sections.body: Manabe went on to help build the first coupled ocean-atmosphere general circulation models (GCMs) at GFDL in the late 1960s and 1970s, extending the one-dimensional insight into full three-dimensional simulations of global circulation — the direct ancestors of today's climate models used by the IPCC. In 2021, Manabe shared the Nobel Prize in Physics — one half jointly with Klaus Hasselmann 'for the physical modelling of Earth's climate, quantifying variability and reliably predicting global warming,' while the other half went separately to Giorgio Parisi for unrelated work on disordered physical systems — a recognition that climate modeling had matured into rigorous, prize-worthy physics. Yet the central number Manabe and Wetherald first estimated is still not pinned down exactly: the IPCC's 2021 Sixth Assessment Report gives a 'likely' equilibrium climate sensitivity range of 2.5 to 4°C for a CO2 doubling, with a best estimate of 3°C — narrower than earlier assessments, but still a real range rather than a single settled number, reflecting genuine ongoing uncertainty in how strongly clouds and other feedbacks amplify or dampen the basic greenhouse response.

lessons.workedExample: A student wants to explain why climate sensitivity is reported as a range (2.5 to 4°C) rather than a single number even after 130 years of study since Arrhenius and nearly 60 since Manabe and Wetherald. The explanation: Manabe and Wetherald's 2°C figure came from a one-dimensional model with fixed relative humidity and no clouds or ocean circulation; every generation of more complete models since has added feedbacks — cloud behavior, ice-albedo changes, ocean heat uptake — that push the estimate up or down depending on how each is represented. The IPCC's 2.5-4°C range reflects that different, individually defensible ways of modeling those feedbacks still produce somewhat different answers, not that the basic physics is in doubt.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks about Manabe's work is testing whether a student can distinguish 'the greenhouse effect is real' from 'we know exactly how much warming a CO2 doubling causes.' A weak answer treats climate sensitivity as a single fixed number. A strong answer explains that Manabe and Wetherald's 1967 estimate of about 2°C was a foundational, physically rigorous calculation, that it agrees in order of magnitude with today's IPCC range, and that the range itself — 2.5 to 4°C, not one value — is the honest current state of the science, driven mainly by unresolved cloud feedbacks rather than any doubt about the basic radiative physics.

questions.prompt: What key physical assumption did Manabe and Wetherald's 1967 model make that produced a more realistic water-vapor feedback than earlier calculations?

options.text: They held absolute humidity fixed as the atmosphere warmed
They held relative humidity fixed as the atmosphere warmed, allowing water vapor content to rise with temperature
They ignored water vapor entirely
They assumed the atmosphere had no water vapor above the surface layer

explanations.a: Fixed absolute humidity was the older, less realistic assumption their model improved upon.
explanations.b: Correct — fixing relative humidity instead let atmospheric moisture increase as temperature rose, producing a more physically realistic amplifying water-vapor feedback.
explanations.c: Water vapor feedback was central to their model, not omitted.
explanations.d: Their model did include water vapor throughout the atmospheric column; this option describes something the model did not do.

questions.prompt: Approximately what surface warming did Manabe and Wetherald's 1967 model estimate for a doubling of CO2?

options.text: About 0.5°C
About 2°C
About 8°C
About 15°C

explanations.a: This is too small; their estimate was several times larger.
explanations.b: Correct — their one-dimensional radiative-convective model produced roughly 2°C of equilibrium warming per CO2 doubling.
explanations.c: This considerably overstates their result.
explanations.d: This is far too large and does not match their published estimate.

questions.prompt: According to the IPCC's 2021 Sixth Assessment Report, what is the 'likely' range for equilibrium climate sensitivity, and what is the best estimate?

options.text: Range of 2.5 to 4°C, best estimate 3°C
Range of 0.5 to 1°C, best estimate 0.75°C
A single fixed value of exactly 2°C with no uncertainty range
Range of 8 to 12°C, best estimate 10°C

explanations.a: Correct — the IPCC AR6 reports a likely range of 2.5 to 4°C with a best estimate of 3°C, narrower than in earlier assessment reports.
explanations.b: This range is far too low compared to the IPCC's assessed values.
explanations.c: The IPCC explicitly reports a range with a best estimate, not a single value with zero uncertainty.
explanations.d: This range is far too high and does not match the IPCC's assessment.

questions.prompt: Order these developments in the history of climate modeling.

items.text: Manabe and Wetherald publish the one-dimensional radiative-convective model
Manabe helps build coupled ocean-atmosphere general circulation models at GFDL
Manabe shares the Nobel Prize in Physics

questions.explanation: The 1967 one-dimensional model came first, followed by the extension into full three-dimensional coupled GCMs in the following years, with the Nobel Prize recognition arriving decades later in 2021.

questions.prompt: Why does climate sensitivity still have a real range (2.5-4°C) rather than one settled value, despite decades of increasingly sophisticated modeling since Manabe and Wetherald?

options.text: Because scientists still doubt whether CO2 absorbs infrared radiation
Because feedbacks such as cloud behavior remain difficult to model precisely and different defensible approaches yield somewhat different answers
Because the original 1967 calculation was later found to be based on incorrect physics
Because climate sensitivity changes randomly from year to year with no stable value

explanations.a: The basic radiative physics of CO2 absorption has been settled since Tyndall's 1861 experiments and is not the source of the remaining uncertainty.
explanations.b: Correct — feedbacks like cloud response are the dominant source of remaining spread in sensitivity estimates, not doubt about the core greenhouse mechanism.
explanations.c: The 1967 model's core physics has held up reasonably well; it was a simplified but sound early estimate, not a flawed one.
explanations.d: Climate sensitivity is a property of the climate system's equilibrium response, not a randomly fluctuating year-to-year quantity.

lessons.label: Ensemble Forecasting and the Reanalysis Era

sections.heading: From one forecast to many
sections.body: Once Lorenz's work established a hard predictability limit for any single deterministic run, the practical response was to stop pretending one run could be trusted at face value. Operational centers began running many forecasts from the same starting point, each with slightly different, equally plausible initial conditions (and sometimes slightly different model physics), and reporting the spread of outcomes rather than one number. The European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) and the U.S. National Centers for Environmental Prediction (NCEP) both launched operational ensemble prediction systems in 1992. A tight cluster of ensemble members forecasting the same outcome signals high confidence; a wide spread signals genuine uncertainty that a single run would have hidden.

sections.heading: Reanalysis: rebuilding the atmosphere's past with today's model
sections.body: A related but separate innovation addressed the historical record rather than the future: reanalysis. Instead of relying on whatever raw observations and forecasting tools existed at a given historical moment, reanalysis reruns one fixed, modern data-assimilation system over decades of historical observations, producing a physically consistent, gridded reconstruction of the atmosphere's past state. ECMWF's ERA5 main record, covering 1979 to the present at hourly resolution on roughly a 31-kilometer grid, was released starting in 2019, superseding the earlier ERA-Interim dataset; the record was later extended back to 1950 in a preliminary back-extension and then to 1940 in a final back-extension released in 2023, so today's ERA5 spans 1940 to the present. Reanalysis products like ERA5 are now the standard reference dataset for studying long-term atmospheric trends and for training newer forecasting methods.

sections.heading: The European-versus-American rivalry, and a new AI challenger
sections.body: The clearest public demonstration of model quality differences came during Hurricane Sandy in October 2012: roughly six to seven days before landfall, ECMWF's model consistently forecast a U.S. East Coast landfall, while NCEP's GFS model forecast Sandy curving harmlessly out to sea. ECMWF was right. Later research (Bassill, 2014) traced the divergence mainly to differing cumulus parameterization schemes rather than resolution or initial data, and the episode drove substantial U.S. investment in upgrading the GFS. More recently, a new kind of competitor emerged: Google DeepMind's GraphCast, published in Science in 2023, is a graph neural network trained on ECMWF's ERA5 reanalysis data that outperformed ECMWF's own operational physics-based model on roughly 90% of over 1,300 verification measures for medium-range forecasts, while producing a 10-day forecast in under a minute rather than the hours a supercomputer needs for a physics-based run. Whether machine-learning emulators like GraphCast can be trusted for genuinely novel extreme events outside their training data, and whether they will replace or merely supplement physics-based models, is an active, unresolved debate in operational forecasting.

lessons.workedExample: A forecaster needs to tell emergency managers how confident to be in a hurricane's predicted landfall location five days out. Running a 50-member ensemble, 40 members show landfall within a 50-mile stretch of coast while 10 show the storm staying offshore — a spread that itself is the useful information, prompting evacuation planning for a wider zone than any single run would suggest. This mirrors the actual 2012 Sandy case: NCEP's single GFS run confidently, and wrongly, kept the storm at sea, while ECMWF's system (and hindsight ensemble analysis) captured the landfall risk days earlier, which is part of why the U.S. subsequently invested heavily in ensemble-based upgrades to its own forecasting.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking about ensemble forecasting or the Sandy case wants to see that a student understands uncertainty as information, not just an obstacle. A weak answer says one model is simply 'better' than another with no mechanism. A strong answer explains that the ECMWF-GFS divergence during Sandy traced to a specific modeling choice (cumulus parameterization), that ensembles turn Lorenz's predictability limit into a quantified probability rather than false certainty, and can weigh the current open question of whether AI systems like GraphCast — trained on reanalysis data rather than built from physical equations — deserve the same operational trust as physics-based models.

questions.prompt: What is the core idea behind ensemble forecasting?

options.text: Running the same model once at the highest possible resolution
Running many forecasts from slightly different plausible initial conditions and treating the spread of outcomes as the uncertainty estimate
Averaging forecasts from the last ten years to predict tomorrow's weather
Running only the ECMWF model repeatedly to double-check for errors

explanations.a: A single high-resolution run does not address the initial-condition uncertainty that ensembles are designed to quantify.
explanations.b: Correct — perturbing the initial conditions across many runs and examining the spread is the defining feature of ensemble forecasting.
explanations.c: This describes a climatological average, not ensemble forecasting.
explanations.d: Ensembles typically combine multiple perturbed runs from one or more models, not simple repetition of an identical run.

questions.prompt: What is reanalysis, as exemplified by ECMWF's ERA5?

options.text: A future weather forecast extended many decades ahead
A reconstruction of the historical atmosphere by rerunning one fixed, modern data-assimilation system over decades of past observations
A survey asking meteorologists to re-rate old forecasts
A method for correcting errors in tomorrow's forecast using yesterday's data

explanations.a: Reanalysis looks backward at historical data, not forward as a long-range forecast.
explanations.b: Correct — reanalysis applies one consistent modern model and assimilation system to historical observations, producing a physically consistent gridded record of the past atmosphere.
explanations.c: Reanalysis is a computational reconstruction, not a survey of expert opinion.
explanations.d: Reanalysis is about reconstructing the past record, not adjusting near-term forecasts.

questions.prompt: What did research find was the main cause of the 2012 divergence between ECMWF's and GFS's Hurricane Sandy track forecasts?

options.text: Differences in grid resolution between the two models
Differing choices of cumulus parameterization scheme
ECMWF using satellite data that GFS lacked access to
A hardware failure in the GFS supercomputer during the forecast window

explanations.a: Research specifically found the divergence was not mainly explained by resolution differences.
explanations.b: Correct — Bassill (2014) traced the differing Sandy track forecasts largely to differences in how each model's cumulus parameterization scheme handled convection.
explanations.c: Data access differences were not identified as the primary cause in the research.
explanations.d: There was no hardware failure; the divergence was a modeling-physics issue, not an equipment malfunction.

questions.prompt: Match each system or dataset to what it is.

right.text: Operational ensemble prediction systems producing many perturbed forecasts instead of one
A reanalysis dataset reconstructing the atmosphere's past state from 1940 to the present
A machine-learning graph neural network trained on reanalysis data that outperformed ECMWF's physics-based model on most verification measures

questions.explanation: Ensemble systems address forecast uncertainty going forward, ERA5 reconstructs the atmosphere's past, and GraphCast is a newer machine-learning forecasting approach trained on that reanalysis data.

questions.prompt: What is the central open debate around AI weather models like GraphCast, as distinct from a settled fact about them?

options.text: Whether they can produce any forecast faster than a physics-based model at all
Whether they can be trusted for genuinely novel or extreme events outside their training data, and whether they will replace or merely supplement physics-based models
Whether they were trained using any real atmospheric data
Whether they have ever outperformed ECMWF on any verification measure

explanations.a: Their speed advantage over physics-based supercomputer runs is already well established, not in dispute.
explanations.b: Correct — the live debate concerns generalization to extreme, out-of-distribution events and the future operational role of AI models alongside physics-based ones.
explanations.c: GraphCast was trained on real ECMWF ERA5 reanalysis data, so this is a settled fact, not a debate.
explanations.d: GraphCast's strong performance on the large majority of verification measures against ECMWF's operational model is an established published result, not an open question.

lessons.label: Open Questions and Live Controversies

sections.heading: Clouds and aerosols: the dominant source of climate-sensitivity uncertainty
sections.body: As earlier lessons showed, climate sensitivity to CO2 doubling is not one settled number but an IPCC-assessed range of about 2.5 to 4°C. The single largest reason that range hasn't narrowed to a point value is clouds. Warming could make low clouds thin out and let more sunlight through, amplifying warming, or thicken and reflect more sunlight, dampening it — different models represent cloud microphysics differently and disagree on which effect wins. Aerosols compound the problem: fine particles from both natural sources and human pollution reflect sunlight directly and also seed brighter, more reflective clouds, meaning they have masked an uncertain fraction of the greenhouse warming that has already occurred. Because the historical aerosol forcing is itself poorly constrained, it propagates directly into uncertainty about how sensitive the climate truly is.

sections.heading: The warming 'hiatus' and the fight over data adjustments
sections.body: From roughly 1998 to 2012, global surface temperature rose more slowly than most climate models projected, a period widely called the warming hiatus or pause. Researchers debated whether this reflected real internal variability — such as increased heat uptake by the deep ocean or a cool phase of Pacific decadal variability — or gaps in the observational data. NOAA's Karl et al. (2015) 'pausebuster' paper revised the sea-surface-temperature record, correcting for a known bias between ship-intake and buoy measurements, and concluded the hiatus had been substantially overstated by incomplete data. The paper triggered a public controversy, including allegations from a NOAA scientist that data-archiving procedures had been rushed, though later independent analyses using satellite and buoy records have broadly supported Karl et al.'s adjustments.

sections.heading: Urban heat islands, hurricane trends, and the limits of downscaling
sections.body: A parallel dispute concerns whether urban warming and changing station siting have artificially inflated the land temperature record. The Berkeley Earth project, launched by physicist Richard Muller specifically to test this skeptical concern with an independent reanalysis of 1.6 billion temperature readings, found that urban-heat-island contamination of the global trend was nearly negligible and that standard homogenization adjustments did not bias the overall warming signal. Hurricane trends remain genuinely harder to pin down: the pre-satellite historical record (before roughly the 1970s-80s) is too inconsistent in coverage and quality to confidently detect long-term frequency trends, even though physical theory and models more confidently predict a shift toward higher-intensity storms and heavier rainfall rates. Compounding this, global climate models use grids roughly 100 kilometers across, far too coarse to resolve a hurricane's core dynamics directly, so projecting realistic individual storms requires specialized high-resolution regional models or statistical downscaling — each with its own assumptions and limitations that keep storm-level projections more uncertain than global-average temperature projections.

lessons.workedExample: A student's fair project claims 'climate models predicted the hiatus was impossible, so the models are broken.' A judge-ready response distinguishes the claims properly: models project a long-term forced trend from greenhouse gases, not a smooth year-by-year path, and internal variability (like ocean heat uptake) can suppress surface warming for a decade or more without contradicting the models' basic physics. The stronger, more defensible framing is that the 1998-2012 slowdown prompted a genuine scientific investigation — including the contested Karl et al. (2015) data revision — rather than being simple proof the underlying greenhouse mechanism established by Tyndall and Arrhenius was wrong.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who raises the hiatus, urban heat islands, or hurricane attribution is testing whether a student can hold two things at once: real, still-open scientific uncertainty, and a well-established underlying mechanism. A weak answer treats any of these controversies as evidence the whole field is unsettled, or alternatively pretends no legitimate debate exists at all. A strong answer names the specific mechanism in dispute (cloud feedback sign, ocean heat uptake, station siting, coarse GCM resolution for storms), cites the actual evidence on each side, and explains why the controversy is bounded — it changes a range or a rate, not the basic physics established by Fourier, Tyndall, and Arrhenius.

questions.prompt: What is identified as the largest remaining source of uncertainty in equilibrium climate sensitivity estimates?

options.text: Uncertainty about whether CO2 absorbs infrared radiation
Cloud feedbacks, compounded by poorly constrained historical aerosol forcing
Disagreement about the current atmospheric CO2 concentration
Uncertainty about the existence of the water-vapor feedback

explanations.a: CO2's infrared absorption has been established science since Tyndall's 1861 experiments and is not the source of remaining uncertainty.
explanations.b: Correct — how clouds respond to warming, and how much aerosols have masked historical warming, are the dominant unresolved factors behind the sensitivity range.
explanations.c: Current CO2 concentration is precisely measured by continuous monitoring programs like the Keeling Curve, not a source of major uncertainty.
explanations.d: The water-vapor feedback's existence and amplifying direction are well established, going back to Manabe and Wetherald's 1967 model.

questions.prompt: What did NOAA's Karl et al. (2015) 'pausebuster' paper argue about the 1998-2012 warming slowdown?

options.text: That the slowdown was entirely due to a drop in atmospheric CO2
That correcting a known bias in sea-surface-temperature measurements showed the slowdown had been substantially overstated by incomplete data
That the slowdown proved climate models were fundamentally wrong about the greenhouse effect
That the slowdown was caused entirely by urban heat island contamination of land stations

explanations.a: CO2 did not drop during this period; that is not the argument the paper made.
explanations.b: Correct — Karl et al. corrected a ship-versus-buoy measurement bias in sea-surface temperatures and argued this explained much of the apparent slowdown.
explanations.c: The paper argued the data itself was incomplete, not that the underlying greenhouse physics was wrong.
explanations.d: The paper concerned ocean surface-temperature measurement bias, not land-station urban heat island effects.

questions.prompt: What did the Berkeley Earth reanalysis, led by physicist Richard Muller, conclude about urban heat island effects on the global land temperature trend?

options.text: That urban heat islands account for most of the observed global warming trend
That urban heat island contamination of the global trend was nearly negligible
That the study was inconclusive and no assessment could be made
That urban stations should be entirely excluded from all future temperature records

explanations.a: Berkeley Earth's finding was the opposite — urban effects were found not to meaningfully explain the global trend.
explanations.b: Correct — despite being organized partly to test this skeptical concern, Berkeley Earth found urban heat island contamination of the global trend to be nearly negligible.
explanations.c: The project reached a definite, published conclusion rather than remaining inconclusive.
explanations.d: The study assessed the size of the urban bias rather than recommending exclusion of urban stations altogether.

questions.prompt: Why is detecting a robust global hurricane frequency trend considered harder than detecting the global average temperature trend?

options.text: Because hurricanes are not affected by ocean temperature at all
Because the pre-satellite historical hurricane record is inconsistent in coverage and quality, complicating long-term trend detection
Because there is no physical theory connecting warming to hurricane behavior
Because hurricanes have become far too rare to study statistically

explanations.a: Ocean temperature is a primary driver of hurricane formation and intensity, not an irrelevant factor.
explanations.b: Correct — inconsistent historical observation coverage and quality before the satellite era makes long-term frequency trends much harder to establish confidently than the global temperature record.
explanations.c: Physical theory and models do offer more confident predictions about intensity and rainfall shifts, even though frequency trends are harder to detect.
explanations.d: Hurricane frequency has not dropped to a level that prevents statistical study; the issue is historical record quality, not current rarity.

questions.prompt: Why is projecting the behavior of individual future hurricanes more difficult than projecting global average temperature?

options.text: Global climate models use grids roughly 100 km across, too coarse to resolve a hurricane's core dynamics directly, requiring downscaling methods with their own added uncertainty
Hurricanes are unaffected by any variable that climate models track
There is no computational method available for simulating hurricanes at all
Global average temperature is actually harder to project than individual storms

explanations.a: Correct — coarse global model resolution cannot capture a hurricane's core structure, so specialized regional models or statistical downscaling are needed, each adding its own uncertainty.
explanations.b: Hurricanes are strongly affected by variables like sea-surface temperature and wind shear that climate models do track, just not at fine enough resolution in global runs.
explanations.c: High-resolution regional models and downscaling techniques do exist for simulating storms; the issue is added uncertainty, not total absence of methods.
explanations.d: Global average temperature is a large-scale, well-constrained quantity and is comparatively easier to project than storm-scale, individual-event behavior.

units.label: Reading Weather and Climate Data

lessons.label: Weather vs. Climate and Climatological Normals

sections.heading: Two different questions about the atmosphere
sections.body: Weather is the instantaneous state of the atmosphere at a place and time: today's high, tomorrow's front, this afternoon's wind gust. Climate is the statistical description of weather over a long window - the mean, the variance, the extremes - at that place. The novelist Robert Heinlein put the distinction memorably in Time Enough for Love (1973): climate is what you expect, weather is what you get. The two operate on wildly different scales of variability. Day-to-day temperature at a mid-latitude station can swing 10-20 degrees Celsius on synoptic weather alone, while the global-mean warming trend since the late 19th century is roughly 1.1-1.2 degrees Celsius total (IPCC AR6, 2021). A single cold snap is a draw from the weather distribution, not a measurement of the climate mean, so it cannot by itself confirm or refute a decadal-scale trend.

sections.heading: The WMO 30-year normal
sections.body: To make climate expectations concrete and comparable, the World Meteorological Organization defines a climatological normal as the 30-year average of a variable at a station, first standardized in 1935 using 1901-1930. WMO practice updates this normal every ten years, so national weather services (NOAA, the UK Met Office, and others) currently report against the 1991-2020 normal, having moved through 1961-1990, 1971-2000, and 1981-2010. A normal is computed straightforwardly - average each calendar day's or month's value across all 30 years at that station - but the choice to roll the window forward every decade means the baseline itself is not fixed: it warms along with the climate.

sections.heading: Why a moving baseline can hide the trend
sections.body: Because the normal updates every decade, what counts as an 'average' summer today already includes a warmer recent decade than what counted as average thirty years ago - a rolling baseline chases the trend it is measuring, which mutes the apparent departure from normal even as the absolute climate keeps warming. WMO addresses this by also recommending a fixed longer reference period, such as 1961-1990, specifically for tracking long-term climate change, alongside the rolling 1991-2020 normal used for everyday forecast and agricultural context. Judges and analysts need both: the rolling normal for 'is today unusual,' the fixed reference for 'has the climate itself shifted.' The 30-year window itself is not arbitrary: it is long enough to average out recurring multi-year natural oscillations, such as ENSO cycles that recur roughly every two to seven years, so a handful of unusually warm or cold El Nino/La Nina years cannot dominate the average, while it is still short enough to stay responsive to a genuinely changing climate mean rather than smearing today's conditions across a century of outdated data. A 10-year window would still be noisy with oscillation-driven swings; a 100-year window would react too slowly to a real, ongoing shift - 30 years is the WMO's compromise between those two failure modes.

lessons.workedExample: On January 30, 2019, Chicago recorded a low near -23 degrees Fahrenheit during a polar vortex outbreak, close to the city's all-time record. A student citing this single day as evidence against global warming is comparing one weather draw to a climate claim - a category error. The correct comparison is Chicago's 1991-2020 normal January low against Chicago's 1961-1990 (or earlier) normal January low: NOAA's normals show the more recent 30-year averages for most U.S. stations running warmer than mid-20th-century normals, even though any given January can still deliver a record cold outbreak, because variability around the mean has not vanished just because the mean has shifted.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'doesn't that cold day/heat wave disprove your climate claim?' to test whether a student can separate signal from noise - the single most common statistical confusion in public climate discourse. A weak answer treats one data point as decisive either way. A strong answer names the relevant normal period, states that weather variance (10-20C swings) dwarfs the climate trend (about 1C per century), and explains that a normal is a 30-year statistic, not a prediction for any single day.

questions.prompt: Under current WMO convention, which 30-year period is the standard climatological normal used by most national weather services today?

explanations.a: 1961-1990 was an earlier standard normal and is now often used only as a fixed long-term reference, not the current rolling normal.
explanations.b: 1971-2000 was the normal period before 1981-2010; it has since been superseded twice.
explanations.c: 1981-2010 was the normal immediately before the current one, replaced when WMO rolled the window forward a decade.
explanations.d: Correct - WMO updates normals every ten years, so 1991-2020 is the current standard 30-year normal.

questions.prompt: Why can't a single record-cold day serve as evidence against a long-term warming trend?

options.text: Because record cold days are always measurement errors
Because day-to-day weather variability is much larger than the size of the century-scale trend
Because climate normals are recalculated every year to erase such records
Because cold records only occur in the Southern Hemisphere

explanations.a: Record cold events are usually real, physically caused weather events (e.g., polar vortex outbreaks), not errors.
explanations.b: Correct - synoptic weather swings of 10-20C dwarf a roughly 1.1-1.2C total global warming signal, so one extreme day is noise relative to the trend.
explanations.c: Normals are recalculated only once per decade under WMO practice, not annually, and recalculation does not erase historical records.
explanations.d: Cold extremes occur in both hemispheres; hemisphere has nothing to do with why one day can't refute a trend.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its correct description.

right.text: The instantaneous state of the atmosphere at a given place and time
The 30-year statistical average WMO updates every decade
The long-run statistical distribution of weather at a place, including its mean and variability

questions.explanation: Weather is a single instantaneous state; climate is the full statistical distribution over time; the climatological normal is the specific 30-year mean WMO defines and updates each decade.

questions.prompt: Order these WMO 30-year normal periods from earliest to most recent as they became the active standard.
questions.explanation: WMO rolls the 30-year normal window forward by one decade each update, so the sequence of active standard periods runs 1961-1990, then 1971-2000, then 1981-2010, then the current 1991-2020.

lessons.label: Time Series, Anomalies, and Baselines

sections.heading: Why analysts subtract before they average
sections.body: An anomaly is a value minus a reference-period mean at that same location: not 'the temperature was 14C' but 'the temperature was 0.8C above its 1961-1990 average.' Climatologists work in anomalies rather than raw values because absolute temperature is dominated by geography - elevation, latitude, coastal proximity - so a raw global average is swamped by the difference between, say, a Siberian station and a Miami station, and that spatial noise has nothing to do with change over time. Anomalies strip out the fixed local climate and leave the departure, which turns out to be spatially coherent: a warm anomaly in one location typically correlates with warm anomalies hundreds of kilometers away, because the same large-scale circulation and forcing drive both. That coherence is what lets a few thousand stations represent the globe.

sections.heading: Assembling a global-mean series
sections.body: Datasets like HadCRUT5 (Morice et al., 2021, from the UK Met Office Hadley Centre and the Climatic Research Unit) and GISTEMP (Lenssen et al., 2019, NASA GISS) grid station and ocean anomalies onto a mesh - HadCRUT5 uses roughly 5-by-5-degree cells - then average the cells with area weighting, typically proportional to the cosine of latitude, so that shrinking high-latitude grid cells do not get over-counted relative to equatorial ones. Cosine weighting is the right function for a geometric reason: on a sphere, a fixed-degree-by-degree grid cell's true surface area shrinks toward the poles in proportion to the cosine of its latitude - a cell at 60 degrees covers roughly half the area of an equatorial cell of the same angular size, and a cell near 90 degrees covers almost none - so weighting each cell's contribution by that same cosine factor exactly cancels the distortion the fixed-degree grid introduces. Ocean anomalies come from ship and buoy sea-surface temperature records folded into the same grid. The global mean for a given month or year is the area-weighted average of all populated cells, which handles the uneven, clustered distribution of stations far better than a simple arithmetic mean of raw station readings would.

sections.heading: Baseline choice moves the line, not the shape
sections.body: Different agencies anchor to different baselines: GISTEMP reports anomalies relative to 1951-1980, HadCRUT5 relative to 1961-1990, and the IPCC's Sixth Assessment Report (2021) frequently references an 1850-1900 'pre-industrial' baseline, under which it states roughly 1.1C of warming through the 2011-2020 decade. Switching baseline shifts every point in the series up or down by a constant, exactly the difference between the two reference-period means - it does not change the slope, the year-to-year variability, or the ranking of warmest years. A series that looks flat under one baseline and rising under another is being misread, not genuinely different.

lessons.workedExample: Suppose a station's 1961-1990 average July temperature is 20.0C and its 2023 July temperature is 21.4C: the HadCRUT-style anomaly is +1.4C. If instead the analyst uses a 1951-1980 baseline where that station averaged 19.6C, the same 2023 July of 21.4C becomes a +1.8C anomaly - a 0.4C jump caused entirely by the 0.4C difference between the two baseline means, not by any change in the raw data. A student who reports '+1.8C is worse than +1.4C' without naming the baseline has compared two different rulers, not two different climates.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'why not just use the actual temperatures?' is testing whether a student understands why climatologists work in departures rather than raw values. A weak answer treats the switch to anomalies as arbitrary convention. A strong answer explains that anomalies are spatially coherent across long distances while raw temperature is dominated by local geography, and can also state which baseline a given figure uses and explain that changing baselines shifts the zero line without altering the trend.

questions.prompt: Why do global temperature datasets report anomalies instead of raw absolute temperatures?

options.text: Because thermometers cannot measure absolute temperature accurately
Because anomalies are spatially coherent over long distances while raw temperature is dominated by local geography
Because international law requires anomaly reporting
Because anomalies are always smaller numbers and easier to plot

explanations.a: Modern thermometers measure absolute temperature accurately; that is not the reason for using anomalies.
explanations.b: Correct - anomalies remove the fixed local climate (elevation, latitude, coastal effects) and leave a departure that correlates well over hundreds of kilometers, letting sparse station networks represent broad regions.
explanations.c: There is no such legal requirement; this is a scientific and statistical convention, not a regulation.
explanations.d: Anomaly magnitudes have nothing to do with why the method is preferred; the reason is spatial coherence, not plot aesthetics.

questions.prompt: A station's anomaly is reported as +1.8C under a 1951-1980 baseline and +1.4C under a 1961-1990 baseline for the same year. What best explains the 0.4C difference?

options.text: The 1961-1990 baseline period itself averaged about 0.4C warmer than the 1951-1980 period
The station's instrument was recalibrated between the two calculations
One of the two anomaly values must be a calculation error
Anomalies are not comparable across different baselines under any circumstances

explanations.a: Correct - switching baselines shifts every anomaly by the difference between the two reference-period means; a warmer reference period produces smaller (or here, larger going the other direction) anomalies relative to the same raw value.
explanations.b: No new instrument reading is involved; only the reference period used in the subtraction changed.
explanations.c: Both values can be correct simultaneously; they are just anomalies relative to different fixed points, not competing measurements.
explanations.d: Anomalies from different baselines are comparable once the constant baseline offset is accounted for; they are not fundamentally incompatible.

questions.prompt: Match each global temperature dataset to its standard reference baseline period.
questions.explanation: GISTEMP anchors to 1951-1980, HadCRUT5 anchors to 1961-1990, and IPCC AR6 commonly reports warming relative to an 1850-1900 pre-industrial baseline.

questions.prompt: Order the steps used to assemble a global-mean temperature anomaly series like HadCRUT5 or GISTEMP.

items.text: Compute each station's or ocean grid point's anomaly relative to its own baseline mean
Place anomalies onto a spatial grid of cells (e.g., 5x5 degrees)
Area-weight each grid cell, typically by cosine of latitude
Average the weighted cells to produce the global-mean anomaly for that month or year

questions.explanation: Anomalies are computed first at the station/ocean-point level, then binned onto a grid, then area-weighted to prevent over-counting shrinking high-latitude cells, and finally averaged into a single global-mean figure.

lessons.label: Trends vs. Variability and Statistical Significance

sections.heading: Fitting a trend and asking whether it's real
sections.body: The simplest way to summarize a warming or cooling signal is ordinary least-squares regression of the variable against time: the slope is the trend, typically reported in degrees per decade, and it comes with a standard error that shrinks as the record gets longer and the year-to-year scatter gets smaller. A trend is only useful if that standard error is small relative to the slope - otherwise the 'trend' could plausibly be zero, and the fit is describing noise. Global mean surface temperature since the 1970s has trended at roughly 0.18-0.20C per decade (NOAA/NASA long-term estimates), a slope that is robustly distinguishable from zero because the record is now five decades long.

sections.heading: Autocorrelation quietly inflates confidence
sections.body: Standard regression assumes each year's data point is an independent draw, but climate variables are autocorrelated - a warm year is more likely to be followed by another warm year because of persistence in the ocean and large-scale circulation, especially El Nino-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) cycles. Treating 40 autocorrelated years as 40 independent samples overstates the effective sample size and makes the trend look more certain than it is. Climate scientists correct for this with an effective-degrees-of-freedom adjustment, following methods like Santer et al. (2000). A common Bartlett-style approximation estimates the effective sample size as N_eff = N(1-r)/(1+r), where N is the raw number of years and r is the lag-1 autocorrelation of the regression residuals - so a residual correlation of r=0.5, for instance, cuts the usable sample size to roughly a third of the raw count, since N_eff/N = (1-0.5)/(1+0.5) = 0.5/1.5 ≈ 1/3. (To 'roughly halve' the sample instead, you would need a weaker persistence of about r=0.33, which gives N_eff/N = 0.67/1.33 ≈ 0.5.) Because the trend's standard error scales with 1/sqrt(N_eff) rather than 1/sqrt(N), this typically widens the confidence interval on a trend once persistence is accounted for - the same data, honestly analyzed, supports a less certain but still valid conclusion.

sections.heading: Cherry-picked start years and the 'hiatus'
sections.body: A trend estimate is sensitive to the endpoints chosen, and a short window starting on an unusually high year can look artificially flat. This is exactly what happened with the so-called global warming 'hiatus': trends computed starting in 1998 - an extreme El Nino year with an anomalously high temperature spike - showed a much smaller slope through roughly 2012 than trends computed from 1970 or from 2000 onward, because starting on a peak biases a short trend downward regardless of the underlying long-term signal. Karl et al. (2015, Science) revisited NOAA's surface temperature record and found that correcting known biases in the sea-surface-temperature data - chiefly a transition-era bias between ship and buoy readings - raised the 2000-2014 trend to a rate comparable to, or even exceeding, the late-20th-century trend, undercutting the case that a real slowdown had occurred at all. Fyfe et al. (2016, Nature Climate Change) took the opposite approach, working with the original uncorrected dataset, and showed that the apparent slowdown was real but modest, driven by a La Nina-dominated ENSO phase, small volcanic aerosol loading, and a solar minimum, and that it disappeared once the record extended past 2014-2016's strong warm years - two different lines of evidence, a data-correction argument and a physical-drivers argument, that converged on the same conclusion: the 'hiatus' was not a break in the long-term warming trend.

lessons.workedExample: A student fits an OLS trend to global temperature anomalies from 1998 to 2012 and gets roughly 0.05C per decade, then claims warming has 'stopped.' A stronger analysis fits the same OLS method to 1970-2023 and gets about 0.18C per decade with a tight confidence interval, then shows that 1998 was an extreme El Nino peak - starting a short trend on a spike mechanically depresses the slope. Extending the short window just eight more years past the 2015-2016 El Nino restores a slope consistent with the longer-term rate, demonstrating the flatness was a start-year artifact, not a change in the physical trend.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge presses on trend claims because start-year cherry-picking is the single most common way real data gets used to argue a false conclusion. A weak answer reports a slope with no confidence interval and no discussion of window choice. A strong answer states the fitting method (OLS), reports uncertainty, explains that autocorrelation widens that uncertainty beyond a naive independent-sample calculation, and shows the same claim tested against at least one other reasonable start year.

questions.prompt: Why does treating autocorrelated climate data as independent samples cause a problem for trend significance?

options.text: It has no effect; autocorrelation only matters for spatial data, not time series
It inflates the effective sample size, making the trend's confidence interval falsely narrow
It always reverses the sign of the trend
It only matters for records shorter than five years

explanations.a: Autocorrelation is a time-series phenomenon (persistence from year to year) and directly affects trend uncertainty estimates.
explanations.b: Correct - because consecutive years are correlated rather than independent, the true effective sample size is smaller than the raw count of years, so uncorrected statistics understate the real uncertainty.
explanations.c: Autocorrelation affects the width of the uncertainty interval, not the sign or direction of the estimated slope.
explanations.d: The effect scales with the strength and persistence of the autocorrelation, not simply with record length; it matters at essentially any length where correlation exists.

questions.prompt: Using the Bartlett-style approximation N_eff = N(1-r)/(1+r), a residual lag-1 autocorrelation of r=0.5 reduces the effective sample size to roughly what fraction of the raw number of years?

options.text: About one third (N_eff/N ≈ 1/3)
About one half (N_eff/N ≈ 1/2)
About two thirds (N_eff/N ≈ 2/3)
It is unchanged; autocorrelation does not affect the count

explanations.a: Correct - N_eff/N = (1-0.5)/(1+0.5) = 0.5/1.5 ≈ 1/3, so half the raw years' worth of independent information is lost and then some.
explanations.b: A halving (N_eff/N ≈ 1/2) corresponds to a weaker persistence of about r=0.33, not r=0.5; plugging r=0.5 into the formula gives one third, not one half.
explanations.c: Two thirds would require a very weak autocorrelation of about r=0.2; r=0.5 is far more persistent and cuts the effective sample to about a third.
explanations.d: The whole point of the correction is that positive autocorrelation shrinks the effective sample size below the raw count.

questions.prompt: Why did trends computed starting in 1998 appear misleadingly flat through roughly 2012?

options.text: Global thermometers were miscalibrated during that period
1998 was an anomalously warm El Nino peak, so starting a short trend there mechanically depresses the fitted slope
The WMO changed its baseline period in 1998
CO2 emissions actually declined between 1998 and 2012

explanations.a: There is no documented widespread miscalibration; the effect is a statistical artifact of the chosen start point, not an instrument problem.
explanations.b: Correct - 1998 was a strong El Nino spike, and a short trend anchored on a peak year is biased toward a flatter slope than the underlying multi-decadal trend.
explanations.c: The WMO's 30-year normal periods update by decade and are unrelated to why a 1998-anchored short trend looks flat.
explanations.d: Global CO2 emissions rose through this period; the flat appearance is a statistical artifact of start-year choice, not a change in the emissions or physical trend.

questions.prompt: Match each named study or event to what it addressed.

left.text: Fyfe et al. (2016, Nature Climate Change)

right.text: Argued that correcting NOAA sea-surface-temperature data biases raised the 2000-2014 warming trend to match or exceed the late-20th-century rate, undercutting the case for a real slowdown
Developed an effective-degrees-of-freedom correction for autocorrelated trend significance testing
An example of a cherry-picked, unusually warm anchor point that mechanically flattens a short trend
Showed the 'hiatus' slowdown was real but modest in the uncorrected data, driven by ENSO phase, small volcanic aerosols, and a solar minimum

questions.explanation: Santer et al. (2000) addressed autocorrelation-corrected significance testing; Karl et al. (2015) showed the apparent slowdown was largely a data-bias artifact once corrected; Fyfe et al. (2016) showed that, in the original uncorrected dataset, the slowdown was real but modest and explained by ENSO, aerosols, and solar forcing; the 1998 start year itself is the textbook case of a start-year artifact.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a defensible trend analysis, from first to last.

items.text: Fit an OLS regression slope to the time series
Compute the standard error, correcting for autocorrelation
Check whether the slope is robust across multiple reasonable start years
Report the trend with its corrected confidence interval and sensitivity to window choice

questions.explanation: A defensible trend claim starts with fitting the slope, corrects the uncertainty for persistence in the data, tests whether the result depends on an arbitrary start year, and finally reports the slope alongside its honest uncertainty and sensitivity.

lessons.label: Distributions in Weather Data: Wind and the Weibull

sections.heading: Wind speed is not normally distributed
sections.body: Wind speed can't go below zero and has a long right tail of occasional strong gusts, so a bell curve fits it poorly. The distribution wind engineers use instead is the two-parameter Weibull: f(v) = (k/c)(v/c)^(k-1) exp[-(v/c)^k], with shape parameter k controlling how peaked or spread the distribution is and scale parameter c setting the characteristic speed. Real wind climates typically have k between about 1.5 and 2.5; the special case k=2 is called the Rayleigh distribution and is the default assumption in wind-resource screening when only a site's mean speed is known, because it needs no separate shape estimate. What sets a site's k within that 1.5-2.5 range is terrain roughness: rougher, more turbulent sites - broken terrain, forests, urban areas, gusty coastal zones - produce a wider, lower-k distribution because the wind speed jumps around more from moment to moment, while smooth, steady-wind sites such as open ocean or high plains produce a more peaked, higher-k distribution because the flow is more consistently close to its mean. Fitting k and c to a year of anemometer data (commonly via maximum likelihood or a method-of-moments fit) lets an analyst reconstruct how often the site sees calm, moderate, and strong winds without storing every 10-minute reading.

sections.heading: The mean wind understates the resource
sections.body: Wind power density scales with the cube of wind speed, P = 0.5 * rho * v^3 per unit swept area, so the quantity that matters for energy yield is the average of v-cubed, not the cube of the average v. Because a Weibull distribution has spread (variance) around its mean, Jensen's inequality guarantees E[v^3] is larger than (E[v])^3 - the gap grows with variance, meaning a windier-than-typical site with a wide, gusty distribution carries meaningfully more energy than its mean speed alone would suggest. Wind engineers formalize this ratio, E[v^3]/(mean v)^3, as the energy pattern factor; using the mean speed cubed as a shortcut for available power routinely and systematically underestimates a site's resource.

sections.heading: Return periods for design, not just resource
sections.body: The same distributional thinking that describes typical operating wind speeds also underlies design wind speeds used in building codes. Rather than fitting the bulk Weibull distribution, codes such as ASCE 7 fit an extreme-value distribution (commonly Gumbel/Type I) to the annual maximum gust at a site, then read off the wind speed with a chosen annual exceedance probability - a '50-year' or '700-year' design wind is the speed expected to be exceeded, on average, once every 50 or 700 years, translating directly into the 2%, or roughly 0.14%, annual probability used to size structural loads in different risk categories and hazard zones across the U.S.

lessons.workedExample: A wind farm site has a fitted Weibull distribution with shape k=2 (Rayleigh) and scale c=8 m/s. The mean wind speed is c*Gamma(1+1/k) = 8*Gamma(1.5) = 8*0.886 = 7.09 m/s. If an analyst naively cubes this mean, they get 7.09^3 = 356 (m/s)^3 worth of relative power. But the true average of v-cubed for this distribution is c^3*Gamma(1+3/k) = 512*Gamma(2.5) = 512*1.329 = 681 (m/s)^3 - nearly double the naive estimate. Sizing a turbine off the mean-cubed shortcut would understate the site's available power by roughly a factor of two.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'why not just use average wind speed to estimate power?' is testing whether a student understands that power is a nonlinear (cubic) function of a variable, so averaging the variable first and cubing second gives the wrong answer whenever there is spread in the distribution. A weak answer reports mean speed cubed as the resource estimate. A strong answer names the Weibull distribution, states k and c for the site, and explains via Jensen's inequality why E[v^3] exceeds (mean v)^3.

questions.prompt: In a Weibull distribution fit to wind speed, what does the shape parameter k control?

options.text: The characteristic (scale) speed of the site, in meters per second
How peaked or spread the distribution of wind speeds is
The exact maximum gust the site will ever record
The turbine's rated power output

explanations.a: The characteristic speed is set by the scale parameter c, not the shape parameter k.
explanations.b: Correct - k controls the shape (peakedness/spread) of the distribution; k=2 is the special Rayleigh case commonly assumed when only mean speed is known.
explanations.c: The Weibull distribution describes a probability density over all speeds and has no hard upper cutoff; it does not itself state a maximum gust value.
explanations.d: Turbine rated power is an engineering spec of the machine, unrelated to the statistical shape parameter of the site's wind distribution.

questions.prompt: Why does estimating wind power from the mean wind speed cubed systematically underestimate the true available power?

options.text: Because wind turbines are inefficient at low speeds
Because power depends on the cube of speed, and by Jensen's inequality the average of v-cubed exceeds the cube of the average v whenever there is spread in the distribution
Because anemometers systematically under-read wind speed
Because the Weibull distribution always has a mean of zero

explanations.a: Turbine efficiency is a separate engineering issue; it does not explain why the statistical shortcut of cubing the mean understates power.
explanations.b: Correct - because power scales with v^3, and the Weibull distribution has spread around its mean, E[v^3] is larger than (mean v)^3; using the shortcut throws away that gap.
explanations.c: This is a statistical, not instrumental, effect; it holds even with a perfectly accurate anemometer.
explanations.d: A Weibull distribution has a positive mean (c times a Gamma function term); it is never zero for physically meaningful shape and scale values.

questions.prompt: Match each wind-related quantity to what determines it.

left.text: Typical day-to-day wind speeds at a site

right.text: E[v^3] from the site's fitted Weibull distribution
A Weibull distribution fit with shape k and scale c
An extreme-value (Gumbel-type) fit to annual maximum gusts, read at a chosen exceedance probability

questions.explanation: Everyday wind speeds are described by the bulk Weibull distribution; true available power needs the distribution's average of v-cubed, not the mean cubed; design wind speeds come from a separate extreme-value fit to annual maxima.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to correctly estimate a site's average available wind power from raw anemometer data.

items.text: Collect a time series of wind speed observations at the site
Fit a Weibull distribution (estimate shape k and scale c) to the observations
Compute the distribution's average of v-cubed, E[v^3] = c^3 * Gamma(1+3/k)
Multiply by 0.5 * air density to get average power density

questions.explanation: The correct sequence is: gather raw speed data, fit the Weibull shape and scale, compute the true average of v-cubed from the fitted distribution (not the mean speed cubed), then convert to power density using the physical power formula.

lessons.label: Extremes, Return Periods, and Record Statistics

sections.heading: Percentiles and the meaning of a threshold
sections.body: Extreme-event indices are usually built from percentiles of a station's own historical distribution rather than a fixed number, so a 'heat wave' means something comparable in Phoenix and in Anchorage. A common convention, used in the ETCCDI climate index set, defines a warm day as one exceeding the local 90th percentile of daily maximum temperature calculated from a baseline period, and a heat wave as several consecutive days above that threshold. Framing extremes as percentile exceedance rather than a hard-coded temperature lets the same statistical machinery apply across climates with very different baselines.

sections.heading: The '100-year event' is a probability, not a calendar
sections.body: A '100-year flood' or '100-year storm' means the event has a 1% probability of being equaled or exceeded in any given year - it is an annual exceedance probability, not a promise the event recurs every hundred years on schedule. Two such events can occur in consecutive years, and a location can go three centuries without one; both are consistent with independent 1%-per-year odds. Because the odds compound over a multi-year exposure, the probability of at least one 100-year event during a 30-year mortgage or building lifetime is 1 - (1 - 0.01)^30, which works out to about 26%, far higher than the '100-year' label intuitively suggests to most people.

sections.heading: A small mean shift moves the tail a lot
sections.body: Because extremes live in the tail of a distribution, a modest shift in the mean can multiply the frequency of crossing a fixed extreme threshold even when the shift itself sounds small. Hansen, Sato, and Ruedy (2012, PNAS) illustrated this with observed summer temperature distributions, showing that a shift of roughly 0.5 standard deviations in the mean corresponded to a large multiplication in the areal frequency of the most extreme (roughly 3-sigma) summer heat categories compared to a mid-20th-century baseline - a small shift in the center produces an outsized change in how often the tail gets crossed, because the tail is exactly where the distribution is thinnest and most sensitive to being pushed.

sections.heading: Two ways to define 'the extremes'
sections.body: Analysts fit extreme-value statistics one of two ways. Block maxima takes the single largest value in each fixed period (each year's hottest day, say) and fits a Generalized Extreme Value (GEV) distribution to that set of annual maxima. Peaks-over-threshold (POT) instead keeps every observation exceeding some high threshold, fitting a Generalized Pareto Distribution (GPD) to the exceedances. POT typically uses far more of the available data, giving more efficient estimates from shorter records, but it requires 'declustering' - grouping nearby exceedances from the same storm so they count as one event rather than several artificially independent ones.

lessons.workedExample: A floodplain map labels a location as inside the '100-year floodplain,' meaning a 1% annual exceedance probability. A homeowner buying a house with a 30-year mortgage asks their risk over the full loan term, not just one year. The correct calculation is 1 - (1 - 0.01)^30 = 1 - 0.99^30 ≈ 1 - 0.740 ≈ 0.26, or about a 26% chance of experiencing at least one such flood before the mortgage is paid off - roughly one-in-four odds, not the ‘once a century, so I'm safe’ intuition the label invites.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'what does 100-year event actually mean?' is checking whether a student can convert a marketing-friendly label into the underlying annual probability and compound it correctly over an exposure window. A weak answer treats '100-year' as a literal recurrence schedule. A strong answer states the 1% annual exceedance probability, shows the compounding calculation for the relevant time horizon, and can distinguish that framing from a percentile-threshold or mean-shift argument about changing frequency.

questions.prompt: What does it mean to call a flood a '100-year flood'?

options.text: It occurs exactly once every 100 years on a fixed schedule
It has a 1% probability of being equaled or exceeded in any given year
It was first recorded 100 years ago
It will not recur for at least 100 years after it happens

explanations.a: A '100-year' label does not imply a fixed schedule; the underlying events are treated as independent year to year, so two can occur in consecutive years.
explanations.b: Correct - it denotes a 1% annual exceedance probability, which is the standard definition used in flood and design-wind statistics.
explanations.c: The label describes a probability, not a historical first-occurrence date.
explanations.d: Independent annual odds mean a repeat the very next year is possible, just unlikely; the label does not guarantee a 100-year gap.

questions.prompt: Approximately what is the probability of at least one 100-year flood occurring during a 30-year period, given independent 1% annual odds?

options.text: About 1%
About 10%
About 26%
About 74%

explanations.a: 1% is the annual probability, not the probability over the full 30-year window; the odds compound across years.
explanations.b: 10% underestimates the compounded probability; simply multiplying 1% by 10 is not how independent annual probabilities combine.
explanations.c: Correct - 1 - (1 - 0.01)^30 ≈ 1 - 0.740 ≈ 0.26, about a 26% chance across the 30-year window.
explanations.d: 74% is actually the complementary probability of NOT experiencing the event over 30 years (0.99^30), not the probability of experiencing it.

questions.prompt: Match each extreme-value approach to the distribution it fits.

right.text: Generalized Extreme Value (GEV) distribution
Generalized Pareto Distribution (GPD)

questions.explanation: Block maxima (e.g., each year's single hottest day) is fit with a GEV distribution; peaks-over-threshold (all exceedances above a high threshold) is fit with a GPD, after declustering correlated exceedances.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for building a peaks-over-threshold (POT) extreme-value analysis.

items.text: Choose a sufficiently high threshold for the variable of interest
Identify all observations exceeding that threshold
Decluster exceedances so correlated events from the same storm count once
Fit a Generalized Pareto Distribution to the declustered exceedances

questions.explanation: POT analysis first sets a high threshold, gathers every exceedance, declusters correlated exceedances from a single event, and only then fits the GPD to the resulting independent exceedances.

lessons.label: Detecting and Attributing Change in a Record

sections.heading: Cleaning the record before trusting it
sections.body: A raw station record accumulates non-climatic jumps that have nothing to do with weather: a station moves to a new site, an observer switches from a liquid-in-glass thermometer to an electronic Maximum-Minimum Temperature System (MMTS, widely adopted across the U.S. Cooperative Observer network in the 1980s), or the time of day readings are taken shifts (time-of-observation bias, corrected following methods from Karl et al., 1986). Homogenization is the process of finding and correcting these artificial breakpoints so the remaining variability reflects climate, not instrumentation history. NOAA's pairwise homogenization algorithm (Menne and Williams, 2009) does this by comparing each station's record against many neighboring stations; a jump that shows up in one station but not its neighbors is flagged as artificial and adjusted, while a shift shared across the whole regional network is left alone as real climate signal.

sections.heading: Finding the breakpoints statistically
sections.body: Breakpoint detection is a formal statistical test, not eyeballing a graph. A widely used method is the Standard Normal Homogeneity Test (Alexandersson, 1986), which scans a difference series between a target station and a reference composite for the point that most improves the fit if the series is split into two segments with different means - that point is flagged as a candidate breakpoint for further investigation against station metadata (moves, equipment logs).

sections.heading: Subtracting out the known wiggles
sections.body: Even a homogenized record still contains large natural swings from El Nino-Southern Oscillation (ENSO), volcanic eruptions, and the 11-year solar cycle, all of which move global temperature independently of any long-term forced trend. Foster and Rahmstorf (2011, Environmental Research Letters) used multiple regression to remove the ENSO signal (via an index like MEI), volcanic aerosol loading (from eruptions such as El Chichon in 1982 and Pinatubo in 1991), and solar irradiance variation from several global temperature datasets, leaving a residual trend that was substantially smoother and more linear than the raw series - a direct demonstration that most of the record's short-term wiggle is explainable natural variability sitting on top of a steadier underlying trend.

sections.heading: Detection is not the same as attribution
sections.body: The IPCC formally separates two questions: detection asks whether the climate system has changed in some statistically demonstrable way, without saying why; attribution asks how much of that detected change is explained by specific causes, typically anthropogenic greenhouse gases versus natural forcings, evaluated with a stated confidence level. The standard attribution method, tracing to Hasselmann's 'optimal fingerprinting' framework (1979, 1993), compares the observed pattern of change against the patterns produced by climate model runs forced only with natural factors and runs forced with both natural and human factors - if observations match the human-plus-natural runs far better than the natural-only runs, the change is attributed, at least in part, to human causes.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher pulls a 100-year station record and finds an abrupt 1.5C jump in 1985 with no matching jump at four nearby reference stations. Checking station metadata confirms the site moved from a rooftop to a grass field that year - a classic non-climatic breakpoint. After applying a homogenization adjustment to remove the artificial 1985 jump, the researcher computes anomalies against the 1991-2020 normal, fits an autocorrelation-corrected OLS trend, and then regresses out ENSO, volcanic, and solar signals following the Foster and Rahmstorf approach. The residual trend is smoother and matches the regional model-based attribution pattern, supporting a real, largely human-driven warming trend at that station rather than an instrumentation artifact.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'how do you know that trend isn't just a bad thermometer or natural cycles?' is testing whether a student can walk the full chain: homogenize the raw data, isolate a defensible trend, remove known natural modes of variability, and only then speak to cause. A weak answer plots raw data and asserts a trend is anthropogenic. A strong answer names a homogenization method, shows awareness of ENSO/volcanic/solar confounders, and correctly distinguishes 'detection' (a change occurred) from 'attribution' (why it occurred), citing model comparison as the tool for the latter.

questions.prompt: A station shows an abrupt 1.5C jump in one year that does not appear in any nearby reference stations. What does this most likely indicate?

options.text: A genuine, highly localized climate shift affecting only that station
A non-climatic breakpoint, such as a station move or instrument change, that homogenization should correct
Proof that ENSO caused a one-year spike
A sign that the station's data should be deleted entirely

explanations.a: A genuine localized climate shift would be an extraordinary claim; the standard interpretation of an isolated jump absent at all neighbors is a station artifact.
explanations.b: Correct - homogenization methods like NOAA's pairwise algorithm flag exactly this pattern (a jump at one station, absent at neighbors) as a candidate non-climatic breakpoint from a station move, instrument change, or observation-time shift.
explanations.c: ENSO produces a broadly regional or global signal correlated across many stations, not an isolated single-station jump.
explanations.d: Homogenization corrects the artificial jump rather than discarding the whole record, preserving the station's otherwise valid data.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between 'detection' and 'attribution' in the IPCC framework?

options.text: Detection identifies that a change occurred; attribution assigns how much of that change is explained by specific causes
Detection is done by satellites; attribution is done by ground stations
Detection requires climate models; attribution never uses climate models
They are two names for the same statistical test

explanations.a: Correct - detection is the statistical demonstration that the climate system has changed; attribution is the separate step of assigning causal contributions, typically via comparing observations to forced and unforced model runs.
explanations.b: The distinction is about the type of scientific claim being made, not which instrument platform collected the data.
explanations.c: It is attribution, not detection, that relies on climate model runs (with and without human forcings) for the fingerprint comparison.
explanations.d: They are explicitly distinct steps in the IPCC framework, addressing different questions (whether vs. why).

questions.prompt: Match each method or study to what it accomplishes in a record-cleaning and trend-isolation workflow.

right.text: Statistically flags the point in a difference series most consistent with an abrupt mean shift
Compares a station against many neighbors to detect and correct non-climatic breakpoints
Used multiple regression to remove ENSO, volcanic, and solar signals, leaving a smoother residual trend

questions.explanation: The pairwise homogenization algorithm corrects breakpoints via neighbor comparison; the SNHT is the statistical test that locates candidate breakpoints; Foster and Rahmstorf's regression approach removes known natural variability from the trend.

questions.prompt: Order the full workflow for producing a defensible, attribution-ready trend from a raw station record.

items.text: Homogenize the raw record to remove non-climatic breakpoints
Compute anomalies relative to a standard baseline period
Fit a trend with an autocorrelation-corrected confidence interval
Regress out known natural modes (ENSO, volcanic, solar) from the trend
Compare the residual pattern against forced and unforced climate model runs for attribution

questions.explanation: A complete workflow homogenizes the raw data first, converts to anomalies against a standard baseline, fits a trend with honest autocorrelation-corrected uncertainty, removes known natural variability, and only then compares against model runs to attribute the remaining trend to specific causes.

units.label: The Synoptic Weather Machine: Air Masses, Fronts & Mid-Latitude Cyclones

lessons.label: Air Masses & Source Regions

sections.heading: Six Letters, Six Source Regions
sections.body: Meteorologists classify air masses with a two-letter code formalized by Tor Bergeron in 1928 as part of the Bergen School's frontal program: a lowercase letter for moisture source (c = continental, dry; m = maritime, moist) and an uppercase letter for thermal source (A = arctic, P = polar, T = tropical). Six combinations matter for North American weather. cP (continental polar) forms over the snow-covered interior of Canada and Siberia. cA (continental arctic) forms over the even colder, ice-covered Arctic Basin and Greenland. mP (maritime polar) forms over the cool North Pacific and North Atlantic. mT (maritime tropical) forms over the Gulf of Mexico, Caribbean, and subtropical oceans. cT (continental tropical) forms over the hot, dry Mexican Plateau and desert Southwest in summer. mA is rare, appearing only where arctic air has a short ocean fetch, as off Iceland.

sections.heading: Why a Source Region Has to Sit Still
sections.body: A patch of air only becomes a true air mass — horizontally uniform in temperature and humidity over hundreds of kilometers — if it lingers over a uniform surface for days to weeks under a stagnant ridge, exchanging heat and moisture with the ground until it equilibrates. That is why source regions are flat and thermally uniform: continental interiors, ice sheets, open subtropical ocean, not mountainous or coastal terrain that would mix the air before it settles. The result is a signature readable directly off a station model. A January cP mass over Saskatchewan sits under a radiational-cooling inversion with surface temperatures of -30 to -40 degrees Celsius and dewpoints nearly as low, because cold air cannot hold much water vapor regardless of relative humidity. A Gulf mT mass, by contrast, arrives with dewpoints in the upper 60s to low 70s Fahrenheit even when the temperature is only in the 80s — the moisture signature that later fuels warm-frontal and dryline convection.

sections.heading: Modification in Transit: Lake-Effect and Continental Warming
sections.body: Air masses never stay pure once they leave their source region. Continental modification is gradual: a cP mass pushing south over the Plains warms diabatically from the ground up, eroding its surface inversion day by day, so air that was -35C in Alberta may arrive in Texas merely cool. Lake-effect modification is fast and dramatic. When cP or cA air crosses the still-warm Great Lakes in early winter — a water-air temperature difference of roughly 13C is the classic rule-of-thumb threshold — the lowest few hundred meters are heated and moistened from below, steepening the lapse rate until convective snow bands organize downwind along the fetch. The November 2014 'Snowvember' event near Buffalo, New York, is the textbook case: successive bands parked over the same southtowns corridor for about two days, burying some neighborhoods under more than five feet of snow while stations just outside the band stayed nearly dry.

lessons.workedExample: A field station near Lake Erie logs -18C with a -20C dewpoint and calm wind under clear skies at midnight — classic unmodified cP air fresh off its source region. Two days later the same station reports continuous snow showers, temperature still near -10C, gusty west winds, and visibility under a mile, while a station forty kilometers south of the lake sees only flurries. Nothing about the air mass's classification changed — it is still cP — but its trajectory crossed open lake water roughly 15C warmer than the air, above the classic 13C development threshold. That fetch was long enough to load the lowest layer with heat and moisture, steepen the lapse rate, and spin up convective snow bands aligned with the wind, producing totals that dwarf anything the source region itself would generate.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe air-mass source regions because confusing 'air mass' with 'the weather right now' is the single most common conceptual slip in a synoptic project. A weak answer says 'a cold front brought cold air.' A strong answer names the source region, explains why that surface produced that specific temperature-dewpoint signature, and — the real test — explains modification: that the same cP air mass can be bone-dry over Winnipeg and dumping three feet of snow forty kilometers downwind of Lake Erie, without changing classification. A judge asking why the dewpoint differs from the source-region value is checking whether the student understands modification versus mere transport.

questions.prompt: A station reports a temperature of -32C and a dewpoint of -34C under calm winds and clear skies, with no recent trajectory over open water. Which air-mass classification best fits this reading?

options.text: mT (maritime tropical)
cP (continental polar)
mP (maritime polar)
cT (continental tropical)

explanations.a: mT air is warm and moist from a Gulf or subtropical-ocean source; it cannot produce a -32C reading.
explanations.b: Correct — extreme cold with a dewpoint nearly matching the temperature, and no maritime moisture source in the trajectory, is the classic cP signature: a continental-interior source region so cold that little moisture is present regardless of relative humidity.
explanations.c: mP air carries a maritime moisture source and is comparatively mild for a polar air mass; it would not reach -32C.
explanations.d: cT forms over hot deserts in summer and is characterized by heat and dryness, the opposite thermal signature.

questions.prompt: Match each air-mass code to its source region.

right.text: Interior Canada / Siberia
Gulf of Mexico / Caribbean
North Pacific / North Atlantic
Mexican Plateau / desert Southwest

questions.explanation: Each code pairs a moisture source (continental vs. maritime) with a thermal source (polar vs. tropical), and each of those source regions is large, flat, and uniform enough to imprint a consistent signature.

questions.prompt: Order the steps by which cold, dry cP air becomes a heavy lake-effect snow producer.

items.text: Cold, dry cP air moves out over much-warmer lake water
The lowest layer of the air mass is heated and moistened from below
The lapse rate steepens and the layer destabilizes
Convective snow bands organize downwind along the fetch

questions.explanation: Modification starts at the surface (heat and moisture added from the warm water), which steepens the lapse rate and only then triggers the organized convection that produces the snow bands.

questions.prompt: Why must a true source region be large, flat, and sit under a stagnant high-pressure ridge?

options.text: So satellites can photograph it without cloud interference
So the air has enough uninterrupted surface contact and time (days to weeks) to equilibrate to a uniform temperature and moisture value
So that fronts are physically prevented from forming there
So the Coriolis effect acts more strongly on the air

explanations.a: Satellite visibility has nothing to do with why a region can imprint uniform properties on air.
