sections.body: When a segment of a squall line's cold pool and its associated rear-inflow jet (RIJ) — a jet of dry, momentum-rich air descending and surging toward the leading edge — become locally intense, that segment bulges forward into the bow echo shape Fujita (1978) first described from his downburst research, distinguishing damaging straight-line wind events from tornado (rotational) damage on the ground. A bow echo's peak winds cluster near the apex of the bow, where the rear-inflow jet reaches the surface with the least resistance, producing swaths of damaging downburst winds and, often, brief spin-up tornadoes near the northern end of the bow where cyclonic shear is enhanced. When repeated bow echoes or an unbroken line sustain damaging wind over a large enough area, the event qualifies as a derecho — a term revived for modern forecasting by Johns and Hirt (1987), who set the defining criteria as a damage swath at least 400 km (250 miles) long with wind gusts of at least 58 mph (50 knots) along most of its length, including several measured or estimated gusts of 75 mph or greater. Beyond wind, MCSs and bow-echo-producing lines remain prolific large-hail producers where embedded supercell-like cells persist within the line, and their combination of downburst clusters, heavy rain, and occasional tornadoes makes them one of the costliest severe-weather categories over a single event.

lessons.workedExample: A squall line crossing Iowa and Illinois develops a pronounced bow echo by late evening as its rear-inflow jet strengthens. Damage surveys afterward trace a continuous corridor of wind damage 480 km long, with widespread 60-70 mph gusts and four separate stations reporting gusts over 80 mph near the bow apexes as the line raced east. Because the swath exceeds 400 km with sustained damaging winds and several gusts above 75 mph, the National Weather Service classifies the event as a derecho under the Johns and Hirt criteria, distinct from an ordinary squall-line wind event.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking about MCSs or derechos wants precision about scale and criteria, since these terms get used loosely in casual weather talk. A weak answer calls any big line of storms a derecho. A strong answer explains the actual structural mechanism — a locally intensified cold pool and rear-inflow jet bowing a line segment forward — and can state the real derecho threshold (a swath of at least 400 km with sustained 58 mph-plus gusts, including several above 75 mph), showing the student knows this is a defined, measured category rather than just 'a bad storm.'

questions.prompt: What physically causes a segment of a squall line to bow forward into a bow echo?

options.text: A tornado embedded in the line pushes the segment ahead of the rest
A locally intensified cold pool and rear-inflow jet accelerate that segment's leading edge forward faster than the rest of the line
The jet stream directly reshapes the radar echo regardless of storm-scale processes
CAPE becomes locally negative, curving the line backward

explanations.a: A bow echo can produce embedded tornadoes, but the bowing shape itself is a cold-pool/rear-inflow-jet process, not caused by a tornado.
explanations.b: Correct — Fujita (1978) tied the bow shape to a locally strengthened cold pool and rear-inflow jet pushing that line segment's surface winds and leading edge forward faster than neighboring segments.
explanations.c: The jet stream can influence the larger environment, but the bow shape itself forms from mesoscale cold-pool and rear-inflow-jet dynamics within the storm system, not direct jet-stream reshaping.
explanations.d: Negative CAPE would suppress convection rather than reshape an existing line's leading edge into a bow.

questions.prompt: Per Johns and Hirt's (1987) derecho criteria, what damage-swath length and wind-gust threshold define the event?

options.text: At least 100 km with any gust over 40 mph
At least 400 km with gusts of at least 58 mph along most of its length, including several gusts of 75 mph or greater
Any length, as long as one tornado is confirmed along the path
At least 400 km but only if the event lasts less than one hour

explanations.a: 100 km and 40 mph fall well short of the Johns and Hirt derecho thresholds, which require a much longer, more intense swath.
explanations.b: Correct — the defining criteria are a swath of at least 400 km (250 miles) with sustained gusts of 58 mph or more, including several gusts of 75 mph or higher.
explanations.c: A derecho is defined by straight-line wind damage over a long swath, not by tornado occurrence, which is a separate hazard sometimes embedded in the same system.
explanations.d: Derechos are long-duration, long-track events typically lasting many hours, not events restricted to under an hour.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

right.text: A jet of dry, momentum-rich air descending and surging toward a squall line's leading edge
Maddox's (1980) defined MCS type: a roughly circular, cold cloud shield at least 100,000 km^2 persisting 6+ hours
Squall-line organization with intense convective cells along the front edge and lighter, uniform rain trailing behind

questions.explanation: An MCC is Maddox's specific large, long-lived, circular MCS category; leading-line/trailing-stratiform describes the classic squall-line radar structure; the rear-inflow jet is the descending flow that intensifies cold pools and can produce bow echoes.

units.label: Observing the Atmosphere: Networks, Radar & Satellite

lessons.label: The Observing System as Forecast Input

sections.heading: Forecasts start with a snapshot, not a model
sections.body: Every numerical forecast begins by describing the atmosphere's current state as precisely as possible — the initial condition a model then evolves forward with physics equations. Lewis Fry Richardson tried this by hand in 1922, hand-computing a six-hour pressure change from observations gathered across Europe; the forecast blew up to an absurd 145 hPa change because his initial wind and pressure fields were not dynamically balanced, and that imbalance triggered spurious high-frequency gravity waves that his raw primitive-equation arithmetic then amplified. Charney, Fjørtoft, and von Neumann's 1950 ENIAC forecast succeeded not by cleaning up the input observations but by changing the equations themselves — adopting the filtered barotropic vorticity equation, which mathematically suppresses those fast gravity-wave modes regardless of how the data were measured. The lesson still held, just from the observing side rather than the equation side: a model is only as good as what it is fed. That principle is why meteorology maintains a standing global observing network rather than relying on satellites or radar alone — the atmosphere is a three-dimensional fluid, and you cannot fully characterize its state from remote sensing of clouds and precipitation without ground-truth of temperature, pressure, humidity, and wind at many altitudes.

sections.heading: The surface layer and the vertical column
sections.body: At the surface, automated stations like ASOS in the United States report temperature, dew point, pressure, wind, visibility, and sky condition roughly hourly at over 900 airport sites, supplemented by finer state and regional mesonets — networks like Oklahoma's Mesonet sample every five minutes, dense enough to catch a frontal passage a national network would miss between reports. METAR is the coded format these stations transmit, decoded automatically by forecast software worldwide. Above the surface, the vertical profile comes chiefly from radiosondes: balloon-borne instrument packages first standardized in the 1930s (building on Pavel Molchanov's 1930 Soviet design) that rise roughly 30 km measuring temperature, humidity, and pressure while GPS tracks wind, launched twice daily at 00 and 12 UTC from roughly 800 sites worldwide under World Meteorological Organization coordination. Commercial aircraft add continuous data between soundings through AMDAR, and moored and drifting ocean buoys — coordinated through the NDBC and international partners — fill in sea-surface conditions.

sections.heading: The gaps that remain
sections.body: Coverage is deeply uneven. Radiosonde sites cluster over land in the Northern Hemisphere; the Southern Ocean, much of Africa, and the open tropical oceans have vast stretches with no routine vertical soundings at all, which is exactly why satellite sounders and, since the 2000s, Argo ocean floats and commercial aircraft data have been pushed hardest to fill oceanic blind spots. This unevenness matters most where it is worst: data-sparse regions are where forecast models diverge most from reality, because the model has the least information to constrain its starting point.

lessons.workedExample: A forecaster is watching a system approaching the Pacific coast from open ocean, where no islands host radiosonde stations for over a thousand miles. The 00 UTC model run shows the upper trough's exact position uncertain by hundreds of kilometers, because between the last Asian sounding and the first US West Coast sounding there is only sparse aircraft data and satellite-derived winds to constrain the analysis. Two competing runs put landfall a full day apart. The forecaster leans on satellite water-vapor imagery to track the trough's motion directly, since it can 'see' where the radiosonde network cannot, and flags the run-to-run instability in the public discussion rather than committing to either solution.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing observing systems is testing whether a student understands that a forecast's uncertainty often traces back to where and how densely the atmosphere was actually measured, not just to the model's physics. A weak answer treats models as self-contained black boxes. A strong answer can name a specific instrument gap — say, the lack of oceanic upper-air soundings — and explain concretely why that gap degrades a forecast for a system approaching from that direction, tying the numbers (twice-daily launches, ~800 global sites) to the consequence.

questions.prompt: Radiosondes are launched from roughly how many sites worldwide, and how often under standard WMO coordination?

options.text: About 800 sites, twice daily at 00 and 12 UTC
About 8,000 sites, once daily at 12 UTC
About 80 sites, four times daily
About 800 sites, continuously

explanations.a: Correct — roughly 800 global sites launch balloon soundings twice daily, at 00 and 12 UTC, under WMO coordination.
explanations.b: The global network is far smaller than 8,000 sites; that overstates coverage by an order of magnitude.
explanations.c: 80 sites would leave far larger data gaps than the actual network has, and launches are twice, not four times, daily.
explanations.d: Radiosondes are single-use balloon flights launched at fixed synoptic hours, not continuous instruments.

questions.prompt: Why did Lewis Fry Richardson's 1922 hand-computed forecast produce an unrealistic result?

options.text: He used the wrong physical equations for atmospheric motion
His unbalanced initial wind and pressure fields triggered spurious gravity waves that the calculation amplified
He had no data at all and simply guessed
Computers of the era could not run his calculation fast enough

explanations.a: His governing primitive equations were sound in principle; the failure came from feeding them a dynamically unbalanced starting state.
explanations.b: Correct — Richardson's initial fields weren't balanced, so the primitive equations generated fast, spurious gravity-wave oscillations that swamped the real pressure tendency.
explanations.c: Richardson did use real observational data gathered across Europe; the problem was that the fields built from it weren't dynamically balanced, not that data was absent.
explanations.d: Richardson computed by hand over weeks; computing speed was not the source of the erroneous result.

questions.prompt: Match each observing platform to what it primarily supplies.

right.text: Hourly surface temperature, wind, pressure, visibility
Vertical profile of temperature, humidity, and wind to ~30 km
En-route atmospheric data from commercial aircraft
Sea-surface temperature and marine conditions

questions.explanation: ASOS/METAR reports surface conditions at fixed stations; radiosondes profile the vertical atmosphere twice daily; AMDAR harvests data from aircraft between soundings; buoys report ocean-surface conditions where land stations don't exist.

questions.prompt: Which region is described as having the sparsest routine upper-air (radiosonde) coverage?

options.text: The continental United States
Western Europe
The open tropical and Southern Ocean regions
East Asia
Coastal Japan

explanations.a: The continental US has a comparatively dense radiosonde network among the described regions.
explanations.b: Western Europe is well covered by land-based sounding sites.
explanations.c: Correct — the open tropical oceans and the Southern Ocean have vast stretches without routine soundings, since radiosonde sites cluster over Northern Hemisphere land.
explanations.d: East Asia has multiple national sounding networks, giving it denser coverage than open-ocean regions.
explanations.e: Coastal Japan hosts operational sounding stations as part of a national network.

lessons.label: How Weather Radar Works

sections.heading: Sending out a pulse and listening for the echo
sections.body: Weather radar works by transmitting short pulses of microwave energy from a rotating dish and measuring how much of that energy bounces back off raindrops, hail, or snow, and how long the return takes. Time delay gives range — the radar simply converts round-trip travel time to distance using the speed of light — while the dish's pointing angle gives direction and elevation. The US operational network, WSR-88D (Weather Surveillance Radar-1988 Doppler, named for its 1988 design year, not its rollout), uses S-band wavelengths near 10 cm, chosen deliberately because longer wavelengths pass through rain with far less signal loss than the shorter wavelengths (C-band near 5 cm, X-band near 3 cm) used by many other countries' networks and by mobile research radars. Roughly 160 WSR-88D radars were installed across the continental US, Alaska, Hawaii, Guam, and Puerto Rico between 1992 and 1997 (first operational unit at Sterling, VA in June 1992; last at North Webster, IN in August 1997), forming NEXRAD, the backbone of US operational radar coverage.

sections.heading: From echo strength to rainfall rate
sections.body: The strength of the returned signal is expressed as reflectivity, Z, which scales with the sixth power of hydrometeor diameter summed over all particles in a radar volume — a physical relationship that makes radar disproportionately sensitive to a few large drops or hailstones. Because Z spans many orders of magnitude, it is displayed logarithmically in decibels of Z, or dBZ, where each 10 dBZ step represents a tenfold jump in the underlying Z value; light rain typically shows around 20-30 dBZ, heavy rain in the 40s, and hail routinely exceeds 60 dBZ. To estimate an actual rainfall rate R from Z, forecasters apply an empirical Z-R relationship; the most widely cited is Marshall and Palmer's 1948 relation, Z = 200 R^1.6, derived from measured raindrop size distributions, though the true relationship varies with rain type and is only an approximation.

sections.heading: What the beam cannot see
sections.body: Radar has systematic blind spots. Because Earth curves away and the beam is aimed slightly upward to clear terrain, the beam's height above ground increases with range — a beam that is a few hundred meters up near the radar can be scanning several kilometers above the surface by the time it reaches a storm 150 km away, so radar can completely overshoot a shallow storm or the near-surface portion of a distant one. Ground clutter from buildings, terrain, and even birds and insects contaminates the lowest scan angles near the radar. And attenuation — signal loss as the beam passes through heavy rain or hail before reaching a target beyond it — is a much bigger problem for the shorter-wavelength C-band and X-band radars than for S-band NEXRAD, sometimes hiding an entire severe cell behind an intervening storm.

lessons.workedExample: A NEXRAD radar scans a supercell 180 km away and reports 55 dBZ at the lowest available tilt, suggesting large hail. But at that range the lowest beam is already more than 3 km above ground due to the upward tilt and Earth's curvature, so the radar is actually sampling hail well aloft in the storm's core, not necessarily what is falling at the surface — the true surface intensity is unknown. A nearer radar 40 km away, where the beam height at the same tilt is under 500 m, would give a far more representative surface estimate, illustrating why forecasters cross-check reflectivity from multiple radars near the edge of range.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about radar fundamentals to check whether a student treats a colorful reflectivity image as ground truth or understands it as an indirect, range-limited measurement. A weak answer reads dBZ values off a screen without noting how far away the storm is. A strong answer explains that beam height grows with range, that heavy attenuation can hide a storm behind another one on shorter-wavelength radars, and that a Z-R relation like Marshall-Palmer's is an approximation, not a direct rain gauge — so a rainfall estimate from radar always carries some uncertainty a gauge network is needed to check.

questions.prompt: Why does the operational WSR-88D network use S-band (about 10 cm) wavelengths instead of shorter C-band or X-band wavelengths?

options.text: S-band dishes are cheaper to manufacture
S-band suffers far less attenuation passing through heavy rain, so distant storms stay visible
S-band cannot detect hail, which simplifies the display
S-band travels faster than shorter wavelengths, giving quicker updates

explanations.a: Cost was not the deciding factor; the choice was driven by beam propagation physics through precipitation.
explanations.b: Correct — longer S-band wavelengths are attenuated much less by intervening rain and hail, so a storm behind another storm remains detectable.
explanations.c: S-band readily detects hail; extreme reflectivity values above roughly 60 dBZ often indicate it.
explanations.d: All radar wavelengths travel at the speed of light; wavelength affects attenuation and resolution, not propagation speed.

questions.prompt: In the Marshall-Palmer Z-R relation, Z = 200 R^1.6, what does this equation let a forecaster estimate?

options.text: Wind speed from Doppler shift
Rainfall rate from measured radar reflectivity
Hail size directly in centimeters
The altitude of the radar beam at a given range

explanations.a: Wind speed comes from Doppler velocity measurements, a separate radar product from reflectivity.
explanations.b: Correct — the Z-R relation converts measured reflectivity Z into an estimated rainfall rate R, based on an empirical raindrop-size relationship.
explanations.c: Reflectivity relates to hail presence qualitatively through very high dBZ values, but the Z-R relation itself is a rainfall-rate formula, not a hail-size formula.
explanations.d: Beam height depends on range, elevation angle, and Earth's curvature, not on the Z-R relation.

questions.prompt: Order these steps in how a weather radar produces a reflectivity estimate, from first to last.

items.text: Radar transmits a short microwave pulse
Pulse reflects off raindrops or hail and returns to the dish
Round-trip time is converted into range to the target
Returned power is converted to reflectivity (Z) and displayed in dBZ

questions.explanation: The radar sends a pulse, waits for the echo, uses the timing to compute distance, and converts the echo's power into the logarithmic dBZ reflectivity value displayed to forecasters.

questions.prompt: Match each radar limitation to its underlying cause.

right.text: Earth's curvature plus the beam's upward tilt raise its height with range
Buildings, terrain, and biota contaminate low-elevation scans close to the radar
Heavy precipitation absorbs and scatters the beam before it reaches a target beyond it

questions.explanation: Overshooting comes from geometry (curvature and beam tilt), clutter from fixed and biological targets near the radar, and attenuation from signal loss passing through intervening precipitation — three distinct causes of missing or distorted data.

lessons.label: Doppler Velocity & Severe-Storm Signatures

sections.heading: Measuring only the piece of motion aimed at the radar
sections.body: Reflectivity tells you where precipitation is; Doppler velocity tells you how it is moving, by measuring the frequency shift between the transmitted pulse and its echo. Crucially, Doppler radar only measures radial velocity — the component of motion directly toward or away from the radar along the beam — not true wind speed or direction, so a target moving perpendicular to the beam registers zero radial velocity even if it is moving fast. Radar Doppler capability became operational with the WSR-88D network beginning in 1988, but the concept was proven earlier: on May 24, 1973, a Doppler radar in Norman, Oklahoma captured the Union City, Oklahoma tornado and its parent mesocyclone in velocity data for the first time, showing a clear couplet of inbound and outbound velocities marking rotation — a landmark result that helped justify building the operational Doppler network.

sections.heading: Reading rotation as a velocity couplet
sections.body: On a base velocity display, a mesocyclone appears as a tight couplet: a patch of inbound (toward-radar) velocity immediately adjacent to a patch of outbound (away-from-radar) velocity, typically spanning 2-10 km — the signature of air rotating around a roughly vertical axis. A tornadic vortex signature, or TVS, is a much smaller, tighter version of that same couplet, sometimes just one or two radar gates wide, associated with the tornado's own circulation embedded inside the broader mesocyclone. Forecasters commonly compute storm-relative velocity, which subtracts the storm's own forward motion from the raw radial velocities, because a fast-moving storm's translational motion can otherwise mask or distort the appearance of rotation within it.

sections.heading: Ambiguity, aliasing, and the tornado-warning decision
sections.body: Doppler radar has an inherent trade-off, set by its pulse repetition frequency (PRF): a higher PRF gives a larger unambiguous velocity range (the Nyquist velocity) but a shorter unambiguous range distance, and vice versa, so returns from beyond the unambiguous range can 'fold' back and appear at the wrong range, while true velocities exceeding the Nyquist velocity wrap around and display as their opposite sign — velocity aliasing. Operational radars use multiple PRFs and automated dealiasing algorithms to reconstruct the true velocity field, though aliasing artifacts still occasionally fool automated storm-tracking software. Operationally, when a forecaster sees a hook echo in reflectivity — a curved appendage on a supercell's southwest flank marking the rain-free area wrapping around the mesocyclone — collocated with a strong low-level rotational couplet in velocity, that combination is the standard basis for issuing a radar-indicated tornado warning, even without a confirmed visual sighting.

lessons.workedExample: A radar operator sees a supercell 60 km southwest of the radar with a classic hook echo in reflectivity. Switching to storm-relative velocity, they find a couplet showing 40 knots inbound next to 35 knots outbound within a 3 km diameter at the lowest tilt — a strong, tight mesocyclone signature well above typical noise. Because the couplet sits directly at the tip of the hook and the rotation is both strong and persistent across successive volume scans, the office issues a tornado warning based on radar alone, before any spotter report arrives, exactly the hook-plus-couplet logic that defines a radar-indicated warning.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about Doppler signatures to see if a student understands that radar velocity is a directional, radar-relative quantity with known artifacts, not a clean wind measurement. A weak answer says radar 'detects tornadoes' without mentioning that it only measures radial velocity or that aliasing can create a false rotation signal. A strong answer explains the inbound/outbound couplet mechanism, distinguishes a mesocyclone-scale couplet from a tighter TVS, and can describe how Nyquist aliasing is corrected — showing they understand both what the instrument reveals and where it can mislead.

questions.prompt: What does Doppler radar velocity actually measure?

options.text: The true wind speed and direction at every point in a storm
Only the component of a target's motion directly toward or away from the radar
Air pressure inside the storm
The size of hydrometeors independent of their motion

explanations.a: True wind requires combining multiple radars or additional assumptions; a single Doppler radar cannot resolve the full wind vector.
explanations.b: Correct — Doppler radar measures only radial velocity, the motion component along the beam toward or away from the radar; cross-beam motion is invisible to it.
explanations.c: Radar measures reflected microwave energy and its frequency shift, not air pressure.
explanations.d: Hydrometeor size relates to reflectivity (Z), a separate product from Doppler velocity.

questions.prompt: What historic event is credited with the first Doppler radar observation of a mesocyclone?

options.text: The 1973 Union City, Oklahoma tornado
The 1988 WSR-88D network's first day of operation
The 1948 Marshall-Palmer rain study
The 1925 Tri-State Tornado

explanations.a: Correct — a Doppler radar in Norman, Oklahoma captured a clear inbound/outbound velocity couplet in the May 24, 1973 Union City tornado's parent storm, an early proof of concept.
explanations.b: 1988 marks when Doppler capability became operational nationwide, well after the Union City proof-of-concept observation.
explanations.c: The Marshall-Palmer study concerned rainfall-reflectivity relationships, unrelated to Doppler velocity or 1973.
explanations.d: The 1925 Tri-State Tornado predates Doppler weather radar entirely.

questions.prompt: Match each velocity signature to its description.

right.text: A broader 2-10 km inbound/outbound velocity pair marking storm-scale rotation
A much tighter, often one-to-two-gate-wide couplet nested inside the mesocyclone
Raw velocity with the storm's own forward motion subtracted out

questions.explanation: The mesocyclone couplet marks broad storm-scale rotation, the TVS is a tighter embedded signature closer to the tornado's own scale, and storm-relative velocity removes the storm's translational motion so rotation is easier to see.

questions.prompt: What causes Doppler velocity aliasing?

options.text: Ground clutter contaminating the lowest elevation scans
A true velocity exceeding the radar's Nyquist velocity, so it wraps around and displays with the wrong sign
Attenuation of the signal by heavy rain along the beam path
The beam overshooting a distant, shallow storm

explanations.a: Ground clutter is a reflectivity contamination issue near the radar, not the mechanism behind velocity aliasing.
explanations.b: Correct — the Nyquist velocity sets the unambiguous velocity range for a given PRF; true velocities beyond it fold over and appear with the wrong sign, requiring dealiasing.
explanations.c: Attenuation reduces signal strength through precipitation; it does not cause velocity values to wrap.
explanations.d: Beam overshoot is a range/geometry issue affecting whether a storm is sampled at all, not a velocity-aliasing mechanism.

lessons.label: Dual-Polarization Radar

sections.heading: Two pulses instead of one
sections.body: Conventional Doppler radar transmits pulses in a single horizontal orientation, so it can measure how much energy comes back but nothing about the shape of what reflected it. Dual-polarization radar transmits pulses in both horizontal and vertical orientations simultaneously and compares the two returns, which lets it infer hydrometeor shape and uniformity, not just quantity. The entire US WSR-88D network was retrofitted with dual-polarization hardware between 2011 and 2013, a multi-year, radar-by-radar upgrade that transformed operational reflectivity-only radar into a shape-sensing instrument without replacing the underlying S-band dishes.

sections.heading: Three new variables and what each reveals
sections.body: Differential reflectivity, ZDR, compares the horizontal and vertical return power in decibels: large raindrops flatten into oblate shapes as they fall, returning more horizontal-polarization energy, so raindrops read positive ZDR, while nearly spherical hail and small drizzle read close to zero. Correlation coefficient, rho-hv, measures how consistently each pulse's horizontal and vertical returns behave relative to each other within a radar volume; a uniform population of similar-shaped raindrops gives values near 0.95-1.0, while a mixed bag of wildly different shapes and sizes — like tumbling hail, or non-meteorological debris — drives rho-hv sharply lower. Specific differential phase, KDP, tracks the cumulative phase shift between horizontal and vertical pulses as they propagate through heavy rain; because it depends on propagation through the medium rather than reflected power, KDP is far less sensitive to radar miscalibration or attenuation, making it especially valuable for estimating rainfall rate in intense convective cores where reflectivity-based estimates saturate.

sections.heading: Two signatures storm chasers watch for
sections.body: A ZDR column is a vertical extension of enhanced ZDR values reaching above the freezing level, produced when a strong updraft physically lofts large, still-liquid raindrops well above the altitude where they would normally have frozen — its presence and depth is a real-time proxy for updraft intensity, tracked operationally since dual-pol became routine. Far more consequential for warning operations is the tornado debris signature, or TDS: when a tornado is actively lofting debris — soil, insulation, vegetation, building material — that debris is irregularly shaped and behaves nothing like raindrops or hail, so correlation coefficient collapses to unusually low values (often below roughly 0.8) precisely where reflectivity and velocity already show a tight rotational couplet. A TDS confirms that a tornado is very likely on the ground and doing damage, distinguishing an actual debris-lofting tornado from a strong rotation signature that has not yet produced a confirmed touchdown.

lessons.workedExample: A supercell shows a tight velocity couplet and a hook echo, the classic tornado-warning combination described in the previous lesson, but the storm has not yet been visually confirmed because it is near dusk with poor visibility. The forecaster checks the correlation coefficient product at the same location and altitude as the couplet and finds rho-hv has dropped to about 0.75, collocated precisely with the rotation — a tornado debris signature. Combined with the existing couplet and hook, this upgrades the office's confidence from 'likely tornado' to 'tornado on the ground, debris confirmed by radar,' language that can go directly into an urgent warning statement even without a spotter report.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing dual-pol wants to see whether a student understands these are shape and uniformity measurements layered on top of reflectivity and velocity, not a redundant display. A weak answer says dual-pol 'shows more detail' vaguely. A strong answer names a specific variable — say, correlation coefficient — explains mechanistically why a mix of irregular debris shapes suppresses it relative to uniform raindrops, and connects that mechanism to why a TDS is treated as stronger confirmation than a velocity couplet alone.

questions.prompt: Why does a tornado debris signature (TDS) show a sharp drop in correlation coefficient (rho-hv)?

options.text: Debris absorbs more microwave energy than rain, reducing overall reflectivity
Debris consists of irregular, varied shapes that behave inconsistently between horizontal and vertical pulses, unlike uniform raindrops
Debris moves faster than the Nyquist velocity, causing aliasing
Debris is always located beyond the radar's maximum unambiguous range

explanations.a: Correlation coefficient measures pulse-to-pulse shape consistency, not overall reflected power; reduced reflectivity is not the mechanism here.
explanations.b: Correct — irregularly shaped, varied debris scatters horizontal and vertical pulses inconsistently, driving correlation coefficient sharply lower than the near-uniform behavior of raindrops.
explanations.c: Velocity aliasing is a Nyquist/PRF phenomenon affecting the Doppler velocity product, unrelated to correlation coefficient.
explanations.d: TDS is a near-storm, low-altitude signature typically well within normal detection range, not a range-ambiguity artifact.

questions.prompt: What does a ZDR column indicate about a thunderstorm?

options.text: The storm is producing large hail exclusively
A strong updraft is lofting large liquid raindrops above the freezing level
The radar beam is being blocked by terrain
The storm has weakened and updraft has collapsed

explanations.a: Hail tends to be more spherical and reads closer to zero ZDR, not the elevated positive values that define a ZDR column.
explanations.b: Correct — a ZDR column is the vertical extension of positive ZDR (indicating oblate liquid drops) above the freezing level, produced by a strong updraft physically carrying those drops aloft before they can freeze.
explanations.c: Beam blockage is a separate radar artifact unrelated to the ZDR variable's meteorological interpretation.
explanations.d: A ZDR column indicates an active, strong updraft, the opposite of a collapsing storm.

questions.prompt: Match each dual-polarization variable to what it primarily measures.

right.text: Shape/oblateness of hydrometeors via horizontal vs. vertical return power
Uniformity of shapes within a radar volume
Rainfall rate via cumulative phase shift, largely immune to attenuation

questions.explanation: ZDR captures shape/oblateness from differential power, correlation coefficient captures how uniform the population of scatterers is, and KDP captures a propagation-phase effect that is robust to calibration and attenuation issues, useful for heavy-rain estimation.

questions.prompt: The entire US WSR-88D network was upgraded to dual-polarization capability during approximately which period?

explanations.a: 1988-1997 was the original WSR-88D installation period, before dual-polarization was added.
explanations.b: Correct — the network-wide dual-polarization retrofit was completed across 2011-2013.
explanations.c: 1948-1950 corresponds to the Marshall-Palmer Z-R work, unrelated to dual-pol hardware.
explanations.d: 1973-1975 corresponds to the early Doppler proof-of-concept era, before dual-polarization existed operationally.

lessons.label: Weather Satellites: Orbits & Channels

sections.heading: Two orbits, two different jobs
sections.body: Geostationary satellites like the US GOES series orbit at roughly 35,786 km above the equator, matching Earth's rotation so they stay fixed over one longitude — GOES-East near 75.2°W and GOES-West near 137°W together watch the Americas continuously. That fixed vantage lets GOES's Advanced Baseline Imager capture a full disk image every 10 minutes and, in targeted mesoscale mode, a small region as often as every 30-60 seconds, which is what lets forecasters watch a single thunderstorm's cloud top pulse in near-real time. Polar-orbiting satellites trade that constant view for resolution and pole-to-pole coverage: the Joint Polar Satellite System, including Suomi NPP and NOAA-20, flies sun-synchronous orbits around 830 km altitude, circling Earth roughly every 101 minutes and crossing any given location only about twice a day, but at far finer spatial resolution than a geostationary platform can achieve from 35,786 km away.

sections.heading: Three channels, three different windows into the atmosphere
sections.body: Visible channel imagery, centered near 0.64 micrometers, records reflected sunlight the way a camera does, so it shows sharp cloud texture and structure but only works during daylight. Infrared channels, such as the 10.3-micrometer 'clean window' band, instead measure emitted thermal radiation, which works day or night and — because temperature falls with altitude through the troposphere — lets a forecaster estimate cloud-top height from cloud-top temperature: colder IR readings mean higher, and usually more vigorous, cloud tops. Water-vapor channels, roughly 6.2-7.3 micrometers, sense radiation from water vapor in the middle and upper troposphere; because that layer is often cloud-free, water-vapor imagery reveals large-scale moisture patterns, jet-stream-related features, and dynamical structure even where no clouds exist to make the pattern visible any other way.

sections.heading: Reading intensity signatures in infrared imagery
sections.body: Two specific IR patterns are severe-weather diagnostics in their own right. An overshooting top is a small, isolated area of anomalously cold cloud-top temperature — colder than the surrounding anvil — marking where an intense updraft has physically punched through the tropopause into the lower stratosphere before sinking back; its presence signals a storm with unusually strong vertical motion. The enhanced-V, documented by McCann in a 1983 study, is a V- or U-shaped area of relatively warm cloud top pointing back toward an overshooting top, forming on the downwind side as stratospheric air diverges around the penetrating updraft; McCann showed this pattern was statistically associated with severe weather at the surface below, giving forecasters a satellite-only clue to severe potential even before a storm is within radar range.

lessons.workedExample: A forecaster monitoring a developing supercell over rural terrain with no nearby radar coverage checks GOES infrared imagery and spots a small, isolated cold spot roughly 8°C colder than the surrounding anvil, with a warm V-shaped notch extending downwind from it — an overshooting top paired with an enhanced-V. Even without radar confirmation, this IR signature is treated as strong evidence of an intense updraft capable of severe weather, prompting the forecaster to issue a severe thunderstorm watch for the area based on satellite alone, then confirm with radar once the storm moves within range roughly 45 minutes later.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about satellite orbits and channels to test whether a student picked the right tool for the right question rather than defaulting to whichever loop looked good. A weak answer treats all satellite imagery as interchangeable 'cloud pictures.' A strong answer explains the geostationary-versus-polar tradeoff (constant view versus finer resolution and better polar coverage), why IR works at night when visible cannot, and can read a specific signature like an overshooting top or enhanced-V as evidence of an actual physical process (updraft strength) rather than just a color on a screen.

questions.prompt: Why can polar-orbiting satellites like those in the Joint Polar Satellite System achieve finer spatial resolution than geostationary satellites like GOES?

options.text: They use a different, more advanced sensor technology unavailable to geostationary satellites
They orbit far closer to Earth (around 830 km) than geostationary satellites (about 35,786 km)
They only observe at night, when the atmosphere is calmer
They stay fixed over one location, allowing longer observation time per pixel

explanations.a: Both orbit types can carry advanced imagers; the resolution difference is primarily an orbital-geometry effect, not a difference in underlying sensor technology.
explanations.b: Correct — flying at roughly 830 km rather than 35,786 km puts polar-orbiting satellites much closer to Earth's surface, which yields finer resolution per pixel.
explanations.c: Polar-orbiting satellites observe day and night on different passes; observation timing is not what drives their resolution advantage.
explanations.d: Staying fixed over one location describes geostationary satellites, not polar orbiters, and is unrelated to resolution.

questions.prompt: A satellite water-vapor channel image shows dry and moist swirls in a cloud-free region of the mid-to-upper troposphere. What does this demonstrate?

options.text: Water-vapor channels only work where clouds are present
Water-vapor channels sense atmospheric moisture directly, revealing structure even without clouds
The image must be a visible-channel image mislabeled as water vapor
Water vapor channels only detect surface-level humidity

explanations.a: Water-vapor channels work precisely because they do not require clouds — they sense the water vapor itself in the middle/upper troposphere.
explanations.b: Correct — because water-vapor channels detect radiation from atmospheric moisture rather than reflected light or cloud tops, they reveal dynamical and moisture structure in otherwise cloud-free air.
explanations.c: Visible imagery requires daylight and shows reflected sunlight/cloud texture, not moisture patterns in clear air; this scenario is consistent with water-vapor, not visible, imagery.
explanations.d: Water-vapor channels are most sensitive to the middle and upper troposphere, not surface-level humidity.

questions.prompt: Match each satellite channel to its primary use.

right.text: Daytime cloud texture from reflected sunlight
Cloud-top temperature/height, day or night, from emitted radiation
Mid/upper-tropospheric moisture and dynamical patterns, even in clear air

questions.explanation: Visible senses reflected sunlight so it needs daylight; infrared senses thermal emission so it works at any hour and maps to cloud-top height via temperature; water vapor senses moisture emission and reveals structure independent of cloud cover.

questions.prompt: What does an overshooting top on infrared satellite imagery indicate?

options.text: A weakening storm whose updraft has collapsed
A small area of anomalously cold cloud top where an intense updraft has punched through the tropopause
Ground clutter contaminating the satellite sensor
The satellite has lost its geostationary lock and is drifting

explanations.a: An overshooting top indicates an unusually strong, active updraft, not a collapsing one.
explanations.b: Correct — an overshooting top is a localized, anomalously cold cloud-top signature marking where a strong updraft has physically penetrated the tropopause before sinking back into the anvil.
explanations.c: Ground clutter is a radar artifact from fixed surface targets; it has no equivalent meaning in satellite infrared imagery.
explanations.d: Overshooting tops are a real meteorological cloud-top signature, unrelated to satellite orbital stability.

lessons.label: Satellite Interpretation of Weather Systems

sections.heading: Reading a cyclone's life cycle in its cloud shape
sections.body: A developing midlatitude cyclone's satellite signature evolves in a recognizable sequence. Early on, clouds along the developing frontal boundary organize into a baroclinic leaf — an elongated, leaf-shaped cloud mass stretched along the region of strongest temperature contrast, thickest where rising air is most vigorous. As the low deepens and begins wrapping cyclonically around its center, that leaf curls into a comma cloud: a dense head of cloud near the low's center trailing a long tail along the cold front, the single most recognizable satellite signature of a mature midlatitude storm and the visual basis generations of forecasters have used to locate a surface low even where no station reports pressure right at the center.

sections.heading: The conveyor belt model and the dry slot
sections.body: Beneath that comma shape, the storm is organized by streams of air moving along coherent three-dimensional paths, formalized as the conveyor belt model developed chiefly by Harrold in 1973 and elaborated by Carlson in 1980 using satellite imagery directly. The warm conveyor belt is a stream of warm, moist air rising ahead of the cold front and curving north and east over the warm front, producing the broad shield of clouds and precipitation that makes up the comma head. The cold conveyor belt flows beneath it from the east, feeding into the low and curving cyclonically around it, often producing a separate band of enhanced precipitation. Between these two moist streams, a tongue of drier, descending air called the dry slot wraps into the storm from the southwest, cutting a visibly clear or thin-cloud notch into the comma head on satellite imagery — its appearance is one of the clearest satellite cues that a storm is entering its most rapidly intensifying phase, since the dry slot marks stratospheric or upper-tropospheric air descending into the storm's core.

sections.heading: Estimating a hurricane's strength from its cloud pattern alone
sections.body: Tropical cyclones present an entirely different challenge: over open ocean, far from any radiosonde or buoy, satellite imagery is often the only observation available, so Vernon Dvorak developed a technique in the 1970s, refined through 1984, to estimate a tropical cyclone's intensity purely from the organization of its cloud pattern in visible or infrared imagery. The Dvorak technique assigns a T-number based on features like central dense overcast size, banding organization, and eye characteristics — a distinct, warm, cloud-free eye surrounded by a tight, cold eyewall indicates a much stronger storm than a ragged, poorly organized cluster of convection — and converts that T-number to an estimated maximum sustained wind speed and central pressure. Despite its subjectivity, Dvorak-based estimates remain a primary tool for operational centers worldwide precisely because most tropical cyclones spend their lives beyond the reach of routine in-situ observation.

lessons.workedExample: A forecaster tracking a Gulf of Mexico system watches its satellite presentation over two days: first a diffuse baroclinic leaf, then a tightening comma shape with a distinct dry slot notching into the northwest side of the comma head. The appearance of that dry slot, indicating descending drier air wrapping into the storm's core, leads the forecaster to note in the discussion that the system is entering rapid intensification, several hours before the nearest surface stations report the pressure drop and wind shift that confirm it — satellite structure anticipated the ground-truth data.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing satellite interpretation wants to know if a student can read structure, not just recite vocabulary. A weak answer names 'comma cloud' and 'dry slot' without explaining what physical process each pattern represents. A strong answer connects the shapes to the underlying airstreams — explaining that the dry slot marks descending air cutting into the moist conveyor belts — and, for tropical systems, can explain why the Dvorak technique exists at all: because most of a hurricane's life is spent where no other observation reaches it.

questions.prompt: Order these cloud-pattern stages in the typical life cycle of a developing midlatitude cyclone, from earliest to most mature.

items.text: Baroclinic leaf
Comma cloud with distinct head and tail
Well-developed dry slot cutting into the comma head

questions.explanation: The storm begins as an elongated baroclinic leaf along the frontal zone, curls into a comma shape as it deepens and wraps cyclonically, and a dry slot appears later still as descending drier air cuts into the comma head during rapid intensification.

questions.prompt: What does the appearance of a dry slot on satellite imagery of a midlatitude cyclone typically indicate?

options.text: The storm is dissipating and precipitation is ending
Drier air is descending and wrapping into the storm's core, often marking rapid intensification
The satellite sensor has malfunctioned in that region
The storm has moved entirely over open ocean

explanations.a: A dry slot is associated with an intensifying, not dissipating, storm; it marks a dynamically active phase, not a weakening one.
explanations.b: Correct — the dry slot marks a tongue of descending drier air wrapping into the storm's core from the southwest, and its clear appearance on satellite is a classic sign of a rapidly intensifying cyclone.
explanations.c: A dry slot is a real meteorological feature with a clear satellite signature, not a sensor artifact.
explanations.d: The dry slot reflects internal storm structure and can appear over land or ocean; it is not defined by the storm's location relative to a coastline.

questions.prompt: Match each conveyor belt model component to its role.

right.text: Warm moist air rising ahead of the cold front, forming the comma head
Air flowing in from the east beneath the warm belt, curving cyclonically around the low
Drier descending air cutting a visible notch into the comma head

questions.explanation: The warm conveyor belt supplies the broad precipitation shield of the comma head, the cold conveyor belt feeds in from the east beneath it, and the dry slot is the descending, drier airstream that carves a clear notch into the cloud pattern, formalized in the conveyor belt model developed by Harrold (1973) and Carlson (1980).

questions.prompt: Why is the Dvorak technique especially important for estimating tropical cyclone intensity?

options.text: It replaces the need for any satellite imagery at all
Most tropical cyclones spend their lives over open ocean, far from radiosonde and buoy coverage, so satellite cloud pattern is often the only available data
It measures wind speed directly using Doppler radar aboard the satellite
It only works after a hurricane makes landfall

explanations.a: The Dvorak technique is itself a satellite-imagery interpretation method — it depends on, rather than replaces, satellite imagery.
explanations.b: Correct — because open-ocean tropical cyclones are usually far from routine in-situ observing networks, Dvorak's cloud-pattern-based estimate is frequently the primary or only intensity estimate available.
explanations.c: Weather satellites used for the Dvorak technique are passive imagers; they do not carry Doppler radar measuring wind speed directly.
explanations.d: The Dvorak technique is applied throughout a storm's oceanic life cycle, not only after landfall — landfall is when in-situ data typically becomes more available, reducing reliance on it.

lessons.label: Measurement Error, Siting & Data Quality

sections.heading: Two very different kinds of error
sections.body: Not all observation error comes from a faulty instrument. Instrument error is the sensor itself reading incorrectly — a miscalibrated thermometer, a radar with a systematic reflectivity bias — and is usually detectable and correctable through routine calibration. Representativeness error is different and often larger: it is the mismatch between what a sensor measures at one precise point and what the surrounding area or the model grid box it is meant to represent is actually doing. A temperature sensor sited over asphalt in a parking lot might be functioning perfectly and still misrepresent the surrounding rural landscape by several degrees, because it is accurately measuring a genuinely unrepresentative microclimate rather than measuring anything wrong. Distinguishing these two matters because they demand different fixes: instrument error is solved by better hardware and calibration, representativeness error is solved by better siting or by explicitly modeling the mismatch.

sections.heading: Where radar geometry itself creates blind spots
sections.body: Radar has a structural error source built into its geometry, beyond any single beam's overshoot at range described earlier: because the radar scans in conical sweeps around a vertical axis, it cannot physically point its beam straight up, leaving a roughly cone-shaped volume directly above the radar — the 'cone of silence' — that is never sampled at all. A storm passing almost directly overhead can vanish from view even though the radar is working correctly, simply because that geometry leaves no beam angle to see it. Forecast offices manage this by relying on neighboring radars whose coverage overlaps that blind cone, which is part of why NEXRAD sites were deliberately spaced to give most of the country coverage from more than one radar.

sections.heading: Siting standards and why error must be characterized, not just minimized
sections.body: Surface stations follow siting standards precisely because exposure changes what a sensor reports without changing anything wrong with the sensor: WMO and national guidelines specify minimum distances from buildings, pavement, and obstructions, standard sensor heights, and shielding from direct solar radiation, because violating them systematically biases readings — an ASOS station near a runway apron can read several degrees warmer on a summer afternoon than a location just a hundred meters away over grass, contaminating a station's climate record with artificial urban-heat-island-like effects that have nothing to do with regional weather. This matters beyond any single reading because data assimilation, the process that blends observations with a model's prior forecast to build the initial condition, formally weights each observation by its estimated error: an observation believed highly accurate is trusted heavily and pulls the analysis toward it, while one with poorly known or large representativeness error is down-weighted. If an observation's error is not properly characterized, it can be given too much or too little influence in ways that actively degrade forecast accuracy rather than improve it.

lessons.workedExample: A state climate office notices a decades-long ASOS station's summer maximum temperatures have crept upward faster than nearby rural stations over the past ten years. A site survey finds a new access road and expanded parking area were built within the siting-standard buffer zone around the sensor several years earlier. The sensor itself passes calibration checks perfectly — this is representativeness error, not instrument error — so the office cannot fix it by recalibrating; instead they flag the record with a documented siting change, since a data-assimilation system pulling this station's readings without that context would otherwise treat a purely local pavement effect as if it were regional warming.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about measurement error and siting because it is where many student projects quietly go wrong: a sensor can be perfectly calibrated and still produce misleading data if its exposure is wrong. A weak answer treats 'the instrument was accurate' as the end of the story. A strong answer separates instrument error from representativeness error, can name a concrete siting violation (pavement, obstruction, wrong height) and its physical consequence, and understands that in operational forecasting this isn't just a data-quality nicety — unaccounted-for error actively corrupts the model's starting point through data assimilation.

questions.prompt: A temperature sensor is perfectly calibrated but sited directly over an asphalt parking lot, reading several degrees warmer than the surrounding rural area. What kind of error is this?

options.text: Instrument error, because the sensor is malfunctioning
Representativeness error, because the sensor accurately measures an unrepresentative microclimate
Range folding, a radar-specific artifact
Velocity aliasing

explanations.a: The sensor is functioning correctly; the problem is what it is exposed to, not a hardware fault, so this is not instrument error.
explanations.b: Correct — the sensor is accurately measuring its immediate surroundings, but those surroundings (pavement) do not represent the broader area it is meant to characterize, which is the definition of representativeness error.
explanations.c: Range folding is a radar range-ambiguity issue unrelated to surface station siting.
explanations.d: Velocity aliasing is a Doppler radar phenomenon, not a surface temperature siting issue.

questions.prompt: What is the radar 'cone of silence'?

options.text: A region where attenuation from heavy rain blocks the beam
The unsampled, roughly cone-shaped volume directly above the radar, since the beam cannot point straight up
An area affected by ground clutter from nearby buildings
The zone beyond the radar's maximum unambiguous range

explanations.a: Attenuation is a signal-loss effect through precipitation, not the geometric cause of the cone of silence.
explanations.b: Correct — because the radar scans in conical sweeps and cannot aim straight upward, a cone-shaped volume directly overhead is structurally never sampled, regardless of storm intensity.
explanations.c: Ground clutter is caused by fixed near-surface targets contaminating low-elevation scans, a different phenomenon from the overhead blind cone.
explanations.d: The unambiguous range limit is set by pulse repetition frequency and affects far-range returns, not the region directly above the radar.

questions.prompt: Match each concept to its consequence for forecasting.

right.text: Systematically biased readings from a faulty sensor, correctable by calibration
A locally accurate reading wrongly treated as representative of a larger area
Observations are trusted in proportion to their estimated error when building the model's initial condition

questions.explanation: Instrument error is a hardware/calibration problem; representativeness error is a mismatch between a point measurement and the area it represents; and data assimilation formally weights every observation by its estimated error, so both error types must be characterized for the process to work correctly.

questions.prompt: Why do siting standards specify minimum distances from pavement, buildings, and obstructions for surface stations?

options.text: To make stations easier for technicians to physically access
To limit representativeness error by keeping the sensor's immediate exposure consistent with the broader area it is meant to characterize
To reduce the cost of installing each station
To prevent range folding in nearby radar data

explanations.a: Siting standards are about measurement quality, not technician convenience; access is a separate operational concern.
explanations.b: Correct — proper siting keeps a station's local exposure representative of the surrounding area, minimizing the gap between what the point sensor reads and what the region is actually doing.
explanations.c: Cost is not the stated rationale for siting standards; the standards exist to protect data quality.
explanations.d: Range folding is a radar phenomenon tied to pulse timing, unrelated to surface station siting standards.

units.label: Numerical Weather Prediction, Ensembles & Forecast Skill

lessons.label: What a Weather Model Is

sections.heading: An initial state, stepped forward
sections.body: A numerical weather prediction (NWP) model does one conceptual thing: it takes a snapshot of the atmosphere's current state — temperature, wind, moisture, pressure — sampled at every point of a three-dimensional grid, and steps that state forward in time using the physical laws that govern fluid motion, heat, and moisture. Each grid point holds a small set of numbers; the model computes how those numbers change over a short timestep (often a few minutes), then repeats the process thousands of times to reach a forecast hours or days out. The grid is the model's eyes: nothing smaller than roughly twice the grid spacing can be represented at all, a limit called the Nyquist constraint. A model with 25 km spacing simply cannot 'see' a 3 km thunderstorm cell — it does not fail to predict the storm so much as the storm does not exist in that model's world.

sections.heading: Global reach versus local detail
sections.body: Because computing every grid point for every timestep is expensive, centers trade resolution against domain size and cost. Global models run over the whole planet at coarser spacing: the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) runs its Integrated Forecasting System (IFS) at about 9 km horizontal resolution — a level its deterministic run reached with the March 2016 upgrade (Cycle 41r2, the TCo1279 grid) — while NOAA's Global Forecast System (GFS) runs near 13 km. Limited-area models instead nest a smaller domain at much finer spacing, borrowing boundary conditions from a global model: NOAA's North American Mesoscale (NAM) model runs at 12 km over North America, and the High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) runs at about 3 km, updated hourly, over the continental United States. The tradeoff is stark — HRRR sees storm-scale structure the global models cannot, but only over one region and only days ahead, while ECMWF's global grid sacrifices that fine detail to forecast the whole planet out past a week. Forecasters routinely consult several models side by side because each is a different compromise between how far it can see and how far ahead it can see. Resolution isn't only horizontal: models also stack a finite number of vertical levels through the atmosphere, and a coarse vertical grid can't resolve fine vertical structure — like a sharp temperature inversion trapping fog near the surface — any more than a coarse horizontal grid can resolve a single thunderstorm. ECMWF's IFS runs 137 vertical levels, versus 127 for GFS, giving it finer vertical detail to go with its finer horizontal spacing.

lessons.workedExample: A forecaster needs Saturday's severe-weather outlook for Oklahoma five days out, then a storm-mode call for Saturday afternoon itself. Five days out, only a global model reaches that far, so they check GFS and ECMWF fields for the large-scale pattern — a trough digging into the Plains — even though at 9-13 km spacing neither model can resolve individual storms; it can only signal favorable ingredients. By Saturday morning, HRRR's 3 km hourly-updated run is in range, and it explicitly shows discrete supercells tracking across the Texas Panhandle because its grid is fine enough to represent a single storm cell rather than just the atmosphere's willingness to produce one.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'what resolution did your model run at, and why does that matter for what you're studying?' because resolution is the single number that tells you what a model can and cannot represent — a student who cites a forecast without knowing its grid spacing hasn't understood their own tool. A weak answer says 'the model was accurate' with no grid spacing mentioned. A strong answer states the spacing, names the tradeoff (a coarser global model forecasts further ahead over more area; a finer regional model sees smaller features but only nearby and only briefly), and explains why that mattered for the phenomenon being studied.

questions.prompt: Why can't a 25 km-resolution global model represent an individual 3 km-wide thunderstorm cell?

options.text: The model's physics equations don't include thunderstorms
Nothing smaller than roughly twice the grid spacing can be represented on that grid
Thunderstorms only form in models run at 3 km resolution
The model's timestep is too long to capture rapid changes

explanations.a: The physics (convection, moisture, heat) is present in every model; the limit is the grid, not the equation set.
explanations.b: Correct — this is the Nyquist-type resolution limit: a feature must span at least about two grid points to be represented at all, so a 3 km storm is simply invisible to a 25 km grid.
explanations.c: Thunderstorms form in the real atmosphere regardless of any model; a coarse model can still signal favorable conditions for them even without resolving individual cells.
explanations.d: Timestep length affects numerical stability and how fast the model runs, not whether a small spatial feature can exist on a coarse grid.

questions.prompt: Match each model to its approximate horizontal resolution.

right.text: ~9 km
~13 km
~12 km
~3 km

questions.explanation: ECMWF's IFS runs near 9 km, GFS near 13 km, both global; NAM runs at 12 km and HRRR at 3 km, both limited-area domains nested inside a global model's boundary conditions.

questions.prompt: What is the main cost of running HRRR's 3 km grid instead of a coarser global grid?

options.text: It cannot be updated more than once a day
It only covers a limited region and a shorter forecast range, not the whole globe
It requires no observations to initialize
It cannot represent wind, only temperature

explanations.a: HRRR is actually updated hourly — more frequently than most global models, not less.
explanations.b: Correct — the computational cost of fine grid spacing is paid for by covering a smaller domain (the continental US) and a shorter forecast horizon than a global model.
explanations.c: Every operational NWP model, HRRR included, is initialized from observations through data assimilation.
explanations.d: HRRR represents the full set of atmospheric variables just like other models; the limitation is domain and range, not which variables it carries.

questions.prompt: Order these steps in how an NWP model produces a forecast.

items.text: Sample the current atmospheric state onto a 3D grid
Apply the governing physical equations to compute change over one short timestep
Repeat the timestep thousands of times
Output the projected state at each forecast hour

questions.explanation: The model starts from a gridded snapshot, advances it one short timestep at a time by applying the physics, repeats that many times, and the running record of states becomes the forecast.

lessons.label: Parameterization & Model Physics

sections.heading: When physics happens below the grid
sections.body: A model's grid can only carry information at the scale of its spacing, but real atmospheric processes — an individual cumulus cloud, the churn of turbulence in the lowest kilometer, the absorption of sunlight by a specific cloud droplet, the wicking of moisture through soil — happen at scales far smaller than even a fine 3 km grid, let alone a 13-25 km global grid. These sub-grid processes still shape the resolved-scale forecast: convection redistributes heat and moisture vertically, turbulence mixes momentum near the surface, radiation heats and cools the column, and the land surface controls how much moisture and heat feed back into the air above. Since the model cannot simulate these processes explicitly, it uses parameterization: a physics-based approximation that estimates the net effect of the sub-grid process on the resolved grid, given only the grid-scale variables it can see. Every operational model carries a suite of parameterization schemes — for convection, cloud microphysics, boundary-layer turbulence, radiation (schemes like RRTMG are widely used), and land-surface exchange (Noah-MP is one common choice) — bundled together as the model's 'physics package.'

sections.heading: The convection-allowing leap
sections.body: Cumulus convection is the parameterization with the largest forecast consequences, and it is where resolution creates a qualitative break, not just a quantitative one. At coarse global-model spacing (roughly 9-25 km), individual thunderstorm updrafts cannot be resolved, so a cumulus parameterization scheme statistically estimates how much heat, moisture, and precipitation a grid cell's worth of unresolved storms would produce. Once grid spacing drops to roughly 4 km or finer, models can begin resolving deep convective updrafts explicitly on the grid itself, so operational configurations built around that threshold — HRRR at 3 km is the standard US example — typically turn the cumulus parameterization off, or nearly off, and let storms form directly from the resolved dynamics; this is the 'convection-allowing' class of model. Grid spacings in between, roughly 5-8 km, sit in the so-called gray zone, where convection is partially resolved and partially parameterized, and neither approach works cleanly — a known source of unreliable storm-mode forecasts. Because every parameterization scheme is a physics-based approximation tuned against past cases, each introduces systematic bias: a convection scheme may consistently trigger storms too early in the diurnal cycle, a boundary-layer scheme may mix too much or too little heat near the surface, and these known biases are exactly what forecasters correct for when they've learned a particular model's tendencies.

lessons.workedExample: Consider two models forecasting a summer afternoon in Kansas: GFS at 13 km relies on a cumulus scheme that estimates a broad area of scattered showers by early afternoon, smearing rainfall across many grid cells because it cannot place an individual storm. HRRR at 3 km, running convection-allowing, instead produces discrete, intense supercell tracks with sharp precipitation gradients, because the storm's updraft is large enough relative to the grid to be resolved directly rather than estimated statistically. The two models are not disagreeing about the atmosphere — they are answering different questions at different scales, and a forecaster who only checked GFS would miss the storm-mode detail entirely.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask 'how did your model handle processes smaller than its grid?' to check whether a student understands that a model output is never raw physics — it is physics plus approximation, and the approximation has known failure modes. A weak answer treats the model as a black box that 'just knows' the weather. A strong answer names a specific parameterized process (convection, boundary-layer mixing, radiation), explains why it had to be approximated rather than resolved, and — ideally — names a known bias that scheme introduces, showing the student read past the forecast plot to the physics underneath it.

questions.prompt: Why must a global model with 13 km grid spacing parameterize convection rather than resolve it directly?

options.text: Convection only occurs in models run for North America
Individual thunderstorm updrafts are far smaller than 13 km, so the grid cannot represent them directly
Parameterization schemes are more accurate than resolving convection explicitly
Global models do not track moisture

explanations.a: Convection is a global atmospheric process; the constraint is grid spacing, not geography.
explanations.b: Correct — an updraft is typically a few kilometers wide at most, well below what a 13 km grid can resolve, so its net effect must be estimated rather than simulated directly.
explanations.c: Parameterized convection is a necessary approximation at coarse resolution, not a superior method; convection-allowing models at finer resolution are generally considered more realistic for storm-scale detail.
explanations.d: Global models carry moisture as a core prognostic variable; that is unrelated to why convection needs parameterizing.

questions.prompt: What roughly defines the 'gray zone' of grid spacing for convection?

options.text: Below 1 km, where even turbulence is fully resolved
Above 25 km, where only global models operate
Roughly 5-8 km, where convection is partially resolved and partially parameterized
Exactly 3 km, the HRRR operational spacing

explanations.a: Sub-kilometer spacing is finer than the gray zone and finer than any operational forecast model discussed here; it is not the gray zone itself.
explanations.b: Coarser global spacings parameterize convection cleanly rather than sitting in the ambiguous gray zone.
explanations.c: Correct — in roughly the 5-8 km range, storm updrafts are large enough to partially show up on the grid but too small to be fully resolved, so neither a full parameterization nor an explicit simulation works cleanly.
explanations.d: 3 km, like HRRR, is fine enough to be considered convection-allowing, generally below the gray zone rather than inside it.

questions.prompt: Match each sub-grid process to the parameterization scheme category that represents it.

left.text: Solar heating of a cloud layer
Turbulent mixing in the lowest kilometer
Moisture exchange with soil and vegetation

right.text: Radiation scheme
Boundary-layer scheme
Land-surface scheme
Cumulus convection scheme

questions.explanation: Each sub-grid process is handled by its own dedicated parameterization category: radiation for heating/cooling by solar and infrared exchange, boundary-layer schemes for near-surface turbulence, land-surface schemes for soil and vegetation exchange, and cumulus schemes for unresolved convection.

questions.prompt: Order these grid spacings from most reliant on parameterized convection to least (fully convection-allowing).

items.text: ~13 km (GFS)
~9 km (ECMWF IFS)
~5-8 km (gray zone)
~3 km (HRRR)

questions.explanation: Coarser global spacings (13 km, 9 km) rely fully on a cumulus scheme; the gray zone partially resolves storms while still parameterizing part of the process; 3 km HRRR is fine enough to resolve storm updrafts directly with the cumulus scheme largely switched off.

lessons.label: Data Assimilation

sections.heading: Blending a forecast with reality
sections.body: Every forecast run needs a starting point — the 'analysis' — but observations alone cannot supply one: weather stations, radiosondes, aircraft, ships, and satellites are scattered unevenly across the globe and never cover every grid point at the exact analysis time. Data assimilation solves this by combining a short-range forecast from the previous cycle (the 'background' or 'first guess,' typically a 6-hour forecast) with all observations that arrived since, weighting each source by its estimated error. The result is the analysis: a physically consistent, gridded best estimate of the atmosphere's true state at that instant, better than either the background alone or the raw observations alone because it exploits the fact that the atmosphere obeys physical laws between observation points. Operational centers repeat this cycle roughly every 6 hours around the clock — background forecast, ingest observations, produce analysis, launch a new forecast that becomes the next cycle's background — so the model is perpetually being nudged back toward reality rather than drifting freely for days.

sections.heading: Two families of method
sections.body: Variational methods (3D-Var and 4D-Var) treat the analysis as an optimization problem: find the atmospheric state that minimizes a cost function balancing closeness to the background against closeness to the observations, weighted by each source's estimated error covariance. 4D-Var extends this over a time window rather than a single instant, using the model's own dynamics to relate observations taken at different times within that window to a single consistent state — ECMWF was an early adopter of operational 4D-Var, implementing it in 1997. Ensemble Kalman filtering (EnKF), developed from Evensen's work in the 1990s, takes a different approach: it runs a small ensemble of forecasts, uses the actual spread across that ensemble to estimate the background error covariance instead of prescribing it, and updates each ensemble member toward the observations accordingly. NOAA's operational system today is a hybrid, blending 4D-Var/EnVar with ensemble-derived background error information to get benefits of both. In every method, the leverage comes from the same place: better and denser observations — especially from satellites, which supply the vast majority of assimilated data over data-sparse oceans — narrow the gap between background and truth, which is why satellite outages or added instrument types measurably change forecast skill in verification studies.

lessons.workedExample: At 00 UTC, a center's 6-hour-old background forecast (valid from the 18 UTC cycle) is compared against the flood of observations that arrived in that window: thousands of aircraft reports, a new swath of satellite radiance data, buoy and ship reports, and the scheduled radiosonde balloon launches from around the globe. The assimilation system does not simply overwrite the background with the nearest observation; instead it weights a radiosonde profile heavily near its location (radiosondes are direct, accurate soundings) while treating a single noisy satellite radiance retrieval more cautiously, and lets the model physics propagate the correction consistently through the surrounding grid. The output — the 00 UTC analysis — becomes the initial condition the model steps forward from, and it also becomes tonight's background for the 06 UTC cycle.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes data assimilation because it exposes whether a student understands where a forecast's starting point actually comes from — many students assume a model just reads off 'the current weather,' when in fact the initial condition is itself a computed estimate with its own uncertainty. A weak answer says the model 'uses observations' with no sense of how they're combined with a prior forecast. A strong answer explains that the analysis blends a short-range background with observations weighted by error, names the roughly 6-hour cycle, and can say why more or better observations (a new satellite instrument, a denser radiosonde network) directly improves the resulting forecast rather than just 'seeming like it should help.'

questions.prompt: Why can't a model simply be initialized from raw observations alone, without a background forecast?

options.text: Observations are always less accurate than any model forecast
Observations are scattered unevenly and never cover every grid point, so a physically consistent full-grid state must be constructed
Regulations require every forecast to start from a prior model run
Observations only exist over land, never over oceans

explanations.a: Observations are often more accurate than the background at their exact location; the issue is coverage and consistency, not accuracy.
explanations.b: Correct — because station, aircraft, and satellite data don't densely cover every grid point, a background forecast fills the gaps and the physics ties everything into one consistent 3D state.
explanations.c: There's no regulatory reason; it's a physical and statistical necessity given uneven observation coverage.
explanations.d: Satellites in particular provide extensive coverage over oceans; the coverage problem is about density and timing, not a total absence over water.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of one data assimilation cycle.

items.text: A short-range background forecast is produced from the previous cycle
New observations arriving in the cycle window are collected
Background and observations are blended, weighted by estimated error, into an analysis
A new forecast is launched from the analysis, becoming the next cycle's background

questions.explanation: Assimilation is a repeating loop: yesterday's short forecast is the background, fresh observations arrive, the two are combined into the analysis, and that analysis both drives the public forecast and seeds the next cycle's background.

questions.prompt: Match each data assimilation approach to its defining idea.
