explanations.d: Clouds substantially reduce net longwave loss compared to clear skies, weakening the inversion even if wind is calm.

lessons.label: Sublayers of the Boundary Layer

sections.heading: From millimeters to the free atmosphere
sections.body: The ABL is not uniform top to bottom; it stacks distinct sublayers with very different physics. Right at a solid or vegetated surface sits a laminar (viscous) sublayer only millimeters thick, where molecular diffusion rather than turbulence dominates heat and momentum transfer — thin enough that it is usually ignored except in detailed surface-exchange work. Just above it, over a rough surface like a crop canopy or a city, is the roughness sublayer, extending a few times the height of the roughness elements themselves (treetops, buildings), where individual wakes and eddies from those obstacles have not yet blended into a statistically uniform flow. Only above the roughness sublayer does the air behave as a horizontally homogeneous turbulent flow that classical similarity theory can describe.

sections.heading: The surface layer: where fluxes are (nearly) constant
sections.body: Above the roughness sublayer sits the surface layer, conventionally taken as roughly the lowest 10% of the ABL's total depth — a few tens of meters at night, up to 100-200 m on a deep convective afternoon. Its defining feature is that turbulent fluxes of momentum, heat, and moisture are approximately constant with height, varying by only about 10% across the layer, which is what makes Monin-Obukhov similarity theory (developed by Monin and Obukhov in 1954) tractable: a single set of surface fluxes and one length scale can describe wind and temperature profiles throughout the layer. This constant-flux assumption is why most flux towers are deliberately installed within the surface layer — a measurement there is treated as representative of the surface exchange itself, not of turbulence that has already changed with height.

sections.heading: The Ekman layer and the mixed layer above
sections.body: Above the surface layer, the wind is no longer governed by surface friction alone; both the pressure-gradient force and Coriolis force come into balance with friction, producing the Ekman layer, named for Vagn Walfrid Ekman, who derived the analogous solution for wind-driven ocean currents in 1905. In this layer wind speed increases and its direction rotates toward the geostrophic wind with height — the classic 'Ekman spiral' — because friction is weaker aloft and the Coriolis force can turn the flow more freely. In a deep daytime convective boundary layer, strong buoyant mixing largely erodes this spiral structure and homogenizes wind, temperature, and moisture through the bulk of the layer — the mixed layer proper — so that fluxes there are no longer constant with height but instead decrease roughly linearly from a maximum near the surface to a minimum (often slightly negative) at the entrainment zone.

lessons.workedExample: A 100 m tower with sensors at 2 m, 10 m, and 80 m measures momentum flux (as friction velocity squared) of 0.09, 0.085, and 0.045 m^2/s^2 respectively on a windy but non-convective morning when the ABL is about 300 m deep. The 2 m and 10 m values differ by under 10%, consistent with both being inside the roughly 30 m surface layer (10% of 300 m) where flux-constancy should hold; the 80 m value has dropped by half, showing it sits well above the surface layer, inside the Ekman-influenced layer where the flux is no longer conserved with height and wind direction has also backed several degrees from the 10 m reading.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'where exactly did you put your sensor, and why there?' to check whether a student understands that the ABL's sublayers have different physics — a flux tower placed above the surface layer is not measuring what the student thinks it is. A weak answer treats 'the boundary layer' as one uniform slab. A strong answer can place their instrument height relative to the roughly-10%-of-ABL-depth surface layer and explain why that placement does or does not justify assuming constant flux with height.

questions.prompt: Order these sublayers from the ground surface upward.

items.text: Laminar (viscous) sublayer
Roughness sublayer
Surface layer (constant-flux layer)
Ekman layer / mixed layer above the surface layer

questions.explanation: Moving upward from a surface: a millimeter-scale laminar sublayer, then the roughness sublayer shaped by individual obstacle wakes, then the surface layer where fluxes are nearly constant, then the Ekman-influenced layer (or well-mixed layer in convective conditions) above.

questions.prompt: Roughly what fraction of total ABL depth does the surface layer occupy?

options.text: About 50%
About 10%
Essentially the entire ABL
A fixed 500 m regardless of ABL depth

explanations.a: 50% would put it well into the Ekman/mixed layer, where fluxes are no longer approximately constant with height.
explanations.b: Correct — the surface layer is conventionally the lowest ~10% of the ABL, ranging from a few tens of meters at night to roughly 100-200 m on a deep convective afternoon.
explanations.c: The surface layer is only the lowest portion; the Ekman/mixed layer above it makes up the bulk of ABL depth.
explanations.d: The surface layer scales with total ABL depth (about 10% of it), not a fixed absolute height.

questions.prompt: What physically causes the Ekman spiral (wind speed and direction changing with height) above the surface layer?

options.text: Surface friction weakens with height while the Coriolis and pressure-gradient forces remain, letting the wind vector rotate toward geostrophic balance
Air temperature reverses sign at that height
The roughness sublayer directly forces the spiral through obstacle wakes
Water vapor condensation drives the spiral

explanations.a: Correct — as frictional drag diminishes with height, the balance among pressure-gradient, Coriolis, and friction forces shifts, rotating and strengthening the wind toward the geostrophic value, per Ekman's (1905) classic solution.
explanations.b: Temperature sign has no direct bearing on the force balance that produces the spiral.
explanations.c: Roughness-sublayer wakes are confined to just above the surface, well below where the Ekman spiral develops.
explanations.d: Condensation is unrelated to the force-balance mechanism that produces the Ekman spiral.

lessons.label: The Convective Boundary Layer in Depth

sections.heading: Thermals, plumes, and a velocity scale for buoyancy
sections.body: The convective boundary layer (CBL) is organized by discrete thermals — narrow, fast-rising plumes of buoyant air born in the superadiabatic surface layer — that broaden and slow as they ascend, surrounded by broader, gentler areas of compensating sinking air. Because the driving force is buoyancy rather than mean wind shear, James Deardorff proposed in 1970 a convective velocity scale, w*, built from the surface buoyancy flux and the mixed-layer depth zi (specifically w* is proportional to the cube root of g/theta times the surface heat flux times zi), which typically comes out to 1-2 m/s for a strongly heated afternoon boundary layer. w* turned out to be the right scaling for turbulence statistics throughout the CBL, replacing the friction-velocity scaling that works for the shear-dominated surface layer, and it remains the standard convective scale used in ABL research and large-eddy simulation.

sections.heading: Top-down and bottom-up mixing
sections.body: Because both the surface (heating) and the entrainment zone (mixing warm free-air down) inject buoyancy into the CBL, turbulent mixing operates from two directions at once — bottom-up mixing driven by surface thermals and top-down mixing driven by parcels sinking after being cooled at the entrainment interface. This dual forcing is why the CBL's mean profiles of potential temperature and moisture end up so flat through the bulk of the layer: rather than a smooth gradient from surface value to free-atmosphere value, theta and humidity are nearly uniform through most of the depth, with essentially all the change concentrated in the thin surface layer at the bottom and the entrainment zone at the top. Deardorff's large-eddy simulations in the 1970s were instrumental in first resolving this top-down/bottom-up structure explicitly, since it is difficult to infer from single-point tower measurements alone.

sections.heading: Penetrative convection and the 20% entrainment rule
sections.body: The strongest thermals do not stop precisely at the mixed-layer top; they overshoot briefly into the stable capping inversion, a behavior called penetrative convection, before sinking back and mixing a parcel of warm inversion air down into the CBL. This process is quantified by the entrainment flux ratio: the ratio of the (negative) heat flux at the CBL top to the (positive) surface heat flux. Deardorff's (1970s) simulations and later observational studies converged on a canonical value near -0.2, meaning roughly 20% of the energy the surface pumps into the CBL as heat flux is effectively spent entraining warm air downward at the top rather than warming the layer directly — a surprisingly large 'overhead cost' that must be included in any simple mixed-layer growth model, or the predicted growth rate comes out too fast.

lessons.workedExample: A CBL has a surface sensible heat flux of 300 W/m^2, a depth zi of 1200 m, and a surface air density near 1.1 kg/m^3 with theta near 300 K. Plugging into w* proportional to [(g/theta) x (H/(rho x cp)) x zi]^(1/3) gives a convective velocity scale of roughly 2 m/s — consistent with the gusty, thermal-driven feel of a hot summer afternoon rather than a steady breeze. If the entrainment heat flux at the CBL top is measured (or assumed via the 20% rule) at about -60 W/m^2, that is 20% of the 300 W/m^2 surface flux, exactly the canonical entrainment ratio, and a mixed-layer growth model that ignores this loss would overpredict how fast zi grows through the afternoon.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about CBL structure to see if a student can move past 'warm air rises' into quantitative territory: naming w* as the relevant velocity scale (not the mean wind speed), and knowing that the CBL's flat theta profile is a two-sided phenomenon (bottom-up plus top-down mixing), not just thermals rising from the ground. Citing the roughly 20% entrainment ratio as a real, named number — rather than treating entrainment as a minor detail — is the clearest signal of depth on this topic.

questions.prompt: Why is the convective velocity scale w* used instead of mean wind speed to characterize turbulence in the CBL?

options.text: CBL turbulence is primarily buoyancy-driven, and w* is built from the surface heat flux and mixed-layer depth to capture that buoyant forcing directly
Wind speed cannot be measured in convective conditions
w* and mean wind speed are always numerically identical
w* only applies to the stable boundary layer, not the CBL

explanations.a: Correct — Deardorff (1970) introduced w* specifically because shear/wind-based scaling (appropriate for the surface layer) fails to organize CBL turbulence, which is dominated by buoyancy.
explanations.b: Wind speed is routinely measured in convective conditions; the issue is that it is not the right scaling variable for buoyancy-driven turbulence.
explanations.c: w* and mean wind speed are physically different quantities and are not generally equal.
explanations.d: w* is specifically a convective (unstable, buoyancy-driven) boundary-layer scale; the stable layer uses different scaling (e.g., friction velocity).

questions.prompt: According to the canonical entrainment flux ratio, roughly what fraction of the surface heat flux is consumed by entrainment at the top of the CBL?

options.text: About 2%
About 20%
About 80%
Essentially 0%

explanations.a: 2% is far too small; observations and Deardorff-era simulations converge on a much larger canonical ratio.
explanations.b: Correct — the entrainment heat flux at the CBL top is canonically about -0.2 times the surface heat flux, i.e., roughly 20%.
explanations.c: 80% would mean entrainment consumes most of the surface energy input, far above the well-established canonical value.
explanations.d: Entrainment is not negligible; ignoring it causes mixed-layer growth models to overpredict how fast the CBL deepens.

questions.prompt: Match each CBL mixing process to its driving location.

right.text: Surface thermals rising from the heated ground
Parcels cooled at the entrainment interface sinking back down
Strong thermals briefly overshooting into the capping inversion before sinking back

questions.explanation: Bottom-up mixing originates at the heated surface; top-down mixing originates at the entrainment zone where cooled parcels sink; penetrative convection is the specific overshoot-and-sink behavior of the strongest thermals at the CBL top.

lessons.label: The Stable Boundary Layer and the Nocturnal Jet

sections.heading: Cooling from the ground up, turbulence in retreat
sections.body: After sunset, the surface radiates longwave energy to space faster than it receives any, and that cooling propagates upward mainly by weak turbulent mixing and, secondarily, by radiative divergence within the air itself, building a stable boundary layer (SBL) that grows only tens to a couple hundred meters deep. Unlike the CBL, turbulence in the SBL is not continuous: buoyancy actively suppresses vertical motion, so the layer often becomes intermittent — bursts of turbulence separated by minutes of near-calm, frequently triggered by passing gravity waves, wind shear instabilities, or a breeze strengthening enough to briefly overcome the stratification. This intermittency makes the SBL notoriously hard to represent in weather and climate models, since standard flux-gradient turbulence closures (built for continuous mixing) tend to either over- or under-mix a layer that is, physically, mixing in fits and starts.

sections.heading: Decoupling and the residual layer above
sections.body: As the SBL deepens through the night, the surface can effectively decouple from the residual layer sitting above it — the well-mixed leftover of the previous day's CBL — because the intervening stable air transmits so little turbulent momentum and heat. Once decoupled, surface friction can no longer efficiently brake the air just above the SBL, and that air is free to respond to the Coriolis force largely unopposed, setting up the conditions for one of the SBL's most striking features.

sections.heading: The Blackadar mechanism and the nocturnal low-level jet
sections.body: Alfred Blackadar explained this feature in 1957: during the day, friction keeps the wind sub-geostrophic and roughly aligned with the pressure-gradient force. At sunset, as the SBL forms and decouples the air above it from surface drag, that friction term effectively vanishes almost immediately, but the wind at that instant is still sub-geostrophic — so the force balance is suddenly unbalanced, and the ageostrophic wind component begins an inertial oscillation, rotating clockwise (in the Northern Hemisphere) around the geostrophic wind vector with a period of 2*pi/f, where f is the Coriolis parameter (about 17 hours at mid-latitudes, shorter toward the poles). Roughly a quarter-period into this oscillation, the ageostrophic component adds constructively to the geostrophic wind, producing a wind speed maximum that can exceed the geostrophic wind itself — the nocturnal low-level jet, typically found a few hundred meters above the ground, just above the shallow SBL, with speeds sometimes 10-20 m/s. Its diurnal on/off switching, its dependence on gravity-wave activity, and the difficulty of resolving intermittent turbulence together make the SBL widely regarded as the least understood of the ABL's major regimes.

lessons.workedExample: At a Great Plains tower, the geostrophic wind is estimated at 12 m/s from due west. At 5 p.m., friction has the actual 10 m wind at about 8 m/s, sub-geostrophic and turned slightly south of the geostrophic direction, as expected under daytime mixing. By sunset the SBL has formed and decoupled the layer above from surface drag; over the next several hours the ageostrophic wind vector rotates clockwise, and around 11 p.m. — a bit over a quarter of the roughly 17-hour inertial period at that latitude — a profiler shows a wind speed maximum near 18 m/s at 200 m, well above the 12 m/s geostrophic value, then decaying back toward geostrophic by early morning as the SBL breaks down and friction reasserts itself.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe the nocturnal jet because it is a clean test of whether a student understands force balance, not just pattern-matching 'wind is stronger at night.' A weak answer says the jet is caused by 'cooling' with no mechanism. A strong answer names the Blackadar (1957) inertial-oscillation mechanism specifically: friction suddenly removed at sunset leaves a sub-geostrophic wind that overshoots as it oscillates back toward balance, and can state that the oscillation period depends on the Coriolis parameter (hence latitude).

questions.prompt: In the Blackadar mechanism, what triggers the inertial oscillation that produces the nocturnal low-level jet?

options.text: The near-sudden loss of surface frictional drag at sunset while the wind is still sub-geostrophic, leaving the force balance suddenly unbalanced
A sudden increase in the geostrophic wind itself at sunset
Direct heating of the air at jet height by residual daytime convection
A drop in atmospheric pressure at the surface each evening

explanations.a: Correct — as the SBL decouples the air above it from surface friction near sunset, the sub-geostrophic wind at that moment is left unbalanced, launching the ageostrophic inertial oscillation Blackadar (1957) described.
explanations.b: The geostrophic wind, set by the large-scale pressure pattern, does not itself jump at sunset; it is the friction term that changes abruptly.
explanations.c: Jet-height air is above the shallow SBL and is not being actively heated by convection at night; the mechanism is inertial, not thermal.
explanations.d: Diurnal surface pressure changes are far too small and are not the driver identified in the Blackadar mechanism.

questions.prompt: Why is the stable boundary layer considered the least understood of the major ABL regimes?

options.text: Its turbulence is often intermittent, driven by gravity waves and shear bursts rather than continuous mixing, which standard closures struggle to represent
It has never been measured directly by instruments
It is always exactly the same depth every night, making it uninteresting to study
It does not involve turbulence at all

explanations.a: Correct — SBL turbulence is patchy and event-driven (gravity waves, shear instabilities) rather than continuous, which is exactly what makes standard flux-gradient turbulence closures perform poorly there.
explanations.b: The SBL is routinely measured with towers, profilers, and sodars; the difficulty is theoretical/modeling, not observational access.
explanations.c: SBL depth varies night to night with wind, cloud cover, and terrain; it is not a fixed value.
explanations.d: The SBL does involve turbulence — just weak, intermittent turbulence rather than the continuous mixing of the CBL.

questions.prompt: Order these stages of a clear-night SBL and nocturnal jet cycle.

items.text: Daytime: friction keeps wind sub-geostrophic and roughly aligned with the pressure-gradient force
Sunset: SBL forms, decoupling the air above it from surface friction
Ageostrophic wind begins an inertial oscillation around the geostrophic vector
About a quarter-period later, ageostrophic and geostrophic components add constructively, producing the jet maximum
Morning: SBL breaks down, friction reasserts, wind decays back toward the daytime sub-geostrophic state

questions.explanation: The cycle runs from daytime frictional (sub-geostrophic) balance, through the sunset loss of friction that triggers the inertial oscillation, to the quarter-period jet maximum, and back to daytime conditions after sunrise breaks up the SBL.

units.label: The Surface Energy Balance

lessons.label: The Surface Energy Budget Equation

sections.heading: A skin with no memory
sections.body: The surface energy balance treats the ground-air interface as an infinitesimally thin skin with negligible heat capacity of its own: whatever radiative energy arrives must be disposed of instantaneously through other pathways, because the skin cannot store it. That bookkeeping is written Rn = H + LE + G, where Rn is net radiation, H is sensible heat flux, LE is latent heat flux, and G is ground (soil) heat flux. All four terms carry units of W/m2, and the equation is really just conservation of energy applied to a control volume with essentially zero thickness. It is the master equation of micrometeorology: everything about how a rye field, a parking lot, or a lake surface heats the air and dries out traces back to how it partitions this budget. Boundary-layer texts such as Oke's Boundary Layer Climates and Stull's An Introduction to Boundary Layer Meteorology build entire chapters around the three ways Rn can be spent.

sections.heading: Sign convention and typical magnitudes
sections.body: The standard convention defines Rn as positive when it delivers energy to the surface, and H, LE, G as positive when they carry energy away from the surface. Under clear midsummer skies near local noon at midlatitudes, Rn commonly reaches 400-600 W/m2 over a well-illuminated, unshaded surface, and that energy is shared out: over moist vegetation LE typically claims the largest share, over dry bare soil H dominates, and G usually takes the smallest bite, on the order of 10-30% of Rn. At night Rn flips negative, typically -50 to -100 W/m2, as the surface radiates more longwave energy than it receives back from the cooler sky. The three consuming terms flip sign in step: G reverses to release stored daytime heat back toward the surface, H commonly reverses to carry warmth downward from air aloft, and LE often drops near zero or reverses as dew forms, releasing latent heat to the cooling surface. This day-night flip is why the ground is warmest in the mid-afternoon, not at solar noon: G keeps charging the subsurface reservoir for a couple of hours after Rn peaks.

sections.heading: The equation rarely balances perfectly in the field
sections.body: In practice, when researchers sum measured H, LE, and G and compare that sum to independently measured Rn, the two sides usually do not match exactly. A widely cited synthesis by Wilson and colleagues (2002), pooling data from FLUXNET towers across dozens of sites, found the measured sum of turbulent and ground fluxes typically fell short of measured Rn by roughly 10-30% on average -- a persistent gap known as the energy balance closure problem. Leading explanations include unmeasured heat storage in the air and canopy between the surface and the sensor height, mesoscale advection carrying energy laterally out of the measurement footprint, and systematic differences in the spatial scales sampled by radiometers versus eddy-covariance instruments. The closure problem is a live research topic, not a solved footnote, which is exactly why a residual in a student's own data is expected, not necessarily a sign of a bad experiment.

lessons.workedExample: A bare desert plot at local noon in July measures Rn = 550 W/m2. Field instruments show H = 400 W/m2 and G = 100 W/m2, both losses from the skin. Because energy must balance, LE = Rn - H - G = 550 - 400 - 100 = 50 W/m2 -- almost all of the net radiation is going into heating the air (H) rather than evaporating water, consistent with a dry surface that has little moisture left to evaporate. Two hours after sunset, Rn has become -80 W/m2 (net loss to space); with LE near zero and H now weakly downward at -10 W/m2, the ground must be releasing G = -70 W/m2 from the day's stored heat to balance the nighttime radiative loss.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'where did the energy go?' to see whether a student treats radiation, convection, and conduction as one accountable system rather than three unrelated measurements. A weak answer reports Rn, H, LE, and G as separate numbers with no check that they close the budget. A strong answer explicitly sums the three sink terms, compares that sum to measured Rn, and interprets the residual (instrument error, storage in vegetation, or an unmeasured advection term) rather than ignoring it -- because real field data on this unit's scale essentially never balances exactly, and knowing why is what separates a data collector from a scientist.

questions.prompt: In the surface energy balance Rn = H + LE + G, why is the surface treated as having zero heat capacity?

options.text: Because real surfaces genuinely cannot absorb any heat
It is a modeling simplification so that all incoming radiative energy must instantaneously appear in the other three fluxes, with none stored in the skin itself
Because G already accounts for all subsurface heat storage, so the surface layer is redundant
Because Rn is always zero at the exact surface

explanations.a: Real surfaces do store heat -- it is the underlying soil/water/vegetation that stores it, which is exactly why G exists as a term.
explanations.b: Correct -- the 'skin' is a mathematical idealization of zero thickness so the balance equation has no storage term of its own; all storage is pushed into G below the skin.
explanations.c: G represents flux into the substrate below the skin, not storage within the zero-thickness skin itself, so it doesn't make the skin assumption redundant.
explanations.d: Rn is generally nonzero at the surface during the day and at night; it is not defined to be zero.

questions.prompt: At 2 AM under clear skies, Rn = -70 W/m2 and LE is approximately 0. If H = -15 W/m2 (downward), what is G?

options.text: G cannot be determined without more data

explanations.a: Correct -- rearranging Rn = H + LE + G gives G = Rn - H - LE = -70 - (-15) - 0 = -55 W/m2, meaning heat is flowing up out of the ground to help balance the radiative loss.
explanations.b: This has the wrong sign; solving the balance equation correctly gives a negative value, since the ground must be releasing stored heat, not absorbing it, at night.
explanations.c: This adds H instead of subtracting it; the balance equation requires G = Rn - H - LE.
explanations.d: The balance equation has exactly the information needed -- three of the four terms are given, so the fourth is fully determined.

questions.prompt: Order these events across a clear 24-hour cycle, from the one that occurs first.

items.text: Rn crosses zero and turns negative near sunset
Rn peaks near solar noon
Ground temperature peaks in the mid-afternoon (after Rn has already started declining)
G reverses to release stored heat back toward the surface overnight

questions.explanation: Rn peaks near solar noon; the ground keeps warming afterward as G continues charging the subsurface, so surface temperature peaks a couple of hours later in mid-afternoon; Rn then crosses zero near sunset as radiative loss overtakes absorption; only after nightfall does G reverse to release the day's stored heat.

questions.prompt: Match each term in Rn = H + LE + G to what it physically represents.

right.text: Net radiative energy exchanged at the surface
Turbulent transport of heat into or out of the air
Energy consumed or released by evaporation/condensation
Conductive flux into or out of the soil/substrate

questions.explanation: Rn is the net radiative surplus or deficit; H is sensible (turbulent, temperature-driven) heat exchange with the air; LE is latent heat tied to phase change of water; G is conduction into or out of the ground.

lessons.label: Net Radiation: The Four-Component Budget

sections.heading: Splitting Rn into shortwave and longwave
sections.body: Rn is not one measurement but the sum of four: Rn = (K-down minus K-up) + (L-down minus L-up). K-down is incoming shortwave (solar) radiation, K-up is the portion the surface reflects, L-down is longwave radiation emitted downward by the atmosphere itself -- water vapor, CO2, and clouds all radiate in the infrared -- and L-up is longwave emitted upward by the surface. The shortwave pair only exists during daylight; the longwave pair operates continuously, day and night, which is exactly why Rn does not simply switch off at sunset but instead goes negative as L-up keeps draining energy with no K-down to offset it.

sections.heading: Albedo sets K-up
sections.body: The ratio K-up / K-down is albedo, and it is almost entirely a surface-property question, not an atmospheric one. Fresh snow reflects 0.8-0.9 of incoming shortwave, grass and most green vegetation sit around 0.20-0.25, dark forest canopy can run as low as 0.08-0.15, and dry desert sand is intermediate at roughly 0.35-0.45. Water is the outlier: at high solar elevation angle its albedo is very low, often under 0.10, because most shortwave refracts into the water column rather than reflecting -- but at low sun angles near sunrise and sunset, specular reflection off the surface pushes water's albedo sharply higher. This is why a snow-covered field and a nearby lake, receiving identical K-down, can differ by hundreds of W/m2 in Rn: the albedo term alone dominates the daytime shortwave budget.

sections.heading: Longwave: Stefan-Boltzmann and the sky's effective temperature
sections.body: L-up is governed by the Stefan-Boltzmann law, L-up = epsilon * sigma * T^4, where sigma = 5.67 x 10^-8 W/(m2 K4) and emissivity epsilon is close to 1 (0.95-0.99) for most natural surfaces. Because T is raised to the fourth power, a surface just a few degrees warmer emits substantially more longwave -- a 300 K surface (27C) emits roughly 460 W/m2, while a 290 K surface (17C) emits about 400 W/m2. L-down depends on the emitting layer of the atmosphere, which under clear skies behaves like a much colder radiator (an effective sky temperature well below surface temperature) because the dominant emitters, water vapor near the surface layer, are relatively dilute; clouds, by contrast, act as near-blackbody emitters at cloud-base temperature and substantially raise L-down, which is the physical reason clear nights cool off far more than overcast ones. Under clear skies, L-down is often modeled directly from surface air temperature and humidity using empirical fits such as the Brutsaert (1975) clear-sky formula, since routinely measuring the full vertical profile of atmospheric emitters is impractical outside of research field campaigns.

lessons.workedExample: At solar noon in summer, a grass field receives K-down = 850 W/m2. With albedo 0.23, K-up = 0.23 x 850 = 195.5 W/m2, so net shortwave is 654.5 W/m2. The grass surface sits at 303 K and emits L-up = 0.97 x 5.67e-8 x 303^4 = 464 W/m2. Under a clear sky, L-down is measured at 340 W/m2, so net longwave is 340 - 464 = -124 W/m2. Total Rn = 654.5 - 124 = 530.5 W/m2, squarely in the expected midday range. Swap the grass for fresh snow at the same K-down: K-up jumps to 0.85 x 850 = 722.5 W/m2, so net shortwave collapses to 127.5 W/m2. The snow surface, held near freezing at 273 K, emits L-up = 0.99 x 5.67e-8 x 273^4 = 312 W/m2; with L-down still 340 W/m2, net longwave is now positive, 340 - 312 = 28 W/m2, because the cold snow surface emits less than the sky delivers. Total Rn = 127.5 + 28 = 155.5 W/m2 -- just under a third of the grass value, not a tenth, since the shortwave term alone (127.5 W/m2) is already about a quarter of grass's Rn and the flipped-sign longwave term adds further to it. Even so, that is still a large suppression of daytime surface heating relative to grass.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who sees a single 'Rn' number in a research log wants to know whether the student understands that Rn is a difference of differences, not a single sensor reading. A weak answer treats Rn as a black box from a net radiometer. A strong answer can explain why a snow-covered plot and a bare-soil plot under the identical sun show wildly different Rn (albedo), and why Rn does not hit zero the instant the sun sets (L-down and L-up keep operating), and can point to which specific term -- K-up via albedo, or L-up via Stefan-Boltzmann -- explains an observed difference between two experimental surfaces.

questions.prompt: Why does Rn typically stay negative rather than zero on a clear night with no shortwave radiation present?

options.text: Because K-up continues at night from moonlight
Because L-up continues to emit while L-down is comparatively small under clear skies, so the longwave difference is negative
Because Rn is defined to equal G at night
Because albedo becomes negative after sunset

explanations.a: Moonlight's shortwave contribution is negligible compared to the fluxes in this budget; K-up is not the reason.
explanations.b: Correct -- with K-down at zero, only the longwave pair remains active, and under clear skies L-down (from a dilute, relatively cold-acting atmospheric emitter) is smaller than L-up, leaving net longwave, and thus Rn, negative.
explanations.c: Rn and G are independent terms in the surface energy balance; Rn is not defined in terms of G.
explanations.d: Albedo is a ratio of reflected to incoming shortwave and is undefined, not negative, when K-down is zero.

questions.prompt: A lake and a nearby dry lakebed of bare, cracked mud receive identical K-down at midday with the sun high overhead. Which factor best explains why the lake likely has lower K-up?

options.text: Water has a lower albedo than dry soil at high sun angle because shortwave mostly refracts into the water column instead of reflecting
Water absorbs longwave radiation more efficiently
Water has a higher emissivity, which lowers K-up
Lakebeds always have higher albedo than any other natural surface

explanations.a: Correct -- at high solar elevation, water's albedo is typically under 0.10 because most incoming shortwave enters the water column rather than reflecting, while dry soil reflects substantially more.
explanations.b: Longwave absorption is a separate process from shortwave reflection (K-up) and does not directly set K-up.
explanations.c: Emissivity governs longwave emission (L-up), not shortwave reflection (K-up); these are different terms in the budget.
explanations.d: Albedo varies widely across natural surfaces, and dry lakebed sediment does not universally exceed every other surface type -- fresh snow, for instance, is far higher.

questions.prompt: Match each surface type to its approximate typical albedo range described in this lesson.

right.text: under 0.10

questions.explanation: Fresh snow is the most reflective natural surface (0.8-0.9); grass sits in the moderate 0.20-0.25 range; water at high sun angle is unusually absorptive (under 0.10) because shortwave refracts in rather than reflecting; dry desert sand is intermediate at 0.35-0.45.

questions.prompt: Order these steps in computing Rn from raw radiometer measurements.

items.text: Measure K-down and K-up separately (or compute K-up from measured albedo)
Compute net shortwave = K-down minus K-up
Measure or compute L-down and L-up (using Stefan-Boltzmann for L-up)
Sum net shortwave and net longwave to obtain Rn

questions.explanation: The four-component budget requires measuring both shortwave components first to get net shortwave, then both longwave components to get net longwave, and only then summing the two differences to arrive at Rn.

lessons.label: Sensible Heat Flux (H)

sections.heading: Heat carried by turbulent eddies
sections.body: Sensible heat flux is the transport of thermal energy by turbulent motion rather than by conduction or radiation -- it is 'sensible' because it changes air temperature you can sense with a thermometer, as opposed to latent heat, which is locked up in a phase change. The standard eddy-covariance definition is H = rho * cp * mean(w' theta'), where rho is air density (about 1.2 kg/m3 at sea level), cp is the specific heat of air (about 1005 J/(kg K)), w' is the instantaneous deviation of vertical wind speed from its mean, and theta' is the instantaneous deviation of potential temperature from its mean. The overbar denotes a time average, typically 30 minutes, over rapid (10-20 Hz) sonic-anemometer measurements. When upward-moving parcels (w' > 0) tend to be warmer than downward-moving parcels (theta' > 0 correlated with w' > 0), the covariance is positive and H is directed upward, away from the surface. Eddy-covariance flux measurements from field campaigns such as the 1968 Kansas experiment (Businger and colleagues) were used to empirically validate the flux-profile relationships predicted by Monin-Obukhov similarity theory (1954), and the two remain closely linked in surface-layer micrometeorology today.

sections.heading: Why H flips sign at sunset
sections.body: During the day the surface is typically warmer than the air just above it, so parcels heated at the surface rise, carrying heat upward: H is positive, and this upward flux is the principal driver of the convective boundary layer's daytime growth -- the classic 'encroachment' picture in which the mixed layer deepens roughly in proportion to the accumulated surface heat input, formalized in slab (jump) models such as the one developed by Tennekes (1973). After sunset, radiative cooling (L-up exceeding L-down, from the previous lesson) drops surface temperature below that of the air just above it. Turbulence collapses because the near-surface air is now stably stratified -- cold, dense air sitting beneath warmer air resists the overturning that generates eddies -- so H typically becomes small and negative (directed downward), representing weak transport of warmth from the residual layer down toward the cooling surface. This same collapse of turbulence is what allows a shallow, strongly stratified nocturnal boundary layer to form, often only tens to a few hundred meters deep, compared to a daytime convective layer that can grow to 1-2 km. The strength of this nocturnal stability also depends on wind: on calm, clear nights radiative cooling wins outright and H stays negative and small in magnitude, but on windy nights mechanically generated turbulence can partly override the stable stratification, mixing the shallow surface layer more vigorously and keeping downward H somewhat larger than on a calm night with identical radiative cooling.

lessons.workedExample: A sonic anemometer over a corn field logs 20-minute statistics: mean(w' theta') = +0.15 m K/s at 1400 local time. Using rho = 1.2 kg/m3 and cp = 1005 J/(kg K), H = 1.2 x 1005 x 0.15 = 181 W/m2, a solidly positive, upward daytime value consistent with sun-warmed crop canopy heating the air above it. At 0300 the same instrument logs mean(w' theta') = -0.01 m K/s, giving H = 1.2 x 1005 x (-0.01) = -12 W/m2 -- a small downward flux, evidence of the stable nocturnal layer where cooling ground pulls a trickle of warmth down from air aloft rather than releasing heat upward.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes H because it is the flux most students conflate with 'just temperature' rather than understanding it as a covariance between vertical motion and temperature fluctuation. A weak answer says 'H is heat going up because the ground is hot.' A strong answer names the actual covariance quantity being measured, explains why a positive correlation between upward motion and warm air (not simply high air temperature) is what produces H, and can explain the physical mechanism behind the day-to-night sign flip -- convective overturning giving way to stable stratification -- rather than treating it as an arbitrary rule.

questions.prompt: In H = rho * cp * mean(w' theta'), what does a positive value of mean(w' theta') physically indicate?

options.text: The air is generally warmer than the ground
Upward-moving air parcels tend to be warmer than downward-moving parcels, so turbulence is net transporting heat upward
Wind speed is increasing over time
The atmosphere is stably stratified

explanations.a: Mean(w' theta') is a covariance between vertical wind and temperature deviations, not a statement about absolute air-vs-ground temperature.
explanations.b: Correct -- a positive covariance means upward-moving parcels (w' > 0) are correlated with positive temperature deviations (theta' > 0), so turbulence is net carrying heat upward.
explanations.c: w' is a deviation from mean vertical wind, not a trend in wind speed magnitude over time.
explanations.d: Stable stratification is associated with suppressed turbulence and typically a negative or near-zero H, the opposite of a strongly positive covariance.

questions.prompt: Why does H typically become small and negative shortly after sunset?

options.text: Because cp changes sign at night
Because the surface cools below the air above it, suppressing convective turbulence and allowing a weak downward transport of warmth
Because rho becomes negative in cold air
Because LE fully replaces H after sunset

explanations.a: Specific heat of air, cp, is a positive physical constant and does not change sign with time of day.
explanations.b: Correct -- radiative cooling makes the surface colder than the air just above it, suppressing the buoyant overturning that generates upward heat transport, leaving a shallow, weak downward flux instead.
explanations.c: Air density rho is always positive; it increases somewhat in cold air but never goes negative.
explanations.d: LE and H are independent terms in the surface energy balance; one does not mechanically replace the other.

questions.prompt: Order these stages of the daily convective boundary layer cycle driven by H.

items.text: Sunrise: surface begins warming faster than the air above it
H becomes strongly positive as convective eddies form
Convective boundary layer deepens through the afternoon
Sunset: surface cools below air temperature, turbulence collapses, H turns weakly negative

questions.explanation: The cycle begins with surface warming at sunrise, which drives convective turbulence and a positive H, which in turn deepens the mixed layer through the day, until sunset reverses the surface-air temperature gradient and collapses turbulence, flipping H negative.

questions.prompt: Match each quantity in the H equation to its typical value or role.

right.text: about 1.2 kg/m3
about 1005 J/(kg K)
the measured turbulent covariance from a sonic anemometer

questions.explanation: rho and cp are near-constant physical properties of air used to convert the covariance into an energy flux, while mean(w' theta') is the actual field-measured turbulence statistic that varies through the day.

lessons.label: Latent Heat Flux and Evapotranspiration (LE)

sections.heading: Two pathways, one flux
sections.body: Latent heat flux, LE, is the rate at which energy is consumed converting liquid water to vapor at the surface -- evapotranspiration, the combination of direct evaporation from soil, open water, and wet leaf surfaces, plus transpiration, water pulled up through plant roots and released as vapor through stomata on leaves. Evaporating water requires energy because breaking hydrogen bonds to free molecules into the vapor phase costs work; that energy is the latent heat of vaporization, Lv, about 2.45 MJ per kilogram of water at typical surface temperatures near 20C (it declines slightly with temperature, from about 2.50 MJ/kg at 0C). LE is simply Lv multiplied by the mass evaporation rate per unit area, so it is the term that directly couples the surface energy balance to the surface water balance: every watt of LE corresponds to a specific, calculable mass of water leaving the surface, and conversely every millimeter of measured evapotranspiration corresponds to a specific energy cost that had to come from Rn.

sections.heading: What controls LE: moisture and resistance, not just energy
sections.body: Available energy is necessary but not sufficient for LE -- a desert receiving 600 W/m2 of Rn cannot sustain large LE if there is no water to evaporate, so the energy is redirected almost entirely to H instead (the low-LE, high-H regime from the previous lesson). The rate is instead governed by two resistances in series: an aerodynamic resistance (how efficiently turbulence removes vapor from just above the surface) and, for vegetation, a surface or stomatal resistance controlling how readily water exits leaf pores. Plants actively regulate this second resistance -- stomata close under water stress or high vapor-pressure deficit to conserve water, which throttles LE even when both energy and soil moisture would otherwise allow more evaporation. John Monteith formalized this coupling in 1965 by extending Howard Penman's 1948 combination equation (originally built for open-water evaporation) into what is now called the Penman-Monteith equation, adding an explicit canopy (stomatal) resistance term; it remains the standard method for estimating crop water use and reference evapotranspiration in agricultural and hydrological science today.

sections.heading: How much of the water cycle actually runs through LE
sections.body: The scale of this flux is easy to underestimate: a global isotope-tracer study by Jasechko and colleagues (2013), analyzing the ratio of heavy to light water isotopes in river, soil, and atmospheric water samples worldwide, estimated that transpiration through plants -- not direct evaporation from soil or open water -- accounts for roughly 80-90% of terrestrial evapotranspiration, making stomatal control the single largest lever on how land surfaces partition their energy budget. That finding reframes LE from a passive physical process into one gated substantially by plant physiology: a cornfield and a bare-soil plot receiving identical rainfall and identical Rn can show very different LE simply because one has leaves regulating the exit of water vapor and the other does not.

lessons.workedExample: A soybean field with well-watered soil is measured with LE = 350 W/m2 sustained over an 8-hour daylight period. Total energy used: 350 W/m2 x 8 x 3600 s = 1.008 x 10^7 J/m2. Dividing by Lv = 2.45 x 10^6 J/kg gives 4.11 kg of water evaporated per square meter, equivalent to about 4.1 mm of water depth lost -- a realistic daily crop evapotranspiration value. Two weeks later, after a dry spell, the same field under identical Rn now shows LE = 120 W/m2 even though soil moisture sensors confirm some water remains in the root zone: the stomata have partially closed under water stress, raising surface resistance and throttling transpiration well below what available energy alone would allow, with the difference in energy now showing up as elevated H instead.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about LE to test whether a student understands that evapotranspiration is resistance-limited, not just energy-limited -- a common naive assumption is 'more sun means more evaporation.' A weak answer stops at 'LE is evaporation using up energy.' A strong answer can explain why a well-watered field and a drought-stressed field under identical Rn produce very different LE, name the two resistances (aerodynamic and stomatal/surface) that govern the rate, and connect LE quantitatively to a real mass of water lost, showing the energy-balance and water-balance sides of the same measurement are the same number in different units.

questions.prompt: A dry, unvegetated desert surface receives Rn = 600 W/m2. Why does LE stay low regardless of this large available energy?

options.text: Because Lv is much higher for dry surfaces
Because there is little to no water available to evaporate, so the energy balance redirects the available energy mainly into H instead
Because desert air has no turbulence at all
Because Rn cannot power LE, only G

explanations.a: Lv, the latent heat of vaporization, is a near-constant property of water and does not change meaningfully based on the dryness of the surface it sits on.
explanations.b: Correct -- LE requires available water to evaporate; without it, energy that could have gone to LE is instead expressed as sensible heat, H, which is exactly the low-LE, high-H regime typical of deserts.
explanations.c: Desert surfaces still generate turbulence, often strong turbulence given large H and steep near-surface temperature gradients; lack of turbulence is not the limiting factor here.
explanations.d: Rn is the shared energy source available to both H and LE (and G); it is not restricted to powering only G.

questions.prompt: Which two resistances does the Penman-Monteith equation combine to determine actual LE from a vegetated surface?

options.text: Aerodynamic resistance and stomatal (surface) resistance
Albedo resistance and Bowen resistance
Radiative resistance and conductive resistance
Thermal resistance and gravitational resistance

explanations.a: Correct -- Monteith's 1965 extension of Penman's equation adds a stomatal (surface) resistance term to the existing aerodynamic resistance term, capturing both how efficiently turbulence removes vapor and how readily plants release it.
explanations.b: Albedo and Bowen ratio are not resistance terms; they belong to the radiation budget and the H/LE partitioning discussion respectively, not the Penman-Monteith formulation.
explanations.c: Neither 'radiative resistance' nor 'conductive resistance' is a term in the Penman-Monteith framework, which is specifically about vapor transport resistances.
explanations.d: Neither of these are terms used in the Penman-Monteith equation.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to convert a measured LE (W/m2) sustained over a known time period into a depth of water evaporated (mm).

items.text: Multiply LE (W/m2) by the duration in seconds to get total energy per area (J/m2)
Divide total energy per area by Lv (about 2.45 MJ/kg) to get mass of water evaporated per area (kg/m2)
Convert kg/m2 of water to an equivalent depth in mm (1 kg/m2 = 1 mm of water depth)

questions.explanation: You first accumulate the flux into total energy, then divide by the latent heat of vaporization to get mass, then convert that areal mass directly to an equivalent depth of water, since 1 kg of water over 1 m2 is exactly 1 mm deep.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its role in evapotranspiration.

right.text: Direct water loss from soil, open water, or wet leaf surfaces
Water released as vapor through plant stomata after uptake by roots
About 2.45 MJ/kg, the energy cost per kilogram of water evaporated
Monteith's 1965 extension of Penman's formula adding stomatal resistance

questions.explanation: Evaporation and transpiration are the two physical pathways that together make up evapotranspiration; Lv is the fixed energy cost per unit mass; the Penman-Monteith equation is the standard formula used to estimate the combined rate for vegetated surfaces.

lessons.label: The Bowen Ratio (beta = H/LE)

sections.heading: One number that summarizes a surface
sections.body: The Bowen ratio, beta = H / LE, is the single most compact description of how a surface partitions its available energy between heating the air and evaporating water. It was introduced by physicist Ira Bowen in a 1926 paper on heat loss from water surfaces, and it remains one of the oldest surviving tools in micrometeorology precisely because it is so cheap to interpret: beta greater than 1 means a surface is spending more energy heating air than evaporating water, beta less than 1 means the reverse. Typical values track surface wetness closely: bare desert commonly runs beta greater than 5 (sometimes into the tens, when almost no water is available at all), semi-arid grassland sits around 0.5, tropical rainforest and open ocean typically stay below 0.5, and a well-irrigated crop can push beta below 0.2, since nearly all its available energy goes into transpiration rather than warming the air.

sections.heading: Soil moisture as the master control, and the Bowen-ratio energy-balance method
sections.body: Because beta is so sensitive to how much water a surface can supply, soil moisture -- not incoming radiation -- is usually the dominant control on beta at a given site: the same field under the same Rn can swing from beta near 0.3 right after rain to beta above 3 during a dry spell, purely as a function of what water remains available to LE. This sensitivity is also what makes the Bowen-ratio energy-balance (BREB) method useful as a measurement technique: rather than needing fast-response sonic anemometers and gas analyzers for direct eddy-covariance measurement, BREB estimates beta from slower, cheaper measurements -- the vertical gradients of temperature and humidity between two heights above the surface, combined through the psychrometric constant gamma (about 0.66 hPa/K). Once beta is known, the available energy (Rn minus G, from earlier lessons) can be partitioned directly: H = [beta / (1 + beta)] x (Rn - G) and LE = [1 / (1 + beta)] x (Rn - G), without ever measuring either flux independently. This made BREB the workhorse method for agricultural and hydrological flux studies for decades before eddy-covariance instrumentation became affordable.

sections.heading: A hidden assumption: the oasis effect
sections.body: BREB's simplicity rests on one assumption worth naming: that the turbulent diffusivities transporting heat and water vapor through the same air are equal, which lets a single measured gradient ratio stand in for both fluxes at once. That assumption holds reasonably well over large, uniform surfaces but can break down under strong horizontal advection -- the classic case is the 'oasis effect,' where warm, dry air blowing off a surrounding desert sweeps across a small irrigated field and supplies extra energy for evaporation beyond what local Rn alone would predict, driving beta sharply negative or otherwise distorting the simple partition. Field practitioners therefore site BREB towers well inside a uniform surface, with enough upwind 'fetch' that the measured gradients reflect the target surface rather than air still carrying the thermal signature of whatever lies upwind.

lessons.workedExample: An irrigated cotton field is measured at midday with Rn = 520 W/m2 and G = 60 W/m2, so available energy is 460 W/m2. Gradient measurements give beta = 0.15. Then H = [0.15 / 1.15] x 460 = 60 W/m2, and LE = [1 / 1.15] x 460 = 400 W/m2 -- a strongly LE-dominated partition typical of well-watered crops. Three weeks later, irrigation has lapsed and the same field under similar Rn and G now shows beta = 2.0: H = [2.0 / 3.0] x 460 = 307 W/m2 and LE = [1 / 3.0] x 460 = 153 W/m2. The available energy barely changed, but the partition flipped almost entirely from LE-dominated to H-dominated, tracking the loss of soil moisture rather than any change in the radiation budget.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about the Bowen ratio to see whether a student can read a single number as a diagnostic of surface water status, not just recite H/LE as a formula. A weak answer defines beta and stops. A strong answer can predict, from a described surface (irrigated crop versus bare desert versus rainforest), roughly where beta should fall and why, can explain that soil moisture -- not Rn -- is usually the variable actually driving observed changes in beta over a season, and understands that BREB is a genuinely different measurement strategy from eddy covariance, trading direct turbulence measurement for gradient measurement plus the energy-balance closure assumption.

questions.prompt: A field's Bowen ratio rises from 0.4 to 3.5 over a three-week dry spell while Rn stays roughly constant. What does this most directly indicate?

options.text: Soil moisture has declined, shifting the energy partition from LE-dominated toward H-dominated
Albedo has increased sharply
The site has become more cloudy
G has become negative

explanations.a: Correct -- with Rn essentially unchanged, a rising beta signals that less available energy is being spent on evaporation and more on heating the air, the classic signature of declining soil moisture during a dry spell.
explanations.b: An albedo change would show up primarily as a change in Rn itself (via K-up), which the scenario says stayed roughly constant, so albedo is not the best explanation here.
explanations.c: Increased cloudiness would tend to change Rn (both K-down and L-down), which is stated to be roughly constant, so this doesn't fit the given scenario.
explanations.d: G's sign is not addressed by the scenario and a change in G's sign would not, by itself, explain a rising H/LE ratio.

questions.prompt: Which surface would this lesson predict has the highest typical Bowen ratio?

options.text: Tropical rainforest
Bare desert
Well-irrigated cropland
Open ocean

explanations.a: Rainforest typically has abundant transpiration and stays below beta = 0.5, the opposite of a high-beta surface.
explanations.b: Correct -- bare desert has almost no water available for LE, commonly pushing beta above 5, the highest range described in this lesson.
explanations.c: Well-irrigated cropland has ample water for transpiration and typically runs beta below 0.2, among the lowest values described.
explanations.d: Open ocean has essentially unlimited surface water for evaporation and typically stays below beta = 0.5.

questions.prompt: Match each surface type to its typical Bowen ratio range from this lesson.

right.text: beta > 5
beta approx. 0.5
beta < 0.5
beta < 0.2

questions.explanation: Beta scales inversely with water availability: bare desert (driest) has the highest beta, semi-arid grassland is intermediate, and tropical forest/ocean and well-irrigated cropland (wettest) have the lowest values, with irrigated crop pushing lowest of all.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the Bowen-ratio energy-balance (BREB) method for estimating H and LE.

items.text: Measure temperature and humidity gradients between two heights above the surface, and independently measure Rn and G to get available energy
Compute beta using the gradients and the psychrometric constant gamma
Partition available energy into H and LE using beta

questions.explanation: BREB first gathers its two independent inputs -- the temperature/humidity gradients (for beta) and the net-radiation/soil-heat-flux measurements (for available energy, Rn minus G) -- then computes beta from the gradients, and only at the end uses beta to split the already-known available energy into H and LE.

lessons.label: Ground Heat Flux and Surface Storage

sections.heading: Conduction into the ground, and thermal admittance
sections.body: Ground heat flux, G, is pure conduction: Fourier's law gives G = -k (dT/dz), where k is the soil's thermal conductivity and dT/dz is the vertical temperature gradient. But conductivity alone doesn't determine how a surface responds to daily heating -- what matters is thermal admittance, mu = square root(k x rho x c), the product of conductivity with volumetric heat capacity (density rho times specific heat c). High-admittance materials -- wet soil, rock, still water -- absorb heat readily without their surface temperature swinging much, because incoming energy is efficiently conducted away into a large thermal mass. Low-admittance materials -- dry sand, loose leaf litter, dry surface soil -- resist that conduction, so the same energy input produces a much larger surface temperature swing, which is why desert sand can be scorching at the surface at noon and near-freezing before dawn while damp soil a few centimeters below barely changes.

sections.heading: The damping depth and the phase-lagged diurnal wave
sections.body: As the diurnal temperature wave propagates downward from the surface, it loses amplitude and its peak arrives later at depth -- both effects follow directly from the heat-conduction equation. The amplitude decays exponentially with depth as exp(-z/D), where D, the damping depth, equals the square root of (2k / (rho c omega)), with omega the wave's angular frequency (2*pi over 24 hours for the diurnal cycle). For typical soils with thermal diffusivity around 5 x 10^-7 m2/s, the diurnal damping depth works out to roughly 0.10-0.20 m: by about three damping depths down (0.3-0.6 m), the daily temperature swing has essentially vanished, which is why root cellars and buried pipes a meter down barely feel the day-night cycle at all. The phase lag is proportional to z/D in radians, meaning the temperature peak at depth D lags the surface peak by roughly 1/(2*pi) of a full cycle, about 3-4 hours, and a full 24-hour phase shift accumulates by a depth of roughly 2*pi*D.

sections.heading: Why G differs so much by land cover
sections.body: Under a closed vegetation canopy, G is typically small, often only 5-10% of Rn at midday, because the canopy intercepts and reflects most incoming radiation before it ever reaches bare soil, and the canopy's own biomass and near-surface air act as an additional heat-storage buffer that isn't captured by a simple soil-conduction G term. Over bare soil with no shading, G can reach 25-30% of Rn at midday, since essentially all incoming radiation strikes and conducts directly into the ground. Urban surfaces -- concrete, asphalt, brick -- combine moderate-to-high thermal admittance with large exposed surface area and structural mass, producing a substantial storage term, often written delta-Qs in the urban energy-balance formulation Q* + QF = QH + QE + delta-Qs (Oke, 1982), where QF is anthropogenic heat and delta-Qs represents heat stored across the entire urban canopy layer -- walls, roofs, pavement -- not just the top few centimeters of soil. That stored heat releases slowly overnight, which is a principal physical driver of the urban heat island effect.

lessons.workedExample: A bare, dry sandy plot and an adjacent irrigated turf plot receive identical Rn = 500 W/m2 at midday. The bare sand, with low thermal admittance and no canopy shading, shows G = 140 W/m2 (28% of Rn), while the turf, shaded by a dense grass canopy with roots holding soil moisture (raising admittance), shows G = 35 W/m2 (7% of Rn). Buried thermometers confirm the pattern: under the sand, a probe at 0.15 m depth (roughly one damping depth) shows a temperature swing about 37% of the surface's amplitude, peaking nearly 4 hours after the surface peak, consistent with the exp(-z/D) decay and z/D phase-lag relationships for a damping depth near 0.15 m.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about G because it is the flux students most often treat as an afterthought, when it actually explains why bare ground and vegetated ground behave so differently under identical sun. A weak answer says 'G is heat going into the soil.' A strong answer can explain why a canopy suppresses G specifically (shading plus a separate storage buffer, not just 'plants are cooler'), can connect thermal admittance to why sand overheats while wet soil doesn't, and recognizes that the same physics scaled up -- higher admittance, more exposed mass, slower nighttime release -- is the mechanistic basis of the urban heat island, not just a vague 'cities are hotter' claim.

questions.prompt: Why does dry desert sand show a much larger surface temperature swing over a day than nearby wet soil under the same Rn?

options.text: Dry sand has higher thermal admittance, so it stores heat more efficiently and swings less
Dry sand has lower thermal admittance, so the same energy input produces a larger surface temperature change
Dry sand has a higher albedo, which directly causes bigger temperature swings
Wet soil receives less Rn than dry sand

explanations.a: This has the relationship backwards -- higher admittance means smaller, not larger, surface temperature swings, because heat conducts away efficiently into the substrate.
explanations.b: Correct -- low thermal admittance (low k*rho*c) means the surface can't efficiently shed absorbed energy into the substrate, so the same energy input produces a much larger local temperature swing.
explanations.c: Albedo affects how much shortwave is absorbed in the first place (via K-up), but it does not directly determine the amplitude of the resulting temperature swing -- that's governed by admittance.
explanations.d: The scenario specifies both surfaces receive identical Rn, so this option contradicts the given setup.

questions.prompt: Under a dense vegetation canopy, why is G typically only 5-10% of Rn, much lower than the 25-30% seen over bare soil?

options.text: Because plants have negative thermal conductivity
Because the canopy intercepts most incoming radiation before it reaches the soil, and canopy biomass provides an additional heat-storage buffer
Because vegetated Rn is always lower than bare-soil Rn
Because roots actively pump heat away from the soil surface

explanations.a: Thermal conductivity cannot be negative for any real material; this is not a physical explanation.
explanations.b: Correct -- shading by the canopy prevents most radiation from directly striking and conducting into the soil, and the canopy's own mass acts as a separate storage buffer not captured by simple soil-conduction G.
explanations.c: The lesson's worked comparison uses identical Rn for both surfaces; the difference in G is not because vegetated Rn is inherently lower.
explanations.d: Root systems take up water, not heat, and are not described as an active heat-pumping mechanism in this lesson.

questions.prompt: Match each surface/system to its typical G as a fraction of Rn described in this lesson.

right.text: 5-10% of Rn at midday
25-30% of Rn at midday
Large storage term (delta-Qs), released slowly overnight, driving the urban heat island

questions.explanation: Canopy shading keeps G smallest under vegetation; unshaded bare soil has the largest simple conductive G; urban surfaces combine admittance and exposed mass into a large storage term that behaves differently from simple soil G and drives nighttime urban warmth.

questions.prompt: Order these depths by how much of the surface diurnal temperature amplitude remains at each, from most remaining to least remaining, given amplitude decays as exp(-z/D).

items.text: z = 0 (the surface itself)
z = 1 damping depth (z = D)
z = 3 damping depths (z = 3D)

questions.explanation: Amplitude decays exponentially with depth, so the surface itself retains the full swing, one damping depth retains about exp(-1) ~ 37% of it, and three damping depths retain only about exp(-3) ~ 5%, essentially damped out.

units.label: Wind, Turbulence, and the Logarithmic Profile

lessons.label: The Logarithmic Wind Profile

sections.heading: Building u(z) from the surface layer
sections.body: In the lowest tens of meters of the atmosphere — the surface layer — turbulent stress is treated as nearly constant with height, so momentum flux does not change much as you climb from 1 m to 30 m. Prandtl's mixing-length argument, developed for pipe and boundary-layer flows in the 1920s, closes the turbulence problem by assuming eddies scale with distance from the surface: mixing length l = kappa*z, where kappa is the von Karman constant, empirically about 0.40. Combining this with the constant-stress assumption and the definition of eddy shear stress produces a shear equation du/dz = u*/(kappa*z), where u* (friction velocity) is defined so that surface stress tau = rho*u*^2. Kappa is not a theoretically derived number — it comes from fitting measured wind profiles, and different field campaigns have returned somewhat different values. The original Kansas experiment fit (Businger et al., 1971) found kappa ~ 0.35; later reanalyses of the same dataset and subsequent campaigns converged on the now-standard kappa ~ 0.40. That roughly 15% spread matters in practice: because u* is solved for as u* = kappa * du/d(ln z), a 15% uncertainty in kappa propagates directly into a 15% uncertainty in any u* derived from a measured wind gradient, which in turn propagates into every quantity built on u* — momentum flux, drag coefficients, and the stability length scales covered in later lessons.

sections.heading: Integrating to the log law
sections.body: Integrating du/dz = u*/(kappa*z) from a reference height z0 (where wind speed is defined as zero) up to height z gives u(z) = (u*/kappa) * ln(z/z0). This is the logarithmic wind profile, the workhorse relation of micrometeorology: plot wind speed against the natural log of height and, in neutral stratification, the points fall on a straight line whose slope is u*/kappa and whose x-intercept is z0. The law strictly holds only for neutral (near-adiabatic) stability in the surface layer, roughly the lowest 10% of the boundary layer; buoyancy in stable or unstable air bends the profile, which is why later stability corrections (Monin-Obukhov theory) are grafted onto this same log form rather than replacing it. Because the log law needs only two parameters, u* and z0, it underlies most practical wind extrapolation — from anemometer height to turbine hub height, from a 2 m weather station to a 10 m WMO standard, or from a rooftop sensor to street level. The constant-stress assumption that the whole derivation leans on is itself only approximate: within the lowest tens of meters, turbulent stress typically varies by just a few percent per 10 m of height, so treating it as constant introduces little error there — but the approximation degrades higher up, as you approach the top of the surface layer where stress starts departing more noticeably from its surface value, which is part of why the log law is confined to that lowest ~10% of the boundary layer rather than applied throughout it.

lessons.workedExample: A weather station reads 3.5 m/s at 2 m height and 5.0 m/s at 10 m, both in neutral stability with z0 = 0.03 m (short grass). Using u(z) = (u*/kappa)*ln(z/z0): at z=10 m, 5.0 = (u*/0.40)*ln(10/0.03) = (u*/0.40)*(5.81), so u* = 5.0*0.40/5.81 = 0.344 m/s. Check at z=2 m: u(2) = (0.344/0.40)*ln(2/0.03) = 0.860*4.20 = 3.61 m/s — close to the observed 3.5 m/s, confirming the profile is consistent with neutral log-law behavior and giving a friction velocity usable to extrapolate to, say, a 30 m turbine hub: u(30) = 0.860*ln(30/0.03) = 0.860*6.91 = 5.94 m/s.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes the log wind profile whenever a project extrapolates wind speed from one height to another — a very common shortcut in student energy or environmental projects. A weak answer just says 'wind is faster higher up.' A strong answer states the log-law form, names u* and z0 as the two fitted parameters, and — critically — states the neutral-stability assumption the law depends on, since applying it uncritically at night (when the boundary layer is often stable) systematically overpredicts near-surface wind and can wreck a turbine-siting estimate.

questions.prompt: In the logarithmic wind profile u(z) = (u*/kappa)*ln(z/z0), what does z0 represent?

options.text: The height at which turbulent stress becomes zero
The height at which the extrapolated wind speed goes to zero
The top of the atmospheric boundary layer
The measurement height of the anemometer

explanations.a: Stress is assumed roughly constant through the surface layer, not zero at z0; z0 is a wind-speed reference, not a stress reference.
explanations.b: Correct — z0 is defined as the height where the log-law extrapolation of wind speed reaches zero; it is a mathematical intercept set by surface roughness, not a place wind is literally measured.
explanations.c: The boundary layer top is typically hundreds to thousands of meters up; z0 is centimeters to meters.
explanations.d: Anemometer height is whatever z the instrument sits at, unrelated to the roughness-set z0.

questions.prompt: The value kappa ~ 0.40 in the log law is known as:

options.text: The drag coefficient
The von Karman constant
The Obukhov constant
The Businger coefficient

explanations.a: The drag coefficient CD is a separate dimensionless ratio relating stress to wind speed squared, covered in a later lesson.
explanations.b: Correct — kappa is the von Karman constant, an empirically determined dimensionless constant (~0.40) from Prandtl's mixing-length closure.
explanations.c: The Obukhov length L is a stability length scale, not this constant.
explanations.d: Businger-Dyer coefficients are the empirical constants in the stability correction functions, a different set of numbers.

questions.prompt: Order the steps used to derive the log wind profile.

items.text: Assume constant turbulent stress with height in the surface layer
Apply mixing-length closure l = kappa*z to get du/dz = u*/(kappa*z)
Integrate du/dz from z0 to z
Obtain u(z) = (u*/kappa)*ln(z/z0)

questions.explanation: The derivation starts from the constant-stress assumption, closes the turbulence with mixing length to get a shear equation, integrates it with height, and arrives at the log form.

questions.prompt: Under what condition does the basic log wind profile (without stability correction) hold?

options.text: Only at night under strong radiative cooling
Only in neutral (near-adiabatic) stratification
At any stability, since kappa absorbs the buoyancy effect
Only above the surface layer, in the mixed layer

explanations.a: Nighttime radiative cooling produces stable stratification, which bends the wind profile away from the simple log form.
explanations.b: Correct — the derivation assumes no buoyant production or suppression of turbulence, i.e., neutral stability, confined to the surface layer.
explanations.c: kappa is a fixed constant; it does not adjust for buoyancy — that correction requires the separate stability functions covered later.
explanations.d: The log law is specifically a surface-layer relation; above it, in the mixed layer, wind speed becomes closer to height-independent.

lessons.label: Roughness Length and Zero-Plane Displacement

sections.heading: Roughness length as a surface fingerprint
sections.body: Roughness length z0, introduced in the log law as the height where extrapolated wind speed vanishes, is not a physical height anyone could stand at — it is a fitted parameter that packages the aerodynamic drag of everything on the ground into one number. Values span nearly four orders of magnitude: smooth sea ice or still water sits near z0 ~ 1e-5 to 1e-4 m; short grass or bare soil is around 0.01 to 0.03 m; row crops and low shrubs run 0.1 to 0.25 m; a mature forest canopy reaches roughly 0.5 to 1.5 m; and dense urban cores with tall, irregular buildings can exceed 1-2 m. A widely used rule of thumb, traceable to Lettau's 1969 formulation relating z0 to obstacle geometry, is that z0 is roughly a tenth of the height of the roughness elements themselves — so a 10 m tall corn crop or forest canopy gives z0 on the order of 1 m, while a 20 cm grass lawn gives z0 near 2 cm. Lettau's actual formula behind that rule of thumb is z0 ~ 0.5*h*(Sf/S), where h is obstacle height, Sf is the frontal (silhouette) area of the average obstacle facing the wind, and S is the ground area per obstacle — so z0 scales with how much wind-facing area the roughness elements present per unit of ground, not with height alone. The 0.1h shortcut is really just this formula evaluated at a 'typical' frontal-area-to-ground-area ratio of about 0.2; sparser or denser obstacle spacing than that shifts z0 up or down from the 0.1h estimate even for the same obstacle height. This scaling reflects that z0 is set by the size and spacing of individual roughness elements (blades, branches, buildings) generating form drag, not by the terrain's large-scale relief.

sections.heading: Zero-plane displacement over tall canopies
sections.body: Over tall, dense roughness — forests, crops, cities — the log law needs a second correction. Air does not effectively 'see' the ground at z=0; instead the whole canopy acts as an elevated, blurred surface, and the log profile is better written as u(z) = (u*/kappa)*ln((z-d)/z0), where d is the zero-plane displacement height. Physically, d approximates the mean height at which momentum is absorbed by the canopy elements, and it commonly runs about 0.6-0.8 times the canopy height h, with 0.7h a standard working value. For a 20 m tall forest, d might be about 14 m, meaning the effective ground for wind-profile purposes sits 14 m above the actual soil, and the log profile only applies to heights safely above d + z0. Ignoring d over tall canopies is a common student-project error: fitting a plain log law through near-canopy wind data without a displacement term produces a spuriously curved or even negative-looking z0, because the coordinate system is missing its true origin.

lessons.workedExample: A student measures wind at 25 m and 35 m above a 20 m tall forest canopy and wants z0 and u*. Using d = 0.7*20 = 14 m, they plot u against ln(z-d): at z=25, z-d=11; at z=35, z-d=21. Suppose u(25)=4.0 m/s and u(35)=5.2 m/s. Then u*/kappa = (5.2-4.0)/(ln21-ln11) = 1.2/0.647 = 1.855, giving u* = 1.855*0.40 = 0.742 m/s. Solving 4.0 = 1.855*ln(11/z0) gives ln(11/z0) = 2.157, so 11/z0 = 8.65, z0 ~ 1.27 m — inside the 0.5-1.5 m range stated above for a mature forest canopy, though still well below the ~0.1h rule-of-thumb estimate (0.1*20 = 2 m), a reminder that real forest z0 depends on canopy density and structure (the Sf/S ratio), not on height alone.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe roughness length and displacement height whenever a project measures wind or flux near trees, crops, or buildings, because forgetting d is the single most common surface-layer mistake in student field data. A weak answer treats every site like open grass and fits a plain two-parameter log law. A strong answer recognizes canopy height, applies d ~ 0.7h, explicitly states that measurements must be taken well above d + z0 for the log law to be valid at all, and can justify the ~0.1h rule for z0 as an obstacle-drag scaling rather than a memorized constant.

questions.prompt: Match each surface type to its approximate roughness length z0.

right.text: ~1e-5 to 1e-4 m
~1-2 m or more

questions.explanation: Roughness length scales with the size and spacing of surface obstacles: smooth ice has almost none, grass has small blades, forests have tall trunks and canopy elements, and cities have large irregular buildings.

questions.prompt: Roughly what fraction of roughness-element height does the rule-of-thumb use for z0?

options.text: About 1/100th
About 1/10th
About 1/2
About equal to element height

explanations.a: 1/100th underestimates the drag contribution of typical roughness elements by an order of magnitude.
explanations.b: Correct — the common rule of thumb, from element-drag scaling arguments like Lettau's, is z0 ~ 0.1 times obstacle height.
explanations.c: 1/2 the element height would make z0 far larger than observed for real vegetated or urban surfaces.
explanations.d: z0 equal to element height would put the wind-vanishing point at the canopy top itself, which observations do not support.

questions.prompt: Why does the log wind profile over a forest need a zero-plane displacement term d?

options.text: Because kappa changes over tall canopies
Because the canopy absorbs momentum well above the actual ground, shifting the effective origin of the log profile upward
Because friction velocity cannot be defined over vegetation
Because z0 is undefined for rough surfaces

explanations.a: The von Karman constant kappa is treated as universal and does not change with canopy type.
explanations.b: Correct — momentum is absorbed throughout the upper canopy rather than at the soil surface, so the profile's effective z=0 origin must be raised by d, typically ~0.7h.
