explanations.b: Correct — spherical particles preserve polarization on backscatter while irregular particles scramble it, so CALIOP's depolarization ratio reveals aerosol shape and therefore type, layer by layer.
explanations.c: Lidar profiles show vertical structure, which helps relate column to surface, but the depolarization channel specifically identifies particle type, not the column-to-surface conversion itself.
explanations.d: CALIOP can operate at night since it uses its own laser source, but that is not what the depolarization channel specifically distinguishes.

questions.prompt: Match each system to what it measures.

right.text: High-resolution tropospheric columns of NO2, SO2, HCHO from orbit
Ground-based aerosol optical depth from standardized sun photometers
Vertical aerosol profiles and particle type via lidar depolarization

questions.explanation: TROPOMI retrieves fine-resolution trace gas columns; AERONET's ground sun photometers give the reference AOD dataset; CALIPSO's CALIOP lidar resolves aerosol vertically and by type.

questions.prompt: Order these satellite instruments by launch date, earliest first.

items.text: TOMS (Nimbus-7)
OMI (Aura)
TROPOMI (Sentinel-5P)

questions.explanation: TOMS launched in 1978, OMI in 2004, and TROPOMI in 2017, each generation adding species coverage or finer spatial resolution.

questions.prompt: Why can't a satellite trace-gas column measurement alone tell you the surface-level concentration a person is breathing?

options.text: Because satellites cannot measure NO2, only ozone
Because the column is a single integrated total from surface to space, and converting it to a surface value requires an assumption about the gas's vertical distribution
Because satellite columns are only accurate at night
Because AERONET must be used instead for any gas measurement

explanations.a: Satellites like OMI and TROPOMI do measure NO2 columns directly, among other species.
explanations.b: Correct — the same column total can correspond to very different surface concentrations depending on whether the gas is well-mixed through a deep boundary layer or trapped in a shallow layer, so a vertical distribution assumption or profile is required to bridge column and surface.
explanations.c: Backscatter retrievals like OMI and TROPOMI require sunlight and are generally daytime measurements, but that is not why column and surface values differ.
explanations.d: AERONET measures aerosol optical depth from the ground, not trace gas columns, and is not a substitute for a vertical profile of the gas in question.

lessons.label: Sampling Networks and Long Records

sections.heading: Mauna Loa and the logic of siting for background air
sections.body: Charles David Keeling began continuous CO2 measurements at Mauna Loa Observatory in Hawaii in 1958, using non-dispersive infrared analysis, and the record he started, now called the Keeling curve, shows both a rising trend, from roughly 316 parts per million in its first full year to past 420 ppm by the early 2020s, and a sawtooth seasonal cycle a few parts per million wide. Mauna Loa was chosen deliberately: at 3,400 meters elevation, far above local vegetation and any nearby city, air arriving at the site is closer to the well-mixed free troposphere than to any local source or sink, which is exactly the property needed to see a global trend rather than a local one. Local plants still leave a fingerprint on the curve itself: the sawtooth is Northern Hemisphere photosynthesis drawing CO2 down each summer and decomposition releasing it again each winter, an amplitude of about 5 to 6 ppm at Mauna Loa's latitude that grows to roughly three times that at high-latitude stations like Barrow, Alaska, where the growing season is short and the land biomass is enormous.

sections.heading: WMO/GAW baseline stations and calibration scales
sections.body: The World Meteorological Organization's Global Atmosphere Watch program, established in 1989, coordinates a worldwide network of baseline stations, including Mauna Loa, Barrow, American Samoa, and the South Pole, all sited specifically to sample background air away from local pollution, with siting criteria that exclude locations near roads, industry, or population centers. A single, shared measurement scale, maintained by a Central Calibration Laboratory and periodically checked through round-robin comparisons between stations, is what lets a CO2 reading from one continent be compared meaningfully to a reading from another decades apart.

sections.heading: Flasks, canisters, and ozonesondes
sections.body: Not every measurement can be continuous. NOAA's cooperative global air sampling network, begun in 1967 as an independent NOAA effort distinct from Keeling's Scripps-run flask program, collects weekly glass or stainless-steel flask samples from roughly fifty sites worldwide and ships them to a central lab for precise analysis, trading time resolution for very high accuracy and the ability to measure many species from one sample. Whole-air canister sampling, often using electropolished stainless-steel SUMMA canisters, works on the same principle for VOCs and halocarbons, collecting a snapshot of ambient air for later gas-chromatographic analysis. Vertical structure requires a different approach: ozonesondes carry an electrochemical concentration cell sensor aloft on a weather balloon, launched weekly at network sites, recording an ozone profile up through the stratosphere until the balloon bursts near 30 to 35 kilometers, typically alongside a radiosonde package measuring temperature, pressure, humidity, and wind.

lessons.workedExample: A student comparing CO2 seasonal cycles at Mauna Loa (about 20 degrees North) and Barrow, Alaska (about 71 degrees North) finds the Mauna Loa cycle swings roughly 5-6 ppm peak-to-trough while Barrow's swings nearly three times as wide. The explanation is not instrument error at either site; it is that Barrow sits close to the vast, seasonally deciduous boreal and tundra biomass of high-latitude North America and Siberia, where summer photosynthesis and winter dieback pull and push atmospheric CO2 far more dramatically than the comparatively small, less seasonal tropical and subtropical vegetation influencing Mauna Loa's free-tropospheric air.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'why was this site chosen?' because siting is the single decision that determines whether a station measures a global background trend or a local pollution episode, and conflating the two invalidates a comparison. A weak answer treats every station's number as interchangeable. A strong answer explains that a baseline station like Mauna Loa is sited at altitude, away from local sources, specifically to see well-mixed background air, while an urban monitoring site is sited to characterize local exposure, and that neither can substitute for the other's purpose.

questions.prompt: Why was Mauna Loa specifically chosen as the site for Keeling's continuous CO2 record starting in 1958?

options.text: Its high elevation and distance from vegetation and cities give air closer to the well-mixed free troposphere, better representing global background CO2
It has the highest local CO2 emissions in the Pacific, making trends easiest to detect
It was the only site with electricity for instruments in 1958
It sits directly over major CO2-emitting industry

explanations.a: Correct — at 3,400 meters and far from local sources, Mauna Loa's air is representative of well-mixed background conditions, which is what makes its record a good proxy for global trends rather than local pollution.
explanations.b: The site was chosen for the opposite reason: minimal local influence, not high local emissions.
explanations.c: Electricity availability was not the deciding factor; the atmospheric representativeness of the site was.
explanations.d: Mauna Loa was chosen to avoid, not sit over, local emission sources.

questions.prompt: Why is the Keeling curve's seasonal cycle amplitude roughly three times larger at Barrow, Alaska than at Mauna Loa?

options.text: Barrow's instruments are less precisely calibrated
Barrow sits closer to vast high-latitude land biomass with a strong, short growing season, producing a much larger seasonal photosynthesis-decomposition swing
Barrow measures CH4 instead of CO2
Mauna Loa's high elevation blocks the seasonal cycle from being detected

explanations.a: Both stations use the same shared calibration scale maintained by the Central Calibration Laboratory; the difference is atmospheric, not instrumental.
explanations.b: Correct — the large, strongly seasonal boreal and tundra biomass near Barrow draws down and releases far more CO2 each year than the vegetation influencing Mauna Loa's free-tropospheric air.
explanations.c: Both stations report CO2 in the Keeling-curve comparison described here.
explanations.d: Mauna Loa's elevation is why it sees a background record at all; it does not block the seasonal cycle, it simply sees a smaller one.

questions.prompt: Match each sampling method to what it is used for.

right.text: High-accuracy, multi-species analysis from a central lab, trading time resolution for precision
VOCs and halocarbons collected for later gas-chromatographic analysis
Vertical ozone profile up through the stratosphere on a weather balloon

questions.explanation: Flask samples are shipped to a central lab for precise multi-species analysis; whole-air canisters preserve a snapshot for VOC/halocarbon GC analysis; ozonesondes carry an electrochemical sensor aloft to profile ozone with altitude.

questions.prompt: Order these events/milestones chronologically.

items.text: Keeling begins continuous CO2 measurement at Mauna Loa
WMO Global Atmosphere Watch program established
Mauna Loa CO2 surpasses 420 ppm

questions.explanation: Keeling's record began in 1958, GAW was established in 1989 to coordinate baseline stations globally, and Mauna Loa's CO2 level passed 420 ppm in the early 2020s.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the shared calibration scale maintained by GAW's Central Calibration Laboratory and checked via round-robin comparisons?

options.text: To let CO2 readings from different stations and decades be compared meaningfully on a common basis
To convert satellite columns into surface concentrations
To classify aerosols by aerodynamic diameter
To reduce interference from PAN and HNO3 in NOx measurements

explanations.a: Correct — a shared reference scale, verified through periodic round-robin comparisons between stations, ensures that a measurement made at one baseline station is directly comparable to one made elsewhere or decades earlier.
explanations.b: Converting satellite columns to surface values requires a boundary-layer or profile assumption, not a gas calibration scale.
explanations.c: Aerodynamic classification is done by cascade impactors, unrelated to a shared gas calibration scale.
explanations.d: Reducing NOx converter interference is a chemiluminescence instrument issue, not a network-wide calibration-scale issue.

lessons.label: Error, Calibration, and Intercomparison

sections.heading: Accuracy, precision, and where each one fails you
sections.body: Precision describes how tightly repeated measurements of the same air cluster together; accuracy describes how close the measured value is to the truth. An instrument can be highly precise and still badly wrong if it has an uncorrected bias, and that bias is often chemical rather than electronic. The clearest atmospheric example is the molybdenum-converter chemiluminescence NOx analyzer: its NO reading is both precise and accurate, but its NO2 reading, derived by converting NO2 to NO and subtracting, is precise yet systematically biased high, because the hot molybdenum surface also reduces other reactive nitrogen species such as PAN and nitric acid. Dunlea and colleagues documented this NOy interference in a widely cited 2007 evaluation, finding the overestimate can be substantial in aged, photochemically processed air masses where PAN has had time to accumulate.

sections.heading: Sampling artifacts on filters
sections.body: Filter-based PM mass measurements carry their own systematic errors, called sampling artifacts, that occur even with a perfectly calibrated balance. Semivolatile species like ammonium nitrate can evaporate off the filter during or after collection, especially in warm conditions or under vacuum, producing a negative artifact that understates true particulate mass. In the opposite direction, organic vapors can adsorb onto the filter medium itself, a positive artifact that overstates organic carbon. Because these artifacts pull in opposite directions and depend on temperature, filter type, and sampling duration, neither can simply be assumed to cancel the other out, and both must be characterized for a given method before its mass number is trusted.

sections.heading: Zero, span, and formal intercomparison
sections.body: Routine calibration counters instrument drift with two reference points: zero air, scrubbed of the target pollutant, sets the baseline, and a span gas of known concentration sets the response slope, typically checked daily to weekly against cylinders traceable to a national standards body. Because no single calibration check catches every failure mode, especially chemical interferences like the NOy problem, the field also relies on formal intercomparison campaigns, where multiple instruments and techniques sample the same air side by side, sometimes in the same smog chamber or at the same field site, specifically to surface disagreements a lab calibration alone would miss. When a final result depends on more than one measured quantity, such as NO2 derived from NOx minus NO, or a photostationary-state calculation combining NO, NO2, and ozone photolysis rate, each input's individual uncertainty must be propagated into the combined result, standard practice being to add independent uncertainties in quadrature rather than simply summing them.

lessons.workedExample: A student calculates NO2 as NOx minus NO using a molybdenum-converter instrument with an NOy interference known, from a Dunlea-style comparison, to add roughly 20% extra signal on aged urban air. If the true NO2 is 25 ppb but the converter's interference adds an extra 5 ppb of falsely converted NOy species, the instrument reports 30 ppb NO2, a 20% high bias that no amount of careful zero/span calibration would catch, because the interference is chemical, not electronic, and a span gas of pure NO2 does not contain the PAN or HNO3 needed to reveal it.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'how do you know your error bars, and did you check for interferences beyond drift?' because a project that only reports instrument-manufacturer precision, without considering chemical interference or sampling artifacts, is reporting a floor on the uncertainty, not the whole picture. A weak answer cites a spec-sheet precision number as if it were the total error. A strong answer names a specific interference or artifact relevant to the method used, states whether zero/span calibration would or would not catch it, and shows how uncertainty was propagated if the reported quantity was derived from more than one measurement.

questions.prompt: A molybdenum-converter chemiluminescence NOx analyzer gives tightly repeatable NO2 readings that are consistently 20% too high in polluted air. What best describes this instrument's performance?

options.text: High precision, low accuracy
Low precision, high accuracy
Low precision, low accuracy
High precision, high accuracy

explanations.a: Correct — tight repeatability is precision, and a consistent 20% high bias from converting PAN and HNO3 alongside NO2 is an accuracy failure; the instrument is precise but not accurate.
explanations.b: The readings are described as tightly repeatable, which is high, not low, precision.
explanations.c: The scenario specifies tight repeatability, ruling out low precision.
explanations.d: A consistent 20% bias means the readings are not close to the true value, so accuracy is low despite the good precision.

questions.prompt: Why can't a routine zero/span calibration catch the NOy interference on a molybdenum-converter NOx analyzer?

options.text: Because zero/span calibration uses pure NO2 or NO reference gases, which do not contain the PAN or HNO3 whose false conversion causes the interference
Because the analyzer is never calibrated with zero air
Because span gas concentrations are always too low to detect any bias
Because zero/span calibration only applies to ozone monitors

explanations.a: Correct — since the reference gases used for calibration are pure target compounds, they cannot reveal a bias that only appears when other reactive nitrogen species like PAN or HNO3 are present in ambient air and get converted alongside NO2.
explanations.b: Zero air is routinely used to set the instrument's baseline; the issue is not the absence of zero calibration but what the calibration gases fail to represent.
explanations.c: Span gas concentration is chosen to bracket expected ambient levels; the problem is compositional, not concentration-related.
explanations.d: Zero/span calibration is standard practice across many instrument types, including NOx analyzers, not only ozone monitors.

questions.prompt: Match each sampling artifact or check to its effect or purpose.

left.text: Volatilization of ammonium nitrate off a filter
Adsorption of organic vapors onto a filter

right.text: Negative artifact, understating true PM mass
Positive artifact, overstating organic carbon
Surfaces disagreements between methods that lab calibration alone would miss

questions.explanation: Semivolatile nitrate evaporating off a filter is a negative mass artifact; organic vapor adsorption is a positive organic carbon artifact; side-by-side intercomparison campaigns catch systematic disagreements that routine single-instrument calibration cannot.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for propagating uncertainty into a derived quantity like NO2 = NOx - NO.

items.text: Determine the individual measurement uncertainty for the NOx reading
Determine the individual measurement uncertainty for the NO reading
Combine the two independent uncertainties in quadrature rather than by simple addition
Report the derived NO2 value together with its propagated uncertainty

questions.explanation: Each input measurement's own uncertainty must be characterized first, then independent uncertainties are combined in quadrature (square root of the sum of squares) rather than added directly, and the final derived value is reported with that combined uncertainty.

questions.prompt: Why do atmospheric chemists run formal side-by-side intercomparison campaigns rather than relying only on each instrument's own zero/span calibration?

options.text: Because zero/span calibration is too expensive to perform routinely
Because some biases, such as chemical interferences, are invisible to a single instrument's own reference-gas calibration and only show up when compared against an independent method
Because intercomparison campaigns replace the need for any further calibration afterward
Because only satellite instruments require intercomparison

explanations.a: Cost is not the stated reason; zero/span calibration remains routine practice alongside intercomparisons.
explanations.b: Correct — a bias like the molybdenum-converter NOy interference is invisible to that instrument's own zero/span check because the reference gases don't include the interfering species, so only comparison against an independent method reveals it.
explanations.c: Intercomparison campaigns complement, not replace, ongoing routine zero/span calibration.
explanations.d: Intercomparison campaigns are conducted for ground-based in-situ instruments as well as satellite and remote-sensing methods.

units.label: Aerosols: Life Cycle, Size Distributions, and Particulate Matter

lessons.label: What Aerosols Are and Where They Come From

sections.heading: Suspended matter, not just smoke
sections.body: An aerosol is technically the whole suspension of solid or liquid particles in a gas, though in practice atmospheric scientists use the word to mean the particles themselves: everything from a single soot grain a few nanometers across to a sea-spray droplet tens of micrometers wide. Sizes span nearly five orders of magnitude, and that range is why no single instrument or single removal process handles the whole population. The largest primary particles are mechanically generated: wind stress tearing droplets off wave crests to make sea salt, and saltation lifting soil grains into mineral dust over arid basins like the Sahara and the Taklamakan. Combustion adds a second primary stream — black carbon (soot) and co-emitted organic carbon from wildfires, cookstoves, diesel engines, and industrial flaring — plus episodic volcanic ash and sulfate from eruptions such as Pinatubo in 1991.

sections.heading: Primary emission versus secondary formation
sections.body: Primary aerosol is emitted directly as a particle; secondary aerosol condenses from gas-phase precursors after they oxidize in the atmosphere, a gas-to-particle conversion covered in depth in the next lesson. Global emission inventories (summarized in IPCC AR6 and earlier AR5 assessments) put natural primary sources far ahead by mass: sea salt around 3,300 teragrams per year and mineral dust around 1,600 teragrams per year, dwarfing anthropogenic primary emissions of black carbon (around 8 teragrams per year) and organic carbon (around 34 teragrams per year). Mass is a misleading yardstick, though — coarse sea salt and dust settle out within hours to days, while fine anthropogenic and secondary particles persist for about a week (see the removal lesson) and dominate both particle number and light scattering over populated regions. So the natural-versus-anthropogenic split flips depending on whether you weigh by mass, by number, or by radiative effect, which is precisely why a report claiming aerosols are 'mostly natural' or 'mostly human' is usually citing only one of those three metrics. Secondary sulfate and secondary organic aerosol, though smaller by mass than sea salt or dust, are disproportionately important for both categories: because they form from gas-phase precursors condensing onto existing particles rather than being mechanically torn or lofted at large sizes, they add mass and number almost entirely within the fine, accumulation-mode range that dominates both light scattering and cloud-condensation-nuclei supply, so a mass budget dominated by sea salt and dust can still describe an atmosphere whose optical and cloud-relevant behavior is set mostly by anthropogenic and secondary sources.

lessons.workedExample: A student building a poster claims 'aerosols are mostly natural, so pollution controls barely matter for particulate matter.' They cite the correct fact that sea salt and dust outweigh soot by mass globally. A judge would push back: over an industrial city, the particles a person actually breathes are dominated by anthropogenic combustion and secondary sulfate/nitrate, not by remote ocean sea salt. The fix is to specify the metric and the location — global mass budget versus urban ground-level exposure are different questions with different answers, and a defensible claim states which one it is answering.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'where did your aerosol come from' because sourcing determines composition, size, and lifetime, and a student who cannot distinguish primary emission from secondary formation usually cannot explain their own data's chemistry either. A weak answer says 'pollution and natural stuff.' A strong answer names specific source types (sea salt, dust, combustion soot, secondary sulfate/organics), states that natural sources dominate global mass while anthropogenic and secondary particles dominate number and optical effects, and ties that split to whichever metric the student's own project actually measured.

questions.prompt: By global mass, which pair of sources dominates the aerosol budget?

options.text: Black carbon and organic carbon from combustion
Sea salt and mineral dust
Secondary sulfate and secondary organic aerosol
Volcanic ash and industrial sulfate

explanations.a: Combustion carbon is a much smaller mass flux globally than the two mechanically generated natural sources.
explanations.b: Correct — wind-driven sea spray and wind-lofted mineral dust each run on the order of thousands of teragrams per year, well above any anthropogenic category by mass.
explanations.c: Secondary aerosol mass is significant regionally but smaller than sea salt and dust in the global total.
explanations.d: Volcanic ash is episodic and industrial sulfate is a much smaller steady flux than sea salt or dust.

questions.prompt: A particle is described as 'primary.' What does that mean?

options.text: It was emitted directly as a particle rather than condensing from a gas
It is the first particle formed each morning
It has the smallest possible diameter
It only forms over the ocean

explanations.a: Correct — primary aerosol enters the atmosphere already as a solid or liquid particle, unlike secondary aerosol which condenses from precursor gases.
explanations.b: Primary refers to emission mechanism, not time of day.
explanations.c: Primary particles include large sea salt and dust, so size is not the defining feature.
explanations.d: Primary sources include continental dust and combustion, not just marine emission.

questions.prompt: Match each aerosol type to its dominant formation mechanism.

right.text: Wave-breaking spray
Wind saltation over arid soil
Incomplete combustion
Gas-to-particle oxidation of SO2

questions.explanation: Sea salt comes from wave action tearing droplets off the ocean surface, dust from wind lofting soil in arid regions, black carbon from incomplete combustion, and secondary sulfate from atmospheric oxidation of sulfur dioxide gas into particulate sulfate.

questions.prompt: Why does the natural-versus-anthropogenic split in aerosol budgets depend on which metric (mass, number, or optical effect) is used?

options.text: Because natural and anthropogenic particles have identical sizes and lifetimes
Because coarse natural particles carry most of the mass but fine anthropogenic/secondary particles dominate number and light scattering
Because instruments cannot measure natural aerosols accurately
Because anthropogenic aerosol does not exist in remote regions

explanations.a: Sizes and lifetimes differ sharply between coarse natural particles and fine anthropogenic ones, which is exactly why the metrics diverge.
explanations.b: Correct — a few large sea salt and dust particles carry most of the mass, while vastly more numerous fine particles dominate number counts and, through their larger total surface area, dominate scattering.
explanations.c: Instrumentation is not the reason the metrics diverge; the physical size distribution is.
explanations.d: Anthropogenic aerosol is smaller in remote regions but the metric divergence is a physical/statistical effect, not an absence issue.

lessons.label: New-Particle Formation and Secondary Aerosol

sections.heading: Nucleation: building a particle from nothing
sections.body: New-particle formation starts with homogeneous nucleation: gas-phase molecules cluster tightly enough to form a stable liquid or solid embryo only about a nanometer across. The classic mechanism is binary nucleation of sulfuric acid (H2SO4, from oxidized SO2) and water vapor, because sulfuric acid's vapor pressure is so low that even trace concentrations (parts per trillion) supersaturate readily. Binary H2SO4-H2O theory alone, however, predicts nucleation rates far below what field campaigns actually observe in the boundary layer — often several orders of magnitude too low, on the order of 10^-4 to 1 cm^-3 s^-1 predicted versus roughly 1-10 cm^-3 s^-1 observed — which sent the field looking for a third ingredient. Ternary nucleation adds a base — ammonia or amines — that stabilizes the acid-water cluster electrostatically, boosting the rate by orders of magnitude even at trace mixing ratios.

sections.heading: What CLOUD at CERN settled and what it opened up
sections.body: The CLOUD chamber experiment at CERN, built to isolate nucleation chemistry under controlled temperature, humidity, and ion conditions, reported in Kirkby et al. (2011, Nature) that ammonia at about 100 parts per trillion by volume increased sulfuric acid nucleation rates by a factor of 100 to 1,000 over the binary case, and that ions (generated with a test particle beam mimicking galactic cosmic rays) further enhanced nucleation, though not enough by themselves to explain observed boundary-layer rates. A follow-up CLOUD result, Kirkby et al. (2016, Nature), showed that oxidized biogenic organic vapors from trees can nucleate new particles even without any sulfuric acid at all, and a related line of work, Almeida et al. (2013, Nature), demonstrated that amines are far more effective than ammonia at stabilizing sulfuric acid clusters, enhancing nucleation rates by orders of magnitude even at parts-per-trillion mixing ratios. Once a cluster survives to a few nanometers, it grows by condensation — vapor molecules (more sulfuric acid, ammonia, and increasingly, oxidized organics) sticking to its surface — up to the roughly 3-10 nanometer size where instruments can finally count it, and further growth into the accumulation mode (next lesson) is often organic-dominated. That organic growth is secondary organic aerosol, SOA: volatile organic compounds (isoprene, monoterpenes from vegetation; aromatics from combustion) get oxidized by OH, ozone, or nitrate radicals into lower-volatility products that condense onto existing particles or self-nucleate. Because SOA yield scales with both precursor emission and oxidant availability, biogenic new-particle-formation events are strongly seasonal and diurnal, typically peaking on warm, sunny afternoons when monoterpene emission and photochemical oxidant production are both highest.

lessons.workedExample: A field campaign near a pine forest records a burst of 3 nm particles at midday, growing to 30 nm by evening — a classic 'banana plot' of new-particle formation. A student explains it as 'the trees released particles.' A stronger explanation: monoterpenes from the pines were oxidized to low-volatility organic vapors, which condensed onto freshly nucleated sulfuric-acid-ammonia clusters, growing them past the Kelvin-effect size barrier where evaporation would otherwise dominate. Naming the two-step process (nucleation, then condensational growth) and the specific precursor chemistry is what separates this from a hand-wave about 'tree particles.'
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes new-particle formation to see if a student understands that a visible aerosol burst is actually a two-stage kinetic competition: nucleation rate versus growth rate, with tiny clusters constantly evaporating unless vapor condenses fast enough to outrun the Kelvin (curvature) effect. A weak answer says 'gases turned into particles.' A strong answer names the precursor (sulfuric acid, ammonia/amines, or biogenic organics), cites that binary H2SO4-H2O nucleation alone underpredicts observed rates, and explains growth as sequential condensation of low-volatility vapors onto the surviving cluster.

questions.prompt: Why does binary H2SO4-H2O nucleation alone fail to explain most observed boundary-layer new-particle-formation rates?

options.text: Sulfuric acid is too abundant to nucleate
It predicts rates far lower than observed; a stabilizing base or organics is usually needed
Water vapor never condenses in the boundary layer
Binary nucleation only happens above the stratosphere

explanations.a: Sulfuric acid's abundance is not the issue; its clusters are simply unstable without additional stabilization at typical atmospheric concentrations.
explanations.b: Correct — CLOUD chamber work showed binary nucleation underpredicts observed rates, and that ammonia, amines, or biogenic organics close most of the gap.
explanations.c: Water vapor readily participates in binary nucleation; the shortfall is in cluster stability, not water availability.
explanations.d: Boundary-layer nucleation is a near-surface tropospheric process, not a stratospheric one.

questions.prompt: What did Kirkby et al. (2011) report about ammonia's effect on sulfuric acid nucleation in the CLOUD chamber?

options.text: Ammonia at ~100 pptv increased nucleation rates by roughly 100-1000 times over binary nucleation
Ammonia suppressed nucleation entirely
Ammonia had no measurable effect at any concentration
Ammonia only mattered above the stratosphere

explanations.a: Correct — trace ammonia dramatically enhanced sulfuric acid nucleation rates in the CLOUD measurements.
explanations.b: The measured effect was a large enhancement, not suppression.
explanations.c: The whole point of the finding was a strong, measurable enhancement even at trace mixing ratios.
explanations.d: The CLOUD chamber results describe tropospheric boundary-layer relevant chemistry, not stratospheric conditions.

questions.prompt: Order the stages of new-particle formation from precursor gas to a detectable particle.

items.text: Precursor gases (e.g., SO2 oxidized to H2SO4) present in the atmosphere
Molecular clustering into a sub-nanometer embryo (nucleation)
Condensational growth of vapor onto the surviving cluster
Particle reaches ~3-10 nm and becomes instrument-detectable

questions.explanation: Formation begins with precursor vapors, proceeds through nucleation into an unstable sub-nanometer cluster, continues via condensational growth that outruns evaporation, and ends once the particle is large enough to count.

questions.prompt: What is secondary organic aerosol (SOA)?

options.text: Soot particles emitted directly from diesel exhaust
Sea salt particles coated in organic film
Low-volatility products of VOC oxidation that condense to form or grow particles
Volcanic ash mixed with sulfate

explanations.a: Diesel soot is primary black carbon, emitted directly as a particle, not SOA.
explanations.b: Organic coatings on sea salt are a mixing/aging phenomenon, not the definition of SOA.
explanations.c: Correct — SOA forms when VOCs are oxidized into lower-volatility products that condense onto particles or nucleate new ones.
explanations.d: Volcanic ash-sulfate mixtures are unrelated to organic vapor oxidation chemistry.

lessons.label: Size Distributions and the Modes

sections.heading: Four modes, one population
sections.body: Atmospheric aerosol size distributions are conventionally split into four modes by diameter. The nucleation mode covers freshly formed clusters below about 10 nanometers, born by the homogeneous nucleation described in the previous lesson. The Aitken mode, roughly 10-100 nanometers, holds particles that survived early growth but haven't yet aged into the accumulation mode; it's named for Aitken, the 19th-century Scottish physicist who pioneered particle counting with an expansion-chamber nuclei counter. The accumulation mode, roughly 100 nanometers to 1-2.5 micrometers, is where condensation, coagulation, and cloud processing pile mass onto particles faster than removal can strip them out — the name reflects that material 'accumulates' here because this size range sits in a lifetime maximum. The coarse mode, above about 2.5 micrometers, holds mechanically generated primary particles like sea salt and mineral dust, which settle out relatively fast under gravity. Each mode is typically parameterized as a lognormal with its own geometric standard deviation, commonly in the range of roughly 1.5 to 2.2, reflecting how tightly or loosely particle sizes cluster around that mode's geometric mean diameter — a narrower, freshly nucleated mode has a smaller geometric standard deviation than a broader, more processed accumulation mode.

sections.heading: Same particles, three different pictures
sections.body: A single population of particles looks completely different depending on how you weight the distribution. Plotted by number, nucleation and Aitken mode particles dominate overwhelmingly — a fresh nucleation burst can add tens of thousands of particles per cubic centimeter, on the order of 10^4 cm^-3, that are individually almost massless, versus a typical background number concentration closer to 10^3 cm^-3 between events. Plotted by surface area, the accumulation mode usually wins, because surface area scales with diameter squared and accumulation-mode particles are both numerous enough and large enough to maximize the product. Plotted by volume or mass, the picture shifts again toward the accumulation and coarse modes, since volume scales with diameter cubed and a single 5-micrometer dust grain outweighs well over a hundred million 10-nanometer clusters. Size distributions are usually plotted as dN/d(log Dp) versus log diameter — a lognormal representation — because atmospheric aerosol populations are well approximated by a sum of two or three lognormal modes, each described by a total number, a geometric mean diameter, and a geometric standard deviation. The accumulation mode's dominance of surface area is why it dominates light scattering (surface area sets scattering cross-section, covered in the optical-properties lesson) and, combined with its long atmospheric lifetime discussed in the removal lesson, why it dominates both visibility haze and cloud-condensation-nuclei supply.

lessons.workedExample: A monitoring station reports a number distribution peaking at 20 nm (huge count, tiny mass) right after a nucleation event, but the PM2.5 mass monitor barely moves. A student concludes 'the pollution event was minor.' The mass instrument is telling the truth about mass, but the number distribution is telling a different, equally true story: a burst of ultrafine particles that will, if they survive coagulation and grow into the accumulation mode over the next day, eventually show up as both haze and CCN. Citing dN/d(log Dp) versus dV/d(log Dp) for the same event, and explaining why they diverge, is the difference between reading one instrument and understanding the aerosol.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'which mode dominates your result' because the same aerosol population can support three contradictory-sounding headlines depending on whether you weight by number, surface, or mass, and a student who reports only one without naming which is being imprecise at best. A weak answer treats 'aerosol concentration' as a single number. A strong answer names the mode structure (nucleation/Aitken/accumulation/coarse), states which weighting (number, surface, or volume/mass) their instrument actually measures, and explains why the accumulation mode punches above its number count for optical and health-relevant effects.

questions.prompt: Match each aerosol mode to its approximate diameter range.

right.text: < 10 nm

questions.explanation: The four conventional modes run from freshly nucleated clusters below 10 nm, through the Aitken mode (10-100 nm), the accumulation mode (roughly 100 nm to 2.5 um), up to coarse mechanically generated particles above about 2.5 um.

questions.prompt: Why does the accumulation mode typically dominate a surface-area-weighted size distribution even though nucleation-mode particles are far more numerous?

options.text: Surface area scales with diameter squared, and accumulation-mode particles are large enough and numerous enough to win that weighting
Nucleation-mode particles have no measurable surface area
Surface area weighting is identical to number weighting
Accumulation-mode particles are always more numerous than nucleation-mode particles

explanations.a: Correct — the diameter-squared scaling of surface area lets fewer, larger accumulation-mode particles outweigh the vastly more numerous but tiny nucleation-mode particles.
explanations.b: All particles have surface area; the issue is how the different powers of diameter shift the weighting.
explanations.c: Surface area weighting and number weighting give different pictures precisely because of the diameter-squared factor.
explanations.d: Nucleation events can vastly outnumber accumulation-mode particles by count; the reversal happens because of the size-squared weighting, not because counts change.

questions.prompt: A single 5-micrometer dust grain can outweigh well over a hundred million 10-nanometer clusters. This illustrates that mass/volume-weighted distributions are dominated by:

options.text: Whichever mode has the most particles by count
Coarse and accumulation-mode particles, because volume scales with diameter cubed
Only the nucleation mode
An average of all modes weighted equally

explanations.a: Count-dominant modes (nucleation, Aitken) are usually mass-negligible, the opposite of what mass weighting shows.
explanations.b: Correct — the diameter-cubed scaling of volume means a comparatively small number of large particles can dominate total mass.
explanations.c: The nucleation mode is the least significant contributor to mass, not the dominant one.
explanations.d: Mass weighting is not an equal average; it is heavily skewed toward larger particles because of the cubic scaling.

questions.prompt: Why is dN/d(log Dp) versus log(diameter) the standard way to plot aerosol size distributions?

options.text: Because atmospheric aerosol populations are well approximated by a sum of lognormal modes spanning orders of magnitude in size
Because linear diameter axes are required by international standards
Because it removes the need to measure particle number
Because all aerosol particles are exactly the same size

explanations.a: Correct — a log-diameter axis compresses the several-orders-of-magnitude size range into a readable plot, and the lognormal form matches how each mode is actually distributed.
explanations.b: There is no such standards requirement; the lognormal convention reflects the physics and statistics of the distributions.
explanations.c: The distribution is a number-concentration plot; it does not eliminate the need to measure number.
explanations.d: Aerosol populations span nucleation through coarse modes, i.e., many different sizes, not one uniform size.

lessons.label: Aerosol Dynamics: Coagulation, Growth, and Aging

sections.heading: Coagulation: collisions that shrink number but not mass
sections.body: Once particles exist, Brownian motion constantly bumps them into one another, and when two particles collide they typically stick (coagulate) into one larger particle. This process was first put on a rigorous mathematical footing by Marian Smoluchowski in the 1910s, whose coagulation equation still underlies aerosol dynamics models today. Coagulation conserves total particle mass but reduces total particle number, and the rate is fastest for small, fast-diffusing particles colliding with larger ones — so a fresh nucleation-mode burst coagulates onto existing Aitken- and accumulation-mode particles far faster than two nucleation-mode particles coagulate with each other. This is a major reason new-particle-formation events often fail to survive to climate-relevant sizes in polluted air: a high background particle surface area acts as a coagulation sink that scavenges the fragile nucleation-mode clusters before they can grow. The timescale is short — a freshly nucleated 10 nanometer particle in a polluted urban background with roughly 10^4 particles per cubic centimeter typically has a coagulational lifetime of only tens of minutes to a few hours, which is why nucleation events are far more likely to survive to climate-relevant sizes in clean background air than in a polluted city center.

sections.heading: Growth by condensation and hygroscopic swelling
sections.body: Separately from coagulation, particles grow (or shrink) by condensation and evaporation of semi-volatile vapors — the same process that drives the growth described in the new-particle-formation lesson, continuing throughout a particle's life as sulfuric acid, ammonia, and oxidized organics partition onto its surface. A related but distinct growth process is hygroscopic: many aerosol species, especially ammonium sulfate and sea salt, are soluble, and as relative humidity rises they take up water. Below a species-specific deliquescence relative humidity (around 80% for ammonium sulfate, around 75% for sodium chloride), the particle stays a dry solid; above it, the solid abruptly dissolves into a saturated droplet and then continues swelling smoothly as RH rises further, described by a growth factor (wet diameter divided by dry diameter) that can reach 1.5-2 or more near saturation. Finally, aerosol composition itself evolves through 'aging': a freshly emitted black-carbon particle is often bare and irregular (fractal-like soot), but within hours to a day it acquires a coating of sulfate, nitrate, or organics from condensation and coagulation, which compacts its structure, raises its density, and changes both its optical absorption efficiency and its hygroscopicity — shifting its mixing state from externally mixed (separate particle types) toward internally mixed (multiple species combined in one particle).

lessons.workedExample: A biomass-burning plume emits bare black-carbon particles with low hygroscopicity, meaning they resist activating into cloud droplets and are poor CCN. A student tracking the plume downwind observes that after several hours its particles activate far more readily. The explanation is aging: condensation of secondary sulfate and organics coats the soot, and coagulation with the ambient accumulation-mode population adds more soluble mass, shifting the particles from externally mixed bare carbon toward an internally mixed, more hygroscopic particle — explaining the change in CCN activity without needing any new emission source.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes coagulation and aging because it is the mechanism that reconciles 'why don't emitted particles stay the way they were emitted' — a question that trips up students who treat aerosol composition as fixed at the source. A weak answer treats a particle's properties as constant from emission to measurement. A strong answer distinguishes coagulation (fewer, bigger particles, same total mass) from condensational and hygroscopic growth (same particle count, more mass or water per particle) from aging (changing composition and mixing state), and can say which one explains a specific downwind change in size, optical, or CCN behavior.

questions.prompt: What does Brownian coagulation conserve, and what does it reduce?

options.text: Conserves particle number, reduces total mass
Conserves total mass, reduces particle number
Reduces both mass and number
Conserves both mass and number

explanations.a: Coagulation does not destroy mass; two colliding particles' mass simply combines into one particle.
explanations.b: Correct — when particles stick together, total mass is unchanged but the number of separate particles drops, since two become one.
explanations.c: Mass is conserved in a coagulation event, only number decreases.
explanations.d: Number decreases every time two particles merge into one, so number is not conserved.

questions.prompt: Whose 1910s work provided the mathematical basis for aerosol coagulation still used in models today?

options.text: Smoluchowski
Aitken
Kirkby
Köhler

explanations.a: Correct — Smoluchowski derived the coagulation equation describing collision rates between particles of different sizes.
explanations.b: Aitken is known for the nuclei counter and the size mode named after him, not the coagulation equation.
explanations.c: Kirkby led the CLOUD nucleation experiments, a different topic from coagulation theory.
explanations.d: Köhler theory describes droplet activation and hygroscopic growth, not coagulation kinetics.

questions.prompt: What happens at a particle's deliquescence relative humidity?

options.text: The particle abruptly dissolves from a dry solid into a saturated droplet
The particle evaporates completely
The particle coagulates with all nearby particles
The particle's chemical composition changes into a different compound

explanations.a: Correct — above the deliquescence RH, a soluble solid particle takes up enough water to dissolve into a concentrated droplet, a sharp phase transition.
explanations.b: Deliquescence adds water rather than removing all mass from the particle.
explanations.c: Deliquescence is a phase-change response to humidity, not a collision process.
explanations.d: The chemical species (e.g., ammonium sulfate) stays the same; only its physical phase and water content change.

questions.prompt: Order the stages of black-carbon aging from fresh emission to a well-processed downwind particle.

items.text: Bare, fractal-like soot emitted from combustion
Condensation of sulfate/organic vapor forms a coating
Coating compacts the particle and raises its density
Particle becomes internally mixed with higher hygroscopicity

questions.explanation: Fresh soot is emitted bare and irregular; condensation deposits a soluble coating; that coating compacts the particle's structure; the end state is an internally mixed, more hygroscopic and CCN-active particle.

lessons.label: Removal: Dry and Wet Deposition

sections.heading: Dry deposition and the Greenfield gap
sections.body: Dry deposition removes particles by direct contact with the surface, without precipitation, and its efficiency is strongly size-dependent in a way that is not intuitive. Very small particles (below about 0.1 micrometer) deposit efficiently because Brownian diffusion moves them quickly across the thin boundary layer next to a surface. Very large particles (coarse mode, above a few micrometers) deposit efficiently too, but for the opposite reason: gravitational settling and inertial impaction pull them down and slam them into obstacles. Particles in between — roughly 0.1 to 1 micrometer, squarely the accumulation mode — are too large to diffuse quickly and too small to settle or impact efficiently, so their dry deposition velocity hits a minimum in this size range, typically down around 0.001-0.01 cm/s versus 1 cm/s or more for sub-10-nanometer or coarse particles. That minimum-efficiency region is called the Greenfield gap, a name borrowed by analogy from Greenfield's (1957) discovery of an equivalent minimum in below-cloud droplet-scavenging efficiency (covered in the wet-removal section below); the dry-deposition-velocity minimum itself is derived independently from resistance-model treatments of surface deposition such as Slinn's (1982) parameterization. It is a major reason accumulation-mode particles, discussed in the size-distribution lesson, persist longest in the atmosphere.

sections.heading: Wet removal and the resulting week-long lifetime
sections.body: Wet deposition removes particles via precipitation through two distinct pathways. Nucleation scavenging (in-cloud removal) happens when a particle acts as a cloud condensation nucleus, activates into a cloud droplet as described by Köhler theory, and then falls out with the droplet if the cloud precipitates — this is the dominant wet-removal pathway globally and it strongly favors accumulation-mode particles because they are the size range most efficient at CCN activation. Below-cloud scavenging (washout) is a secondary pathway in which falling raindrops or snow physically intercept and collect particles beneath the cloud base via impaction and diffusion; Greenfield (1957) was the first to characterize this pathway's own size-dependent collection minimum, the result that later lent its name to the dry-deposition Greenfield gap described above. Because the Greenfield gap slows dry removal and CCN activation strongly favors accumulation-mode particles for in-cloud removal, that same size range that dry deposition struggles to remove is also removed relatively inefficiently between precipitation events, giving accumulation-mode aerosol its characteristically long atmospheric residence time — commonly cited as roughly a week in the free troposphere, compared to hours to about a day for coarse particles that settle out under gravity, and just minutes to hours for the smallest ultrafine particles, which are rapidly lost to coagulation onto larger particles rather than to gravity or precipitation at all. That week-long lifetime is long enough for accumulation-mode aerosol to be transported across an ocean basin before it is finally rained out or diffuses to the surface.

lessons.workedExample: A student compares two pollution events: a dust storm and a persistent regional sulfate haze. The dust settles out within a day near its source, visible as a sharp concentration spike that decays fast, because coarse particles fall efficiently by gravity. The sulfate haze, made of accumulation-mode particles, persists for the better part of a week and is measured hundreds of kilometers downwind, because it sits in the Greenfield gap for dry deposition and requires precipitation and CCN activation to be scavenged. Explaining the different decay timescales by naming the size-dependent removal mechanism, rather than just 'dust is heavier,' is the mechanistic answer a judge is looking for.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about removal because atmospheric lifetime is what converts an emission rate into an actual atmospheric burden, and 'how long does your aerosol stay up' is a direct test of whether a student understands that removal efficiency is not uniform across sizes. A weak answer says 'gravity brings particles down eventually.' A strong answer names the Greenfield gap, explains why accumulation-mode particles are removed inefficiently by both dry deposition and below-cloud washout, and identifies in-cloud CCN activation and precipitation (nucleation scavenging) as the process that ultimately ends their roughly week-long lifetime.

questions.prompt: Why does dry deposition velocity have a minimum for accumulation-mode particles (~0.1-1 um)?

options.text: They are too large for efficient Brownian diffusion and too small for efficient gravitational settling or impaction
They are chemically inert and cannot stick to surfaces
They only exist above the boundary layer
Surfaces actively repel this size range electrostatically

explanations.a: Correct — this size range falls between the two efficient removal regimes (diffusion for very small particles, settling/impaction for very large ones), producing the Greenfield gap.
explanations.b: Chemical inertness is not the mechanism; the effect is purely about the size-dependent physics of transport to a surface.
explanations.c: Accumulation-mode particles are present within the boundary layer just like other sizes; their removal rate, not their presence, is what dips.
explanations.d: There is no electrostatic repulsion mechanism invoked in the Greenfield gap; it is a transport-efficiency minimum.

questions.prompt: Which researcher's 1957 work on particle collection by droplets gives the Greenfield gap its name?

options.text: Greenfield
Smoluchowski
Kirkby
Köhler

explanations.a: Correct — Greenfield's 1957 study of collection efficiency by water droplets identified the size-dependent minimum now named for him.
explanations.b: Smoluchowski's early-1900s work concerns particle-particle coagulation, a different process from droplet collection efficiency.
explanations.c: Kirkby is associated with the CLOUD nucleation experiments, not deposition/collection efficiency.
explanations.d: Köhler theory concerns droplet activation thermodynamics, not the size-dependent collection efficiency named the Greenfield gap.

questions.prompt: What is nucleation scavenging?

options.text: A particle acting as a CCN, activating into a cloud droplet, and being removed if the cloud precipitates
Raindrops falling below cloud base and physically intercepting particles
A particle evaporating completely in dry air
Gravitational settling of coarse dust particles

explanations.a: Correct — nucleation scavenging is the in-cloud pathway where CCN activation into a droplet leads to removal upon precipitation.
explanations.b: That description is below-cloud (washout) scavenging, a distinct pathway from nucleation scavenging.
explanations.c: Evaporation in dry air is not a removal-by-precipitation process.
explanations.d: Gravitational settling of coarse particles is part of dry deposition, not wet nucleation scavenging.

questions.prompt: Order these particle categories from shortest to longest typical atmospheric lifetime.

items.text: Coarse-mode dust (efficient gravitational settling)
Accumulation-mode sulfate/organic haze (Greenfield gap, needs precipitation)
Freshly nucleated ultrafine particles (fast diffusional loss/coagulation)

questions.explanation: Fresh ultrafine particles are lost within minutes to hours via rapid diffusion to surfaces or coagulation onto larger particles; coarse dust settles within roughly a day under gravity; accumulation-mode particles, caught in the Greenfield gap and requiring cloud processing to be scavenged, persist roughly a week.

lessons.label: PM2.5 and PM10: Composition and Exposure

sections.heading: An aerodynamic, not a physical, cutoff
sections.body: PM2.5 and PM10 are defined by aerodynamic diameter — the diameter of a spherical, unit-density particle that would settle and deposit in the respiratory tract the same way the actual particle does — not by a literal ruler measurement. PM10 admits particles with aerodynamic diameter below about 10 micrometers; PM2.5 (also called 'fine' particulate matter) admits those below about 2.5 micrometers. Because aerodynamic diameter depends on shape and density as well as physical size, a porous, low-density soot aggregate and a dense, compact salt crystal of the same physical size can fall into different aerodynamic bins. PM2.5 maps closely onto the accumulation mode from the size-distribution lesson, while the PM10-minus-PM2.5 'coarse' fraction is dominated by mechanically generated dust, pollen, and sea salt. This composition science — what PM2.5 and PM10 are actually made of — is distinct from the regulatory concentration limits set for those size cuts, which live in environmental and public-health standards rather than in the underlying atmospheric chemistry covered here.

sections.heading: Composition, mass closure, and why penetration depth matters
sections.body: PM2.5 mass is typically reconstructed from measured chemical components in a mass-closure calculation: sulfate, nitrate, and ammonium (secondary inorganic species, often traveling together as ammonium sulfate and ammonium nitrate salts), organic carbon and elemental carbon (from combustion and secondary organic aerosol), plus smaller contributions from crustal/dust elements and trace metals. A widely used framework, the IMPROVE equation developed for U.S. visibility monitoring, sums these species with density and hygroscopic-growth correction factors to reconstruct total fine-particle mass from speciated filter measurements, and a good mass closure (reconstructed mass close to gravimetrically measured mass) is a standard data-quality check. The reason the size cut itself matters for health is penetration depth: particles above about 10 micrometers are filtered out in the nose and upper airway; the PM10 fraction reaches the tracheobronchial region; PM2.5 penetrates deep into the alveolar region of the lungs, and the smallest ultrafine particles (well below PM2.5's cutoff) can cross into the bloodstream, which is why fine-particle composition science is the mechanistic partner to any exposure or health finding. The species mix behind that same PM2.5 mass number varies enormously by source: a wildfire-smoke sample is typically dominated by organic carbon and elemental carbon, often together making up 60-80% of the fine mass, with comparatively little sulfate or nitrate, while a traffic-corridor sample skews toward elemental carbon from diesel exhaust plus a larger secondary-nitrate contribution from vehicle NOx oxidation, and a regional summertime haze sample is often sulfate- and ammonium-dominated instead — three very different chemical fingerprints that can register as the same PM2.5 mass concentration.

lessons.workedExample: A monitoring station's PM2.5 mass filter reads 15 micrograms per cubic meter, and speciated analysis finds sulfate, nitrate, ammonium, organic carbon, and elemental carbon summing to 13.5 micrograms per cubic meter after applying standard density and hygroscopic-growth factors. That is a mass closure of 90%, a reasonable result. A weaker closure (say 60%) would signal a missing species (often unmeasured water or crustal material) or a measurement artifact, and a student should be able to say which component the discrepancy most likely points to, rather than reporting the closure percentage without diagnosing it.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes composition because 'PM2.5' as a single mass number hides very different underlying mixtures — a wildfire-smoke PM2.5 sample and a traffic-corridor PM2.5 sample can have the same mass concentration and wildly different sulfate/organic-carbon/elemental-carbon ratios with different health implications. A weak answer treats PM2.5 as one substance with a single toxicity. A strong answer names the size cut as an aerodynamic-diameter definition, breaks the mass into its major chemical components, and connects the fine-particle size range specifically to deep lung (alveolar) penetration rather than just saying 'PM2.5 is bad for you.'

questions.prompt: What does 'PM2.5' technically mean?

options.text: Particles with a physically measured diameter under 2.5 micrometers
Particles with an aerodynamic diameter under about 2.5 micrometers
Particles emitted from exactly 2.5 sources
Particles with a mass under 2.5 micrograms

explanations.a: The cutoff is defined by aerodynamic behavior, not a direct physical-size measurement, which is why shape and density matter.
explanations.b: Correct — PM2.5 is defined by aerodynamic diameter, the equivalent diameter of a unit-density sphere with the same settling behavior.
explanations.c: The '2.5' refers to a size cutoff in micrometers, not a count of sources.
explanations.d: PM2.5 refers to a size cutoff, not an individual particle mass threshold.

questions.prompt: Why can a porous soot aggregate and a dense salt crystal of similar physical size fall into different PM size bins?

options.text: Aerodynamic diameter depends on shape and density, not just physical size
Soot is always classified as coarse mode by definition
Salt crystals are never included in PM measurements
PM bins are assigned randomly by instrument calibration

explanations.a: Correct — because the size cut is aerodynamic, a low-density porous particle settles differently than a compact dense one of the same physical dimension, shifting its aerodynamic bin.
explanations.b: Soot is not defined by size class alone; its aerodynamic classification depends on its specific morphology and density.
explanations.c: Salt (sea salt) is a real and often significant PM component, particularly in coastal PM10.
explanations.d: Bin assignment follows physical settling behavior, not random calibration.

questions.prompt: Match each PM2.5 mass-closure component category to an example species or source.

right.text: Sulfate, nitrate, ammonium
Organic carbon and elemental carbon
Soil-derived elements (e.g., aluminum, silicon compounds)

questions.explanation: Mass-closure reconstruction sums secondary inorganic salts (sulfate/nitrate/ammonium), carbonaceous material (organic and elemental carbon), and a smaller crustal/dust contribution to reconstruct total measured PM2.5 mass.

questions.prompt: Why does the PM2.5 size cut matter specifically for respiratory penetration depth?

options.text: Particles above ~10 um are filtered in the nose/upper airway, while PM2.5-range particles penetrate to the deep alveolar region
All particle sizes penetrate to the same depth in the lungs
PM2.5 particles are too large to enter the respiratory tract at all
Penetration depth depends only on chemical composition, not size

explanations.a: Correct — larger particles are captured by upper-airway filtering, while the fine PM2.5 size range reaches deep into the alveolar region of the lungs.
explanations.b: Penetration depth is strongly size-dependent, which is exactly why the PM10/PM2.5 distinction exists.
explanations.c: PM2.5's small size is precisely what lets it bypass upper-airway filtering and reach deep lung tissue.
explanations.d: Size is the primary driver of penetration depth; composition affects toxicity once deposited, not how far the particle travels into the airway.

lessons.label: Aerosol Optical Properties

sections.heading: Scattering, absorption, and single-scattering albedo
sections.body: Light hitting an aerosol particle is either scattered (redirected without energy loss to the particle) or absorbed (converted to heat within the particle). Extinction, the total loss of a beam's intensity passing through an aerosol layer, is the sum of scattering and absorption. The ratio that separates the two is single-scattering albedo (SSA), scattering divided by extinction: an SSA of 1 means a purely scattering particle, an SSA near 0 means a strongly absorbing one. Composition sets SSA almost entirely. Sulfate and most secondary organic aerosol are essentially pure scatterers, with SSA close to 1, which is why sulfate haze cools the surface by reflecting sunlight back to space. Black carbon is the opposite extreme, with SSA commonly cited in the range of roughly 0.2-0.6 depending on size and mixing state, meaning it absorbs a large fraction of the light it intercepts, warms the surrounding air layer, and (especially once aged and coated, as in the aerosol-dynamics lesson) can even warm the climate system rather than cool it despite being a tiny fraction of global aerosol mass.

sections.heading: Size sets the scattering regime; the column integral is AOD
sections.body: Whether a particle scatters efficiently, and how that scattering depends on wavelength, is governed by the ratio of particle size to the wavelength of light. When the particle is much smaller than the wavelength (roughly a tenth or less), scattering follows the Rayleigh regime, where scattering efficiency scales steeply with wavelength to the inverse fourth power — the reason the clear sky is blue. When particle size is comparable to the wavelength, which is the regime most accumulation-mode aerosol actually falls into for visible light (~0.4-0.7 micrometers), the full Mie solution to Maxwell's equations is required, and scattering becomes much less wavelength-dependent and more forward-peaked. That wavelength dependence is captured empirically by the Ångström exponent, which describes how aerosol optical depth (AOD) falls off with increasing wavelength; a large Ångström exponent (roughly 2 or more) indicates a population dominated by small, sub-micron particles (typical of urban pollution and smoke), while a small or near-zero exponent indicates coarse-particle-dominated conditions like dust or sea salt, where scattering is nearly wavelength-independent. AOD itself is the vertical, column-integrated extinction due to aerosol — a single dimensionless number per wavelength, routinely retrieved by sun photometers (such as the AERONET network) and satellite instruments, that summarizes how much a full atmospheric column dims incoming sunlight. Globally and annually averaged, AOD at 550 nm is typically around 0.1-0.2, with much higher values (0.5 or more) over major dust and biomass-burning source regions during active episodes. Aging also changes the optical picture: once black carbon acquires a coating of sulfate or organics, the coating can act as a lens that focuses additional light onto the absorbing core, enhancing absorption by a factor of roughly 1.5 or more compared to the same amount of bare, uncoated black carbon.

lessons.workedExample: A sun photometer measures AOD of 0.35 at 440 nm and 0.15 at 870 nm on a hazy urban day. Computing the Ångström exponent from that pair of wavelengths gives a value near 1.2, indicating a fine-particle-dominated haze consistent with urban secondary sulfate and organic aerosol rather than dust. If the same station recorded AOD of 0.30 at 440 nm and 0.27 at 870 nm during a dust outbreak, the near-flat spectral dependence (Ångström exponent near 0.15) would instead point to coarse mineral dust in the Mie-to-geometric-optics regime. Reporting the exponent, not just the AOD value, is what lets a student infer particle size from a purely optical measurement.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about optical properties because AOD alone cannot say whether an aerosol layer is warming or cooling the surface — that sign flips entirely on composition and SSA, which most students conflate with mass concentration. A weak answer treats all aerosol as simply blocking sunlight. A strong answer distinguishes scattering from absorption, states that SSA (set by composition, e.g., sulfate near 1 versus black carbon near 0.2-0.6) determines whether the net radiative effect is cooling or warming, and can use the Ångström exponent from AOD measured at two wavelengths to infer whether the population is fine or coarse.

questions.prompt: What does single-scattering albedo (SSA) near 1 indicate about a particle?

options.text: It is a nearly pure scatterer, absorbing very little light
It absorbs almost all incoming light
It has no optical effect at all
It is always a coarse-mode particle

explanations.a: Correct — SSA is scattering divided by extinction, so a value near 1 means nearly all extinguished light was scattered rather than absorbed.
explanations.b: An SSA near 0, not near 1, would indicate strong absorption.
explanations.c: An SSA of 1 still means the particle extinguishes light (via scattering); it is not optically inert.
explanations.d: SSA reflects composition/absorptivity, not particle size class.

questions.prompt: Why does black carbon's low SSA (roughly 0.2-0.6) make it a warming aerosol despite being a small fraction of global aerosol mass?

options.text: A low SSA means it absorbs a large share of intercepted light and converts it to heat rather than reflecting it
Low SSA means it has an unusually large physical size
Low SSA means it stays in the atmosphere longer than any other aerosol
Low SSA has no relationship to radiative warming or cooling

explanations.a: Correct — the low SSA directly reflects strong absorption, which heats the surrounding air layer rather than reflecting sunlight, giving black carbon a warming rather than cooling effect.
explanations.b: SSA describes absorptivity, not physical size.
explanations.c: SSA is an optical property and is not what sets atmospheric lifetime.
explanations.d: SSA directly determines the balance between scattering (cooling) and absorption (warming), so it is central to the radiative sign, not unrelated to it.

questions.prompt: A large Ångström exponent (~2) derived from AOD at two wavelengths most likely indicates:

options.text: A population dominated by small, sub-micron (fine-mode) particles
A population dominated by coarse dust or sea salt
An atmosphere with no aerosol at all
A particle population entirely in the Rayleigh regime for gas molecules

explanations.a: Correct — steep wavelength dependence (high Ångström exponent) is characteristic of fine, sub-micron particles like urban pollution or smoke.
explanations.b: Coarse-dominated populations (dust, sea salt) show a near-flat spectral dependence and a low Ångström exponent, the opposite pattern.
explanations.c: A defined Ångström exponent requires measurable AOD at both wavelengths, so it implies aerosol is present, not absent.
explanations.d: The Ångström exponent describes aerosol particles in the Mie-adjacent regime, not gas-molecule Rayleigh scattering.

questions.prompt: Order these steps from raw sun-photometer measurement to inferring aerosol particle size.

items.text: Measure AOD at two distinct wavelengths
Compute the Ångström exponent from the wavelength dependence of AOD
Compare the exponent's magnitude to fine- vs coarse-mode reference behavior
Infer whether the aerosol population is fine-particle-dominated or coarse-particle-dominated

questions.explanation: The workflow starts with multi-wavelength AOD measurement, uses that spectral dependence to compute the Ångström exponent, compares its magnitude against known fine/coarse behavior, and concludes which size regime dominates the sampled aerosol.

units.label: Tropospheric Ozone and Photochemical Smog

lessons.label: The Leighton Relationship and Photostationary State

sections.heading: A three-reaction merry-go-round
sections.body: Tropospheric ozone chemistry starts with a cycle that, on its own, makes no net ozone at all. Sunlight below about 420 nm splits nitrogen dioxide: NO2 + hv -> NO + O(3P). The freed oxygen atom is so reactive it combines almost instantly with the abundant O2 in air, with a third body M carrying off excess energy: O(3P) + O2 + M -> O3 + M. That ozone molecule then reacts with the NO just produced in the first step, regenerating NO2: NO + O3 -> NO2 + O2. Run all three continuously and you get a closed loop -- NO2 photolyzes, ozone forms, ozone titrates back to NO2 -- with no net change in the total oxidant supply. Philip Leighton described this null cycle formally in his 1961 book on photochemical air pollution, and the relationship now carries his name.

sections.heading: The photostationary-state equation
sections.body: Because the three reactions run fast relative to how quickly NOx concentrations change over an hour, the system settles into a photostationary state where ozone production from photolysis balances ozone loss to NO titration. Setting the forward and reverse rates equal gives the Leighton relationship: [O3] = j(NO2)[NO2] / (k[NO]), where j(NO2) is the NO2 photolysis rate constant (set by sun angle and cloudiness) and k is the rate constant for NO + O3. Equivalently, the ratio [NO2]/[NO] tracks k[O3]/j(NO2). The equation is a diagnostic, not a source of new ozone: measure any three of the four quantities and the fourth is predictable, and field campaigns have used exactly this check since the 1970s to cross-validate fast-response NO, NO2, and O3 instruments. When observed ozone exceeds what the relationship predicts from NO and NO2 alone, that excess is the signature of an additional oxidant supply -- peroxy radicals converting NO to NO2 without consuming ozone -- which is the subject of the next lesson.

sections.heading: Why titration, not production, dominates near fresh NOx
sections.body: The practical consequence shows up at street level: air heavy with fresh NO from tailpipes has ozone concentrations well below the regional background, because the NO + O3 reaction is consuming ozone as fast as it arrives. Ozone monitors near busy roads often read lower than suburban monitors nearby for exactly this reason -- a pattern sometimes mistaken for cleaner air when it is really just active titration of a locally produced pollutant. The Leighton cycle explains this local dip perfectly; a closed null cycle has no mechanism to raise the total oxidant pool, so it cannot by itself explain the buildup of ozone to unhealthy levels that shows up downwind of a city by afternoon.

lessons.workedExample: A monitoring station at noon reports [NO2] = 20 ppb, [NO] = 4 ppb, j(NO2) = 0.008 per second, and k(NO+O3) at its typical daytime value near 298 K. Plugging these into [O3] = j(NO2)[NO2] / (k[NO]) after converting ppb to molecules per cm^3 predicts the ozone level consistent with a pure photostationary state. If the station's actual ozone reading instead runs 40% higher than this prediction, that gap is the tell-tale sign of peroxy radicals (RO2, HO2) also converting NO to NO2 -- an oxidant pathway the three-reaction Leighton cycle does not include, and the mechanism the next lesson builds out.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'if NO2 photolysis makes ozone, why doesn't the Leighton cycle alone explain smog?' is testing whether a student actually worked through the mass balance rather than memorizing 'sunlight plus NOx makes ozone.' A weak answer restates the three reactions without noticing they form a closed loop. A strong answer states plainly that the cycle is a null cycle -- one ozone destroyed for every one made -- and names the missing ingredient (peroxy radicals converting NO to NO2 without touching ozone) as the actual source of net production, which signals the student understands ozone build-up requires breaking the NO-O3 titration step, not just running the photolysis step harder.

questions.prompt: Why does the three-reaction Leighton cycle (NO2 photolysis, O + O2 -> O3, NO + O3 -> NO2) produce zero net ozone by itself?

options.text: Because NO2 photolysis is too slow to matter at ground level
Because the ozone made in step two is consumed again in step three, closing a loop with no net oxidant gain
Because O(3P) atoms are too unstable to ever react with O2
Because NO and NO2 cannot coexist in sunlight

explanations.a: j(NO2) is fast enough during daylight to matter a great deal -- the issue is not photolysis rate but what happens to the ozone produced.
explanations.b: Correct -- every ozone molecule made by O + O2 is immediately available to react with the NO released by the same photolysis event, so the cycle is self-titrating and adds no net oxidant.
explanations.c: O(3P) is highly reactive and combines with O2 almost instantly; that step is not the bottleneck.
explanations.d: NO and NO2 coexist constantly in daylight air -- their ratio is exactly what the photostationary-state equation tracks.

questions.prompt: A researcher measures [NO], [NO2], and j(NO2) and finds the observed [O3] is substantially higher than the Leighton relationship predicts. What does this gap indicate?

options.text: The instruments must be miscalibrated, since the Leighton relationship always holds exactly
Some process besides O3 + NO is converting NO to NO2, adding oxidant the simple cycle doesn't account for
j(NO2) was measured at night
The air mass has no NOx at all

explanations.a: Instrument error is possible in any measurement, but the well-documented, systematic direction of this gap in NOx-VOC-rich air points to real chemistry, not noise.
explanations.b: Correct -- peroxy radicals (RO2, HO2) can convert NO to NO2 without consuming ozone, which lets ozone accumulate beyond what the three-reaction null cycle alone predicts.
explanations.c: j(NO2) is essentially zero at night, which would predict near-zero photostationary ozone, not an excess.
explanations.d: The scenario requires measurable NO and NO2 to compute the Leighton prediction in the first place.

questions.prompt: Put these three reactions of the Leighton cycle in the order they occur, starting from sunlight hitting NO2.

items.text: NO + O3 -> NO2 + O2
NO2 + hv -> NO + O(3P)

questions.explanation: Photolysis splits NO2 into NO and an oxygen atom first; that atom combines with O2 to form ozone second; the newly formed ozone then reacts with the NO from the first step to regenerate NO2 third, closing the loop.

questions.prompt: Match each Leighton-relationship quantity to what it physically represents.

right.text: How fast sunlight splits NO2 into NO and O(3P); depends on sun angle and cloud cover
Tracks k[O3]/j(NO2) in the photostationary state
Governs how quickly ozone titrates back to NO2 once NO is present
