The most frequently observed speed, the mode, sits below the mean and is given by v_mode = c x ((k-1)/k)^(1/k); for the coastal worked-example site (k = 1.9, c = 7.8 m/s) that works out to a mode near 5.3 m/s, well under the roughly 6.9 m/s mean, a concrete illustration of the right-skew described qualitatively above.

sections.heading: Rayleigh: the one-parameter shortcut
sections.body: Setting k = 2 collapses the Weibull into the Rayleigh distribution, f(v) = (2v/c^2) exp(-(v/c)^2), which needs only the mean speed to fully specify, since mean = c times the square root of pi over two, about 0.886c. Because full time-series measurements are not always available, IEC 61400-1 and many early resource assessments default to Rayleigh as a reasonable global-average shape whenever only the long-term mean speed is known. It systematically understates variability at gusty sites, where true k often runs 1.5-2, and overstates it at steady sites, where k frequently reaches 2.5-3.5, so a Rayleigh-only estimate is a starting approximation, not a substitute for fitting a real k to measured data whenever an actual anemometer record exists.

lessons.workedExample: A met mast logs one year of 10-minute wind speeds at 50 m. Binning them into a histogram shows a long right tail: most 10-minute periods sit between 4 and 9 m/s, but a handful exceed 20 m/s during winter storms. Fitting a Weibull curve to that histogram yields k = 1.9 and c = 7.8 m/s, a fairly broad shape consistent with a mid-latitude coastal site influenced by frontal storms. A nearby ridge site with the same 7 m/s mean speed but steadier synoptic-scale flow fits k = 3.4 and c = 7.6 m/s, a narrower curve with fewer calms and fewer extreme gusts. Even though both sites report almost the same mean, their k values tell an engineer the coastal site will see more high-wind cut-out events and more near-zero output hours.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks why fit a Weibull instead of just reporting mean and standard deviation is testing whether the student understands that turbine output depends on the full shape of the speed distribution, not just its center, because power scales with the cube of speed and a handful of high-speed hours contribute disproportionate energy. A weak answer says Weibull is the standard wind curve without explaining k or c. A strong answer names the shape parameter's physical meaning, cites a fitted k for the actual dataset, and explains why two sites with equal means can have very different energy yields depending on how peaked or spread their distributions are.

questions.prompt: In the Weibull pdf f(v) = (k/c)(v/c)^(k-1)exp(-(v/c)^k), what does a low shape parameter k (around 1.5) typically indicate about a site?

options.text: Very steady winds clustered near one speed
A broad distribution with more calm periods and occasional strong gusts
That negative wind speeds occur regularly
That the scale parameter c must equal the mean speed exactly

explanations.a: That describes a high k, not a low one; steady sites have narrow, peaked distributions.
explanations.b: Correct — low k produces a broad, right-skewed shape with many near-calm hours and occasional strong gusts, typical of storm-influenced coastal sites.
explanations.c: The Weibull distribution is defined only for v >= 0, so it never assigns probability to negative speeds regardless of k.
explanations.d: c is close to but not equal to the mean; the mean equals c times a Gamma-function factor that depends on k.

questions.prompt: Which value of the shape parameter k reduces the Weibull distribution to the Rayleigh distribution?

explanations.a: k = 1 gives an exponential-shaped distribution, not Rayleigh.
explanations.b: k = 1.5 is a common broad-site value but does not simplify to the named Rayleigh form.
explanations.c: Correct — setting k = 2 collapses the two-parameter Weibull into the one-parameter Rayleigh distribution.
explanations.d: k = 3 describes a narrower, more peaked distribution, not the Rayleigh case.

questions.prompt: Match each site description to its approximate Weibull shape parameter.

left.text: IEC default resource estimate using only the mean speed

right.text: k roughly 1.5-1.9
k roughly 3-3.5
k = 2.0 exactly (Rayleigh assumption)

questions.explanation: Gusty, storm-driven coastal sites tend toward a low k with a broad spread; steady plateau or trade-wind sites tend toward a high k with a narrow spread; the IEC/Rayleigh default fixes k at exactly 2 as a global-average compromise when no site-specific shape data exist.

questions.prompt: Order the steps in fitting a Weibull curve to a site's measured wind data.

items.text: Record wind speed time series from an anemometer
Bin the recorded speeds into a histogram
Fit shape (k) and scale (c) parameters to the histogram
Compare the fitted Weibull curve against the observed histogram shape

questions.explanation: Fitting requires raw measured data first, then binning it into a histogram, then estimating k and c from that histogram, and finally checking the fitted curve against the data it was fit to.

lessons.label: Mean Wind vs the Energy-Containing Speed

sections.heading: Mean speed from the Weibull parameters
sections.body: Once a Weibull distribution is fit to a site, its mean wind speed follows directly: mean = c times Gamma(1 + 1/k), where Gamma is the Gamma function, the continuous extension of the factorial (Gamma(n) = (n-1)! for integers). For k = 2, the Rayleigh case, Gamma(1.5) is the square root of pi over two, about 0.886, so mean = 0.886c. For k = 1, the distribution flattens toward an exponential shape and Gamma(2) = 1, so mean = c exactly. This single formula is why analysts can report a site's average speed the moment they know k and c, without re-averaging raw data.

sections.heading: Why the cube dominates: energy is not linear in speed
sections.body: The kinetic energy flux carried by moving air scales as v^3, not v, because it is the product of the mass flow rate (proportional to v) and the specific kinetic energy per unit mass (proportional to v^2). That cubic relationship means small numbers of high-speed hours contribute disproportionately to total annual energy, and it also means mean(v^3) is not equal to mean(v)^3. Jensen's inequality guarantees mean(v^3) is always greater than or equal to mean(v)^3 for any variable with real spread, and the gap widens as the distribution gets broader — exactly the situation a low-k, spread-out Weibull describes.

sections.heading: The energy pattern factor Ke
sections.body: That gap is captured by the energy pattern factor, Ke = mean(v^3) / mean(v)^3, a dimensionless number describing how much energy is hiding in a distribution's tail relative to what its bare mean speed would suggest. For the Rayleigh case (k = 2), Ke works out to about 1.91. Broader distributions (lower k) push Ke higher; narrower, more peaked distributions (higher k) push Ke down toward 1. Using mean-speed-cubed as a stand-in for mean available power, instead of correcting it by Ke, is the single most common error in a back-of-envelope wind energy estimate, and at a typical Rayleigh-like site it understates available energy by nearly a factor of two. In general, Ke(k) = Gamma(1 + 3/k) / [Gamma(1 + 1/k)]^3, the closed form whose k = 2 special case produces the Rayleigh value of 1.91 above. At a broader, low-k site with k = 1.5, that formula gives Ke of about 2.7 — noticeably higher than Rayleigh's 1.91 — meaning a mean-speed-cubed estimate at such a site would understate available energy by nearly a factor of three, not just two.

lessons.workedExample: A site is well-described by a Rayleigh distribution (k = 2) with scale c = 8 m/s. Its mean speed is 0.886 x 8 = 7.09 m/s. A naive estimate cubes that mean directly: 7.09^3 = 356 m^3/s^3. But the true mean(v^3), computed as c^3 x Gamma(2.5) = 512 x 1.329 = 681 m^3/s^3, is nearly double. The ratio, 681/356 = 1.91, is exactly the Rayleigh energy pattern factor. Anyone who estimated power from the mean speed alone at this site would have understated the available energy by almost half.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this specific point because using mean wind speed cubed to estimate available power is the single most common mistake in student and even amateur industry wind-energy estimates, routinely understating yield by roughly half at typical Rayleigh-shaped sites. A weak answer treats mean speed as if it were interchangeable with mean power. A strong answer names the energy pattern factor Ke, explains it via the cube law and Jensen's inequality, and shows the correction actually applied to the site's own numbers rather than just gesturing at 'the wind is variable.'

questions.prompt: Given a Weibull fit with shape k and scale c, what is the correct formula for the mean wind speed?

options.text: mean = c
mean = c x Gamma(1 + 1/k)
mean = k x c
mean = c / k

explanations.a: mean = c only in the special case k = 1; in general it depends on k through the Gamma function.
explanations.b: Correct — the Weibull mean is c times Gamma(1 + 1/k), which reduces to about 0.886c when k = 2.
explanations.c: There is no such linear relationship between k and c that gives the mean this way.
explanations.d: Dividing c by k is not the correct closed-form expression for the Weibull mean.

questions.prompt: Why is mean(v^3) always greater than or equal to mean(v)^3 for a real wind-speed distribution with spread?

options.text: Because wind speed is always measured in whole numbers
Because of Jensen's inequality applied to the convex function v^3, which makes the gap grow with the distribution's spread
Because air density changes with wind speed
Because the Weibull distribution is only defined for k = 2

explanations.a: Measurement precision or rounding has nothing to do with this mathematical relationship.
explanations.b: Correct — cubing is a convex operation, so by Jensen's inequality the average of the cubes exceeds the cube of the average whenever the underlying values vary, and more spread means a bigger gap.
explanations.c: Air density is treated as constant in this comparison; it does not drive the mean(v^3) vs mean(v)^3 gap.
explanations.d: The Weibull distribution is defined for any k > 0; k = 2 is just the Rayleigh special case.

questions.prompt: Match each Weibull shape to its approximate energy pattern factor Ke.

right.text: Ke close to 1 (little hidden tail energy)
Ke about 1.91
Ke noticeably above 1.91

questions.explanation: Ke rises as the distribution broadens (lower k) because more of the total energy sits in a long high-speed tail relative to the mean, and it falls toward 1 as the distribution narrows (higher k) because there is little tail left to hide energy in.

questions.prompt: Order these approaches to estimating a site's annual energy from least to most accurate.

items.text: Cube the mean wind speed only
Multiply mean-speed-cubed by the site's energy pattern factor Ke
Integrate v^3 directly over the site's measured wind-speed distribution or time series

questions.explanation: Cubing the bare mean speed ignores distribution spread entirely and understates energy the most; multiplying by Ke corrects for that spread using a single summary factor; directly integrating v^3 over the real distribution or raw time series uses no shortcut and is the most accurate.

lessons.label: Wind Power Density

sections.heading: The physics: kinetic energy flux through a disk
sections.body: Air moving at speed v through a cross-sectional area A carries a kinetic energy flux P = 0.5 x rho x A x v^3, the product of the mass flow rate (rho x A x v) and the kinetic energy per unit mass (0.5 v^2). Dividing by area gives the wind power density, P/A = 0.5 x rho x v^3, in watts per square meter. This is the theoretical power available in the wind stream itself, before any machine extracts energy from it; a real turbine can capture at most about 59.3 percent of this figure under the Betz limit, but that ceiling is a separate, turbine-side question — power density is purely a resource-side metric used to characterize a site independent of any specific hardware.

sections.heading: Standard air density and why the time-averaged value matters
sections.body: Standard air density, rho = 1.225 kg/m^3, is defined at 15 degrees Celsius and sea-level pressure (1013.25 hPa) under the ICAO standard atmosphere. Because wind is gusty and variable, the meaningful site metric is not P/A evaluated at the mean speed but the time-averaged mean power density, 0.5 x rho x mean(v^3), which folds in the energy pattern factor from the cube-law relationship: mean(v^3) = c^3 x Gamma(1 + 3/k) for a fitted Weibull distribution with shape k and scale c. This matters even more once measurement height enters the picture: wind speed climbs with height above ground, so a v^3 measured at hub height differs sharply from one measured at a shorter reference mast. Because turbine hub heights have grown well past the 50 m reference used to define the classification below — many modern turbines sit at 80-120 m — the wind speed at hub height is usually higher than at 50 m due to shear, following a power-law profile v(z) = v_ref x (z/z_ref)^alpha with a shear exponent alpha commonly around 0.14 over open, low-roughness terrain. A site rated Class 4 using 50 m data can look meaningfully stronger once its actual hub-height power density is recomputed.

sections.heading: NREL's seven-class wind power scheme
sections.body: To let developers grade sites on a common scale, the Solar Energy Research Institute (SERI, the predecessor to today's National Renewable Energy Laboratory, NREL) and Pacific Northwest Laboratory published a seven-class wind power classification in the 1986 Wind Energy Resource Atlas of the United States, based on mean power density at a 50 m reference height: Class 1 is below 200 W/m^2 (mean speed below about 5.6 m/s), rising through Class 4 at 400-500 W/m^2 (about 7.0-7.5 m/s), up to Class 7 above 800 W/m^2 (above about 8.8 m/s). Utility-scale wind development traditionally targeted Class 3 and above, roughly 300 W/m^2 or 6.4 m/s and up, as the threshold of economic viability, though modern taller towers and larger rotors have since made many Class 2 sites viable as well.

lessons.workedExample: Using the Rayleigh site from the previous lesson (k = 2, c = 8 m/s, mean(v^3) = 681 m^3/s^3), the mean wind power density is P/A = 0.5 x 1.225 x 681 = 417 W/m^2. Checked against the NREL scheme, 417 W/m^2 falls inside the Class 4 band (400-500 W/m^2), a solid but not top-tier wind resource. If the same site instead fit a narrower distribution with k = 3.4 at the same c = 8 m/s (roughly the same 7 m/s mean), mean(v^3) would be closer to c^3 x Gamma(1 + 3/3.4), lowering both Ke and the resulting power density — a reminder that two sites with the same mean speed do not automatically earn the same class rating.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks for the computed power density and its NREL class because that pairing is the standard way to state 'how good is this site' in the wind industry, and it forces the student to show real arithmetic rather than an impression. A weak answer cites only the mean wind speed as if it were the site quality metric. A strong answer computes the mean power density from the fitted distribution's mean(v^3), states the units correctly as W/m^2, and places the number in the correct NREL class band with the corresponding speed range.

questions.prompt: What is the standard (ICAO, sea-level, 15C) air density value used in wind power density calculations?

explanations.a: 1.0 kg/m^3 is not the standard reference value used in the industry.
explanations.b: Correct — 1.225 kg/m^3 is the ICAO standard atmosphere density at sea level and 15C, the reference used for turbine power curve certification.
explanations.c: 1.5 kg/m^3 overstates standard sea-level air density.
explanations.d: 9.8 corresponds to the acceleration of gravity in m/s^2, not an air density value.

questions.prompt: Which expression correctly gives wind power density?

options.text: P/A = rho x v
P/A = 0.5 x rho x v^2
P/A = 0.5 x rho x v^3
P/A = rho x v^3

explanations.a: This omits both the 0.5 factor and the cube on speed; it describes momentum flux, not power.
explanations.b: This is the kinetic energy per unit mass form, not the power flux through an area, and it uses the wrong power of v.
explanations.c: Correct — power density is the product of mass flow rate (rho x A x v) and specific kinetic energy (0.5 v^2), divided by area, giving 0.5 x rho x v^3.
explanations.d: This is missing the 0.5 factor from the kinetic energy term.

questions.prompt: Match each NREL wind power class to its approximate mean power density band at 50 m.

right.text: Below 200 W/m^2
Above 800 W/m^2

questions.explanation: The NREL seven-class scheme spans below 200 W/m^2 for Class 1 up through above 800 W/m^2 for Class 7, with Class 4 sitting in the middle band at 400-500 W/m^2.

questions.prompt: In the worked example, a Rayleigh site with mean(v^3) = 681 m^3/s^3 was computed to have a mean power density of about 417 W/m^2. Which NREL class does that fall into?

options.text: Class 2
Class 3
Class 4
Class 6

explanations.a: Class 2 covers 200-300 W/m^2, well below the computed 417 W/m^2.
explanations.b: Class 3 covers 300-400 W/m^2; 417 W/m^2 is just above that band.
explanations.c: Correct — 417 W/m^2 falls inside the Class 4 band of 400-500 W/m^2.
explanations.d: Class 6 requires 600-800 W/m^2, far above the computed value.

lessons.label: Fitting Weibull Parameters

sections.heading: Method of moments and maximum likelihood
sections.body: The method of moments (MoM) estimates k and c from the sample mean and standard deviation: the coefficient of variation, stdev/mean, is inverted numerically to solve for k via the Gamma-function relationship, and c then follows from mean/Gamma(1+1/k). It is fast and simple but can be biased at low k, where the distribution is most skewed. Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) instead iteratively finds the (k, c) pair that maximizes the probability of observing the actual recorded samples, using an approach like Newton-Raphson to solve the resulting pair of nonlinear equations. MLE is statistically more efficient and is the default in most modern wind software, but it is more sensitive to data gaps and to autocorrelation between consecutive readings, since it implicitly assumes independent samples.

sections.heading: The energy-conserving method and the graphical log-log method
sections.body: WAsP (the Wind Atlas Analysis and Application Program, developed at Denmark's Riso National Laboratory starting in the 1980s) instead fits an energy-conserving Weibull: it forces the fitted curve to reproduce the site's true mean(v^3), not just its mean speed, because accurate energy yield is the entire purpose of a wind atlas. A separate, older technique is the graphical log-log method: taking the double log of the Weibull survival function, ln(-ln(1-F(v))) = k ln(v) - k ln(c), produces a straight line when plotted against ln(v). A linear regression through binned cumulative-probability data then gives k directly as the slope and c from the intercept, which makes it a fast visual diagnostic even before running dedicated fitting software.

sections.heading: Goodness of fit, and when one Weibull isn't enough
sections.body: Fit quality can be checked with the R^2 of the graphical log-log regression, or with a chi-square or Kolmogorov-Smirnov test comparing the fitted CDF to the empirical one. In practice, an R^2 above about 0.98-0.99 on the log-log regression is considered a good unimodal fit; this lesson's own monsoon-site worked example below scored only 0.83, the signal that prompted splitting the record into two regimes. A single Weibull curve breaks down at sites with two physically distinct wind regimes superimposed: coastal locations with a strong diurnal sea-breeze cycle layered on synoptic-scale flow, or monsoon-influenced regions where wet-season and dry-season winds differ sharply, both producing a bimodal, two-humped histogram that no unimodal Weibull can fit well. Calm-dominated records, such as sheltered inland valleys with many near-zero-wind hours, likewise violate the smooth near-zero behavior the Weibull pdf assumes. Analysts handle these cases by fitting a mixture of two separate Weibull distributions, one per regime, weighted by the fraction of time each regime occurs.

lessons.workedExample: An analyst has one year of 10-minute data from a monsoon-affected site. A single Weibull fit gives an R^2 of only 0.83 on the log-log regression, with visible curvature, and the raw histogram clearly shows two humps: one near 3 m/s and one near 9 m/s. Splitting the record into monsoon months (40 percent of hours) and dry months (60 percent) and fitting each separately gives k=3.0, c=9.5 m/s for the monsoon regime and k=2.2, c=3.4 m/s for the dry regime. Combining the two as a weighted mixture raises the fit quality sharply and gives a far more accurate annual energy estimate than forcing one curve through both humps.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe fitting-method choice because it reveals whether a student simply clicked 'fit Weibull' in software or actually understands what the fit optimizes for. A weak answer cannot say which method was used or why, and shows a single smooth curve laid over a visibly bimodal histogram without comment. A strong answer names the method (method of moments, MLE, or WAsP's energy-conserving approach), explains why matching mean(v^3) matters more than matching mean speed for yield estimates, and recognizes and corrects for a site where the unimodal Weibull assumption breaks down.

questions.prompt: What does the method of moments use to estimate the Weibull parameters k and c?

options.text: The sample mean and standard deviation of the wind-speed data
The single highest wind speed ever recorded
The elevation and latitude of the site
The turbine's rated power curve

explanations.a: Correct — the coefficient of variation (stdev/mean) is inverted numerically to solve for k, and c follows from the mean and the fitted k.
explanations.b: The single maximum value belongs to extreme-value analysis, not the method-of-moments fit to the whole distribution.
explanations.c: Elevation and latitude affect air density and climate but are not inputs to the moment-matching equations.
explanations.d: The turbine's power curve is unrelated to fitting the resource's speed distribution.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes WAsP's energy-conserving Weibull fit from a simple mean-speed fit?

options.text: It ignores the shape parameter k entirely
It forces the fitted curve to match the site's true mean(v^3), not just its mean speed
It only works for k = 2 (Rayleigh) sites
It replaces the Weibull distribution with a normal distribution

explanations.a: WAsP's method still fits both k and c; it does not discard the shape parameter.
explanations.b: Correct — because energy yield is what a wind atlas exists to predict, WAsP's fit is constrained to reproduce the site's actual mean(v^3) rather than only matching the mean speed.
explanations.c: The energy-conserving approach applies for any k, not only the Rayleigh special case.
explanations.d: WAsP still fits a Weibull distribution; it does not switch families to a normal distribution.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the graphical log-log Weibull fitting method.

items.text: Compute the empirical cumulative distribution function from binned speed data
Transform with ln(-ln(1-F(v))) on the y-axis and ln(v) on the x-axis
Fit a straight line by linear regression
Read k from the slope and back out c from the intercept

questions.explanation: The empirical CDF must be built from the data first, then transformed into the linearizing double-log form, then fit with a regression line, and only then can k and c be read off from the slope and intercept.

questions.prompt: Match each site type to the reason a single unimodal Weibull fit fails there.

left.text: Coastal site with a strong diurnal sea breeze

right.text: Two physically distinct diurnal wind regimes superimposed, producing a bimodal histogram
Sharply different wet-season and dry-season wind regimes
Excess near-zero-wind hours that violate the smooth Weibull shape near v = 0

questions.explanation: Sea-breeze sites mix two daily flow regimes into one bimodal histogram, monsoon sites mix two seasonal regimes, and calm-dominated valleys pile up too many near-zero hours for the Weibull's smooth low-speed behavior — all three require a mixture model rather than one Weibull curve.

lessons.label: Extreme Winds & Return Periods

sections.heading: Resource statistics vs design statistics
sections.body: Everything in the earlier lessons — Weibull fits, mean(v^3), power density — describes the long-term average energy a site can produce, drawn from the bulk of a 10-minute or hourly wind-speed record. Structural design asks a completely different question: not how much energy the site typically delivers, but how strong the worst storm it will ever see is likely to be, drawn instead from the extreme tail of the record. A turbine perfectly sited for energy yield can still fail structurally in a rare storm if its blades, tower, and foundation are not rated for the site's extreme gust climate, while over-designing every site for extremes it will never see wastes money on unneeded steel.

sections.heading: Gumbel and GEV fitting to annual maxima
sections.body: The standard approach, the block maxima method, takes the single highest wind speed recorded in each year of a multi-year record and fits an extreme-value distribution to that annual-maxima series. Fisher and Tippett's 1928 extreme value theorem showed that block maxima of many underlying distributions converge to one of three limiting forms, unified today as the Generalized Extreme Value (GEV) family. Gumbel formalized the most widely used special case, the light-tailed Type I distribution, in his 1958 book Statistics of Extremes, and it remains the default choice for wind-gust extremes because measured annual-maxima wind records typically fit it well. From the fitted distribution, the wind speed with a 1-in-50 annual exceedance probability is read off as the 50-year extreme wind speed. A crucial caveat: extrapolating a 50-year return level from a 20-year record — as in this lesson's own worked example — carries wide statistical uncertainty, since the fit is anchored on only 20 annual-maxima points to predict an event rarer than the record itself; IEC guidance recommends at least several years of measured data, ideally extended with long-term reanalysis records, before the resulting Vref is trusted for design.

sections.heading: IEC 61400-1 turbine classes and Vref
sections.body: The IEC 61400-1 standard converts that 50-year extreme, expressed as a 10-minute mean called Vref, into a small set of turbine classes so a manufacturer can certify one design against a bounded range of site severities instead of every possible site: Class I at Vref = 50 m/s for the most exposed sites, such as typhoon-prone coasts; Class II at Vref = 42.5 m/s; and Class III at Vref = 37.5 m/s for calmer, mostly inland continental sites. A site's measured or estimated 50-year extreme gust is compared against these thresholds to select an appropriate turbine class; installing a Class III turbine at a site whose real extreme exceeds 37.5 m/s risks structural failure in the design storm, while over-classing a calm site wastes money on unnecessarily reinforced towers and blades.

lessons.workedExample: A 20-year met-mast record's annual maximum 10-minute wind speeds are fit to a Gumbel distribution with location parameter 25 m/s and scale parameter 3.5 m/s. The 50-year return level is x = location + scale x (-ln(-ln(1 - 1/50))) = 25 + 3.5 x 3.90 = about 38.7 m/s. That value exceeds the IEC Class III threshold of 37.5 m/s but stays comfortably under the Class II threshold of 42.5 m/s, so a Class III turbine would be structurally undersized for this site, while a Class II-rated machine is the appropriate, correctly matched choice.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about extreme-value analysis separately from resource statistics because a project can look like a great average energy site while still being a structural liability if the extreme-gust climate was never analyzed. A weak answer conflates 'how windy is it on average' with 'how strong is the worst storm,' or states a Vref number without explaining how it was derived. A strong answer names the block-maxima method, the Gumbel or GEV fit applied to it, and correctly maps the resulting 50-year extreme onto the matching IEC 61400-1 turbine class.

questions.prompt: What does the block maxima method do when preparing data for extreme-wind analysis?

options.text: Averages every recorded wind speed across the whole multi-year record
Extracts the single highest wind speed recorded in each year and fits an extreme-value distribution to that series
Fits a Weibull distribution to the full 10-minute time series
Discards any year containing a storm

explanations.a: Averaging the whole record produces the mean speed used for resource statistics, not extreme-value statistics.
explanations.b: Correct — block maxima pulls out one annual maximum per year and fits an extreme-value distribution, such as Gumbel or GEV, to that reduced series.
explanations.c: Fitting a Weibull to the full record describes resource-statistics work, not extreme-value analysis.
explanations.d: Storm years are exactly the years extreme-value analysis needs; discarding them would defeat the purpose.

questions.prompt: Under IEC 61400-1, what is the reference wind speed Vref for a Class I turbine?

options.text: 30 m/s
50 m/s

explanations.a: 30 m/s is not one of the three standard IEC 61400-1 class reference speeds.
explanations.b: 37.5 m/s is the Class III reference speed, for the calmest of the three standard classes.
explanations.c: 42.5 m/s is the Class II reference speed, the middle of the three.
explanations.d: Correct — Class I, the most severe standard class, is defined with Vref = 50 m/s.

questions.prompt: Match each IEC 61400-1 turbine class to its 50-year reference wind speed Vref.

right.text: 50 m/s

questions.explanation: IEC 61400-1 assigns Vref = 50 m/s to Class I, the harshest standard class, 42.5 m/s to Class II, and 37.5 m/s to Class III, the calmest of the three.

questions.prompt: Order the steps in a full extreme-wind design assessment.

items.text: Collect a multi-year wind-speed record
Extract the single highest wind speed recorded in each year
Fit a Gumbel or GEV distribution to the annual-maxima series
Compute the 50-year return-period wind speed from the fitted distribution
Compare the result against IEC 61400-1 class Vref thresholds to select a turbine class

questions.explanation: A multi-year record must exist before annual maxima can be extracted, the extracted series is what an extreme-value distribution is fit to, the fitted distribution yields the 50-year return level, and only then can that value be compared against the IEC class thresholds to pick a turbine.

lessons.label: Air Density, Altitude & Standardization

sections.heading: What moves air density: temperature, pressure, elevation, humidity
sections.body: Air density follows the ideal gas law, rho = P / (R x T), with R about 287.05 J/(kg K) for dry air. Because power density scales linearly with rho, in P/A = 0.5 x rho x v^3, any of four inputs shifts a site's energy yield even at a fixed wind speed. Higher temperature lowers density, since warm air expands and its molecules spread out. Higher pressure raises density. Higher elevation lowers both pressure and density together, since there is less atmosphere pressing down from above. And, counter to intuition, higher humidity slightly lowers density, because water vapor molecules, at about 18 grams per mole, are lighter than the nitrogen-oxygen mix they displace, at about 29 grams per mole, when temperature and pressure are held fixed — moist air is actually less dense than dry air at the same conditions. This folds directly into the ideal gas calculation via the virtual temperature, T_v = T / (1 - 0.378 x e/P), where e is the vapor pressure and P the total pressure; using T_v in place of T in rho = P/(R x T_v) accounts for humidity's density-lowering effect without a separate correction factor.

sections.heading: The altitude effect, quantified
sections.body: Using the standard-atmosphere lapse-rate model, air density falls roughly exponentially with elevation, dropping to about 86-88 percent of the sea-level value of 1.225 kg/m^3 by 1500 m, and to roughly 74 percent by 3000 m. Because power density is linear in rho, a turbine at 1500 m gets roughly 12-14 percent less power than an identical machine at sea level for the exact same wind speed. That correction matters enormously for the many strong wind resources that sit on elevated plateaus and ridgelines, from Andean sites to high plains and plateau regions worldwide, where the wind measurement alone tells only part of the energy story.

sections.heading: Standardizing measured records to reference conditions
sections.body: To compare sites fairly, and because IEC turbine power-curve certification is defined at the standard air density of 1.225 kg/m^3, a measured record taken under non-standard density must be corrected before its numbers are comparable. The usual approach scales the measured power density, or the power curve itself, by the ratio of actual site density to standard density, rho_site / rho_std, computed either from the site's own logged temperature and pressure or from a standard-atmosphere estimate based on elevation alone. Skipping this correction is a common source of overstated energy-yield projections at high-elevation or hot-climate sites, since an accurately measured wind speed can still produce a misleadingly high modeled power output if it is run through a sea-level-density power curve.

lessons.workedExample: A proposed wind farm sits at 1800 m elevation with an average site temperature of 20 C (293 K) rather than the 15 C standard. Using the barometric formula, pressure at 1800 m is about 815 hPa versus 1013 hPa at sea level. Applying the ideal gas law with the site's actual temperature gives rho = 81,500 Pa / (287.05 x 293 K) = about 0.97 kg/m^3. Compared to the standard 1.225 kg/m^3, that is a ratio of about 0.79, meaning the site's true power density is roughly 21 percent lower than a sea-level-standard power curve would predict at the same wind speed. A developer who skipped this correction would overstate the site's annual energy yield by roughly a fifth.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about density correction because it is the step most often skipped in enthusiastic yield projections, especially at high-elevation or hot-climate sites where altitude and temperature effects compound each other. A weak answer treats wind speed as if it alone determines power output everywhere. A strong answer computes an actual or standard-atmosphere density ratio for the specific site's elevation and temperature, explains that P/A scales linearly with rho, and states the resulting output deficit or surplus in concrete percentage terms rather than only in the abstract.

questions.prompt: Holding temperature and pressure constant, what happens to air density as humidity increases?

options.text: Density increases, because water adds mass to the air
Density decreases slightly, because water vapor molecules are lighter than the dry-air molecules they displace
Density is unaffected by humidity
Density increases sharply, doubling under saturated conditions

explanations.a: Water vapor molecules are lighter than the average dry-air molecule, so adding water vapor at fixed T and P lowers density rather than raising it.
explanations.b: Correct — at about 18 g/mol, water vapor is lighter than the roughly 29 g/mol nitrogen-oxygen mix it displaces, so more humid air is slightly less dense at the same temperature and pressure.
explanations.c: Humidity does have a measurable, if small, effect on air density at fixed temperature and pressure.
explanations.d: The humidity effect on density is small, on the order of a percent or two, not a doubling.

questions.prompt: What is the standard reference air density used for IEC turbine power-curve certification?

explanations.a: 1.0 kg/m^3 understates the standard reference value.
explanations.b: Correct — 1.225 kg/m^3, the sea-level, 15C ICAO standard atmosphere value, is the density at which IEC turbine power curves are defined.
explanations.c: 1.4 kg/m^3 overstates the standard reference value.
explanations.d: 0.9 kg/m^3 is closer to a high-altitude site's density than the sea-level standard.

questions.prompt: Match each change in a variable to its effect on air density (holding the other variables fixed).

right.text: Density decreases (warmer air expands)
Density increases
Density decreases (less atmosphere overhead)
Density decreases slightly (water vapor is lighter than the air it displaces)

questions.explanation: Temperature and elevation both lower density but through different mechanisms (thermal expansion vs. reduced overhead atmosphere), pressure raises it directly through the ideal gas law, and humidity lowers it slightly because water vapor is less dense than the dry air it displaces.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to standardize a measured wind record to reference air density conditions.

items.text: Log the site's temperature and pressure, or estimate density from elevation via the standard atmosphere
Compute the site's actual air density using the ideal gas law
Compute the ratio of site density to the standard reference density (1.225 kg/m^3)
Scale the measured power or power curve by that density ratio

questions.explanation: Standardization needs raw temperature and pressure data (or an elevation-based estimate) first, then the ideal gas law converts that into an actual site density, then that density is compared to the 1.225 kg/m^3 standard as a ratio, and only then is the measured power or power curve rescaled by that ratio.

units.label: The Solar Resource: Irradiance, Geometry & Insolation

lessons.label: The Solar Constant & Extraterrestrial Irradiance

sections.heading: A number that isn't quite constant
sections.body: The total solar irradiance (TSI) — the power the Sun delivers per square meter to a surface facing it, just outside Earth's atmosphere, at Earth's mean distance — is close to 1361 W/m^2. For decades textbooks quoted 1366-1367 W/m^2, a figure inherited from 1970s-80s satellite radiometers whose optical baffles scattered stray light into the detector and inflated the reading. NASA's SORCE mission, using the Total Irradiance Monitor (TIM) launched in 2003, redesigned the instrument's aperture and light trap and measured a lower, more accurate value. Kopp and Lean published the revised figure in 2011, and TSI ~1361 W/m^2 is now the accepted reference value used in solar-resource work. The lesson is not really about the Sun changing — it is that the number itself is a calibrated measurement with its own instrumental history and error bars, not a physical constant handed down complete.

sections.heading: Why the value swings through the year
sections.body: Earth's orbit is an ellipse with eccentricity about 0.0167, so distance to the Sun varies, and irradiance scales as the inverse square of that distance. At perihelion (early January, roughly 147.1 million km) TSI runs about 1408 W/m^2; at aphelion (early July, roughly 152.1 million km) it drops to about 1317 W/m^2 — a swing of roughly +/-3.3% around the 1361 W/m^2 mean, about 6.6-6.7% peak to peak. A more precise correction engineers actually apply is the eccentricity factor Eo = 1 + 0.033*cos(360*n/365), multiplying the 1361 W/m^2 mean by Eo for day-of-year n to get the extraterrestrial irradiance on that specific date, rather than relying on the coarser perihelion/aphelion snapshots alone. Because perihelion falls in Northern Hemisphere winter, the Southern Hemisphere actually receives slightly more extraterrestrial energy at its summer solstice than the north does at its own summer solstice — a fact that surprises most students, since seasonal temperature is dominated by axial tilt and day length, not this smaller orbital effect.

sections.heading: The ceiling on any ground measurement
sections.body: The top-of-atmosphere (TOA) irradiance on a horizontal surface, TSI times the cosine of the solar zenith angle, sets the physical ceiling that no ground-based pyranometer reading, clear or cloudy, can exceed. Every subsequent lesson in this unit — air mass, clearness index, insolation — is defined as a fraction of this ceiling, so getting comfortable with the ~1361 W/m^2 baseline and its known annual swing is the foundation the rest of the unit is built on.

lessons.workedExample: A team is validating a rooftop pyranometer against a clear-sky model. On July 3 (near aphelion), their model uses TSI = 1317 W/m^2 as the extraterrestrial input; on January 3 (near perihelion), it should use TSI = 1408 W/m^2. If they instead hard-code the textbook mean of 1361 W/m^2 year-round, their predicted clear-sky GHI is biased low by roughly 3% in January and high by roughly 3% in July — exactly the kind of error a judge will spot when a July 'this matches great' claim is compared against a January dataset that quietly used the same constant.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'where did your solar-input number come from?' to check whether a student is reciting a memorized constant or understands it as a measured, revised quantity that also depends on time of year. A weak answer says '1366 W/m^2, the solar constant' with no context. A strong answer cites the SORCE/TIM revision to ~1361 W/m^2, explains why the old radiometers ran high, and shows the day-of-year eccentricity correction was actually applied in the calculation rather than left as a footnote.

questions.prompt: Why was the solar constant revised downward from ~1366 W/m^2 to ~1361 W/m^2?

options.text: The Sun's output measurably decreased between the two measurement eras
NASA's SORCE/TIM instrument (launched 2003) had a redesigned aperture that reduced stray-light scattering into the detector
Earth's orbit shifted slightly closer to circular
The new figure includes only visible light, not the full spectrum

explanations.a: The Sun's actual output did not drop by this much on this timescale; the change is instrumental, not solar.
explanations.b: Correct — TIM's redesigned optical baffle and light trap cut stray-light scatter that had biased earlier radiometers high, per the Kopp and Lean (2011) analysis.
explanations.c: Orbital eccentricity did not change; it still drives the ~+/-3.3% seasonal swing around the revised mean.
explanations.d: TSI is a broadband, full-spectrum measurement in both the old and revised figures.

questions.prompt: TSI is higher at perihelion (early January) than at aphelion (early July) because:

options.text: Earth's axial tilt points the Northern Hemisphere toward the Sun in January
Irradiance falls off with the inverse square of Sun-Earth distance, and Earth is closer to the Sun in January
Solar activity (sunspot cycle) peaks every January
The atmosphere is thinner in January, letting more radiation through

explanations.a: Axial tilt explains seasons and day length, not this orbital-distance effect on TSI itself.
explanations.b: Correct — Earth's elliptical orbit (eccentricity ~0.0167) brings it closer to the Sun around January 3, and irradiance scales as 1/distance^2.
explanations.c: The 11-year sunspot cycle is unrelated to Earth's annual orbital position.
explanations.d: Atmospheric thickness affects ground irradiance, not the extraterrestrial TSI value itself.

questions.prompt: Order these irradiance quantities from largest to smallest ceiling.

items.text: TSI perpendicular to the beam (~1317-1408 W/m^2)
TOA irradiance on a horizontal surface at typical daytime zenith angle
Clear-sky GHI reaching the ground at noon

questions.explanation: TSI on a surface facing the Sun is the absolute ceiling; multiplying by cos(zenith) for a horizontal surface lowers it further; atmospheric scattering and absorption lower it again by the time it reaches the ground as GHI.

lessons.label: Solar Geometry & Sun Position

sections.heading: Declination and hour angle: the two orbital clocks
sections.body: Two angles locate the Sun in the sky at any instant. Declination (delta) is the angle between the Sun's rays and Earth's equatorial plane; it swings from -23.44 degrees at the December solstice to +23.44 degrees at the June solstice because Earth's rotation axis is tilted 23.44 degrees from its orbital plane, and it is well approximated by delta = 23.44 * sin(360/365 * (n + 284)) using day-of-year n (the Cooper 1969 approximation). Hour angle (H) tracks the Sun's apparent motion through the day: 15 degrees per hour, zero at local solar noon, negative in the morning, positive in the afternoon — a direct consequence of Earth's 360-degree rotation in 24 hours.

sections.heading: From delta, H, and latitude to zenith and azimuth
sections.body: Given declination, hour angle, and observer latitude (phi), the solar zenith angle (theta_z, measured from straight up) follows from cos(theta_z) = sin(phi)sin(delta) + cos(phi)cos(delta)cos(H); solar elevation is simply 90 degrees minus theta_z. Solar azimuth (the compass direction of the Sun) requires a second equation involving the same three inputs and determines whether the Sun is in the southeast or southwest sky at a given hour for a Northern Hemisphere site. These equations, standard in texts like Duffie and Beckman's Solar Engineering of Thermal Processes, let you compute the Sun's exact position for any date, time, and location without a table lookup — the same math that drives every solar-tracker controller and PV siting tool. The same declination and latitude inputs also give the sunrise/sunset hour angle directly, from cos(H_sunset) = -tan(phi)*tan(delta): plugging in H_sunset converts straight to day length (2*H_sunset/15 degrees-per-hour) and to the clock times of sunrise and sunset once combined with solar noon, so a team scheduling a multi-hour outdoor data run can compute their usable daylight window before ever stepping outside.

sections.heading: Solar noon isn't clock noon: the equation of time
sections.body: Solar noon — when the Sun crosses the local meridian and hour angle H=0 — rarely lines up with 12:00 on a clock, for two independent reasons. First, longitude within a time zone shifts solar noon by 4 minutes per degree of longitude offset from the zone's reference meridian. Second, the equation of time (EoT) corrects for Earth's elliptical, tilted orbit causing the Sun to run 'fast' or 'slow' relative to average clock time; EoT ranges from about -14 minutes in mid-February to about +16 minutes in early November. A solar-tracker or sundial that ignores EoT can be off by half an hour at its worst point in the year, which matters when timing peak irradiance windows.

lessons.workedExample: Find solar noon on November 3 at longitude 84 degrees W in a time zone referenced to 75 degrees W (Eastern Time). The longitude correction is 4 min/degree * 9 degrees = 36 minutes, added because the site is west of the reference meridian, so the Sun reaches that meridian later in clock time (same rule as checkpoint q2: farther west means a later solar noon). The equation of time on November 3 is near its yearly maximum, about +16 minutes, meaning the true Sun crosses the meridian 16 minutes before mean clock time, which pulls solar noon earlier by that amount. Net correction to clock noon (12:00): +36 minutes (longitude) - 16 minutes (EoT) = +20 minutes, so solar noon falls at roughly 12:20 local clock time (before accounting for daylight saving offset, which shifts the clock reading by another hour if in effect).
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing solar geometry wants to see whether a student can place the Sun for their own test date and site rather than assuming 'solar noon = 12:00' and 'the panel points due south at max output all day.' A weak answer treats the Sun's position as roughly fixed through a data-collection session; a strong answer computes hour angle and declination for the actual test times, explains why their solar-noon peak was offset from clock noon by a specific number of minutes (longitude plus equation-of-time), and uses that to justify their measurement window.

questions.prompt: What physically causes solar declination to vary between -23.44 degrees and +23.44 degrees over the year?

options.text: Earth's orbital eccentricity (~0.0167)
The 23.44-degree tilt of Earth's rotation axis relative to its orbital plane
The equation of time
Atmospheric refraction near the horizon

explanations.a: Eccentricity governs the Sun-Earth distance and the ~+/-3.3% TSI swing, not declination.
explanations.b: Correct — axial tilt is why the subsolar point migrates between the tropics, tracing out declination's annual range.
explanations.c: The equation of time corrects clock time against true solar time; it does not cause declination.
explanations.d: Refraction bends light near the horizon but does not drive the seasonal declination cycle.

questions.prompt: A site is at longitude 90 degrees W, inside a time zone referenced to 75 degrees W. Ignoring the equation of time, how does this longitude offset shift solar noon relative to clock noon?

options.text: No shift — longitude within a time zone doesn't matter
Solar noon occurs 60 minutes later than clock noon (at ~13:00)
Solar noon occurs 60 minutes earlier than clock noon (at ~11:00)
Solar noon occurs 15 minutes later than clock noon

explanations.a: Longitude within a time zone matters at 4 minutes of offset per degree away from the reference meridian.
explanations.b: Correct — 15 degrees west of the reference meridian * 4 min/degree = 60 minutes; being farther west means the Sun reaches that meridian later in clock time.
explanations.c: The offset is later, not earlier, because the site is west of the reference meridian.
explanations.d: 15 minutes would correspond to less than 4 degrees of offset, not the 15-degree gap given.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to compute solar zenith angle for a given date, time, and site.

items.text: Compute declination from day-of-year
Compute hour angle from local solar time
Combine declination, hour angle, and latitude via cos(theta_z) = sin(phi)sin(delta)+cos(phi)cos(delta)cos(H)
Read off zenith angle (and elevation = 90 - theta_z)

questions.explanation: Declination and hour angle are computed independently from date and clock time respectively, then combined with latitude in the zenith-angle formula, which finally yields elevation.

lessons.label: DNI, DHI & GHI: The Three Components

sections.heading: Three ways to slice sunlight at the ground
sections.body: Direct normal irradiance (DNI) is the power per area arriving as a beam straight from the Sun's disk, measured on a surface held perpendicular to that beam — what you would sense staring straight at the Sun with a small aperture. Diffuse horizontal irradiance (DHI) is everything else: sunlight scattered by air molecules, aerosols, and clouds, arriving from all directions across the sky dome, measured on a flat horizontal surface. Global horizontal irradiance (GHI) is what a flat horizontal sensor actually reads, and it is the sum of both contributions once DNI is projected onto the horizontal: GHI = DNI * cos(theta_z) + DHI, where theta_z is the solar zenith angle. This identity, sometimes called the closure equation, is the backbone of every solar-resource dataset — if measured or modeled DNI, DHI, and GHI do not satisfy it to within instrument uncertainty, one of the three is wrong. Quality-control networks like BSRN don't leave that tolerance vague: a station's three-component readings are typically flagged when the closure residual exceeds roughly a few percent of GHI, or on the order of 15-25 W/m^2 in absolute terms near midday, whichever check catches the problem first — numbers worth matching if a team is building their own QC pass on co-located sensors.

sections.heading: Why the technology dictates which component matters
sections.body: Concentrating solar technologies — parabolic troughs, power towers, concentrating PV — can only focus a collimated beam, so they respond almost entirely to DNI; a hazy or thin-cirrus sky can gut DNI while GHI drops only modestly, because scattered light still arrives as diffuse. Conventional flat-plate PV panels and flat-plate thermal collectors, by contrast, accept light from the whole sky, so they respond to whatever irradiance actually lands on their tilted plane, the plane-of-array (POA) irradiance, which blends a geometrically reprojected beam component with the diffuse sky and any ground-reflected light. This is why utility-scale trough plants like the historic SEGS installations in California's Mojave Desert are sited specifically for high, reliable DNI (desert climates with few aerosols and little cloud), while rooftop PV is deployed almost anywhere GHI is adequate, humid coastlines included.

sections.heading: Typical magnitudes on a clear day
sections.body: Near solar noon on a clear day at low latitude with the Sun near zenith, GHI commonly approaches 1000 W/m^2, split roughly 80-90% beam and 10-20% diffuse under very clean, dry air; DNI itself can reach 900-950 W/m^2 under excellent conditions. As zenith angle increases toward morning, evening, or higher latitude, cos(theta_z) shrinks, DNI's horizontal contribution drops sharply, and the diffuse fraction of GHI rises — a pattern this unit returns to when defining the clearness index.

lessons.workedExample: A pyrheliometer (tracking, measures DNI) reads 850 W/m^2 while a co-located horizontal pyranometer (measures GHI) reads 700 W/m^2 at a moment when the solar zenith angle is 35 degrees (cos 35 degrees ~= 0.819). The beam's horizontal contribution is DNI * cos(theta_z) = 850 * 0.819 ~= 696 W/m^2. Since GHI = DNI*cos(theta_z) + DHI, DHI ~= 700 - 696 = 4 W/m^2 — physically implausible for a real clear sky, which should show at least 60-100 W/m^2 of diffuse light. The tiny residual signals a calibration or shading problem in one of the two instruments, exactly the kind of closure check a rigorous data-collection team runs before trusting a sensor.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'which irradiance component does your setup actually respond to?' because conflating GHI with what a tilted or concentrating collector receives is one of the most common science-fair errors in solar projects. A weak answer treats 'sunlight' as one undifferentiated quantity and quotes a GHI number for a concentrating design. A strong answer names DNI, DHI, and GHI explicitly, states which one drives their specific hardware, and — if they have two co-located sensors — shows the closure equation was checked as a data-quality step.

questions.prompt: Which component of solar irradiance is most critical for a concentrating solar power (CSP) trough plant?

options.text: DHI, because troughs concentrate scattered light most efficiently
DNI, because only a collimated beam can be focused by mirrors onto a receiver
GHI, because it is the total energy regardless of source direction
None — CSP output is independent of irradiance component

explanations.a: Diffuse light arrives from the whole sky and cannot be focused to a line or point by a concentrating mirror.
explanations.b: Correct — concentrating optics require a collimated source, so CSP output tracks DNI closely and suffers badly under hazy or thin-cloud skies even when GHI holds up.
explanations.c: GHI mixes beam and diffuse; a CSP plant cannot use the diffuse portion, so GHI overstates its usable resource.
explanations.d: CSP output is strongly, directly dependent on DNI.

questions.prompt: GHI = 650 W/m^2 and DHI = 120 W/m^2 at a moment when theta_z = 40 degrees (cos 40 degrees ~= 0.766). Using GHI = DNI*cos(theta_z) + DHI, what is DNI?

explanations.b: 530 W/m^2 is GHI minus DHI before dividing by cos(theta_z) — the projection step was skipped.
explanations.c: 850 W/m^2 overshoots; check the subtraction and division order.
explanations.d: 120 W/m^2 is DHI itself, not the solved-for DNI.

questions.prompt: Match each irradiance quantity to its defining description.

right.text: Beam irradiance on a surface perpendicular to the Sun
Scattered sky irradiance on a horizontal surface
DNI*cos(theta_z) + DHI on a horizontal surface

questions.explanation: DNI is the tracking-perpendicular beam measurement, DHI is the horizontal diffuse-only measurement, and GHI is their horizontal-plane sum via the closure equation.

lessons.label: Air Mass & Atmospheric Attenuation

sections.heading: Air mass: how much atmosphere the beam crosses
sections.body: Air mass (AM) is the ratio of the actual atmospheric path length the Sun's beam travels to the shortest possible path — straight up, Sun at zenith. The simple approximation AM = 1/cos(theta_z) works well until the Sun gets low, where it blows up unrealistically because it ignores Earth's curvature and atmospheric refraction. Kasten and Young published a refined formula in 1989 that stays accurate down to the horizon: AM = 1 / [cos(theta_z) + 0.50572*(96.07995 - theta_z)^-1.6364], with theta_z in degrees. AM=1 means the Sun is directly overhead; AM=2 roughly corresponds to a 60-degree zenith angle; near the horizon AM approaches about 38, not infinity, because curvature caps the path length.

sections.heading: AM1.5 as the industry's reference spectrum
sections.body: A zenith angle of about 48.2 degrees gives AM~1.5, a mid-latitude, mid-morning-ish Sun angle chosen decades ago as a representative average condition for terrestrial PV. The ASTM G173 standard spectrum, split into AM1.5 direct (beam only) and AM1.5 global (beam plus diffuse, tilted 37 degrees toward the sun), is the reference every commercial solar panel is rated against under standard test conditions. A panel's nameplate wattage assumes this specific spectral shape and 1000 W/m^2 total irradiance — real-world air mass drifting away from 1.5 measurably shifts a panel's output even at the same total irradiance, because different photovoltaic materials respond unevenly across the spectrum.

sections.heading: What actually attenuates the beam
sections.body: Four processes remove energy from sunlight passing through the atmosphere. Rayleigh scattering by air molecules follows a wavelength^-4 dependence, so it strips blue and violet light preferentially — the reason skies are blue and the direct beam reddens at low sun, when a long low-angle path scatters away most of the short wavelengths before the beam reaches an observer. Aerosol scattering and absorption (dust, smoke, haze, pollution) is quantified by the Linke turbidity factor (TL), first proposed by Linke in 1922 and revised by Kasten in the 1980s-90s, which expresses how many 'ideal dry, clean atmospheres' worth of extra attenuation the real sky adds — TL~2 for very clean air, TL~6-7 for polluted haze. Water vapor absorbs strongly in specific near-infrared bands — notably around 940 nm and 1130 nm — and stratospheric ozone, typically a column of roughly 300 Dobson units, absorbs UV below about 320 nm, both carving distinct notches out of the AM1.5 spectrum that a plain scattering model would miss.

lessons.workedExample: At theta_z = 60 degrees, the simple formula gives AM = 1/cos(60) = 1/0.5 = 2.0. The Kasten-Young formula gives AM = 1/[cos(60) + 0.50572*(96.07995-60)^-1.6364] = 1/[0.5 + 0.50572*(36.08)^-1.6364]. Computing (36.08)^-1.6364 ~= 0.00283, so the correction term is ~0.00143, giving AM = 1/0.50143 ~= 1.994 — nearly identical to the simple estimate at this moderate angle. At theta_z = 85 degrees, though, 1/cos(85) blows up to ~11.5, while Kasten-Young yields a much more physically sensible ~10.3, showing the correction term matters most precisely where the simple formula breaks down: low Sun angles near sunrise and sunset.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge tests air-mass understanding to see whether a student treats 'more atmosphere = less power' as a vague intuition or an actual computed quantity tied to their test conditions. A weak answer says panels perform worse in the morning 'because there's more air in the way' with no number attached. A strong answer computes AM for their specific test zenith angle, explains that AM1.5 is the rating-standard baseline their panel was calibrated against, and can name at least one specific attenuator (Rayleigh scattering, aerosol/turbidity, water vapor, or ozone) rather than lumping all atmospheric loss into one undifferentiated 'haze.'

questions.prompt: Why does the simple AM = 1/cos(theta_z) formula fail badly near the horizon, and what does the Kasten-Young (1989) refinement fix?

options.text: It ignores ozone absorption, which the refinement adds back in
It treats the atmosphere as flat/infinite, diverging to infinity, while Kasten-Young accounts for Earth's curvature and caps the path length near the horizon
It uses the wrong solar constant value
It doesn't account for the Linke turbidity factor

explanations.a: Ozone absorption is a spectral effect, not the reason the plane-parallel geometry formula diverges.
explanations.b: Correct — 1/cos(theta_z) assumes a flat, infinitely extended atmosphere, so it goes to infinity as theta_z approaches 90 degrees; Kasten-Young's empirical correction accounts for curvature, keeping AM near 38 at the horizon instead of infinite.
explanations.c: The solar constant is irrelevant to the geometric air-mass calculation.
explanations.d: Turbidity describes aerosol attenuation magnitude, not the geometric path-length formula.

questions.prompt: Why does the direct solar beam appear redder at sunrise/sunset than at midday?

options.text: Ozone absorbs red light near the horizon
Rayleigh scattering (proportional to wavelength^-4) preferentially removes blue/violet light over the longer low-angle path, leaving more red/orange in the transmitted beam
The Sun's actual emitted spectrum shifts redder at low angles
Water vapor absorption increases red light transmission at low angles

explanations.a: Ozone's absorption is in the UV, not the visible red end, and isn't the driver of the reddening effect.
explanations.b: Correct — the strong wavelength^-4 dependence of Rayleigh scattering strips short (blue) wavelengths out of the beam much faster than long (red) ones as air mass increases.
explanations.c: The Sun's emitted spectrum does not change with the observer's local geometry.
explanations.d: Water vapor absorbs in specific near-infrared bands; it does not selectively transmit red visible light.

questions.prompt: Order these zenith angles from lowest to highest air mass (AM).

items.text: theta_z = 0 degrees (AM = 1)
theta_z ~= 48.2 degrees (AM ~= 1.5)
theta_z = 60 degrees (AM ~= 2)
theta_z = 85 degrees (AM ~= 10)

questions.explanation: Air mass increases monotonically as zenith angle increases from directly overhead toward the horizon, since the beam crosses more atmosphere at a shallower angle.

lessons.label: The Clearness Index & Sky Conditions

sections.heading: Normalizing GHI against its own ceiling
sections.body: The clearness index kt is the ratio of measured global horizontal irradiance to the extraterrestrial horizontal irradiance for that same moment and location: kt = GHI / H0, where H0 is TSI times cos(theta_z) adjusted for the day's Earth-Sun distance (Lesson 1). Dividing out the geometry this way turns a raw, location- and time-dependent GHI number into a dimensionless 0-to-1 measure of how much of the physically possible sunlight actually got through the sky that day or hour. A dense overcast might read kt~0.1-0.2; a hazy but sunny day might sit around kt~0.5-0.6; an exceptionally clean, dry, high-Sun clear sky can reach kt~0.75-0.8. Because it strips out latitude, season, and time of day, kt is the standard variable meteorologists use to classify and compare sky conditions across completely different sites and dates.

sections.heading: Using kt to split beam from diffuse
sections.body: Knowing kt alone lets you estimate how the measured GHI divides between beam and diffuse, because cloudier skies are diffuse-dominated while clear skies are beam-dominated. Orgill and Hollands published an early piecewise correlation between kt and the diffuse fraction (DHI/GHI) in 1977; Erbs, Klein, and Duffie refined it into a smoother, widely used piecewise-polynomial correlation in 1982 (Erbs et al.). Both share the same qualitative shape: at low kt (heavy cloud), nearly all the transmitted light is diffuse and the diffuse fraction approaches 1; as kt climbs through the mid-range the diffuse fraction falls steeply; at high kt (very clear skies) the diffuse fraction levels off at a floor around 0.15-0.2, since even a cloudless sky always scatters some light via Rayleigh and aerosol scattering. These decomposition models let a modeler estimate DNI and DHI separately from a GHI-only measurement or satellite product, which is common because GHI-only pyranometers are far cheaper and more common than tracking pyrheliometers.

sections.heading: Clear-sky models as the zero-cloud reference
sections.body: To say a given kt represents 'cloudy' versus 'clear,' you need a reference for what a cloudless sky would produce at that same site and moment — that is what a clear-sky model provides. The Ineichen-Perez model (2002) is a compact, widely used parameterization driven mainly by Linke turbidity, giving a fast clear-sky GHI/DNI/DHI estimate. REST2 (Gueymard, 2008) is a more detailed spectral model that separately accounts for aerosol optical depth, precipitable water vapor, and ozone column, trading simplicity for higher accuracy. Comparing a real-time kt or measured GHI against one of these clear-sky baselines is exactly how solar-forecasting systems flag cloud events in near-real time.

lessons.workedExample: At a given hour, H0 (extraterrestrial horizontal irradiance) is calculated as 950 W/m^2 from the site's zenith angle and day-of-year. A pyranometer reads GHI = 620 W/m^2, giving kt = 620/950 ~= 0.65 — a moderately clear, slightly hazy sky. Applying the Erbs-type correlation shape for this mid-to-upper kt range predicts a diffuse fraction near 0.25-0.3, so DHI is estimated at roughly 155-185 W/m^2 and the remaining beam-derived horizontal component at roughly 435-465 W/m^2, from which DNI can be recovered by dividing by cos(theta_z) — all without ever installing a tracking pyrheliometer.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about clearness index to see whether a student can characterize 'how sunny was your test day' quantitatively instead of narratively. A weak answer says 'it was pretty sunny' or reports raw GHI numbers with no context for whether that represents a clear or hazy sky at that time and place. A strong answer computes kt against the extraterrestrial ceiling for the actual test conditions, and — if they needed DNI or DHI but only measured GHI — explains they used a published diffuse-fraction correlation (Erbs or Orgill-Hollands) rather than guessing the split.

questions.prompt: The clearness index kt is defined as:

options.text: DNI divided by DHI
GHI divided by the extraterrestrial horizontal irradiance (H0) for the same time and location
GHI divided by 1361 W/m^2 (the solar constant)
The Linke turbidity factor

explanations.a: That ratio is unrelated to clearness index; DNI and DHI are separate components, not kt's definition.
explanations.b: Correct — kt normalizes measured GHI against the extraterrestrial horizontal ceiling for that exact moment, removing geometry so different times/places can be compared.
explanations.c: Dividing by the bare solar constant ignores zenith angle and Earth-Sun distance, so it isn't kt.
explanations.d: Linke turbidity is a separate aerosol-attenuation quantity used in clear-sky models, not the clearness index itself.

questions.prompt: As kt decreases from a clear-sky value (e.g., 0.75) toward an overcast value (e.g., 0.15), what happens to the diffuse fraction DHI/GHI, according to the Erbs-type correlation?

options.text: It decreases toward zero
It stays constant regardless of kt
It increases, approaching close to 1 under heavy overcast
It becomes undefined below kt = 0.3

explanations.a: The diffuse fraction moves the opposite direction — it rises, not falls, as skies get cloudier.
explanations.b: The whole point of the Erbs/Orgill-Hollands correlations is that diffuse fraction varies systematically with kt.
explanations.c: Correct — under heavy cloud almost none of the transmitted light is a direct beam, so nearly all of it is diffuse, pushing DHI/GHI toward 1.
explanations.d: The correlation is defined continuously across the kt range, including low values.

questions.prompt: Match each named model/correlation to what it is used for.

right.text: Piecewise correlation estimating diffuse fraction from clearness index
Compact clear-sky model driven mainly by Linke turbidity
Detailed spectral clear-sky model using aerosol, water vapor, and ozone inputs

questions.explanation: Erbs et al. split GHI into beam/diffuse fractions via kt; Ineichen-Perez is a fast turbidity-based clear-sky reference; REST2 is a higher-fidelity spectral clear-sky model needing more atmospheric inputs.

lessons.label: Insolation, Peak Sun Hours & Tilt

sections.heading: Insolation: irradiance integrated over time
sections.body: Insolation is the time-integral of irradiance — energy per area, not power per area — typically reported as daily or annual totals in kWh/m^2/day or kWh/m^2/year. Where GHI tells you the instantaneous rate of solar energy delivery, daily insolation tells you the whole day's haul, and it is the number that actually determines how much energy a fixed solar installation collects. NREL's National Solar Radiation Database compiles decades of satellite-and-ground-station-derived insolation maps for the US; sunny desert Southwest sites like southern Arizona commonly average around 6-7 kWh/m^2/day of GHI annually, while cloudier northern and coastal sites average roughly 3.5-4.5 kWh/m^2/day — nearly a two-fold difference in resource that directly scales expected PV output.

sections.heading: Peak sun hours: a sizing shortcut with a physical basis
sections.body: Because photovoltaic panels are rated at Standard Test Conditions of exactly 1000 W/m^2, daily insolation in kWh/m^2/day is numerically identical to 'peak sun hours' — the number of hours an equivalent, constant 1000 W/m^2 sun would need to shine to deliver that same day's total energy. A site averaging 5.5 kWh/m^2/day has '5.5 peak sun hours,' and a nameplate 5 kW array there yields roughly 5 kW * 5.5 h * (a system derate factor, commonly ~0.75-0.85 for inverter, wiring, temperature, and soiling losses) ~= 20-24 kWh/day. This shortcut is why installers quote peak sun hours rather than raw GHI when sizing a system — it converts directly into expected daily production.

sections.heading: Why tilt and orientation change the number you actually capture
sections.body: GHI is measured on a flat horizontal surface, but most PV arrays are tilted, so the energy an array actually intercepts — plane-of-array (POA) insolation — differs from GHI by a geometric reprojection of the beam plus, for tilted surfaces, a ground-reflected (albedo) term that a horizontal sensor never sees. As a rule of thumb for a south-facing (Northern Hemisphere) fixed array optimizing annual output, tilting the panel to roughly the site's latitude angle balances summer and winter Sun paths and typically raises annual insolation captured by something on the order of 10-25% above a flat horizontal surface at mid-latitudes, though the true optimum tilt is usually a few degrees shallower than latitude because diffuse sky light is best captured closer to horizontal. Trackers push this further: single-axis tracking commonly adds on the order of 15-25% more annual energy than an optimally tilted fixed array, and dual-axis tracking on the order of 30-40% more, at the cost of moving parts and additional expense.

lessons.workedExample: A team compares two identical 300 W panels: one horizontal, one tilted to the site's 35-degree latitude and facing south. Local annual-average GHI is 5.0 kWh/m^2/day. The horizontal panel captures close to that 5.0 kWh/m^2/day directly. The tilted panel, applying a representative mid-latitude POA gain of ~18% for a latitude-tilt fixed array, captures roughly 5.0 * 1.18 ~= 5.9 kWh/m^2/day. Over a year that is the difference between about 1825 kWh/m^2 and 2154 kWh/m^2 of collected insolation per unit area — a gap the team should report explicitly rather than quoting a single site GHI figure for both configurations.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about insolation and tilt to catch students who report a single 'sunniness' number for their site and apply it uniformly to any panel orientation. A weak answer cites GHI from a weather app and assumes that is what their tilted array collected. A strong answer distinguishes GHI (horizontal) from plane-of-array insolation (their panel's actual tilt and orientation), states the tilt they used and roughly why, and — if sizing a system — converts insolation into peak sun hours to justify an expected energy-output number rather than an unsupported guess.

questions.prompt: A site has 5.5 kWh/m^2/day of insolation. Approximately how many 'peak sun hours' does that represent, and why?

options.text: 24 hours, because the Sun is up somewhere on Earth at all times
5.5 hours, because PV panels are rated at 1000 W/m^2, so kWh/m^2/day is numerically equal to hours of equivalent full-strength sun
12 hours, the typical day length
1000 hours, matching the STC irradiance value

explanations.a: Peak sun hours describes one site's daily insolation collapsed into an equivalent full-sun duration, not global daylight.
explanations.b: Correct — since STC rating power is defined at 1000 W/m^2, 5.5 kWh/m^2 of daily energy is exactly equivalent to 5.5 hours at that reference intensity.
explanations.c: Day length and peak sun hours are related but not the same number; peak sun hours is always less than actual day length because irradiance varies through the day.
explanations.d: 1000 W/m^2 is the reference power density, not a duration; it should not appear as an hours value.

questions.prompt: Why does a south-facing (Northern Hemisphere), latitude-tilted fixed PV array typically capture more annual insolation than an identical horizontal array at the same site?

options.text: Tilting increases the panel's surface area
Tilting reduces the average angle between the panel surface and the incoming beam across the year, capturing more of the beam component plus some ground-reflected light
Tilted panels run cooler, which alone accounts for the gain
There is no meaningful difference between horizontal and tilted annual insolation

explanations.a: Panel area is unchanged by tilting; only its orientation relative to the Sun changes.
explanations.b: Correct — tilting toward the Sun's average path reduces the incidence angle over the year and can add a ground-reflected (albedo) contribution a horizontal surface misses, raising captured insolation.
explanations.c: Cooler operation affects electrical efficiency, not the insolation (energy) actually striking the panel, which is a separate, larger geometric effect.
explanations.d: The difference is typically on the order of 10-25% at mid-latitudes for a well-chosen tilt, which is meaningful for system sizing.

questions.prompt: Order these array configurations from lowest to highest typical annual energy capture at a fixed mid-latitude site (same panel, same location).

items.text: Horizontal (flat) fixed panel
Fixed panel tilted near latitude angle, south-facing
Single-axis tracker
Dual-axis tracker

questions.explanation: A flat horizontal panel captures the least; a well-chosen fixed tilt improves on it; single-axis tracking adds further gain by following the Sun in one axis; dual-axis tracking, following both axes, captures the most.

lessons.label: Spectral & Temporal Variability of Sunlight

sections.heading: Sunlight is a spectrum, not a single number
sections.body: The reference AM1.5 global spectrum (ASTM G173) spreads its ~1000 W/m^2 total across wavelengths roughly as: a small ultraviolet share below 400 nm (only a few percent of total energy), a large visible share between 400-700 nm (a bit over 40%), and the largest single share in the near-infrared beyond 700 nm (a bit over half of total energy). Different photovoltaic technologies harvest this spectrum unevenly. Crystalline silicon, with a bandgap near 1.1 eV, converts light up to about 1100 nm but wastes energy above the bandgap as heat; thin-film technologies like CdTe or amorphous silicon have different bandgaps and different spectral response curves; multi-junction cells stack several bandgaps to capture more of the spectrum at the cost of complexity. Because air mass and atmospheric water vapor reshape the spectrum through the day (higher air mass and haze push relatively more of the surviving energy into red/near-infrared, per Lesson 4's Rayleigh-scattering discussion), a panel's real-world spectral mismatch relative to its AM1.5 rating condition varies hour to hour, and technologies with narrower spectral response are more sensitive to that mismatch than broadband crystalline silicon.

sections.heading: Clouds create variability on a completely different timescale
sections.body: Passing cumulus clouds can cut point-sensor GHI by 80% or more within tens of seconds as a cloud edge crosses the Sun, then let it rebound just as fast — a ramp rate far steeper than anything driven by the sun's slow geometric motion through the day. This sub-minute variability is a real operational headache for grid operators managing high-penetration solar: inverters must ride through rapid swings, and utilities must hold reserve generation ready to backfill sudden drops. Researchers characterize this with quantities like the variability index and cloud-speed-derived ramp statistics, work associated with groups studying solar forecasting such as Lave and Kleissl's irradiance-variability research in the 2010s.

sections.heading: Why spreading sensors out smooths the swings
sections.body: A single rooftop sensor sees the full brunt of a cloud shadow passing directly overhead, but a fleet of PV systems spread across a city or region rarely all sit under the same cloud at once — different sites' ramps partly cancel in the aggregate. Mills and Wiser's 2010 Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory analysis of wide-area geographic diversity found that aggregating output across many dispersed PV sites substantially reduces the short-timescale variability seen at any single site, smoothing the second-to-minute swings even though the slower daily and cloud-system-scale variability remains. This is a key argument for geographically distributed solar deployment over a single large concentrated plant, when short-term grid stability is a concern.

lessons.workedExample: A single rooftop pyranometer logs GHI at 1-second resolution during a partly cloudy afternoon and shows repeated drops from 900 W/m^2 to under 150 W/m^2 within 20-30 seconds as cumulus clouds cross the Sun, then equally fast recoveries.
