A nearby utility operator instead looks at the combined output of 200 rooftop systems spread across the metro area at the same 1-second resolution: because the clouds cover different neighborhoods at different times, the aggregate output's fastest drops are far shallower and slower than any single rooftop's — illustrating exactly the geographic-smoothing effect Mills and Wiser documented, and why a single point sensor overstates the variability challenge for a large distributed fleet.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge raises spectral or temporal variability to see whether a student treats 'the sun's power' as a single steady number or understands it as a variable quantity with structure in both wavelength and time. A weak answer reports a single averaged irradiance value for an entire test session spanning variable cloud cover, or assumes any PV technology converts a given W/m^2 identically. A strong answer either logs at high enough time resolution to show cloud-driven ramps explicitly, or explains that their panel's spectral response interacts with changing air mass and cloud conditions in a way a single broadband irradiance number does not fully capture.

questions.prompt: In the AM1.5 reference solar spectrum, which wavelength band carries the largest share of total energy?

options.text: Ultraviolet (below 400 nm)
Visible light (400-700 nm)
Near-infrared (beyond 700 nm)
All three bands carry exactly equal shares

explanations.a: UV is only a small fraction, a few percent, of total AM1.5 spectral energy.
explanations.b: Visible light is a large share, a bit over 40%, but not the largest single band.
explanations.c: Correct — near-infrared beyond 700 nm carries a bit over half of the total AM1.5 spectral energy, the single largest share.
explanations.d: The three bands are notably uneven, with near-infrared dominating.

questions.prompt: Why does a single rooftop pyranometer typically show much sharper, faster irradiance swings on a partly cloudy day than the aggregated output of many PV sites spread across a city?

options.text: Aggregated systems use better sensors that filter out noise
Individual clouds rarely cover an entire dispersed fleet simultaneously, so ramps at different sites partially cancel in the aggregate, per Mills and Wiser's (2010) geographic-diversity findings
Larger fleets are always installed in cloud-free regions
Aggregation removes all irradiance variability entirely, including daily and seasonal swings

explanations.a: The effect is statistical/geographic, not about sensor quality.
explanations.b: Correct — because cloud shadows are localized, a dispersed fleet rarely experiences the same cloud edge at the same instant, so individual ramps partly average out at the aggregate level.
explanations.c: Site selection for cloud-free climate is unrelated to why aggregation smooths short-term variability.
explanations.d: Aggregation smooths short-timescale (seconds-to-minutes) variability specifically; it does not eliminate slower daily or seasonal irradiance patterns.

questions.prompt: Order these sources of solar output change from fastest to slowest timescale.

items.text: A cumulus cloud edge crossing the Sun (ramp within tens of seconds)
The Sun's daily rise-to-set elevation change
Seasonal change in day length and Sun angle across months

questions.explanation: Cloud-edge ramps operate on a seconds-to-minutes timescale, far faster than the hours-long diurnal elevation change, which in turn is far faster than the months-long seasonal cycle in day length and Sun path.

units.label: Measuring the Resource: Instruments & Remote Sensing

lessons.label: Cup & Vane Anemometry

sections.heading: A drag imbalance turned into rotation
sections.body: A cup anemometer mounts three (rarely four) hemispherical or conical cups on light spokes around a vertical spindle. Wind striking the concave face of a cup produces more drag than wind striking the convex back of the cup on the opposite side of the rotor, so the assembly spins at a rate that is, to first order, proportional to wind speed. That proportionality is exactly where the instrument's oldest known flaw hides: the drag differential is not linear, and the rotor's own rotational inertia means it does not track a gust and a lull with equal fidelity.

sections.heading: Overspeeding: why turbulence makes cups read high
sections.body: In a rising gust, the cup rotor accelerates quickly because the aerodynamic torque driving it up scales with the square of the relative wind speed. In the following lull, the rotor decelerates only as fast as friction and the now-smaller driving torque allow it to spin down, so it coasts above the true instantaneous speed. Averaged over a turbulent record, the fast-up, slow-down asymmetry biases the mean reading high — a behavior meteorological instrument engineers documented as early as Patterson's 1926 studies of cup-anemometer dynamics. In the sustained, gusty flow typical of a wind-resource site, this overspeeding bias is commonly on the order of one to three percent, larger for higher-inertia, slower-responding rotors and in more turbulent terrain.

sections.heading: Classifying and calibrating the instrument
sections.body: IEC 61400-12-1, the standard governing wind turbine power-performance measurement, assigns cup anemometers a numerical classification describing the expected measurement uncertainty across the full matrix of wind speeds, turbulence intensities, air densities, and inflow angles the sensor will see in the field — a tighter class number (often grouped informally as class 1 versus the looser class 2) means the manufacturer has characterized and bounded that error surface more completely, not simply that the cups spin more smoothly. Achieving a class rating requires calibration traceable through MEASNET, the Measuring Network of Wind Energy Institutes formed in the 1990s to harmonize wind-tunnel calibration procedures across accredited European test labs so that a slope-and-offset calibration certificate from one lab means the same thing as one from another.

sections.heading: The wind vane's simpler job
sections.body: Direction is measured separately, usually with a counterweighted vane that aligns itself with the flow; its accuracy is governed less by drag physics than by damping ratio and distance constant, which determine how quickly it settles after a wind shift rather than oscillating around it.

lessons.workedExample: A campaign logs a class-1.7A cup anemometer at 60 m on a coastal mast where 10-minute turbulence intensity averages 18%. The raw annual mean speed comes out to 7.42 m/s. Cross-checking against a co-located sonic anemometer with no moving parts shows the cup reading is biased about 1.8% high, consistent with published overspeeding rates for that turbulence level — so the analyst applies a documented correction rather than treating the cup record as ground truth, dropping the corrected mean to roughly 7.29 m/s before it feeds the energy-yield model.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about overspeeding because it separates a student who copied a wind-speed number off a data logger from one who understands that the instrument itself has a physics-driven bias. A weak answer says cup anemometers 'can be slightly inaccurate.' A strong answer explains that the bias comes specifically from the square-law torque response being faster on the accelerating side than the decelerating side, names the rough one-to-three-percent magnitude, and connects it to why classified, MEASNET-calibrated instruments and sonic cross-checks matter for a bankable measurement.

questions.prompt: Why does a cup anemometer tend to overestimate wind speed in turbulent flow?

options.text: The cups wear down over time and spin more freely
The rotor accelerates faster in gusts than it decelerates in lulls, because driving torque scales with the square of wind speed
Cold temperatures make the bearings spin faster than the true wind speed
The vane pulls the cup rotor in the direction of the wind, adding extra speed

explanations.a: Bearing wear changes friction over years of service but is not the source of the well-documented turbulence-driven overspeeding bias.
explanations.b: Correct — the asymmetric response (fast up, slow down) driven by the square-law torque relationship means the time-averaged reading sits above the true mean in gusty flow.
explanations.c: Temperature affects bearing friction and air density but is not the mechanism behind overspeeding.
explanations.d: The vane and cup rotor are mechanically independent instruments; the vane measures direction only.

questions.prompt: What does an IEC 61400-12-1 class rating (e.g., class 1 versus class 2) primarily describe?

options.text: The physical size of the cups
The expected measurement uncertainty of the anemometer across the range of wind speeds, turbulence, and inflow conditions it will encounter
How many years the instrument is warrantied for
The color coding used to identify the manufacturer

explanations.a: Cup size varies by model but is not what the class number encodes.
explanations.b: Correct — the classification bounds expected uncertainty across an operating envelope, so a tighter class means better-characterized performance across real field conditions, not just a smoother-spinning rotor.
explanations.c: Warranty length is a commercial term unrelated to the IEC classification.
explanations.d: Manufacturers are not identified by class number.

questions.prompt: Match each term to what it addresses in a cup-and-vane measurement setup.

right.text: Harmonized, traceable wind-tunnel calibration across accredited labs
Positive bias in mean wind speed caused by asymmetric gust/lull response
Measures wind direction by aligning with the flow

questions.explanation: MEASNET standardizes calibration traceability, overspeeding is the turbulence-driven positive bias in cup readings, and the vane's job is direction rather than speed.

questions.prompt: Order these steps in getting a trustworthy cup-anemometer wind speed record, from first to last.

items.text: Anemometer is calibrated in a MEASNET-traceable wind tunnel
Instrument is mounted on the mast at its rated exposure and boom length
Raw 10-minute wind speed averages are logged over the campaign
Overspeeding and other class-based corrections are applied before the mean feeds the resource estimate

questions.explanation: Calibration happens before deployment, mounting establishes valid exposure before data collection, raw averages are logged during the campaign, and corrections are applied afterward before the number is used.

lessons.label: Sonic Anemometers

sections.heading: Measuring wind with the speed of sound itself
sections.body: A sonic anemometer has no moving parts. Instead, pairs of transducers face each other across a short fixed path — typically two paths for a 2D horizontal sensor, three for a full 3D unit — and fire ultrasonic pulses at each other, both directions at once. Wind blowing along a path speeds up the pulse traveling downwind and slows the one traveling upwind; measuring that pair of transit times gives the wind-speed component along that path directly, with no calibration curve to drift and nothing to wear out mechanically. Three non-parallel paths are enough to reconstruct the full 3D wind vector by vector algebra.

sections.heading: A free temperature measurement, almost
sections.body: The speed of sound itself depends on air temperature, so a sonic anemometer's transit-time measurements also yield what is called the sonic or virtual temperature — accurate enough for turbulence work, though it is subtly different from a true thermometer reading because it is also weakly sensitive to humidity through its effect on air density. This dual output is why sonics dominate boundary-layer and eddy-covariance research: a single instrument delivers wind and a fast temperature proxy from the same physical measurement.

sections.heading: The tradeoff: flow distortion instead of overspeeding
sections.body: Sonics escape cup overspeeding entirely, but they introduce a different error: the transducer heads and their supporting arms are solid objects sitting directly in the flow they are trying to measure, so the airflow is locally accelerated and deflected around the sensor's own hardware before it reaches the measurement volume. This flow distortion varies with wind direction relative to the sensor's orientation and can bias readings by a few percent in certain sectors, which is why the current edition of IEC 61400-12-1 added wind-tunnel characterization requirements for sonic anemometers, mirroring the cup-anemometer classification but built around flow-distortion rather than inertial bias.

sections.heading: Why turbulence work demands the extra speed
sections.body: Sonics are typically sampled at 10 to 20 Hz, far faster than the once-per-second or slower response of a cup rotor's mechanical inertia allows. That speed matters because turbulent eddies that transport momentum and heat through the boundary layer have timescales of a fraction of a second to a few seconds; resolving them — as eddy-covariance flux measurements and turbine load assessments require — needs a sensor that can track wind fluctuations at that rate, which is precisely what a mechanical cup rotor cannot do.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher installing turbulence-monitoring instruments on a nacelle-height boom compares a cup anemometer sampled at 1 Hz against a 3D sonic sampled at 20 Hz for the same 10-minute record. The two report nearly identical mean wind speeds, but the sonic's power spectrum shows real turbulent energy out past 5 Hz that the cup's mechanical inertia simply cannot follow — the cup record looks artificially smooth above about 1 Hz. Because the study needs turbulence intensity and gust structure for a fatigue-load estimate, not just a 10-minute mean, the sonic is the only one of the two instruments that can supply the answer.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes sonic anemometry to see if a student understands that swapping instruments trades one error source for another rather than eliminating error altogether. A weak answer says sonics are 'more accurate' than cups with no mechanism. A strong answer names the time-of-flight principle, explains that removing moving parts removes overspeeding but introduces transducer flow distortion, and ties the 10-20 Hz sampling rate to a specific need — resolving turbulent eddies — rather than treating faster sampling as generically better.

questions.prompt: How does a sonic anemometer determine wind speed along a measurement path?

options.text: By timing how long an ultrasonic pulse takes to travel downwind versus upwind between two transducers
By measuring the drag force on a fixed acoustic panel
By counting rotations of a small internal fan
By measuring the Doppler shift of reflected sunlight

explanations.a: Correct — the wind speeds up the downwind pulse and slows the upwind pulse; the transit-time difference along each path gives that path's wind component.
explanations.b: Sonic anemometers have no acoustic panel measuring drag; that describes a different kind of sensor entirely.
explanations.c: A sonic anemometer has no internal fan or moving rotor — that describes a cup anemometer instead.
explanations.d: Sonic anemometers use sound, not light; Doppler shift of light describes a wind LIDAR, not a sonic anemometer.

questions.prompt: What error source affects sonic anemometers in place of cup-style overspeeding?

options.text: Flow distortion from the transducer heads and support arms sitting in the measured airflow
Bearing friction increasing over years of use
Rotor inertia causing a lag between gusts and lulls
Magnetic interference from nearby power lines

explanations.a: Correct — because sonics have no moving parts, their dominant bias comes from the sensor's own hardware locally distorting the flow it is trying to measure, which varies by wind direction.
explanations.b: Sonic anemometers have no bearings; this describes a cup anemometer's aging failure mode.
explanations.c: Rotor inertia and the gust/lull lag describe cup overspeeding, which sonics do not experience since they have no rotor.
explanations.d: Magnetic interference is not the documented error source addressed by sonic anemometer classification standards.

questions.prompt: Order these from lowest to highest typical sampling rate.

items.text: Mechanical cup anemometer (roughly 1 Hz or slower response)
Sonic anemometer at the low end of typical use (10 Hz)
Sonic anemometer at the high end of typical use (20 Hz)

questions.explanation: Mechanical inertia caps a cup anemometer's effective response well below sonic sampling rates, and sonics are commonly run anywhere from 10 to 20 Hz depending on the application.

questions.prompt: Match each sonic anemometer feature to what it enables or reflects.

right.text: Eliminates mechanical overspeeding bias
Yields a fast virtual temperature alongside wind data
Characterizes flow-distortion uncertainty for sonic sensors via wind-tunnel testing

questions.explanation: No moving parts removes rotor inertia bias, the temperature dependence of sound speed gives a bonus virtual temperature, and wind-tunnel characterization standardizes how flow-distortion error is quantified for sonics.

lessons.label: Met Masts & Measurement Campaigns

sections.heading: Why the tower has to be tall
sections.body: A meteorological mast for wind-resource assessment is built to reach the altitudes turbines actually sweep, typically 60 to well over 100 meters — tall enough that its topmost sensors sit near or above modern hub heights rather than extrapolating far upward from a short tower. Masts are either guyed lattice structures or free-standing tubular poles; lattice masts are lighter and cheaper at height but present more structural material to distort the airflow they are trying to measure.

sections.heading: Getting the sensor out of the tower's own wake
sections.body: Any tower, however open its lattice, casts a wake — a zone of reduced and turbulent flow on its downwind side. Anemometers are therefore mounted on horizontal booms that project the sensor well clear of the structure, with IEC 61400-12-1 specifying minimum boom lengths (commonly expressed as a multiple of the tower's cross-sectional diameter) and requiring that the boom point toward the site's prevailing wind direction. Data collected when the wind blows from the tower's shadow sector — through roughly the arc directly behind the boom — are flagged and excluded from the valid dataset rather than corrected, because the flow distortion there is too severe to model reliably.

sections.heading: Redundancy: measuring shear, not just one height
sections.body: A single measurement height cannot tell an analyst how wind speed changes with altitude, yet that vertical wind shear directly affects how much energy a turbine's full rotor disk will see and is central to extrapolating a resource estimate up to hub height. Campaigns therefore instrument multiple heights on the same mast — often three or more — partly to fit a shear profile (commonly a power-law exponent) and partly for redundancy: if a sensor at one height fails or its record is disturbed by icing, the other heights preserve usable data and let analysts cross-check for consistency.

sections.heading: Twelve months is the floor, not the target
sections.body: Wind resource varies strongly by season — winter storm tracks, summer thermal patterns, monsoon reversals — so a valid campaign runs a minimum of about twelve months to capture one full annual cycle before its mean is considered representative. Even a full year, however, is only one sample of interannual variability; because any single year can run anomalously windy or calm, serious assessments extend campaigns to two years or more where feasible, or use measure-correlate-predict (MCP) techniques that regress the short on-site record against a long-running nearby reference station to estimate a more robust long-term mean.

lessons.workedExample: A developer mounts anemometers at 40 m, 60 m, and 80 m on an 80 m lattice mast, with booms oriented into the site's dominant southwesterly flow. After nine months, a lightning strike damages the 60 m boom. Because two other heights are still logging clean data, the campaign continues rather than restarting, and after reaching twelve full months the analyst fits a shear exponent from the 40 m and 80 m records, excludes the roughly 20-degree sector directly behind each boom where tower-shadow flags tripped, and then runs an MCP regression against a 15-year regional airport station to adjust the on-site year, which happened to run about 4% calmer than the long-term average, up to a more representative long-term mean.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about mast design and campaign length because it reveals whether a student understands that a wind-resource number is a carefully constructed statistic, not a raw sensor reading. A weak answer says 'we put an anemometer up for a while and averaged it.' A strong answer explains boom length and tower-shadow exclusion as controlling for a real, physical measurement artifact, names multi-height redundancy as serving both shear estimation and failure tolerance, and can explain why twelve months is a floor rather than a sufficient sample of interannual variability.

questions.prompt: Why are anemometers mounted on booms extending away from a met mast rather than directly on the tower?

options.text: To make the instrument easier to reach for maintenance
To get the sensor clear of the wake and flow distortion the tower structure itself creates
Because IEC standards require all sensors to face north
To reduce the total weight the tower has to support

explanations.a: Maintenance access is a minor secondary concern; it is not why boom length is specified in the standard.
explanations.b: Correct — the tower disturbs the airflow around it, so booms are sized and oriented to place the sensor outside that disturbed zone, particularly clear of the wake behind the structure.
explanations.c: IEC 61400-12-1 specifies boom length and orientation toward the prevailing wind, not a fixed compass direction.
explanations.d: Boom length is chosen for flow-distortion reasons, not to manage structural load.

questions.prompt: What is the main reason a valid wind measurement campaign requires a minimum of about twelve months?

options.text: To let the anemometer's bearings wear in and stabilize
To capture one full annual cycle of seasonal wind variability before treating the mean as representative
Because MEASNET calibration certificates expire after exactly one year
To satisfy insurance requirements unrelated to the wind data itself

explanations.a: Bearing wear-in is not a meaningful factor in campaign-length requirements.
explanations.b: Correct — wind resource varies by season, so a full year is the floor for capturing that annual cycle, though interannual variability means even a year is not a complete picture.
explanations.c: Calibration certificate validity periods are a separate, unrelated consideration.
explanations.d: Insurance is not the driver of the twelve-month minimum in the measurement standard.

questions.prompt: Match each measurement-campaign concept to what it addresses.

right.text: Removes data disturbed by the mast's own wake
Estimates vertical shear and provides failure redundancy
Adjusts a short on-site record using a long-term reference station

questions.explanation: Tower-shadow exclusion removes wake-corrupted data, multiple heights serve shear estimation and redundancy, and MCP corrects a short campaign toward a long-term representative mean.

questions.prompt: Order these campaign steps from first to last.

items.text: Mast is erected with booms sized and oriented per IEC 61400-12-1
Anemometers log data across multiple heights over at least twelve months
Tower-shadow sector data are flagged and excluded
On-site record is adjusted against a long-term reference via MCP if needed

questions.explanation: The mast and booms are installed first, data collection runs across the campaign, invalid shadow-sector data are removed during quality control, and long-term adjustment happens last using the cleaned record.

lessons.label: Remote Sensing: LIDAR & SODAR

sections.heading: Measuring wind without a tower at all
sections.body: Instead of placing a sensor at each height, a ground-based Doppler wind LIDAR fires laser pulses skyward and analyzes the light scattered back by naturally occurring aerosols carried along with the wind. The backscattered light is Doppler-shifted by the aerosols' motion along the beam, and that shift gives the wind speed component along the beam direction at whatever range the return is timed to. Commercial units such as WindCube and ZephIR have made this practical for wind-resource work, letting a single ground-mounted instrument profile wind speed and direction from near the surface up past typical hub heights without erecting a single meter of tower.

sections.heading: Acoustic SODAR: the same idea with sound
sections.body: SODAR (sonic detection and ranging) uses the same Doppler logic but with acoustic pulses instead of laser light, detecting the backscatter caused by turbulent temperature fluctuations in the air rather than aerosols. SODAR was historically cheaper than LIDAR and remains useful in some applications, but it is more sensitive to ambient noise, has a shorter effective range in calm, low-turbulence conditions, and has been increasingly displaced by LIDAR as laser-based units have come down in cost.

sections.heading: Reconstructing wind from a cone, not a point
sections.body: Neither instrument can measure a full 3D wind vector along a single vertical beam, so both use a conical scan strategy: the beam is swept around a cone at a fixed elevation angle, sampling radial velocity at several azimuth angles as it goes, and a sinusoidal fit to those radial-velocity measurements around the circle (the velocity-azimuth display, or VAD, technique) recovers the horizontal wind speed and direction at each height. This retrieval carries a built-in assumption: that the wind is horizontally homogeneous across the full diameter of the scan circle, which at greater heights can span well over a hundred meters.

sections.heading: Where that assumption breaks: complex terrain
sections.body: On flat, unobstructed ground the homogeneity assumption holds well and remote-sensing devices agree closely with a calibrated mast anemometer at the same height. Over hills, ridges, forest edges, or other complex terrain, however, the wind field genuinely varies across the scan disk — speeding up over a ridge crest on one side, slowing in its lee on the other — so the VAD-derived wind vector is a distorted average rather than a true point measurement, introducing a terrain-dependent bias. Verification campaigns run by groups including DNV and the Consortium for Advancing Remote Sensing (CFARS) have repeatedly shown remote-sensing devices agreeing with reference masts to within about two percent on flat terrain, with that agreement degrading measurably as terrain complexity increases, which is why remote sensing is typically paired with at least a shorter reference mast in complex sites rather than used entirely alone.

lessons.workedExample: A developer deploys a ground-based LIDAR at a flat agricultural site alongside an existing 80 m reference mast to cross-validate before removing the mast. Over three months the LIDAR's 100 m wind speed tracks the mast anemometer within about 1.5%, consistent with published flat-terrain verification results, so the team accepts the LIDAR as the primary sensor for the remaining campaign. At a second, ridge-top site the same model of LIDAR is deployed without a co-located mast; post-campaign review flags this as a risk, because the site's complex terrain means the VAD scan's horizontal-homogeneity assumption is likely violated and the reported wind speed may carry an unverified bias.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes remote sensing because students often treat 'no moving parts, no tower' as simply better than a mast, missing that it trades one set of assumptions for another. A weak answer says LIDAR is 'more advanced' than an anemometer. A strong answer explains the VAD conical-scan retrieval, names the horizontal-homogeneity assumption it depends on, and can say specifically why that assumption — and therefore the instrument's accuracy — degrades in complex terrain rather than flat terrain.

questions.prompt: What physical quantity does a Doppler wind LIDAR actually measure to infer wind speed?

options.text: The Doppler shift of laser light backscattered from aerosols carried by the wind
The drag force on a fixed reflective panel
The transit time of an ultrasonic pulse between two fixed transducers
The temperature difference between two heights

explanations.a: Correct — aerosol motion along the laser beam Doppler-shifts the backscattered light, and that shift gives the wind component along the beam.
explanations.b: LIDAR has no panel measuring drag; that is not how the instrument works.
explanations.c: Ultrasonic transit time describes a sonic anemometer, not a LIDAR.
explanations.d: Temperature difference is not what a Doppler wind LIDAR measures, though SODAR does exploit temperature-driven turbulence for its backscatter.

questions.prompt: What assumption does the velocity-azimuth display (VAD) conical-scan retrieval rely on, and why does that matter in complex terrain?

options.text: It assumes the wind is horizontally homogeneous across the scan circle, which can be violated by terrain-driven flow variation over hills or ridges
It assumes the air is free of all aerosols, which fails near coastlines
It assumes the instrument is mounted exactly at hub height, which fails on short masts
It assumes wind direction never changes during the scan

explanations.a: Correct — the VAD fit treats the wind as uniform across the full scan disk, an assumption that breaks down where terrain causes real spatial variation in the flow.
explanations.b: LIDAR actually requires aerosols to generate a backscatter signal; their absence would reduce signal, not violate the VAD assumption.
explanations.c: VAD retrieval works at any scanned height, not only hub height.
explanations.d: The VAD technique fits a sinusoid to azimuthal variation and does not assume direction is constant during the scan; it assumes spatial homogeneity instead.

questions.prompt: Match each remote-sensing term to its description.

right.text: Uses acoustic pulses and temperature-turbulence backscatter
Fits radial velocities around a scan cone to recover the horizontal wind vector
Documented roughly 2% flat-terrain agreement between remote sensors and reference masts

questions.explanation: SODAR relies on acoustic backscatter from turbulence, VAD is the sinusoidal-fit retrieval technique, and CFARS/DNV campaigns quantified flat-terrain agreement near 2%.

questions.prompt: Order these from least to most likely to introduce terrain-driven bias into a remote-sensing wind measurement.

items.text: Flat, open agricultural terrain
Gently rolling terrain with modest elevation change
Ridge-top site with steep upwind and downwind slopes

questions.explanation: The horizontal-homogeneity assumption behind VAD retrieval holds best on flat terrain and is progressively more violated as terrain complexity and slope increase, with a steep ridge site being the most challenging case.

lessons.label: Pyranometers & Pyrheliometers

sections.heading: Two ways to turn light into a voltage
sections.body: A thermopile pyranometer works thermally: a black, broadband-absorbing disk under one or two glass domes heats up when it absorbs solar radiation, and a stack of thermocouples (the thermopile) converts the resulting temperature difference against a reference into a small voltage proportional to total hemispheric irradiance. A silicon photodiode pyranometer instead uses a solar cell as the sensing element, converting incident photons directly to current. Photodiode units are cheaper and respond almost instantly, but the silicon's photovoltaic response only covers roughly 400-1100 nanometers, missing much of the near-infrared that a thermopile's black coating absorbs across the full solar spectrum — so a photodiode pyranometer's reading can drift several percent off a thermopile's under changing cloud cover or air mass, because the spectral mix of sunlight shifts throughout the day and with atmospheric conditions.

sections.heading: ISO 9060: grading the instrument
sections.body: ISO 9060 sorts pyranometers into a performance hierarchy historically labeled secondary standard, first class, and second class, ranked from tightest to loosest specification on response time, temperature dependence, directional error, stability, and other characteristics. A secondary-standard instrument is the type used at reference stations and for bankable resource assessments; first-class units are common in commercial monitoring networks; second-class instruments trade accuracy for low cost in less demanding applications.

sections.heading: Two errors even a good pyranometer carries
sections.body: Thermal, or zero, offset is a small negative reading — commonly on the order of a few watts per square meter — that appears even at night or under zero irradiance, caused by the black sensor radiating infrared heat outward to a colder sky faster than it receives it, cooling the thermopile junction below the reference and producing a spurious negative signal; ventilated pyranometers reduce this by keeping the dome and body at a more uniform temperature. Cosine response error is separate: an ideal pyranometer's signal should scale with the cosine of the angle between the sun and the sensor's vertical axis, but real domes refract and partially reflect light non-ideally at oblique angles, so the actual response departs from the ideal cosine law — an error that grows worst at low solar elevation, near sunrise and sunset, when the sun's rays strike the dome at a steep angle.

sections.heading: Pyrheliometers: isolating the direct beam
sections.body: A pyranometer measures total (global) irradiance from the whole sky; a pyrheliometer instead measures only direct normal irradiance (DNI), the beam coming straight from the sun's disk, which is what concentrating solar technologies and tracking photovoltaic systems actually use. To do that, a pyrheliometer is built with a narrow field of view — a few degrees wide — that excludes most diffuse skylight while still capturing the small circumsolar glow immediately around the sun, and it is mounted on a two-axis solar tracker that keeps it pointed continuously at the moving sun throughout the day.

lessons.workedExample: A bankability study needs DNI data for a proposed concentrating solar plant. The site's existing station uses a first-class thermopile pyranometer for GHI but has no pyrheliometer, so DNI has to be modeled from GHI and diffuse measurements instead of measured directly, adding uncertainty the developer's lenders flag. The team upgrades the station with a tracker-mounted pyrheliometer and a secondary-standard pyranometer, and during commissioning notices the pyranometer reads about -3 W/m^2 at night under a clear, cold sky — a textbook thermal offset — which the data-processing pipeline flags and zeroes out rather than treating as a real negative-irradiance measurement.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about pyranometer classes and error sources because solar-resource projects live or die on whether the instrument's stated accuracy is understood, not just trusted. A weak answer says 'the sensor measures sunlight.' A strong answer distinguishes thermopile from photodiode sensing physics, names a specific ISO 9060 class appropriate to the study's stakes, and can explain thermal offset and cosine error as two distinct, well-characterized error sources rather than lumping all inaccuracy together as 'sensor noise.'

questions.prompt: Why can a silicon photodiode pyranometer disagree with a thermopile pyranometer under changing cloud cover?

options.text: The photodiode's spectral response only covers roughly 400-1100 nm, so it misses near-infrared light the thermopile absorbs, and clouds shift the spectral mix of sunlight
The photodiode has a slower response time than the thermopile
The thermopile stops working whenever clouds are present
The photodiode can only measure direct beam radiation, not diffuse light

explanations.a: Correct — the photodiode's limited spectral range means its reading is sensitive to the spectral composition of incoming light, which changes with clouds and air mass, unlike the broadband thermopile.
explanations.b: Photodiodes respond faster than thermopiles, not slower, so this does not explain the disagreement.
explanations.c: Thermopile pyranometers continue functioning normally under cloud cover; that is not the source of the discrepancy.
explanations.d: Both instrument types measure hemispheric (global) irradiance, not direct beam only; that describes a pyrheliometer instead.

questions.prompt: What causes thermal (zero) offset in a thermopile pyranometer?

options.text: The black sensor radiates infrared energy to a colder sky faster than it receives it, cooling the thermopile junction below reference
Dust accumulating on the glass dome over several months
Electrical interference from nearby power lines
The instrument's internal battery running low

explanations.a: Correct — net infrared loss to a cold sky cools the sensing element below the instrument's reference temperature, producing a small spurious negative signal even with no shortwave irradiance present.
explanations.b: Dust accumulation causes a separate, gradual sensitivity loss but is not the mechanism behind thermal offset.
explanations.c: Electrical interference is not the documented cause of thermal offset in these instruments.
explanations.d: Battery condition is unrelated to the physics of thermal offset.

questions.prompt: Match each instrument or error to what it does or measures.

right.text: Measures direct normal irradiance via a narrow field of view on a solar tracker
Grows largest at low solar elevation angles near sunrise and sunset
Ranks pyranometers from secondary standard down to second class

questions.explanation: A pyrheliometer isolates the direct beam with a tracker, cosine error is worst at oblique sun angles, and ISO 9060 sets the accuracy hierarchy for pyranometers.

questions.prompt: Order these pyranometer grades from tightest (most accurate) to loosest specification under ISO 9060's historical naming.

items.text: Secondary standard
First class
Second class

questions.explanation: ISO 9060's historical hierarchy runs from secondary standard (tightest specification, used for reference and bankable measurements) through first class to second class (loosest, lowest cost).

lessons.label: Reference Networks & Satellite Retrieval

sections.heading: BSRN: the ground-truth backbone
sections.body: The Baseline Surface Radiation Network (BSRN), established in the early 1990s under the World Meteorological Organization and World Climate Research Programme, is a global set of stations chosen specifically to produce the highest-quality surface radiation measurements available — secondary-standard instruments, rigorous calibration schedules, and standardized quality control at every site. BSRN is deliberately small, on the order of a few dozen stations worldwide, because its purpose is not broad coverage but serving as an accuracy anchor: the dataset every satellite-derived and modeled irradiance product gets validated against.

sections.heading: NSRDB and the modeled alternative
sections.body: Most solar sites will never have a station anywhere nearby, which is why NREL built the National Solar Radiation Database (NSRDB): a gridded, satellite-derived dataset covering large regions at roughly kilometer-scale resolution and sub-hourly time steps, built from radiative transfer and semi-empirical models rather than a physical sensor at every point. It lets a developer pull a multi-decade irradiance record for essentially any location without ever installing an instrument there, at the cost of accepting a modeled rather than measured number.

sections.heading: Turning satellite images into irradiance
sections.body: The core technique behind most satellite-derived irradiance products is the Heliosat method, developed in the 1980s: a geostationary weather satellite's visible-channel imagery is used to compute a cloud index by comparing each pixel's reflectance to its clear-sky and fully-overcast reference values, and that cloud index is then translated into an estimate of how much of the top-of-atmosphere solar radiation actually reaches the surface. Commercial products such as SolarAnywhere apply this same general family of methods, refined with additional atmospheric inputs like aerosol optical depth and water vapor, to generate the bankable-grade irradiance datasets project developers actually purchase.

sections.heading: How much the two disagree, and when it matters
sections.body: Under typical conditions, satellite-derived global horizontal irradiance (GHI) tracks ground measurements reasonably well, with reported biases often cited around five percent against a well-maintained ground station, though errors grow substantially under broken or fast-moving cloud, where a single satellite pixel can span several kilometers and average away real sub-pixel variability the ground sensor actually experiences. Direct normal irradiance (DNI) is harder still: because DNI depends sensitively on whether the beam path to a specific point is clear or obstructed by even thin cloud, satellite-derived DNI carries meaningfully larger errors than GHI. For that reason, satellite datasets are routinely trusted for early-stage site screening and multi-decade long-term context, but a bankable financing-grade assessment still typically installs a ground station for at least a year or two and uses it to bias-correct the satellite record, rather than relying on the modeled data alone.

lessons.workedExample: A developer screens twelve candidate sites across a region using only NSRDB satellite-derived GHI and DNI, ranking them by estimated annual energy yield with no ground instrument installed anywhere. The top three sites then each receive a ground station with a secondary-standard pyranometer and pyrheliometer for an eighteen-month campaign. At one site, the ground data shows DNI running about 9% below the satellite estimate, consistent with that site sitting in a zone of frequent thin, broken cirrus the coarse satellite pixel underrepresents — a correction large enough to change the project's financial return, which is exactly the gap a screening-only satellite study would have missed.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes ground-versus-satellite data because it tests whether a student can justify a real methodological tradeoff rather than just citing a data source. A weak answer treats satellite and ground data as interchangeable. A strong answer explains the Heliosat cloud-index mechanism in outline, states that DNI carries larger satellite-retrieval error than GHI and can explain why (beam-path sensitivity to sub-pixel cloud), and can say specifically when a modeled dataset is good enough (screening) versus when it needs ground validation (bankable financing).

questions.prompt: What is the primary purpose of the BSRN network, given that it includes only a few dozen stations worldwide?

options.text: To provide the highest-accuracy reference measurements that satellite and modeled irradiance products are validated against
To provide dense global coverage for every solar project site
To replace all satellite-derived irradiance products
To measure only wind speed, not solar irradiance

explanations.a: Correct — BSRN prioritizes instrument quality and calibration rigor over station count, functioning as the accuracy anchor other datasets are checked against.
explanations.b: BSRN's small station count means it was never designed for dense global coverage; that role falls to gridded modeled datasets like NSRDB.
explanations.c: BSRN complements rather than replaces satellite products; the two serve different purposes.
explanations.d: BSRN measures surface radiation (solar irradiance), not wind.

questions.prompt: Why does satellite-derived DNI typically carry larger errors than satellite-derived GHI?

options.text: DNI depends sensitively on whether the direct beam path is clear, so thin or sub-pixel cloud that a coarse satellite pixel misses still substantially affects the true beam value
DNI is measured with a less accurate ground instrument than GHI
Satellites cannot detect direct sunlight at all
DNI values are always higher than GHI, so any percentage error looks larger

explanations.a: Correct — because DNI is an all-or-nothing beam measurement sensitive to any obstruction along the sun-to-point path, sub-pixel cloud variability that a satellite averages away produces disproportionately large DNI errors.
explanations.b: Ground pyrheliometers used for DNI are not inherently less accurate than pyranometers; the error described here is in the satellite retrieval, not the ground reference instrument.
explanations.c: Satellites do detect solar radiation reaching the surface; the issue is retrieval accuracy for the direct-beam component specifically, not total inability to sense it.
explanations.d: The larger DNI error is a real retrieval accuracy issue tied to beam-path sensitivity, not simply an artifact of DNI's numeric scale.

questions.prompt: Match each item to its role in solar resource data.

right.text: Small, highest-accuracy global reference network
Gridded, satellite-derived dataset covering broad regions
Converts satellite cloud-index imagery into surface irradiance estimates

questions.explanation: BSRN anchors accuracy with few, excellent stations; NSRDB provides broad modeled coverage; Heliosat is the underlying retrieval method converting satellite imagery to irradiance.

questions.prompt: Order these steps in a typical project's use of solar resource data, from earliest to latest in project development.

items.text: Screen many candidate sites using satellite-derived (e.g., NSRDB) data only
Install a ground station with calibrated pyranometer/pyrheliometer at top candidate sites
Run a ground campaign for a year or more
Bias-correct the satellite record against the ground data for the bankable estimate

questions.explanation: Satellite data is cheap and broad, so it screens many sites first; ground instrumentation follows at the shortlisted sites; the campaign then runs long enough to be meaningful; and the final bankable number corrects the long satellite record using that ground data.

lessons.label: Measurement Uncertainty & Data Quality

sections.heading: Building the uncertainty budget piece by piece
sections.body: No single number describes how trustworthy a resource measurement is; instead, analysts build an uncertainty budget that itemizes each independent source of error and combines them. Calibration uncertainty comes from the wind-tunnel or radiometric calibration itself — a MEASNET-traceable cup anemometer calibration might carry roughly one to two percent uncertainty in its slope. Mounting uncertainty covers flow distortion from the boom, tower, or transducer geometry discussed elsewhere in this unit. Classification uncertainty is the operating-envelope error bound an IEC class rating or ISO 9060 class assigns to the instrument. And transfer uncertainty appears whenever a measurement is extrapolated or adjusted — projecting a mast reading up to hub height, or bias-correcting a satellite record against a shorter ground campaign — since that adjustment step introduces its own error on top of the original measurement.

sections.heading: Combining errors: root-sum-square, not simple addition
sections.body: Because these error sources are largely independent of one another, analysts do not simply add their percentages; they combine them in quadrature — the root-sum-square, or square root of the sum of each component's squared uncertainty — which is smaller than a straight sum because independent random errors partially cancel rather than all pushing in the same direction at once. A campaign with, say, 1.5% calibration uncertainty, 1% mounting uncertainty, and 2% classification uncertainty combines to roughly 2.7% overall, not 4.5%.

sections.heading: Data recovery: how much of the record has to survive
sections.body: Sensors ice over, loggers lose power, cables fail. Because gaps are unavoidable, campaigns set a minimum data-recovery (availability) threshold — commonly around 90 percent of the intended record — below which the dataset is considered too incomplete to support a confident annual estimate, and gap-filling or campaign extension is required instead. Automated quality-control routines catch problems continuously rather than waiting for a post-campaign review: range checks flag physically impossible readings, rate-of-change checks catch a sensor jumping implausibly between consecutive readings, flatline detection catches a stuck sensor reporting the identical value for too long, and for solar data, closure checks compare whether measured global, direct, and diffuse irradiance are physically consistent with one another (GHI should approximately equal DNI times the cosine of the solar zenith angle plus DHI) — a mismatch flags an instrument that has drifted or fouled.

sections.heading: Why the final number amplifies wind uncertainty more than solar
sections.body: How that combined instrument uncertainty propagates into the number that actually matters — predicted energy output — differs sharply between the two resources. A wind turbine's power output scales roughly with the cube of wind speed, so a given percentage error in the measured mean wind speed propagates into roughly three times that percentage error in the energy estimate; a 3% wind-speed uncertainty becomes something closer to a 9% energy-output uncertainty. Solar energy yield, by contrast, scales close to linearly with irradiance, so a 3% irradiance uncertainty stays roughly a 3% uncertainty in energy output. That cube-law amplification is exactly why wind measurement campaigns invest so heavily in tightly classified, well-calibrated instruments — the same percentage sloppiness costs far more downstream than it would in a solar assessment.

lessons.workedExample: A wind campaign's uncertainty budget totals 1.5% calibration, 1.2% mounting/flow-distortion, 1.8% classification, and 1.0% MCP transfer uncertainty. Combined in quadrature, the overall wind speed uncertainty comes to about 2.8%. Because energy output scales roughly with the cube of wind speed, the analyst reports an energy-estimate uncertainty near 8.4% rather than treating the 2.8% wind-speed figure as the bottom line — a distinction that directly affects how a lender prices the project's financing risk. A parallel solar campaign at a comparably instrumented site, with similar total instrument uncertainty of about 3%, reports an energy-estimate uncertainty close to that same 3%, since irradiance-to-yield scaling is roughly linear.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about uncertainty propagation because it is the single clearest test of whether a student understands that a measurement's error does not stop at the sensor. A weak answer states an instrument's accuracy spec and stops there. A strong answer builds a budget from named, independent sources, combines them in quadrature rather than by simple addition, cites the roughly 90% data-recovery threshold as a real go/no-go gate, and can explain why the same percentage wind-speed error costs roughly three times as much in the final energy number as an equivalent solar irradiance error does.

questions.prompt: Why do analysts combine independent uncertainty sources in quadrature (root-sum-square) rather than by simple addition?

options.text: Because independent random errors partially cancel rather than all acting in the same direction, so RSS gives a smaller, more realistic combined estimate than a straight sum
Because simple addition is mathematically impossible with percentages
Because IEC standards forbid adding percentages directly
Because quadrature combination always produces a larger number, which is more conservative

explanations.a: Correct — for independent error sources, RSS reflects that they do not all push the reading the same direction simultaneously, giving a realistic combined figure smaller than the simple sum.
explanations.b: Adding percentages is mathematically fine; RSS is used because it better represents how independent errors actually combine, not because addition is impossible.
explanations.c: There is no such prohibition; RSS is a statistical convention, not a regulatory rule.
explanations.d: RSS combination produces a smaller number than simple addition, not a larger one, so this describes the opposite of what actually happens.

questions.prompt: A campaign has 3% uncertainty in its measured mean wind speed. Roughly how much uncertainty does that translate to in the predicted energy output, and why?

options.text: Roughly 9%, because turbine power output scales approximately with the cube of wind speed
Roughly 3%, because energy output scales linearly with wind speed
Roughly 1%, because errors shrink when propagated through the power curve
Roughly 27%, because power scales with the square of the cube of wind speed

explanations.a: Correct — because power scales roughly with wind speed cubed, a given percentage wind-speed error propagates to about three times that percentage in energy output.
explanations.b: Linear scaling describes solar irradiance-to-yield, not wind, where the cube-law relationship applies instead.
explanations.c: Errors amplify through the cube-law power curve; they do not shrink.
explanations.d: The cube-law relationship triples the percentage error, not raises it to a further power.

questions.prompt: Match each automated QC check to what it catches.

right.text: Physically impossible readings outside plausible bounds
A sensor stuck reporting the same value repeatedly
Inconsistency between measured GHI, DNI, and DHI

questions.explanation: Range checks catch impossible values, flatline detection catches stuck sensors, and closure checks catch solar-component inconsistency using the GHI/DNI/DHI relationship.

questions.prompt: Order these uncertainty-budget components as they are typically identified in building a wind measurement's total uncertainty, from the instrument's own calibration outward to the final adjustment.

items.text: Calibration uncertainty from the wind-tunnel test
Mounting/flow-distortion uncertainty from boom and tower geometry
Classification uncertainty across the operating envelope
Transfer uncertainty from extrapolation or long-term adjustment

questions.explanation: The budget starts at the instrument's own calibration, adds uncertainty from how it is physically mounted, folds in the envelope-wide classification bound, and finally accounts for any extrapolation or long-term transfer applied to reach the reported estimate.

units.label: Resource Assessment: From Short Records to Bankable Estimates

lessons.label: The Measure-Correlate-Predict Framework

sections.heading: A short record standing in for a 20-30 year climate
sections.body: A developer rarely gets more than one or two years of on-site met-mast data before financing decisions are due, but a wind or solar project has to be sized against the long-term climate it will operate in for 20-30 years. Measure-correlate-predict (MCP) bridges that gap: pair the short on-site record with a long-running reference dataset (a nearby airport station or a reanalysis product) over the same concurrent months, fit a statistical relationship between the two, then apply that relationship to the reference's full multi-decade history to reconstruct what the site's long-term wind speed would have been. The output is not a measurement, it is an inference — and its quality depends entirely on how well the fitted relationship holds outside the window it was fitted on.

sections.heading: Simple regression and why it isn't enough
sections.body: The most basic MCP approach runs ordinary least-squares regression of concurrent site wind speed against reference wind speed, giving a slope and intercept applied to every reference value. The problem is regression dilution: OLS minimizes squared error by pulling predictions toward the mean, which systematically shrinks the variance of the predicted long-term site record even when the mean is roughly right. Rogers, Rogers, and Manwell (2005) compared several MCP algorithms and found this variance loss was a real, measurable failure of the simple linear method. Two fixes are standard: the variance-ratio method rescales the regression to explicitly preserve the reference-to-site variance ratio, and the matrix (bin) method sorts concurrent data into direction-and-speed bins and derives a separate transfer relationship per bin, capturing effects a single global slope cannot.

sections.heading: The load-bearing assumption: stationarity
sections.body: Every MCP method rests on one assumption: the statistical relationship between site and reference, fitted over a handful of concurrent months, remains valid across decades of reference data the site was never measured against. This is stationarity, and it can silently fail — a new building near the reference station changes its exposure, a wind farm built upwind of the reference tower distorts its wake-affected readings, or the reference simply sits in a different sub-regional flow regime that decouples from the site in certain wind directions. Analysts test this by splitting the concurrent period and checking whether the fitted relationship is stable across seasons or sub-periods; if it is not, MCP output should be treated as lower-confidence regardless of how clean the regression fit looks.

lessons.workedExample: A met mast records 14 months on-site, averaging 6.8 m/s. A nearby airport station has 30 years of hourly data. Over the same 14 concurrent months the airport averaged 7.5 m/s, but its own 30-year mean is 7.2 m/s — those 14 months happened to be a below-normal period for the airport too. A variance-ratio MCP fit gives slope 0.92; since the fitted line must pass through the concurrent-period means (6.8 = 0.92 x 7.5 + intercept), the intercept works out to -0.1 m/s. Applying that relationship to the airport's full 30-year mean of 7.2 m/s (not just the concurrent 14 months) yields a predicted long-term site mean of 0.92 x 7.2 + (-0.1), about 6.5 m/s — below the raw on-site average here, since the correction is doing real work reconciling two different reference periods.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks why the team didn't just report their measured on-site average as the site's wind resource. A weak answer treats the measured mean as the answer. A strong answer explains that any single 12-18 month window can sit above or below the true long-term climate, names the reference dataset and MCP method used to correct for that, and can say in one sentence what would break the correction — an unstable site-reference relationship, i.e. non-stationarity.

questions.prompt: Why does simple ordinary-least-squares MCP tend to underestimate the variance of the predicted long-term wind speed record?

options.text: OLS regression always overestimates the mean
Regression dilution pulls predictions toward the mean, shrinking variance
Reanalysis data has no variance to begin with
The reference station's instruments are less precise than the site mast

explanations.a: OLS regression does not systematically bias the mean; the documented problem is variance, not mean level.
explanations.b: Correct — this is regression dilution, the effect Rogers, Rogers, and Manwell (2005) identified as a weakness of simple linear MCP.
explanations.c: Reanalysis and station reference data both carry real year-to-year variance; that is not the source of the error.
explanations.d: Instrument precision is a separate, smaller issue; the dominant, well-documented effect is the statistical pull of regression toward the mean.

questions.prompt: What is the core assumption an MCP long-term correction depends on?

options.text: That the site and reference are within 1 km of each other
That the statistical relationship fitted on the concurrent period stays valid across the reference's full multi-decade record
That both datasets use the same anemometer brand
That the site has at least 5 years of on-site data

explanations.a: Proximity helps but is not the load-bearing assumption; distant, well-correlated references are routinely used.
explanations.b: Correct — this is stationarity, and if it fails, the corrected long-term estimate is unreliable no matter how clean the concurrent-period fit was.
explanations.c: Instrument brand matching is irrelevant; what matters is the statistical relationship between the two records.
explanations.d: MCP exists precisely because sites usually have far less than 5 years of on-site data; that is the problem it solves, not a precondition.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a measure-correlate-predict analysis.

items.text: Collect on-site data concurrent with a long-running reference record
Fit a statistical relationship (regression, variance-ratio, or matrix) between site and reference over the concurrent period
Test the relationship for stability across sub-periods or seasons
Apply the fitted relationship to the reference's full long-term record to predict the site's long-term climate

questions.explanation: MCP starts with concurrent measurement, fits the transfer relationship on that overlap, checks it for stability before trusting it, then applies it to the reference's decades of data the site itself was never measured against.

questions.prompt: Match each MCP method to what distinguishes it.

right.text: Single global slope/intercept; prone to regression dilution
Explicitly rescaled to preserve the site-to-reference variance ratio
Fits a separate transfer relationship per direction-and-speed bin

questions.explanation: Simple regression is the naive baseline that loses variance; variance-ratio methods correct for that loss directly; matrix methods go further by not assuming one relationship holds across all wind directions and speeds.

lessons.label: Long-Term Reference Data & Reanalysis

sections.heading: What a reanalysis actually is
sections.body: A reanalysis is not a collection of raw observations; it is the output of a fixed numerical weather model repeatedly fed decades of historical observations — satellite soundings, radiosondes, surface stations, ships and buoys — through data assimilation, producing a physically consistent, gap-free gridded record. ERA5, produced by ECMWF under the Copernicus program, runs at roughly 31 km (0.25°) horizontal resolution, hourly, and now extends back to 1940. MERRA-2, produced by NASA's Global Modeling and Assimilation Office, runs coarser at roughly 50 km resolution, hourly, from 1980 onward. Because the same model generates the entire record, reanalysis wind speed is internally consistent across 80+ years in a way no single set of surface stations, with their equipment changes and site moves, ever is.

sections.heading: Reanalysis vs. the nearby station as an MCP reference
sections.body: A nearby airport or synoptic station measures wind directly at a fixed, known location, but its record is only as long as the station has existed and is vulnerable to instrument changes, relocations, and land-use shifts around the site — an airport runway expansion or new hangar can quietly shift a station's wind climate mid-record. Reanalysis avoids those discontinuities and reaches back further, but its 31-50 km grid cell cannot resolve local terrain, so it systematically misrepresents near-surface wind over complex topography or through sharp roughness transitions the model grid smooths away. In practice, analysts favor reanalysis for the length and physical consistency of the record and treat a well-sited nearby station, when one exists, as a valuable cross-check rather than a substitute.

sections.heading: Why one measured year is never the answer
sections.body: Wind climate varies year to year because large-scale circulation patterns shift the storm tracks that drive it — the El Nino-Southern Oscillation and the North Atlantic Oscillation are the best-documented drivers, favoring stronger or weaker wind years across whole regions for a season or more. Which single year a developer happens to measure can shift the predicted long-term average wind speed by several percent, and considerably more at some sites — and because wind power scales roughly with the cube of speed, that swing in speed translates into an even larger swing in energy. A single measured year, however carefully instrumented, is a sample from a distribution, not the distribution itself; only a multi-decade reference anchors the estimate to the actual long-term mean.

lessons.workedExample: A site's 14-month met-mast campaign happens to fall during a La Nina episode that historically strengthens wind flow across the Great Plains. The ERA5 record at that grid cell shows the concurrent measurement period averaged 8% above the site's own 20-year ERA5 mean. Reporting the raw on-site average without correction would overstate the long-term wind resource by roughly that same margin — exactly the gap MCP against the 20-year ERA5 record is built to catch, since a 20-year window averages over multiple ENSO and NAO phases instead of landing inside just one of them.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks why the team needed ERA5 or MERRA-2 at all when they had their own tower data. The weak answer treats the on-site record as sufficient on its own. The strong answer names the specific reanalysis product and its resolution, explains that a 1-2 year tower record cannot distinguish a normal year from an anomalous one, and can point to a physical driver — ENSO or NAO — as the reason wind climate varies year to year in the first place.

questions.prompt: Roughly what horizontal grid resolution does ERA5 provide?

options.text: About 1 km
About 31 km
About 500 km
About 5 km

explanations.a: 1 km is far finer than any global reanalysis; that resolution requires local mesoscale or CFD modeling, not ERA5.
explanations.b: Correct — ERA5's native grid is about 0.25 degrees, roughly 31 km, hourly, from ECMWF's Copernicus program.
explanations.c: 500 km is far coarser than ERA5; that would barely resolve continental-scale features.
explanations.d: 5 km is finer than ERA5's native grid; some downscaled wind-atlas products reach that scale, but not ERA5 itself.

questions.prompt: Why is a single measured year insufficient to characterize a site's long-term wind resource?

options.text: Anemometers wear out after 12 months
Large-scale circulation patterns like ENSO and the NAO shift regional wind climate year to year, so one year is a sample, not the long-term mean
Wind turbines cannot be sized without exactly 30 years of data
Reanalysis products only publish 12-month averages

explanations.a: Instrument wear is a real maintenance issue but is not why single-year measurements are statistically insufficient.
explanations.b: Correct — documented year-to-year swings driven by circulation patterns like ENSO and the NAO mean any single year can sit well above or below the true multi-decade mean.
explanations.c: There is no fixed 30-year requirement; the point is that the reference period must be long enough to average over multiple circulation phases, and reanalysis records of 20-40+ years serve that purpose.
explanations.d: Reanalysis products publish hourly data across their full multi-decade record, not just 12-month averages.

questions.prompt: Match each long-term reference source to its defining tradeoff.

right.text: Direct local measurement, but vulnerable to instrument and site-exposure changes over its record
Finer ~31 km grid, hourly, extending back to 1940
Coarser ~50 km grid, hourly, extending back to 1980

questions.explanation: A station gives direct measurement at a fixed point but a shorter, discontinuity-prone record; ERA5 and MERRA-2 both give long, physically consistent gridded records, differing mainly in resolution and start date.

questions.prompt: Order these from finest to coarsest horizontal resolution.

items.text: On-site met mast (point measurement)
ERA5 (~31 km grid)
MERRA-2 (~50 km grid)

questions.explanation: A met mast is a single point; ERA5's grid cell is roughly 31 km across; MERRA-2's grid cell is coarser still at roughly 50 km, which is why neither reanalysis product resolves local terrain the way a point measurement does.

lessons.label: Spatial Extrapolation & Wind Atlases

sections.heading: One mast, many turbines
sections.body: A resource assessment rarely has the luxury of a met mast at every turbine position — typically one or a few masts stand in for a site that may host dozens of machines spread across ridgelines and valleys. The wind atlas method, formalized by Troen and Petersen in the 1989 European Wind Atlas and implemented in the WAsP software from what was then Riso National Laboratory in Denmark, solves this by working in two stages. First it strips the mast's measured wind of all local effects — terrain height, surface roughness, sheltering obstacles — to back out a regional geostrophic wind representative of the wider area. Then it re-applies terrain, roughness, and obstacle models for any other point in the domain to predict the wind there, at any height.

sections.heading: The linear flow model and where it comes from
sections.body: WAsP's orographic module models how hills and ridges speed up or slow down flow using linearized perturbation theory for flow over low, gentle terrain, developed by Jackson and Hunt (1975). Separately, a roughness-change model tracks how internal boundary layers grow downwind of transitions between surface types (forest to open field, land to water), and an obstacle model accounts for sheltering by buildings or tree lines. Combined, these let a single mast generate a full wind resource map across a site in minutes rather than requiring a mast at every turbine. The catch is in the name: linear. The model assumes flow stays attached to the terrain surface: valid over smooth, rolling hills, but not once slopes get steep enough that the flow separates and recirculates on the lee side.

sections.heading: RIX: knowing when linear stops being valid
sections.body: Bowen and Mortensen (1996) proposed the ruggedness index, RIX, as a simple, computable warning flag: the percentage of terrain within a given radius of a site that exceeds a critical slope, commonly taken as 0.3 (about 17 degrees). A site with RIX near zero sits in gently rolling terrain where WAsP's linear assumptions hold reasonably well. As RIX rises, so does the likelihood of flow separation the linear model cannot represent, and Mortensen and Petersen (1997) showed that the difference in RIX between the reference mast and the target turbine site (delta-RIX) correlates with WAsP's prediction error, systematically overpredicting wind speed on steep, separated lee slopes (the model keeps extrapolating attached-flow acceleration instead of the speed deficit real flow separation produces). Above roughly 10-15% RIX, or a large delta-RIX between mast and turbine, analysts typically abandon the linear model in favor of computational fluid dynamics or mesoscale-microscale coupled models before finalizing turbine micro-siting.

lessons.workedExample: A met mast sits on a gentle ridge with RIX of 2%. Three proposed turbine positions sit on a steeper downwind slope with RIX of 15%, giving a delta-RIX of 13 percentage points. Following the Bowen and Mortensen relationship, this flags a high risk that WAsP's linear model overpredicts the true wind speed (missing the speed deficit from lee-side flow separation and recirculation) at those three positions. The assessment team re-runs those positions through a CFD model instead of trusting the linear WAsP output, and micro-siting shifts one turbine 150 meters upslope to avoid the separated-flow zone entirely.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks how the team knows a single mast's data is representative of every turbine location across a site that might span a kilometer of varied terrain. A weak answer assumes uniform wind across the site. A strong answer names the extrapolation model used (WAsP or equivalent), explains it is a linear flow model with a known breakdown point, and can state the ruggedness metric — RIX — used to check whether that breakdown point has been crossed at this site.

questions.prompt: What does the RIX ruggedness index measure?

options.text: The average wind speed at a site
The percentage of terrain within a radius of a site that exceeds a critical slope
The number of turbines that fit on a site
The height of the met mast above ground

explanations.a: RIX is a terrain-shape metric, not a wind-speed metric; it flags where a flow model's assumptions are likely to fail.
explanations.b: Correct — Bowen and Mortensen (1996) defined RIX as the fraction of terrain steeper than a critical slope (commonly 0.3), as a proxy for flow separation risk.
explanations.c: RIX says nothing about turbine count or spacing; it is purely a terrain ruggedness measure.
explanations.d: Mast height is an instrumentation parameter, unrelated to the terrain-ruggedness calculation behind RIX.

questions.prompt: Why does WAsP's linear flow model lose accuracy in steep, rugged terrain?

options.text: It was never calibrated with any real wind data
The linear perturbation theory it is built on assumes attached flow, which breaks down once slopes are steep enough to cause flow separation
It only works for offshore sites
It requires more than one met mast to run at all

explanations.a: WAsP's underlying models, including Jackson and Hunt's (1975) orographic theory, are grounded in fluid dynamics and validated against measurement; the issue is the range of terrain they were built for, not lack of calibration.
explanations.b: Correct — the model assumes flow stays attached to the terrain surface, an assumption steep slopes violate by causing separation and recirculation the linear model cannot represent.
explanations.c: WAsP is used onshore and offshore; terrain complexity, not shore proximity, is what limits its linear assumptions.
explanations.d: The wind atlas method is specifically designed to extrapolate from a single mast; it does not require multiple masts to run.

questions.prompt: Order the stages of the WAsP wind atlas method.

items.text: Measure wind at the met mast
Strip local terrain, roughness, and obstacle effects to derive a regional geostrophic wind
Re-apply terrain, roughness, and obstacle models for the target location
Predict wind speed at any other point and height in the domain

questions.explanation: The method first strips the mast's measurement down to a site-independent regional wind, then rebuilds local effects for wherever the prediction is needed, producing an estimate at a location that was never directly measured.

questions.prompt: Match each WAsP sub-model to what it accounts for.

right.text: Speed-up or slow-down of flow over hills and ridges
Internal boundary-layer growth downwind of a surface-type transition
Sheltering by buildings or tree lines

questions.explanation: WAsP combines three separate physical effects — terrain-driven speed-up, roughness transitions, and obstacle sheltering — each modeled separately and then combined to predict wind at a target location.

lessons.label: From Resource to Energy & the Uncertainty Budget

sections.heading: Convolving the resource with the machine
sections.body: A long-term-corrected wind speed distribution is not yet an energy number. To get gross energy, the analyst convolves the site's wind speed distribution (typically fit as a Weibull distribution) with the turbine manufacturer's power curve, which maps wind speed to electrical output, summing the energy each speed bin contributes weighted by how often that speed occurs. The equivalent for solar is convolving the plane-of-array irradiance distribution with the PV system's performance model. This gross figure, sometimes called the theoretical or free-stream energy, is the ceiling: it assumes every turbine sees undisturbed wind and every panel operates at rated efficiency with no downtime, which no real plant achieves.

sections.heading: The loss stack
sections.body: Gross energy is walked down to net energy through a stack of losses, each with its own uncertainty. For wind, wake losses come first and are usually largest — downwind turbines sit in the velocity deficit of upwind machines, historically modeled with the Jensen (1983) wake model or the closely related Park model from Katic, Hojstrup, and Jensen (1986), both of which represent the wake as an expanding cone of reduced wind speed. After wakes come availability (turbine and grid downtime), electrical losses, curtailment, and performance losses like blade soiling or icing. A representative stack might run wake losses around 8%, availability 97%, and electrical plus other losses a further few percent, compounding gross energy down to a net figure roughly 15-20% below the theoretical ceiling.

sections.heading: P50, P90, and why lenders don't finance the average
sections.body: Each stage of that pipeline — the long-term wind correction, the power curve, every loss category — carries its own uncertainty, and these are combined in quadrature (square root of the sum of squares) into a total uncertainty on the net annual energy estimate. That uncertainty is then reported as an exceedance-probability curve: P50 is the median expected annual energy, the value equally likely to be exceeded or not in any given year. P90 is the value expected to be exceeded in 9 years out of 10 — a more conservative number sitting below P50 by roughly 1.28 standard deviations if the distribution is treated as normal. P99 sits further below still, around 2.33 standard deviations under P50. Lenders size debt against P90 or P99, not P50, because a loan has to be serviced even in a below-average year; P50 is the right number for equity investors pricing the expected long-run return, but it is the wrong number for setting a debt repayment schedule a bad wind year could break.

lessons.workedExample: A project's gross energy from the power-curve convolution is 100 GWh/year. Applying an 8% wake loss, 97% availability, and 5% combined electrical and other losses brings net P50 energy to 100 x 0.92 x 0.97 x 0.95, about 84.8 GWh/year. The combined uncertainty on that estimate is assessed at 8% (one standard deviation). A one-year P90 estimate is then roughly 84.8 GWh minus 1.28 times 8% of 84.8 GWh, or about 76.1 GWh/year — the figure a lender would size a debt-service schedule against, some 10% below the P50 figure the developer would quote as the project's expected output.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks why the number in the lender's term sheet is lower than the number in the developer's marketing deck. A weak answer treats P50 as the only number that matters.
