A strong answer explains that P50 is the statistical median while P90 and P99 are conservative, low-probability-of-exceedance figures built from the same uncertainty budget, and can explain in one sentence why debt financing needs the conservative number even though the expected (P50) case is higher.

questions.prompt: What does a P90 annual energy estimate represent?

options.text: The energy value expected to be exceeded in 9 out of 10 years
The maximum possible energy the plant could ever produce
The energy produced in the single best year on record
The average of the ten best forecasts submitted by different consultants

explanations.a: Correct — P90 is the exceedance-probability value expected to be met or exceeded in 90% of years, sitting below the P50 median.
explanations.b: The theoretical maximum is the gross, undisturbed-wind energy figure before any losses; P90 is a conservative net figure, not a ceiling.
explanations.c: P90 is a statistical exceedance value derived from the full uncertainty distribution, not a record from any single observed year.
explanations.d: P90 comes from propagating uncertainty through one project's resource-to-energy pipeline, not from averaging separate forecasts.

questions.prompt: Why do lenders typically size debt against P90 or P99 rather than P50?

options.text: P50 is illegal to use in financial contracts
P90/P99 are conservative, low-probability-of-exceedance figures, so debt sized against them can still be serviced in a below-average wind year
P90 is always a higher number than P50
Turbine manufacturers only warranty performance at the P90 level

explanations.a: There is no such restriction; P50 is used routinely, just for equity return expectations rather than debt sizing.
explanations.b: Correct — a loan must be serviceable even in a bad wind year, so lenders use the more conservative P90/P99 figures that sit below the P50 median.
explanations.c: P90 is lower than P50 by construction, since it represents a higher-confidence, more conservative exceedance level.
explanations.d: Turbine power-curve warranties are a separate mechanism from the statistical Pxx exceedance framework used for financing.

questions.prompt: Order the steps from wind resource to a financeable energy estimate.

items.text: Convolve the long-term wind speed distribution with the turbine power curve for gross energy
Apply the loss stack (wakes, availability, electrical, other) to get net P50 energy
Combine category uncertainties in quadrature into a total uncertainty
Report P50, P90, and P99 exceedance values from that uncertainty

questions.explanation: Energy assessment starts with the physical convolution of resource and machine, walks that gross figure down through real-world losses to a net median, then layers uncertainty on top to produce the exceedance values lenders and investors actually use.

questions.prompt: Match each loss or model to what it represents in the resource-to-energy pipeline.

right.text: Models the wind speed deficit downwind of a turbine (wake loss)
Accounts for turbine and grid downtime reducing energy capture
Method for combining independent uncertainty categories into one total

questions.explanation: Wake models quantify one specific physical loss; availability is a separate operational loss category; quadrature combination is the statistical step that turns many independent uncertainty sources into the single total used to build the Pxx curve.

lessons.label: Solar Resource Assessment Specifics

sections.heading: Building a Typical Meteorological Year
sections.body: Rather than run a full multi-decade record through every simulation, solar analysts compress it into one representative 8,760-hour Typical Meteorological Year (TMY). The method traces back to Hall, Prairie, Anderson, and Boes at Sandia National Laboratories in 1978: for each calendar month, the method computes the Finkelstein-Schafer statistic comparing that month's cumulative distribution of irradiance, temperature, wind, and humidity against the long-term distribution for that same month across all available years, ranks candidate months by how closely they match the long-term climate, and selects the most typical month from among the years available, smoothing the splice points between selected months so the composite year has no discontinuous jumps. TMY3, produced by Wilcox and Marion at NREL in 2008, updated the method with satellite-era irradiance data, and it remains the industry-standard input for PV simulation software.

sections.heading: Satellite-ground blending
sections.body: Ground pyranometer stations measure irradiance directly and accurately but are sparse and short-lived; geostationary satellites, by contrast, provide irradiance estimates derived from cloud cover across nearly every point on Earth going back to the late 1990s, but with real bias relative to ground truth, since irradiance is inferred from reflected cloud brightness rather than measured directly. The standard solution mirrors wind's measure-correlate-predict logic: a short, high-quality ground measurement campaign at the site is used to bias-correct the much longer satellite-derived record, combining the satellite record's length and spatial coverage with the ground campaign's local accuracy.

sections.heading: From horizontal irradiance to the tilted panel
sections.body: None of this data is useful until it is converted from global horizontal irradiance (GHI), what a flat sensor measures, into plane-of-array (POA) irradiance at the actual tilt and azimuth of the panels. The simplest, isotropic (Liu-Jordan) transposition model treats diffuse sky radiation as uniform in all directions, which understates irradiance near the sun. Hay and Davies (1980) improved on this by splitting diffuse radiation into an isotropic background plus a circumsolar component that scales with direct beam intensity. The Perez model (1990) went further still, adding a horizon-brightening term and empirically fitting all three components against irradiance data from dozens of sites worldwide; it is now the industry standard in tools like PVsyst and NREL's System Advisor Model. Soiling — dust, pollen, and bird droppings accumulating on panels between rain events — is layered on afterward as a site-specific loss, monitored with paired soiling stations (one cleaned regularly, one left to accumulate) and capable of exceeding 5-8% in dry, dusty climates without regular cleaning.

lessons.workedExample: A site's satellite-derived record spans 2005-2025 but is known to run a few percent low relative to ground truth. A one-year ground pyranometer campaign in 2024 bias-corrects the full satellite record, similar to a wind MCP correction. The resulting long-term GHI series is then run through the Perez model to compute POA irradiance for panels tilted at the site's latitude, since the isotropic model would understate irradiance during the clear, sun-facing conditions that produce most of the site's annual energy. A soiling loss of 3%, measured from a paired soiling-station campaign at the site, is subtracted from the final POA-based energy estimate.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks why the team didn't just use the site's measured horizontal irradiance directly in their energy calculation. A weak answer treats GHI as the finished input to the energy model. A strong answer explains that GHI must be transposed to the panel's actual tilt using a model like Perez or Hay-Davies, and can name at least one additional site-specific loss, such as soiling, that a horizontal-irradiance number alone would miss entirely.

questions.prompt: What statistic does the Sandia TMY method use to select the most representative month from among the years available?

options.text: The Finkelstein-Schafer statistic comparing candidate-month and long-term distributions
A simple average of monthly GHI totals
The single year with the highest annual energy yield
A random draw weighted by year

explanations.a: Correct — the Finkelstein-Schafer statistic, introduced by Hall, Prairie, Anderson, and Boes (1978) at Sandia, ranks candidate months by how closely their distribution matches the long-term climate distribution.
explanations.b: A simple monthly average would smooth out the distribution shape the Finkelstein-Schafer statistic is specifically designed to preserve.
explanations.c: Selecting the highest-yield year would bias the TMY toward an atypical, sunnier-than-normal climate, defeating the purpose of a 'typical' year.
explanations.d: The method is a deliberate ranking against a long-term distribution, not a random selection.

questions.prompt: Why does the Perez (1990) transposition model outperform the simple isotropic (Liu-Jordan) model?

options.text: It ignores diffuse radiation entirely
It adds circumsolar and horizon-brightening components instead of treating diffuse sky radiation as uniform in all directions
It only works for horizontal panels
It requires no ground irradiance data at all

explanations.a: The Perez model still accounts for diffuse radiation; it refines how that diffuse component is distributed across the sky rather than dropping it.
explanations.b: Correct — Perez adds circumsolar and horizon-brightening terms on top of the isotropic background, capturing that diffuse sky radiation is brighter near the sun and near the horizon, not uniform.
explanations.c: Perez is specifically used for tilted, plane-of-array transposition; the isotropic model it improves on is the one more prone to error on tilted surfaces.
explanations.d: Perez was empirically fit against measured irradiance data from many ground sites; it depends on that ground data existing.

questions.prompt: Order these irradiance transposition models from simplest to most refined treatment of diffuse sky radiation.

items.text: Isotropic (Liu-Jordan): diffuse radiation uniform in all directions
Hay-Davies (1980): adds a circumsolar component scaled to beam irradiance
Perez (1990): adds circumsolar plus horizon-brightening, empirically fit to many sites

questions.explanation: Each model layers on more physical detail: isotropic assumes uniformity, Hay-Davies adds the brighter region around the sun, and Perez adds both that and a horizon-brightening term, calibrated against real multi-site data.

questions.prompt: Match each solar resource concept to what it addresses.

right.text: Bias-corrects a long, cloud-derived irradiance record with a short accurate ground campaign
Converts horizontal irradiance to the irradiance a tilted panel actually receives
Accounts for dust and debris accumulation reducing panel transmittance between rain events

questions.explanation: These are three distinct corrections applied at different stages: blending fixes the input data source, transposition fixes the geometry, and soiling accounts for a physical loss neither of the first two captures.

lessons.label: Bankability, Standards & Independent Review

sections.heading: What makes an assessment bankable
sections.body: A resource assessment is bankable when a lender who has never met the analyst can trust it enough to size a multi-million-dollar loan against it. That trust does not come from a good model; it comes from a documented, auditable methodology: every data source disclosed, every long-term correction and loss category justified with a stated uncertainty, and the full uncertainty budget combined transparently into the reported P50/P90/P99 figures. A bankable report is one a second qualified analyst, given the same inputs, could substantially reproduce. Reports that assert a number without showing the chain of corrections behind it, however sophisticated the underlying model, are not bankable regardless of accuracy.

sections.heading: IEC 61400-15-1 and the push for a common standard
sections.body: For most of the wind industry's history, every consultancy described a site's conditions with its own terminology and layout, so a lender comparing two assessments had to reconcile each report's private conventions before it could compare anything. IEC 61400-15-1, Edition 1.0, published in March 2025 by IEC technical committee 88 after its final draft went to national-committee vote the previous year, is the first International Standard to define a common framework for assessing and reporting site suitability input conditions for onshore and offshore wind power plants. Its scope is deliberately bounded: defining, measuring and predicting the long-term meteorological and wind-flow characteristics at the site; integrating those with wind turbine and balance-of-plant characteristics; characterizing environmental extremes and other plant design drivers; and setting documentation and reporting requirements so the assessment is traceable. It fixes the minimum parameter set a report must carry — wind speed distribution, the 50-year extreme wind, mean and extreme ambient turbulence intensity, wind shear, inflow angle, temperature, air density — and specifies a machine-readable data-exchange format for them, so a reviewer receives the same fields in the same form no matter who did the work. It complements the design standards IEC 61400-1 and 61400-3 rather than superseding them.

sections.heading: What the standard does not cover
sections.body: It is worth being precise about the boundary, because it is easy to over-credit a standard. IEC 61400-15-1 governs the input conditions and the paper trail — the wind and atmospheric parameters that bear on a turbine's structural integrity, and how they must be documented. It does not standardize the energy-yield calculation or the uncertainty budget behind P50 and P90; that sits downstream, in the companion part of the 61400-15 series covering assessment and reporting of the wind resource and energy yield. So a project can be fully compliant with 61400-15-1 and still owe a lender a separate, carefully argued case for how its loss factors and uncertainties were derived.

sections.heading: The independent engineer and what operational data revealed
sections.body: Lenders typically require an independent engineer (IE) — a third-party firm with no stake in the project's outcome — to review or substantially re-perform the developer's own energy assessment before financial close, then monitor construction and verify performance testing afterward. That check exists because the industry's own operational record gave lenders reason to insist on it: benchmarking studies comparing pre-construction P50 estimates against years of actual operational production, including reviews published by major independent engineering firms such as DNV, found that the wind industry had historically over-predicted energy yield, with early-era assessments running several percent above what plants actually delivered. That systematic bias drove refinements to wake modeling, more conservative loss assumptions, and the wider push toward standardized reporting.

lessons.workedExample: A developer's pre-construction assessment reports P50 annual energy of 100 GWh. Five years of operational SCADA data show an actual average of 92 GWh/year, an 8% shortfall. An operational back-analysis traces the gap to wake losses that were underestimated by the original wake model and turbine availability that ran below the assumed 97%. That single project's back-analysis feeds into the consultancy's broader benchmarking dataset alongside dozens of other projects, the kind of aggregated evidence that independent engineering firms' benchmarking reviews draw on, and the finding pushes the firm toward more conservative wake-loss assumptions on its next pre-construction assessment.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks how the team knows their energy estimate is trustworthy rather than just plausible-looking. A weak answer points only to the sophistication of the model used. A strong answer names a real standard or review mechanism — IEC 61400-15-1's framework for reporting site input conditions, or the role of an independent engineer — and can cite that historical operational data has shown pre-construction estimates were once systematically too high, which is exactly why that independent check exists. Naming the standard's limits (it fixes the inputs and the documentation, not the yield calculation) is stronger still.

questions.prompt: What is the primary role of the independent engineer (IE) in a project financing?

options.text: To design the turbine layout for the developer
To review or re-perform the developer's energy assessment on behalf of the lender, with no stake in the project's outcome
To sell the electricity generated by the plant
To manufacture the wind turbines used on site

explanations.a: Turbine layout and micro-siting are the developer's or its consultant's job; the IE's role is independent review, not design.
explanations.b: Correct — the IE is a third party, appointed by or for the lender, that checks the developer's assessment before financial close and monitors performance afterward.
explanations.c: Power sales are handled through offtake agreements, unrelated to the IE's technical due-diligence role.
explanations.d: The IE has no manufacturing role; it is a technical and financial due-diligence function.

questions.prompt: What did benchmarking of pre-construction P50 estimates against operational data, including reviews by independent engineering firms, historically find?

options.text: Pre-construction estimates were systematically too low compared to actual production
Pre-construction estimates were systematically too high compared to actual production
Pre-construction estimates exactly matched operational results in nearly all cases
Operational data could not be compared to pre-construction estimates at all

explanations.a: The documented historical pattern ran the opposite direction: assessments over-predicted, not under-predicted, energy yield.
explanations.b: Correct — the wind industry historically over-predicted energy yield relative to actual operational production, a finding that drove more conservative modeling and the push toward standardized reporting.
explanations.c: A close match is what the industry has worked toward since, but it was not the historical finding that motivated the independent-review and standardization push.
explanations.d: Operational back-analysis is precisely the comparison of actual production against the original P50 estimate; the comparison is the whole method.

questions.prompt: Which of these does IEC 61400-15-1 actually standardize?

options.text: The method for calculating a project's P50 energy yield and its uncertainty budget
The set of site wind and atmospheric input conditions a report must contain, and how they are documented and exchanged
The commercial terms of the loan agreement between developer and lender
The structural design requirements the turbine itself must meet

explanations.a: Deliberately out of scope — the energy-yield assessment and its uncertainty framework are handled by the companion part of the 61400-15 series, not by 15-1.
explanations.b: Correct — 15-1 defines the minimum set of site suitability input parameters, the documentation needed for traceability, and a machine-readable format for exchanging them.
explanations.c: Financing terms are commercial, not technical; no IEC standard governs them.
explanations.d: Turbine design requirements live in IEC 61400-1 and 61400-3; 15-1 complements those standards rather than superseding them.

questions.prompt: Order the stages of a project's assessment moving from pre-construction to lessons learned.

items.text: Developer produces a P50/P90 energy assessment
Independent engineer reviews or re-performs the assessment for the lender
Project is financed and constructed
Operational back-analysis compares actual production to the original P50 estimate

questions.explanation: The developer's original estimate is checked by an independent party before money is committed, the plant is then built and operated, and only years later does operational back-analysis reveal whether the original estimate held up, feeding lessons back into future assessments.

questions.prompt: Match each bankability element to its function.

right.text: Defines a common framework for assessing and reporting a site's wind and environmental input conditions
Provides a lender with an unbiased third-party check of the developer's assessment
Compares actual production against the original pre-construction estimate to reveal systematic bias

questions.explanation: The standard fixes the common language and the minimum set of site input conditions a report must carry, an independent engineer fixes the conflict-of-interest problem in who checks the numbers, and back-analysis is the feedback loop that shows whether the whole process is actually working.

units.label: Landmark Work & Open Debates

lessons.label: Weibull, Justus & the Statistics of Wind

sections.heading: From Steel to Wind: Weibull's 1951 Distribution
sections.body: The two-parameter Weibull distribution that every wind-resource report leans on was not built for wind at all. Waloddi Weibull, a Swedish engineer, published it in 1951 as "A Statistical Distribution Function of Wide Applicability," derived from weakest-link failure theory: a chain (or a steel fiber, or a ball bearing) breaks at its single weakest flaw, and Weibull showed that class of process produces a specific skewed shape controlled by two knobs. The shape parameter k sets how peaked and symmetric the curve is; the scale parameter c (sometimes A) sets the characteristic speed. When k = 2, the Weibull distribution collapses to the simpler Rayleigh distribution, which is why many wind-energy textbooks quietly treat Rayleigh as a special case rather than a separate model.

sections.heading: Justus Makes It the Wind Industry's Default
sections.body: Wind speed is, like a failure process, bounded below by zero and long-tailed above, so meteorologists tried fitting it to a Weibull curve in the 1970s. Justus, Hargraves, Mikhail, and Graber (1978, Journal of Applied Meteorology) supplied the piece that made it practical: simple formulas to estimate k and c directly from a site's mean wind speed and standard deviation, without needing a full multi-year histogram. Their estimator approximates the shape parameter as k = (sigma/v-bar)^(-1.086) and the scale as c = v-bar / Gamma(1 + 1/k), turning two summary statistics into a full distribution. Paired with an empirical vertical shear model — commonly the 1/7 (about 0.14) power-law exponent, a simplified stand-in for the neutral-stability wind profile — this gave developers a complete pipeline from a short low-height measurement to an energy estimate: fit Weibull at mast height, extrapolate to hub height, integrate against the turbine's power curve.

sections.heading: Where the Statistic Breaks
sections.body: That pipeline still underlies the extrapolation methodology used within power-curve testing procedures like IEC 61400-12, but both halves are now openly challenged. A single two-parameter Weibull curve under-fits sites with a genuinely bimodal wind climate — coastal sea-breeze regimes or terrain with two dominant synoptic flow directions — where the real histogram has two humps a smooth Weibull curve cannot represent, pushing some analysts toward mixed-Weibull fits instead. And the fixed 1/7 exponent assumes near-neutral atmospheric stability; as turbines climbed from 50 m hub heights toward 120-160 m, and as day-night stability swings became impossible to ignore at that height, that fixed exponent stopped being defensible on its own — setting up the stability-resolved theory in the next lesson.

lessons.workedExample: A met mast records a mean wind speed of 7.5 m/s and a standard deviation of 3.2 m/s at 50 m. Using the Justus-style relation (k approximated from the ratio of standard deviation to mean), the site fits roughly k = 2.5, c = 8.5 m/s — more peaked, less spread than the Rayleigh (k = 2) case. Extrapolating to a 100 m hub height with the 1/7 power law gives v_100 = 7.5 x (100/50)^(1/7) = 7.5 x 1.104 = about 8.3 m/s, the number that then feeds the turbine's power curve for an annual energy estimate.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about a project's Weibull fit because reciting "wind is Weibull-distributed" proves nothing — every wind-energy textbook says so. What separates real understanding is diagnosing the fit: can the student say what their shape parameter k came out to, and does it match what their raw histogram actually looks like? A strong answer notices a right-skewed or bimodal histogram and explains why (sea breeze, mixed synoptic regimes) rather than forcing a Weibull curve onto it. A weak answer treats the distribution as a black-box step nobody has to justify.

questions.prompt: Weibull's 1951 distribution was originally developed to model which phenomenon?

options.text: Weakest-link failure of materials, such as fracture strength in steel
Daily rainfall totals
Radioactive decay rates
Wind turbine blade noise spectra

explanations.a: Correct — Weibull (1951) built the distribution from weakest-link failure theory for materials like steel fibers and ball bearings; wind-speed modeling came later, borrowing the same math.
explanations.b: Rainfall totals are more commonly modeled with gamma or mixed distributions in hydrology, not Weibull's original application.
explanations.c: Radioactive decay follows an exponential law, unrelated to Weibull's weakest-link derivation.
explanations.d: Turbine acoustics use entirely different models; this has no connection to Weibull's 1951 paper.

questions.prompt: In the two-parameter Weibull distribution used for wind speeds, what special case does a shape parameter of k = 2 produce?

options.text: The Rayleigh distribution
The normal (Gaussian) distribution
The uniform distribution
The Poisson distribution

explanations.a: Correct — the Rayleigh distribution is exactly the Weibull distribution with k = 2, which is why many wind-resource tools list it as a simplified default.
explanations.b: The normal distribution is symmetric and unbounded on both sides; Weibull's wind-speed form is bounded at zero and typically skewed.
explanations.c: A uniform distribution has constant probability across a range, nothing like the Weibull's decaying tail.
explanations.d: The Poisson distribution describes discrete event counts, not a continuous speed variable.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the Justus-era wind resource assessment workflow.

items.text: Measure a short-term wind speed record at mast height
Fit Weibull shape (k) and scale (c) from the record's mean and standard deviation
Extrapolate the fitted distribution to hub height using a power-law exponent
Integrate the extrapolated distribution against the turbine's power curve for an energy estimate

questions.explanation: Justus's method starts from raw mast data, fits the Weibull parameters from simple summary statistics, extrapolates the resulting distribution vertically to hub height, and only then combines it with the turbine's power curve to produce an energy yield.

questions.prompt: Match each term to what it controls in wind resource statistics.

right.text: The curve's peakedness and skew
The characteristic wind speed scale
Vertical wind shear used to extrapolate to hub height

questions.explanation: k governs the shape of the wind-speed frequency curve, c sets its characteristic speed, and the power-law exponent describes how wind speed is assumed to change with height when extrapolating a measurement to hub height.

lessons.label: Monin-Obukhov Similarity & the Field Campaigns That Fixed It

sections.heading: Monin and Obukhov's 1954 Similarity Theory
sections.body: The 1/7 power law from the previous lesson is a convenient fiction: it assumes the atmosphere is always near-neutral, when in reality buoyancy constantly reshapes how wind shears with height. Monin and Obukhov addressed this in 1954 with a similarity theory for the atmospheric surface layer. They combined the surface friction velocity, the surface heat flux, and buoyancy into a single length scale — the Obukhov length, L — that measures the ratio of mechanical turbulence production to buoyant production or destruction. Their similarity hypothesis states that, once heights are non-dimensionalized as z/L, the dimensionless wind-shear and temperature-gradient functions (called phi_m and phi_h) take a universal form, the same at any site, given the local surface fluxes.

sections.heading: The Kansas 1968 Experiment Measured the Functions
sections.body: A hypothesis needs numbers. In 1968, a field campaign on flat, homogeneous grassland near Manhattan, Kansas instrumented several mast levels to measure wind, temperature, and turbulent fluxes simultaneously. The resulting analysis, published as Businger, Wyngaard, Izumi, and Bradley (1971, Journal of the Atmospheric Sciences), empirically fit phi_m and phi_h as functions of z/L across unstable, neutral, and stable conditions — coefficients still called the Businger-Dyer relationships after a related 1974 review by Dyer that offered slightly revised constants. In their most common form, phi_m = (1 - 16 z/L)^(-1/4) for unstable conditions (z/L < 0) and phi_m = 1 + 4.7 z/L for stable conditions (z/L > 0), with phi_m = 1 at neutral (z/L = 0) recovering the plain logarithmic profile. These functions turned Monin-Obukhov similarity theory (MOST) from an elegant idea into a usable formula for correcting the wind profile by atmospheric stability rather than assuming one fixed shape.

sections.heading: Why Wind Assessment Still Leans on It — and Still Argues
sections.body: MOST-based, stability-corrected extrapolation is more physically honest than a fixed power-law exponent: it lets shear steepen on calm, stable nights and flatten during convective, well-mixed afternoons, using measured heat flux rather than a guess. It underlies IEC power-curve testing procedures and the profiles used to cross-check LIDAR against masts. But the Kansas data came from flat, short grass, low mast levels, and a narrow stability range — applying its coefficients above roughly 100 m, over forests, complex terrain, or open water stretches the theory well past where it was validated. In very stable conditions, some researchers argue turbulence structure stops scaling with height at all — so-called z-less scaling — a departure from MOST that remains unresolved.

lessons.workedExample: Compare two nights at the same site. On a convective afternoon, measured sensible heat flux is strongly positive, giving a large negative Obukhov length (L = -50 m); phi_m at 50 m is well below 1, meaning shear is weak and the profile is nearly well-mixed. On a clear, calm night, heat flux reverses sign, giving a small positive L (L = +20 m); phi_m at the same height is now well above 1, meaning shear near the surface is much steeper. A single fixed 1/7 exponent applied to both nights would underestimate hub-height wind speed in the first case and overestimate it in the second.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge pushes on this because it separates a team that memorized "use the log law" from one that understands why the log law needs a correction at all. A strong answer names the Obukhov length as the controlling scale, explains that stability (not just height) sets the shear, and can say what stability regime their site data actually showed. A weak answer recites "logarithmic wind profile" without ever connecting it to measured heat flux or day/night differences.

questions.prompt: What does the Obukhov length physically represent in Monin-Obukhov similarity theory?

options.text: A length scale reflecting the ratio of mechanical to buoyant turbulence production
The average spacing between instrument masts in a field campaign
The wavelength of the dominant turbulent eddy at a site
The height at which wind speed first reaches zero

explanations.a: Correct — the Obukhov length is built from friction velocity, surface heat flux, and buoyancy, and represents the height scale where mechanical and buoyant turbulence production are comparable.
explanations.b: Instrument spacing is an experimental design choice, not a physical quantity derived from the theory.
explanations.c: Eddy wavelength is a turbulence-spectrum concept, not what the Obukhov length quantifies.
explanations.d: Wind speed does not reach exactly zero at a finite height in this theory; that description does not match the Obukhov length.

questions.prompt: Why was the flat, homogeneous grassland site of the 1968 Kansas experiment well suited to testing Monin-Obukhov similarity theory?

options.text: It minimized terrain and roughness complications, isolating the stability effects the theory predicts
It was the first site where offshore wind turbines were installed
It let researchers avoid measuring surface heat flux entirely
It was chosen because it had the tallest meteorological masts ever built

explanations.a: Correct — flat, uniform grassland removed terrain and roughness variability as confounders, letting the campaign isolate how stability alone shapes the wind and temperature profiles.
explanations.b: The Kansas experiment was a land-based grassland campaign, not an offshore installation.
explanations.c: Surface heat flux measurement was central to the experiment, since it is required to compute the Obukhov length.
explanations.d: The Kansas masts were modest instrumented towers, not exceptionally tall; height was not the point of the site choice.

questions.prompt: Order these milestones in the development of Monin-Obukhov similarity theory.

items.text: Monin and Obukhov publish the similarity theory (1954)
The Kansas field campaign collects surface-layer flux and profile data (1968)
Businger, Wyngaard, Izumi, and Bradley publish the empirical stability functions (1971)
Stability-corrected extrapolation is embedded in wind-industry testing standards

questions.explanation: The theoretical framework came first in 1954, the Kansas experiment supplied the data in 1968, the empirical functions were published from that data in 1971, and only afterward did the stability-corrected approach become embedded in industry standards.

questions.prompt: Match each atmospheric stability regime to its typical wind-shear behavior near the surface.

right.text: Weaker shear; wind well-mixed with height
Classic logarithmic wind profile
Stronger shear concentrated near the surface

questions.explanation: Buoyant convection mixes momentum vertically in unstable conditions, weakening shear; neutral conditions produce the textbook logarithmic profile; suppressed turbulence in stable conditions traps strong shear close to the ground.

lessons.label: The European Wind Atlas & WAsP

sections.heading: Troen & Petersen's 1989 Risoe Method
sections.body: Weibull statistics and Monin-Obukhov shear correction tell you how wind behaves at one point; they say nothing about moving that knowledge across terrain. Troen and Petersen closed that gap in 1989 with the European Wind Atlas, published by Risoe National Laboratory in Denmark. Their method uses the geostrophic drag law, which relates the free-atmosphere geostrophic wind (driven by large-scale pressure gradients) to the surface friction velocity through the local surface roughness, via a form of Rossby-number similarity. Running that relationship at a reference station strips out the site's local roughness and terrain, producing a "generalized" or site-independent regional wind climate. Reversing the process at a new location — stepping back down through that site's own roughness changes and orographic features — regenerates a site-specific wind climate without needing new geostrophic data.

sections.heading: WAsP Becomes the Industry Standard
sections.body: Risoe implemented the method as software: the Wind Atlas Analysis and Application Program, WAsP, still maintained today by DTU after Risoe's merger into the university. WAsP paired two models. The roughness-change model classifies land cover into standard roughness-length classes, from open water and short grass at the smooth end through farmland and villages to forests and cities at the rough end, and tracks how wind adjusts as it crosses each change of surface. The orographic model is a linearized potential-flow solution in the tradition of Jackson & Hunt (1975) hill-flow theory, which predicts how wind speeds up over hills and ridges. Through the 1990s and 2000s it became the near-universal tool for turning a single reference mast into a full site wind resource map, driving micrositing decisions for thousands of turbines worldwide.

sections.heading: RIX Exposes the Complex-Terrain Failure
sections.body: WAsP's orographic model is linear, which means it assumes flow stays attached to the terrain surface rather than separating and recirculating — an assumption that fails on steep slopes. Bowen and Mortensen (1996) introduced the Ruggedness Index, RIX: the fraction of terrain around a site steeper than a critical slope, commonly set at 30%. They showed that the difference between a target site's RIX and the reference mast's RIX, called Delta-RIX, correlates loglinearly with WAsP's prediction error. That gave developers a diagnostic that could flag an untrustworthy prediction before construction rather than after a project underperformed, and pushed the most rugged sites toward CFD-based flow solvers while WAsP-plus-RIX screening remained standard on gentler terrain.

lessons.workedExample: A developer uses a valley-floor reference mast to predict output on a nearby ridge. The mast's surroundings compute to a low RIX of about 5%; the ridge's surroundings compute to a high RIX of about 45%, giving a Delta-RIX of roughly 40 percentage points. That large a gap flags the WAsP prediction as unreliable for the ridge — steep enough terrain that flow likely separates there, violating the linear model's core assumption — signaling the team should re-run the site with a CFD flow solver instead of trusting the WAsP output directly.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe RIX because it distinguishes "we ran the standard industry tool" from "we know when the standard tool is lying to us." A strong answer names RIX or Delta-RIX as a documented diagnostic, reports whether their own site is flagged, and explains why steep terrain breaks a linear flow assumption. A weak answer treats a WAsP output number as ground truth regardless of how rugged the terrain actually is.

questions.prompt: What role does the geostrophic drag law play in the Troen & Petersen (1989) method?

options.text: It relates the free-atmosphere geostrophic wind to surface friction velocity via surface roughness, enabling a site-independent regional wind climate
It measures the exact speed-up of wind over a specific hill
It calculates a turbine's power curve from its rotor diameter
It corrects for instrument calibration drift on a met mast

explanations.a: Correct — the geostrophic drag law is the physical link that lets the method strip out one site's local roughness to build a regional climate, then reapply a different site's roughness and terrain to predict conditions there.
explanations.b: Hill-induced speed-up is handled separately by WAsP's linearized orographic flow model, not the geostrophic drag law itself.
explanations.c: Power curves are turbine-specific engineering data, unrelated to the geostrophic drag law.
explanations.d: Instrument calibration is a measurement-quality issue handled before any wind atlas modeling begins.

questions.prompt: Match each name or term to its role in the European Wind Atlas method.

right.text: Authors of the original European Wind Atlas methodology
Software implementing the roughness and orographic downscaling method
Ruggedness diagnostic introduced by Bowen & Mortensen (1996)

questions.explanation: Troen and Petersen authored the underlying method; WAsP is the Risoe/DTU software that implements it; RIX is the later diagnostic that flags where the software's linear flow assumption is likely to fail.

questions.prompt: Order the steps WAsP uses to move a wind climate from a reference mast to a new target site.

items.text: Estimate the geostrophic wind driving the regional flow
Strip out the reference site's roughness and terrain to build a generalized, site-independent wind climate
Reapply the target site's own roughness and terrain to the generalized climate
Produce the target site's specific wind climate and energy estimate

questions.explanation: WAsP first works up to a geostrophic estimate from the reference station, strips its local surface effects to generalize the climate, then works back down through the new site's own surface effects to arrive at a site-specific prediction.

questions.prompt: A large Delta-RIX between a reference mast and a target turbine site most directly signals what?

options.text: That the target terrain is rugged enough that WAsP's linear flow model is likely unreliable there
That the reference mast's instruments need recalibration
That the target site definitely has more energy than the reference site
That the two sites share an identical wind climate

explanations.a: Correct — Delta-RIX quantifies how much rougher/steeper the target terrain is relative to the reference, and a large gap is exactly the warning sign Bowen and Mortensen linked to larger WAsP prediction errors.
explanations.b: RIX is a terrain-ruggedness measure, not a check on instrument calibration.
explanations.c: A large Delta-RIX signals unreliable prediction, not a guaranteed direction of energy difference.
explanations.d: A large Delta-RIX means the two sites differ substantially in terrain ruggedness, the opposite of similarity.

lessons.label: Angstrom, Prescott & the Solar-Resource Models

sections.heading: Angstrom's 1924 Sunshine-to-Radiation Bridge
sections.body: Wind resource assessment leans on masts; early solar resource assessment leaned on sunshine, because direct radiation sensors (pyranometers) were rare and expensive in the early twentieth century, while a Campbell-Stokes recorder — a glass sphere that burns a trace onto a card as the sun crosses the sky — was cheap and already deployed at many weather stations. Anders Angstrom proposed in 1924 a linear regression connecting daily global solar radiation to the fraction of possible sunshine hours, n/N, observed by that inexpensive instrument. His original formula referenced the radiation expected on a hypothetical completely clear day at the site, a reference value that itself had to be estimated.

sections.heading: Prescott's 1940 Fix and the Standard Form
sections.body: Prescott revised the equation in 1940, replacing that hard-to-know clear-day reference with extraterrestrial radiation, H0 — a quantity computable exactly from latitude, date, and solar geometry, with no measurement needed at all. The result is the now-standard Angstrom-Prescott equation, H = H0 (a + b n/N), with regression coefficients a and b calibrated locally. Default globally-averaged values near a = 0.25 and b = 0.50 are still embedded in reference frameworks such as the FAO-56 crop reference-evapotranspiration guideline, carrying a 1920s sunshine-recorder equation well beyond its original solar-engineering purpose.

sections.heading: Perez's All-Sky Models Take Over the PV Era
sections.body: Photovoltaic design needs more than a daily total: it needs irradiance split into direct beam and diffuse components, then reprojected onto a tilted panel. Perez and collaborators built separation models that use a clearness-index parameterization to split measured global horizontal irradiance into its beam and diffuse parts, and, in Perez et al. (1990), an anisotropic transposition model that treats the sky as three zones — a circumsolar disc, a horizon band, and an isotropic background — rather than assuming diffuse light arrives uniformly from the whole sky. That transposition model is now embedded in nearly every commercial PV yield tool.

sections.heading: Resetting the Baseline: Kopp & Lean's Lower Solar Constant
sections.body: Every one of these models ultimately references the extraterrestrial solar constant. A 1990s-era canonical value near 1365-1366 W/m^2 stood for decades until Kopp and Lean (2011, Geophysical Research Letters) combined NASA's SORCE Total Irradiance Monitor with improved radiometric laboratory calibration to report 1360.8 plus or minus 0.5 W/m^2 at the 2008 solar minimum — a downward revision traced to instrument calibration error, not a real change in the sun. The International Astronomical Union adopted 1361 W/m^2 in 2015, resetting the H0 baseline that every Angstrom-Prescott and clear-sky irradiance calculation ultimately depends on.

lessons.workedExample: A site at a given latitude and date has computed extraterrestrial radiation H0 = 32 MJ/m^2/day, with 8 sunshine hours measured out of 12 possible daylight hours (n/N = 0.667). Using default Angstrom-Prescott coefficients a = 0.25 and b = 0.50: H = 32 x (0.25 + 0.50 x 0.667) = 32 x 0.583 = about 18.7 MJ/m^2/day of estimated global radiation — a full-day irradiance estimate built entirely from a sunshine-hour count and computed geometry, no pyranometer required.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe the Angstrom-Prescott coefficients because many teams plug numbers into the formula without knowing where a and b came from or why they might not fit the local site. A strong answer explains that a and b are regionally calibrated, states whether they used a default or a locally fit value, and can name what H0 represents. A weak answer treats the equation as an unexplained black box and cannot say what would change if the site were at a different latitude.

questions.prompt: Why did Prescott (1940) revise Angstrom's original 1924 equation?

options.text: To replace the hard-to-know clear-day radiation reference with computable extraterrestrial radiation
To add a correction for cloud droplet size
To remove the need for any sunshine-hour data
To convert the equation from daily to hourly time steps

explanations.a: Correct — Prescott swapped the original clear-day reference, which itself needed estimating, for extraterrestrial radiation H0, which can be computed exactly from geometry alone.
explanations.b: Cloud droplet size is not a variable in either the Angstrom or Prescott formulations.
explanations.c: The revised equation still requires the sunshine fraction n/N; Prescott changed the reference term, not that input.
explanations.d: The Angstrom-Prescott equation remains a daily-total formulation; Prescott's change was about the reference radiation term, not the time step.

questions.prompt: Kopp and Lean's 2011 revision changed the accepted solar constant from roughly what value to what value?

options.text: From about 1365-1366 W/m^2 down to about 1360.8 W/m^2
From about 1200 W/m^2 up to about 1361 W/m^2
From about 1361 W/m^2 up to about 1400 W/m^2
From about 1366 W/m^2 down to about 1000 W/m^2

explanations.a: Correct — improved SORCE/TIM measurements and lab calibration lowered the accepted value from the 1990s-era 1365-1366 W/m^2 to about 1360.8 W/m^2, later rounded to 1361 W/m^2 by the IAU.
explanations.b: 1200 W/m^2 is far too low to have ever been the canonical solar constant.
explanations.c: The revision moved the value down, not up, and 1400 W/m^2 was never the canonical figure.
explanations.d: 1000 W/m^2 is roughly typical peak surface irradiance under clear sky, not the extraterrestrial solar constant.

questions.prompt: Match each person or model to their contribution to solar resource modeling.

right.text: Original sunshine-fraction-to-radiation regression
Replaced the clear-day reference with extraterrestrial radiation
Anisotropic sky model for tilted-surface irradiance transposition

questions.explanation: Angstrom proposed the original regression, Prescott fixed its reference term, and Perez later built the three-zone sky model used to project irradiance onto tilted PV panels.

questions.prompt: Order these developments in solar-resource modeling chronologically.

items.text: Angstrom's original sunshine-to-radiation equation (1924)
Prescott's revision referencing extraterrestrial radiation (1940)
Perez's anisotropic tilted-surface transposition model (1990)
Kopp & Lean's revised solar-constant measurement (2011)

questions.explanation: Angstrom's equation came first in 1924, Prescott revised its reference term in 1940, Perez's transposition model followed in 1990 for the PV era, and Kopp & Lean reset the underlying solar-constant baseline in 2011.

lessons.label: Global Stilling & the Wind-Drought Debate

sections.heading: McVicar's 2012 Global Synthesis Names 'Stilling'
sections.body: Every wind resource number so far in this unit assumes the historical wind record used to calibrate it is representative of the future. McVicar and colleagues (2012, Journal of Hydrology) tested that assumption by pulling together many independently published station wind-speed trend studies across multiple continents. They found a broad, though not universal, decline in near-surface (typically 10 m) wind speed at many mid-latitude land stations, developing from roughly the 1960s-1980s onward — a phenomenon they termed terrestrial stilling. It mattered well beyond wind energy: near-surface wind drives evaporative demand, so the same trend worried irrigation planners and hydrologists as much as wind developers.

sections.heading: Competing Explanations
sections.body: Three broad mechanisms were debated as the cause. First, increased surface roughness from vegetation growth, afforestation, and urban development, which can physically slow near-surface flow. Second, large-scale atmospheric circulation shifts tied to decadal ocean-atmosphere oscillations, which alter the pressure gradients that drive surface wind. Third, non-climatic artifacts — anemometer relocations, sensor-height changes, and instrument replacements across long station records — that can masquerade as a climate trend. No single explanation cleanly fit every region, and the debate stayed open through the following decade. The reported declines were on the order of a few percent per decade at many stations, with North America, Europe, and East Asia showing the strongest and most consistent signal across networks.

sections.heading: Zeng's 2019 Reversal Reframes the Cause
sections.body: Zeng and colleagues (2019, Nature Climate Change) used in-situ station records to show the decades-long stilling trend reversed globally around 2010, with land wind speeds recovering. Because vegetation and urban roughening change too slowly to explain a trend reversing within a single decade, the authors argued that decadal-scale wind variability is driven mainly by internal ocean-atmosphere oscillations rather than land-surface roughening, undercutting that explanation as the dominant driver. They estimated the post-2010 strengthening raised potential wind energy by about 17 percent (plus or minus 2 percent) over 2010 to 2017. Crucially, they attributed only part of the observed rise in United States wind-farm capacity factor to that wind recovery — about 37 percent of it, roughly a third — leaving the remaining majority to non-climatic causes such as taller towers, larger rotors, and improved turbine technology.

sections.heading: The Resource-Risk Lesson
sections.body: Together, the two studies show that a wind resource assessment built from any single 10-20 year historical record risks capturing one phase of a multi-decadal oscillation rather than a stable long-term average — understating or overstating the true long-term resource depending on which phase the record happened to catch. That risk compounds directly into the same P50/P90 uncertainty problem that plagues pre-construction yield estimates across the wind industry. Because the McVicar-to-Zeng swing spanned several percent of mean wind speed within a decade, even a decade-long baseline can sit entirely within one phase of the oscillation.

lessons.workedExample: A developer's 2008 resource assessment relies on a 2000-2008 mast record, sitting near the tail end of the stilling trend, giving a measured mean wind speed of 6.2 m/s. Once the post-2010 reversal is included in a longer record through 2018, the true long-term average comes out closer to 6.6 m/s — meaning the original short-record assessment understated the site's long-term resource by roughly 6 percent. The same short-record risk could just as easily run the other direction if a site's baseline had instead been measured during a strengthening phase followed by renewed stilling.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask how long a wind record is and whether the team checked it for a trend, because a resource claim built on one short baseline conflates decadal ocean-atmosphere variability with genuine site climatology. A strong answer names the stilling-and-reversal literature, reports how many years of data underlie their estimate, and flags the direction of risk if their record is short. A weak answer treats a single year or one short measurement campaign as a definitive, unbiased resource figure.

questions.prompt: What phenomenon did McVicar et al. (2012) name after synthesizing terrestrial wind-speed trend studies?

options.text: "Stilling" — a widespread decline in near-surface land wind speed
"Blocking" — a stall in upper-atmosphere jet stream movement
"Amplification" — a rise in extreme wind gust frequency
"Decoupling" — a loss of correlation between surface and upper-level wind

explanations.a: Correct — McVicar et al. (2012) synthesized station records showing a broad decline in near-surface terrestrial wind speed and termed the phenomenon "stilling."
explanations.b: Blocking refers to stalled upper-atmosphere weather patterns, an unrelated meteorological concept not what this study named.
explanations.c: The study documented a decline in mean wind speed, not a rise in gust extremes.
explanations.d: Decoupling between surface and upper-level wind is not the term or finding from this synthesis.

questions.prompt: What did Zeng et al. (2019) conclude about the cause of decadal wind-speed variability, based on the post-2010 reversal?

options.text: The reversal happened too fast for land-surface roughening, pointing instead to internal ocean-atmosphere oscillations as the main driver
Vegetation growth and urbanization fully explained both the decline and the reversal
No reversal was found; stilling continued unabated after 2010
Instrument errors alone explained the entire multi-decade trend

explanations.a: Correct — because a reversal within about a decade is far too fast for slow-changing land-surface roughening, Zeng et al. argued internal ocean-atmosphere oscillations were the dominant driver of the decadal pattern.
explanations.b: The study specifically argued against vegetation/urban roughening as the dominant explanation, precisely because it changes too slowly to explain a decade-scale reversal.
explanations.c: The paper's central finding was that stilling reversed around 2010, not that it continued.
explanations.d: The paper used in-situ records to identify a real physical reversal, not an instrument-driven artifact.

questions.prompt: United States wind-farm capacity factor rose over 2010-2017. How much of that rise did Zeng et al. (2019) attribute to the recovery in wind speed itself?

options.text: About 37 percent of it — roughly a third, with the rest from turbine and siting improvements
Essentially all of it, since capacity factor tracks wind speed directly
About 17 percent of it, the same figure as the potential-wind-energy gain
None of it — capacity factor gains came entirely from taller towers

explanations.a: Correct — the wind-speed recovery accounted for roughly a third (about 37 percent) of the observed United States capacity-factor increase; the larger remaining share came from non-climatic factors like taller towers, larger rotors, and better turbines.
explanations.b: Wind speed was only one contributor. Turbine technology and siting improved substantially over the same years, so attributing the whole gain to wind speed overstates the climate signal.
explanations.c: The 17 percent (plus or minus 2 percent) figure is the rise in potential wind energy from the wind-speed recovery, a different quantity from the share of the capacity-factor increase it explains.
explanations.d: The study found the wind-speed recovery did contribute a substantial share, roughly a third, so the climate contribution was not zero.

questions.prompt: Match each candidate cause of the stilling trend to its category of mechanism.

right.text: Land-surface roughening mechanism
Large-scale atmospheric circulation mechanism
Non-climatic measurement artifact

questions.explanation: Vegetation and urban growth act by physically roughening the land surface; ocean-atmosphere oscillations act by shifting large-scale circulation; instrument changes are artifacts of the measurement record rather than a real climate signal.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the global stilling and reversal story chronologically.

items.text: Widespread decline in near-surface terrestrial wind speed begins (roughly 1960s-1980s)
The declining trend begins reversing in station observations (around 2010)
McVicar et al. publish a global synthesis documenting the stilling trend (2012)
Zeng et al. publish the finding that the stilling trend has reversed (2019)

questions.explanation: The decline itself began decades earlier, the observed reversal started around 2010, McVicar's synthesis of the decline was published in 2012, and Zeng's paper documenting and explaining the reversal followed in 2019.

lessons.label: The P90 Gap & the LIDAR-vs-Mast Controversy

sections.heading: The Industry's Overprediction Problem
sections.body: Every method in this unit feeds into one final number: the pre-construction annual energy production (AEP) estimate, expressed as a P50 (the value expected to be exceeded half the time) and a more conservative P90 (expected to be exceeded 90 percent of the time). For years the industry's P50 estimates ran optimistic. A 2021 industry-wide review published in Wind Energy Science, drawing on large operating fleets in the United States, found the average P50 overprediction bias had narrowed to roughly 3.5-4.5 percent after methodology reforms that followed around 2011 — down from a larger bias typical of earlier-vintage projects. Put differently, many real projects' long-run output has landed close to what their headline P50 promised — the expected-case number used for equity returns and marketing — while P90, the more conservative figure lenders typically size project debt against, was usually cleared with room to spare.

sections.heading: Where the Error Compounds
sections.body: The final AEP figure is a stack of the methods covered earlier in this unit: a Weibull curve fit to a short wind record, vertical extrapolation to hub height through a shear model, a terrain correction from a linear or CFD flow model, and finally wake, availability, and curtailment losses layered on top. A mis-fit resource distribution, a shear extrapolation run in the wrong stability regime, or a WAsP prediction applied in high-Delta-RIX complex terrain does not stay a local error — it propagates straight through to the financial forecast that determines how a project gets financed.

sections.heading: Can Remote Sensing Retire the Tall Mast?
sections.body: Ground-based and floating LIDAR, and historically SODAR, measure wind speed directly across the full rotor-swept height by timing the Doppler shift of light or sound scattered off the moving air, rather than measuring low and extrapolating upward — in principle removing shear-extrapolation error entirely. Early units, though, struggled with accuracy in complex terrain and in turbulent or icing conditions, so lenders were slow to treat them as bankable substitutes for a tall reference mast. The Consortium for the Advancement of Remote Sensing (CFARS) ran multi-year side-by-side verification campaigns comparing LIDAR against mast measurements across varied terrain, and its published results, together with classification and acceptance guidance from DNV, gradually built enough confidence for financiers to accept LIDAR as mast-equivalent or mast-supplementing evidence on many projects. Combining wind-resource, wake-model, and remote-sensing verification uncertainty into one defensible, bankable P90 number remains an open problem — different consultants combine these correlated uncertainty sources differently, so estimates for the same site can still vary meaningfully between reports.

lessons.workedExample: A pre-construction report projects P50 = 250 GWh/yr and P90 = 210 GWh/yr for a wind farm. After ten years of operation, measured average output comes in at 235 GWh/yr — about 6 percent below P50, landing between the two figures but noticeably closer to P50 (15 GWh/yr away) than to P90 (25 GWh/yr away). Investigating the shortfall, the team traces roughly half the gap to underestimated wake losses between turbines and the other half to a shear-extrapolation error, because the original met mast was shorter than the eventual hub height and had to extrapolate further than the data supported.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe the P50/P90 gap because it tests whether a team understands their own uncertainty, not just their point estimate. A strong answer can state what exceedance level their number represents and names at least one specific source of prediction bias in their own project, such as shear extrapolation or terrain complexity, rather than treating a single number as exact. A weak answer presents a P50 as a guaranteed outcome and cannot say how confident that number actually is.

questions.prompt: What does a wind farm's "P90" energy estimate represent?

options.text: The production level expected to be exceeded 90 percent of the time over the project's life
An estimate that is correct 90 percent of the time
The maximum possible output the turbines could ever produce
90 percent of the P50 estimate by definition

explanations.a: Correct — a P90 is a conservative exceedance-probability estimate: actual output is expected to exceed it 90 percent of the time, making it a lower, more bankable figure than P50.
explanations.b: P90 describes an exceedance probability for production, not a probability that the number itself is accurate.
explanations.c: P90 is a conservative, not maximal, estimate; it is set well below any theoretical maximum output.
explanations.d: P90 is derived from the site's own uncertainty distribution, not a fixed fraction of P50 — the exact ratio varies by project.

questions.prompt: According to the 2021 industry-wide review of large U.S. wind fleets, how has average P50 overprediction bias trended since around 2011?

options.text: It narrowed to roughly 3.5-4.5 percent after methodology reforms, though a real overprediction bias persisted
It disappeared completely, with P50 estimates now landing exactly on measured output
It reversed into a systematic underprediction of over 20 percent
It has never been measured across an actual operating fleet

explanations.a: Correct — the review found bias narrowed after 2011-era methodology reforms but did not vanish, settling around 3.5-4.5 percent overprediction on average.
explanations.b: The review found a persisting bias, not a bias that fully disappeared.
explanations.c: The documented bias remained an overprediction, not a reversal into large underprediction.
explanations.d: The review specifically used large real operating fleets to measure this bias, not a hypothetical or unmeasured quantity.

questions.prompt: What is LIDAR's main advantage over a traditional met mast for wind resource assessment?

options.text: It measures wind speed directly across the full rotor-swept height instead of extrapolating from a lower measurement
It is immune to all terrain and weather effects
It eliminates the need for any Weibull fitting
It measures air temperature more accurately than a mast

explanations.a: Correct — LIDAR profiles wind speed directly through the rotor-swept height using Doppler shift, avoiding the vertical extrapolation error that a shorter mast measurement requires.
explanations.b: LIDAR still has documented accuracy challenges in complex terrain and turbulent or icing conditions, so it is not immune to environmental effects.
explanations.c: The wind-speed distribution measured by LIDAR still needs to be fit to a Weibull curve for resource assessment, just like mast data.
explanations.d: LIDAR is a wind-measurement instrument; temperature accuracy is not its distinguishing advantage over a mast.

questions.prompt: Order the stages of the pre-construction annual energy production estimate where error can compound.

items.text: Fit a wind-speed distribution from a short measured record
Extrapolate the distribution vertically to hub height using a shear model
Correct for terrain effects using a flow model
Apply wake, availability, and curtailment losses to produce the final AEP

questions.explanation: The AEP estimate builds up in this order: distribution fitting, vertical shear extrapolation, terrain flow correction, and finally the loss adjustments that produce the number used for financing.

questions.prompt: Match each organization or study to its role in the P90 gap and remote-sensing debate.

right.text: Ran multi-year LIDAR-vs-mast verification campaigns
Publishes classification and acceptance guidance for remote sensing
Quantified the average P50 overprediction bias across real operating projects

questions.explanation: CFARS ran the side-by-side verification campaigns comparing LIDAR to masts, DNV publishes the guidance that shapes what financiers will accept as bankable, and the 2021 fleet review quantified how far real P50 estimates ran from actual measured output.

units.label: Advanced Topics & Applications

lessons.label: Complex-Terrain & Nonlinear Flow Modeling

sections.heading: Where the Linear Model Comes From — and Where It Fails
sections.body: Most commercial wind resource software still leans on a genuinely old idea: linearized flow theory. Jackson and Hunt (1975) showed that for gentle, rolling terrain you can treat the wind as a small perturbation on the undisturbed flow and solve the linearized flow equations in closed form, producing a fast prediction of speed-up over a hill crest and slow-down in a valley. Troen and Petersen (1989, the 'European Wind Atlas') turned that theory into the linearized flow model that sits inside WAsP (the Wind Atlas Analysis and Application Program), built at Denmark's Risø National Laboratory and still the industry's default for a first-pass resource map. (A related but separate Risø/DTU spectral model, LINCOM, traces to Troen and de Baas's 1986 paper and ships in companion tools like WAsP Engineering for complex-terrain and offshore load work — it is not the engine inside standard WAsP.) The catch is the word 'linear': the math only holds for gentle slopes and attached flow. WAsP itself flags this with the ruggedness index (RIX) — the fraction of terrain within 3500 m of a point that exceeds a 16.7° critical slope. A high RIX, or a large difference in RIX between the met mast and the turbine site ('delta-RIX'), is WAsP telling you its own answer is no longer trustworthy.

sections.heading: Flow Separation and Recirculation
sections.body: Past that critical slope, air can no longer follow the terrain contour. On the lee side of a steep ridge the flow detaches, curling into a recirculation zone — a pocket of slow, reversed, highly turbulent air — rather than the smooth accelerated stream a linear model assumes. A turbine sited in or near that zone sees lower energy capture than predicted and higher fatigue loading than it was designed for, because linear models by construction cannot represent detached flow; they simply keep extrapolating a speed-up that is no longer physically there. This is the single most common reason a post-construction energy assessment undershoots a linear-model pre-construction estimate on ridge-top and escarpment sites, and it is why IEC 61400-1 formally distinguishes 'complex terrain' sites — steep slopes, cliffs, gorges — as requiring a different modeling approach rather than a correction factor bolted onto WAsP.

sections.heading: CFD/RANS and Mesoscale-to-Microscale Coupling
sections.body: The fix is to stop linearizing and solve the flow numerically. RANS (Reynolds-Averaged Navier-Stokes) solvers with a k-epsilon or similar turbulence closure — commercial tools like WindSim or Meteodyn WT — discretize the terrain into a 3-D mesh and iterate the full nonlinear equations, letting separation, recirculation, and wake-like structures emerge from the physics instead of being assumed away. That accuracy costs hours of compute per wind direction instead of seconds. In practice, developers couple scales: a mesoscale model like WRF (Weather Research and Forecasting) is run over tens to hundreds of kilometers at a few-kilometer resolution to establish the regional wind climate and its directional distribution, and that climate is then downscaled into the microscale CFD model to produce a turbine-resolution resource map — the standard mesoscale-to-microscale workflow behind most bankable complex-terrain assessments today.

lessons.workedExample: A developer proposes eight turbines along a ridge with a 20° lee slope — well past WAsP's 16.7° RIX threshold. The only met mast sits on the gentler windward slope, so delta-RIX between mast and three of the eight turbine positions is large. A first-pass WAsP run predicts a clean speed-up, projecting a mean wind speed of 9.4 m/s at the ridge-top positions. Because the delta-RIX flag is high, the assessor reruns those three positions in a RANS/CFD model instead: it resolves a recirculation bubble on the lee slope that WAsP's linear math cannot see, cutting predicted wind speed there by roughly 8% and flagging elevated turbulence intensity. The three turbines are microsited 150 m windward, off the separation zone, before construction.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who knows wind resource assessment will ask 'why not just use WAsP everywhere — it's free and fast?' A weak answer treats WAsP as a generic wind calculator. A strong answer names the actual failure mode: WAsP linearizes the flow equations, so it cannot represent detachment, and its own RIX diagnostic exists precisely to warn the user when a site has left the model's valid range. Naming RIX, describing what recirculation physically does to a turbine's output and loads, and explaining why RANS/CFD costs more compute but earns it on steep terrain shows the student understands the tool's assumptions, not just its interface.

questions.prompt: What does a high WAsP ruggedness index (RIX) value at a site indicate?

options.text: The terrain is flat and WAsP's predictions there are especially reliable.
Local slopes exceed the critical angle the linear flow model was built for, so its predictions are less trustworthy.
The site has unusually high average wind speed.
The met mast used to characterize the site was too short.

explanations.a: The opposite — RIX rises with steep, complex terrain, not flat terrain.
explanations.b: Correct — RIX measures the fraction of terrain steeper than the 16.7° critical slope, flagging where linear theory (Jackson and Hunt, 1975) breaks down.
explanations.c: RIX measures terrain steepness, not wind speed magnitude.
explanations.d: Mast height is a separate measurement issue unrelated to the RIX diagnostic.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a mesoscale-to-microscale coupled workflow for a complex-terrain resource map.

items.text: Run a mesoscale WRF simulation over the broader region
Extract the regional wind climate and directional distribution
Downscale that climate into a microscale RANS/CFD model of the site
Produce a turbine-resolution resource map

questions.explanation: WRF first establishes the large-area wind climate; that climate is then fed into a finer CFD model of the actual terrain, which resolves local speed-up and separation to produce the site-specific map.

questions.prompt: Match each tool to its role in wind flow modeling.

right.text: Fast linearized model for gentle terrain, flags its own limits via RIX
Nonlinear numerical solver that resolves separation and recirculation on steep terrain
Mesoscale simulation providing the regional wind climate for downscaling

questions.explanation: WAsP is the fast linear tool (Troen and Petersen, 1989) with a built-in validity check; RANS/CFD numerically solves the full nonlinear flow for steep terrain; WRF supplies the mesoscale climate that gets downscaled.

questions.prompt: Why does a turbine sited in a lee-slope recirculation zone typically underperform its linear-model pre-construction estimate?

options.text: Recirculation locally raises air density, which lowers turbine power.
Linear models assume attached flow and cannot represent the slower, more turbulent detached air actually present there.
Recirculation zones have stronger, steadier wind than the model predicted.
WAsP always overestimates the surface roughness length in recirculation zones.

explanations.a: Air density is essentially unchanged by flow separation; it is driven by temperature and pressure, not recirculation.
explanations.b: Correct — the linear math extrapolates a speed-up that no longer exists once flow detaches, so it overstates wind speed and understates turbulence.
explanations.c: Recirculation zones are slower and far more turbulent, not stronger and steadier.
explanations.d: The error is in the flow-separation physics the model cannot represent, not specifically in a roughness length input.

lessons.label: Offshore & Coastal Wind Resource

sections.heading: A Smoother, but Not Simpler, Boundary Layer
sections.body: Water is aerodynamically far smoother than land, but the smoothness is not fixed — it depends on the wind itself. Charnock (1955) proposed that the sea-surface roughness length z0 scales with the wind's own friction velocity through a dimensionless Charnock parameter (commonly around 0.011-0.018), because a stronger wind raises steeper waves that in turn roughen the surface it blows over. The result is still tiny compared to land: at typical operating wind speeds z0 offshore runs about 0.1-1 mm, versus centimeters to meters for cropland, forest, or urban terrain, so the classic logarithmic wind profile grows more slowly with height and turbulence intensity offshore is often only 6-8% versus 15-20% onshore. The complication is thermal: land heats and cools quickly, keeping daytime onshore flow close to neutral, while the sea surface changes temperature slowly, so the air above it is often distinctly warmer or cooler than the water for days at a time. That produces frequent, persistent stable or unstable stratification offshore, which the simple neutral log-law does not capture — offshore assessments lean on Monin-Obukhov similarity with a stability correction far more routinely than onshore ones do.

sections.heading: The Coastal Internal Boundary Layer
sections.body: Exactly at the coastline the surface roughness jumps discontinuously from land to sea (or the reverse), and the air does not adjust instantly. A new internal boundary layer (IBL) grows from the shoreline downwind, its depth increasing with distance traveled over the new surface (fetch); within the IBL the profile reflects the new surface, while air above it still carries the old surface's imprint. Near-shore turbines, roughly the first 5-20 km offshore, sit inside this transition zone, where wind speed and shear can change rapidly with distance from shore — sometimes accelerating as roughness drops, sometimes complicated by sea-breeze thermal circulations — making a resource estimate extrapolated from an onshore mast unreliable close to the coast.

sections.heading: Measuring It: FINO Masts and Floating LIDAR
sections.body: Because offshore towers are expensive, only a handful of fixed research masts exist to ground-truth everything else. Germany's FINO1 (North Sea, operating since 2003), FINO2 (Baltic Sea, 2007), and FINO3 (North Sea, 2009) instrumented masts to roughly 100 m and became the reference datasets for validating the marine boundary layer physics above. Floating LIDAR buoys — remote-sensing units that profile wind by Doppler-shifted laser return instead of cup anemometers on a mast — were validated against these fixed masts under frameworks like the Carbon Trust's Offshore Wind Accelerator roadmap (2013), and are now accepted in bankable resource campaigns, letting developers profile deep water sites where a fixed mast would be prohibitively costly.

lessons.workedExample: A campaign compares two floating LIDAR buoys off the same coastline: one 3 km offshore, one 25 km offshore. Both see the same synoptic wind direction, but the near-shore buoy shows 6% lower mean wind speed and visibly higher shear than the far buoy — a signature of still being inside the coastal internal boundary layer, where the flow has only partly adjusted from the rougher land upstream. The assessor concludes the near-shore turbine positions cannot simply borrow the far buoy's wind speeds and instead builds a fetch-dependent correction, validated against both FINO-style stability corrections and the two buoys' own vertical profiles, before finalizing the site's energy yield.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes offshore assessment to see whether a student has grasped that 'offshore' is not just 'onshore with less friction.' A weak answer says water is smoother so wind is faster, full stop. A strong answer adds that the roughness itself depends on wind speed (Charnock), that stability corrections matter more offshore because sea-surface temperature lags the air, and that near-shore turbines sit inside a still-adjusting internal boundary layer rather than the fully developed marine profile — and can point to FINO or floating LIDAR data as the evidence base rather than an assumption.

questions.prompt: According to the Charnock (1955) relation, what does the sea-surface roughness length z0 depend on?

options.text: A fixed constant, the same at all wind speeds
The wind's own friction velocity, since stronger wind raises steeper waves that roughen the surface
Water depth alone
The distance from the nearest coastline

explanations.a: Charnock's whole point is that z0 is not fixed — it scales with the wind-generated wave state.
explanations.b: Correct — the Charnock relation ties z0 to friction velocity through a roughly constant Charnock parameter, because the wind builds the waves that then roughen the surface it blows over.
explanations.c: Water depth affects wave dynamics in shallow water but is not the variable in Charnock's relation.
explanations.d: Distance from shore governs the internal boundary layer, a separate effect from Charnock roughness.

questions.prompt: Why do offshore wind assessments rely on stability corrections (Monin-Obukhov) more heavily than typical onshore assessments?

options.text: Because offshore turbulence intensity is higher than onshore, requiring more correction
Because sea-surface temperature changes slowly, so the air above it is often persistently warmer or cooler than the water, producing frequent stable or unstable stratification
Because offshore wind speeds never exceed neutral-stability thresholds
Because floating LIDAR cannot measure temperature

explanations.a: Offshore turbulence intensity is typically lower than onshore, not higher.
