explanations.b: Correct — the sea's thermal inertia keeps its surface temperature nearly steady while air temperature varies, so non-neutral stratification is common and persistent offshore.
explanations.c: Stability departs from neutral regardless of wind speed; it is a thermal, not purely mechanical, effect.
explanations.d: Modern floating LIDAR buoys typically carry temperature and other met sensors alongside the wind profiler.

questions.prompt: Order these locations from least to most affected by the coastal internal boundary layer for a given onshore-to-offshore wind direction.

items.text: 25 km offshore
10 km offshore
3 km offshore
At the coastline

questions.explanation: The internal boundary layer grows with fetch downwind of the roughness discontinuity, so the site closest to shore is least adjusted to the new (sea) surface and most affected, while the farthest site has had the most fetch to develop a fully marine profile.

questions.prompt: Match each offshore measurement platform to its description.

right.text: Fixed North Sea research mast operating since 2003, instrumented to about 100 m
Fixed Baltic Sea research mast operating since 2007
Remote-sensing platform validated against fixed masts, now accepted for bankable deep-water campaigns

questions.explanation: FINO1 (North Sea, since 2003) and FINO2 (Baltic Sea, since 2007) are fixed research masts; floating LIDAR was validated against masts like these before being accepted as a lower-cost substitute in deep water.

lessons.label: Solar & Wind Forecasting

sections.heading: The Baseline You Have to Beat: Persistence and NWP
sections.body: The simplest forecast of all is persistence: assume the next interval looks like the last one (or, for solar, that today's clear-sky index repeats tomorrow). Persistence is embarrassingly hard to beat a few minutes to an hour ahead, because weather genuinely does not change much that fast — any fancier model that cannot clear this bar is worthless operationally. Beyond a few hours, numerical weather prediction (NWP) models such as GFS, ECMWF, or the high-resolution HRRR take over, integrating the physical equations of the atmosphere forward from an observed initial state. NWP skill improves with horizon relative to persistence, but degrades with lead time as small initial-condition errors amplify — the same chaotic sensitivity that limits any weather forecast, wind or solar.

sections.heading: Satellite Cloud-Motion Nowcasting
sections.body: In the gap between persistence and NWP — roughly 15 minutes to 6 hours ahead — solar forecasting leans on satellites instead of physics. Consecutive geostationary images (GOES, Meteosat) are compared to derive cloud motion vectors, and clouds are advected forward under a 'frozen cloud' assumption to predict where they will be. Hammer and colleagues (1999) coupled this cloud-motion approach to a satellite-based irradiance retrieval model, turning tracked cloud position into a predicted ground-level GHI and DNI at a specific plant — the approach behind most commercial intra-day solar forecasting services today, since it captures the cloud edges that actually drive output far better than an NWP model's coarser cloud scheme. (The retrieval model itself — turning a satellite cloud index into a ground-level irradiance value for one image at a time — traces to Perez and colleagues' 2002 operational model, which shows up again in the case-study lesson as the engine behind retrospective, multi-year satellite irradiance records.)

sections.heading: Ramp Events and Skill Metrics
sections.body: Grid operators care less about average accuracy than about ramps: a wind farm's output ramping sharply upward at sunset as a nocturnal low-level jet forms and accelerates, then collapsing again near sunrise as convective mixing erodes the jet, or a solar plant's output falling 80% in minutes as a cloud edge crosses it. A forecast that is accurate on average but misses ramps is operationally dangerous, because ramps are exactly when reserve capacity has to be scheduled. Forecast quality is reported with RMSE and MAE against measured output, but the number that matters for comparison is a skill score — typically one minus the model's RMSE divided by persistence's RMSE — because it answers the only question that matters: did this model actually beat the free baseline.

sections.heading: Two Different Jobs: Siting versus Operating
sections.body: It is easy to conflate resource assessment with forecasting because both produce numbers about wind or sun, but they answer different questions on different timescales. A long-term climatology — years of reanalysis or measured data, reduced to a P50/P90 energy estimate — answers where and how large to build a plant, once, before construction. A forecast answers what the plant will produce in the next minutes to days, repeatedly, to bid into a market or schedule reserves. Confusing the two means asking a forecast model to justify financing, or asking historical climatology to dispatch tomorrow's grid — neither tool is built for the other's job.

lessons.workedExample: A solar developer benchmarks three forecast methods for a plant on a partly cloudy afternoon: persistence, an NWP-only forecast, and a satellite cloud-motion-vector forecast, all issued for the next two hours. Persistence's RMSE is 140 W/m^2 because it cannot see the cloud bank moving in from the west. The NWP forecast, at coarse spatial resolution, smooths the cloud field and gets RMSE 110 W/m^2. The satellite CMV forecast tracks the actual cloud edge and gets RMSE 65 W/m^2, for a skill score of 1 - 65/140 = 0.54 against persistence — a clear win in exactly the 15-minute-to-2-hour window where cloud tracking outperforms both the naive baseline and coarse NWP.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this distinction because students often present a single wind or solar 'model' as if resource assessment and forecasting were the same task with the same output. A weak answer treats a P90 resource estimate and an hour-ahead forecast as interchangeable numbers. A strong answer states plainly that climatology sites the plant once, using years of data, while forecasting operates it continuously on short horizons, and can explain why persistence is the correct baseline for judging any operational forecast rather than an arbitrary strawman.

questions.prompt: Why is a persistence forecast used as the baseline that other forecast methods must beat?

options.text: Because it is the most physically sophisticated method available
Because weather changes little over very short intervals, making persistence hard to beat at short horizons and a fair test of whether a fancier model adds real skill
Because grid operators are legally required to use it
Because it is the only method that works for solar power

explanations.a: Persistence is the simplest possible method, not a sophisticated one — it just repeats the last observed value.
explanations.b: Correct — at short horizons the atmosphere hasn't had time to change much, so persistence is a strong, free baseline; any paid or complex model has to demonstrably beat it to be worth using.
explanations.c: There is no such legal requirement; it is a methodological convention for measuring skill.
explanations.d: Persistence is used for both wind and solar forecasting, not solar alone.

questions.prompt: What does Hammer and colleagues' (1999) satellite cloud-motion approach actually predict?

options.text: Wind speed several days ahead using NWP output alone
Ground-level solar irradiance a few minutes to hours ahead, by tracking cloud motion in satellite imagery and feeding it into an irradiance retrieval model
Long-term annual energy yield for financing purposes
Cloud height using radar reflectivity

explanations.a: This is a solar, not wind, method, and it operates on much shorter horizons than multi-day NWP.
explanations.b: Correct — cloud motion vectors from consecutive satellite images are advected forward and combined with an irradiance model to forecast GHI/DNI at a specific plant.
explanations.c: That is the job of long-term resource assessment/climatology, a separate task from short-horizon forecasting.
explanations.d: The method tracks horizontal cloud motion for irradiance forecasting, not cloud height via radar.

questions.prompt: Order these forecasting approaches from shortest to longest effective lead time.

items.text: Persistence
Satellite cloud-motion-vector nowcasting
Numerical weather prediction (NWP)

questions.explanation: Persistence is strongest only minutes ahead; satellite cloud tracking fills the roughly 15-minute-to-6-hour gap; NWP integrates atmospheric physics and becomes the better choice beyond that, out to days ahead.

questions.prompt: Match each task to the tool built for it.

left.text: Deciding where and how large to build a plant
Bidding output into tomorrow's electricity market
Scheduling grid reserves around a possible ramp

right.text: Long-term resource climatology (P50/P90)
Day-ahead NWP-based forecast
Short-horizon ramp forecast with skill-score validation

questions.explanation: Siting relies on multi-year climatology; day-ahead market bids rely on NWP-based forecasts; reserve scheduling around ramps needs a forecast specifically evaluated on its ability to catch rapid changes.

lessons.label: Variability, Complementarity & Resource Correlation

sections.heading: Sub-Hourly Variability Has Different Causes for Wind and Solar
sections.body: A single wind turbine's output is spiky on the scale of seconds to minutes because turbulent eddies pass through the rotor plane, and on the scale of minutes to an hour because gusts and lulls ride on top of the mean wind. A single solar array's output is spiky on the scale of seconds to minutes for a very different physical reason: passing cumulus cloud edges cast shadows that can drop plane-of-array irradiance by 70-90% in under a minute, then release it just as fast. Both signals look similarly jagged on a plot, but a mitigation strategy that treats them as the same problem — say, adding the same amount of battery buffering — will be sized wrong, because the driving physics, turbulent eddies versus cloud advection, are different processes.

sections.heading: Geographic Smoothing
sections.body: Spread a fleet of turbines or solar arrays across a region instead of one site, and the fleet's aggregate output is dramatically less spiky than any single site's, even though average energy stays about the same. This is not magic — it happens because individual sites' short-term fluctuations are not perfectly correlated with each other. A cloud shading one array is not shading an array 40 km away at the same instant; a gust hitting one turbine is not hitting a turbine on the far side of a wind farm at the same instant. NREL's WIND Toolkit and related studies of spatially dispersed fleets show that as geographic dispersion increases, aggregate output variance falls and the fleet's minimum output rises, which is exactly why grid operators favor geographically distributed portfolios over one large single-site plant of the same nameplate capacity.

sections.heading: Diurnal and Seasonal Complementarity
sections.body: Wind and solar are also anti-correlated on longer, predictable cycles, which is why hybrid wind-solar plants are attractive rather than just convenient. Solar output is confined to daylight and peaks near solar noon by definition. Wind, in many mid-latitude regions, is often strongest at night, because after sunset the surface layer decouples from friction and a nocturnal low-level jet can accelerate well above daytime near-surface wind speeds, while daytime convective mixing that stirs faster air down to turbine height fades. Seasonally, many temperate and continental climates see wind resource peak in winter, driven by stronger synoptic storm tracks, while solar resource peaks in summer from longer days and a higher sun angle — an offsetting pattern researchers call complementarity, quantified in studies across regions from Texas to Europe.

sections.heading: Resource Correlation Length
sections.body: How far apart do two sites need to be before their variability is genuinely independent? That distance is the resource's correlation length, and it differs by driver and timescale. Turbulence-driven wind variability decorrelates over kilometers; synoptic-scale wind systems (fronts, cyclones) keep sites correlated over hundreds of kilometers. Cloud-driven solar variability decorrelates over just a few to tens of kilometers, since an individual cumulus field is that size, while large-scale cloud systems correlate sites over a much broader area. The portfolio implication is direct: diversification only reduces variability once site spacing exceeds the relevant correlation length for the timescale you care about — clustering sites inside that length buys little real smoothing.

lessons.workedExample: A utility comparing two portfolios of equal nameplate capacity — one 200 MW solar plant at a single site, one 200 MW portfolio spread across five solar sites 60 km apart plus a co-located wind fleet — finds the single site's five-minute output swings by as much as 60% of capacity on a partly cloudy day. The dispersed portfolio, because its sites are spaced beyond the roughly 10-20 km correlation length of that day's cumulus field, swings by only 22% at the same timescale, and its nighttime output floor is higher because the wind fleet, riding a nocturnal low-level jet, is producing while the solar sites are dark — both geographic smoothing and diurnal complementarity acting together.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this concept to catch a common shortcut: claiming 'more sites reduce variability' without explaining why. A weak answer stops at 'diversification helps.' A strong answer names the actual mechanism — imperfect spatial correlation below a specific decorrelation distance — and separately names why wind and solar smooth each other on a daily and seasonal cycle rather than a sub-hourly one, showing the student can tell a statistical smoothing effect apart from a physical anti-correlation effect instead of lumping every variability fix into one vague bucket.

questions.prompt: Why does spreading a fleet of solar arrays across a wide region reduce the fleet's aggregate short-term variability?

options.text: Because clouds never pass over a dispersed fleet
Because individual sites' short-term fluctuations, driven by local cloud cover, are not perfectly correlated with each other once sites are far enough apart
Because dispersed arrays receive more total sunlight than a single site
Because inverters at multiple sites synchronize their output electronically

explanations.a: Clouds still pass over every site; the point is that they don't shade every site at once.
explanations.b: Correct — geographic smoothing comes from imperfect spatial correlation of local fluctuations, not from eliminating cloud cover.
explanations.c: Total average energy is roughly the same; smoothing changes variability, not the mean resource.
explanations.d: This is a physical/statistical effect of independent local weather, not an electrical synchronization mechanism.

questions.prompt: In many mid-latitude regions, why is wind resource often strongest at night while solar is, by definition, zero?

options.text: Because turbines are only switched on after sunset
Because after sunset the surface layer decouples from friction and a nocturnal low-level jet can accelerate well above daytime near-surface wind speeds
Because air density is lower at night, spinning turbines faster
Because grid demand is higher at night, pulling more wind online

explanations.a: Turbines run continuously whenever wind conditions allow; there is no nighttime-only switch.
explanations.b: Correct — nocturnal decoupling and the low-level jet are the physical mechanism behind stronger nighttime wind at hub height in many regions.
explanations.c: Air density differences between day and night are small and not the driver of this diurnal pattern.
explanations.d: Demand does not drive how much wind the atmosphere physically produces.

questions.prompt: Order these variability drivers from shortest to longest typical spatial decorrelation distance.

items.text: Turbulent wind eddies at a single turbine
An individual cumulus cloud field over a solar fleet
A synoptic-scale weather system (front or cyclone)

questions.explanation: Turbulent eddies decorrelate over meters to kilometers, an individual cumulus field over roughly tens of kilometers, and synoptic weather systems keep sites correlated over hundreds of kilometers.

questions.prompt: Match each complementarity pattern to its physical driver.

left.text: Wind stronger than solar at night
Wind resource peaking in winter, solar in summer
Two solar sites 60 km apart having largely independent short-term output

right.text: Nocturnal low-level jet decoupling from surface friction after sunset
Stronger winter storm tracks versus longer, higher-sun summer days
Site spacing exceeding the correlation length of the local cumulus cloud field

questions.explanation: Nighttime wind strength ties to the low-level jet; winter-wind/summer-solar seasonality ties to storm tracks versus sun angle and daylength; independent short-term solar output across sites ties to exceeding the local cloud field's correlation length.

lessons.label: Climate Change & the Non-Stationary Resource

sections.heading: Global Climate Model Wind Projections
sections.body: Wind resource assessment has always treated the historical record as a stand-in for the future, but global climate model ensembles increasingly suggest that assumption is shaky. Karnauskas and colleagues (2018), analyzing a multi-model ensemble of CMIP5-generation global climate simulations, found projected declines in near-surface wind power density across much of the Northern Hemisphere mid-latitudes — including large parts of North America and Europe — under higher-emissions scenarios, alongside projected increases over parts of the tropics and Southern Hemisphere, tied to a weakening pole-to-equator temperature gradient that eases the mid-latitude storm track driving those winds. Follow-on regional studies using the newer CMIP6 generation of models, such as a 2022 analysis of the North Sea, have continued to find measurable projected shifts in offshore wind resource there, reinforcing that the change is not a one-off artifact of a single older model generation.

sections.heading: Global Dimming and Brightening
sections.body: Solar resource has its own, better-documented non-stationarity: Wild and colleagues (2005) compiled surface radiation measurements worldwide and found surface solar radiation declined by roughly 2% per decade from the 1950s through the 1980s — 'global dimming' — before reversing into a 'brightening' trend at many stations from the mid-1980s onward. A 2009 update confirmed the brightening continued into the 2000s across Europe and the United States. The driver is not a change in the sun or in cloud cover alone but anthropogenic aerosols: rising industrial pollution scattered and absorbed sunlight and altered cloud reflectivity through the mid-20th century, and clean-air regulations that cut aerosol emissions in many regions from the 1980s onward let more sunlight back through. A 20-year historical solar dataset spanning this transition is not measuring one stable climate; it is measuring two different aerosol regimes.

sections.heading: Decadal Teleconnections: NAO and ENSO
sections.body: Even without a long-term trend, regional wind and solar resource swings year to year and decade to decade with large-scale ocean-atmosphere patterns. The North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) — the pressure difference between the Icelandic Low and Azores High — modulates the strength and track of Atlantic storms; its positive phase tends to bring stronger, more zonal winds and wind resource across northern Europe while weakening them over the Mediterranean, and it can persist in a given phase for multiple years. El Nino-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) similarly shifts regional wind and cloud patterns on a roughly 2-7 year cycle, altering both wind and solar resource in affected regions. Neither pattern is a long-term trend, but both mean a 'representative' short measurement window can simply have caught an unusual phase.

sections.heading: Why This Breaks the Stationarity Assumption Behind MCP
sections.body: Measure-correlate-predict (MCP) extends a short on-site measurement campaign into a bankable long-term estimate by correlating it against a long-term reference station and assuming that correlation holds into the future — a stationarity assumption baked into the method's logic. Dimming-and-brightening trends, shifting storm tracks, and multi-year NAO or ENSO phases are all evidence that the wind and solar climate is not statistically stable over the decades MCP methods are built to bridge. That does not make MCP useless, but it means the 'long-term' reference record used to correct a short campaign may itself be drifting, and a resource assessment that treats 20-30 years of history as a fixed target is quietly assuming away exactly the non-stationarity the climate record shows.

lessons.workedExample: A solar developer builds a bankable P50 yield estimate from a 25-year historical irradiance record at a European site spanning 1990-2015. Because that window falls entirely within the post-1980s brightening period documented by Wild and colleagues, the historical record already shows a mild upward trend in measured surface irradiance from reduced regional aerosols — meaning a naive average of the full 25 years understates the resource available in the most recent, brightest years and would have understated it further if aerosol reductions continue. A careful assessor checks whether the trend is a genuine continuing brightening or a plateau before extrapolating the P50 forward, rather than assuming the 25-year average is a stationary target.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes this topic because measure-correlate-predict and long-term resource averages are taught as if the underlying climate were fixed, and many students never question that premise. A weak answer treats 'more years of data' as automatically better. A strong answer names a specific non-stationary driver — aerosol-driven dimming/brightening, a shifting storm track, or a persistent NAO/ENSO phase — and explains concretely why it undermines the assumption that a historical reference record represents the future the plant will actually operate in.

questions.prompt: What did Wild and colleagues (2005) identify as the primary driver of the mid-20th-century 'global dimming' trend in surface solar radiation?

options.text: A measurable decrease in the sun's total output
Rising anthropogenic aerosols scattering and absorbing sunlight and altering cloud reflectivity
A permanent increase in average cloud cover unrelated to human activity
Instrument drift in the ground radiation sensors used

explanations.a: Solar output variation is far too small to explain a roughly 2%-per-decade surface trend; the driver was atmospheric, not solar.
explanations.b: Correct — rising industrial aerosol emissions through the mid-20th century scattered and absorbed sunlight and modified clouds, producing the dimming; falling aerosols after the 1980s produced the reversal into brightening.
explanations.c: The trend reversed after the 1980s in step with aerosol policy changes, which a permanent cloud-cover shift would not explain.
explanations.d: The dimming and brightening pattern was confirmed across many independent stations and instrument types, ruling out simple instrument drift.

questions.prompt: What does the measure-correlate-predict (MCP) method assume that decadal climate variability calls into question?

options.text: That wind speed and solar irradiance are always positively correlated
That the statistical relationship between a short on-site record and a long-term reference station stays stable (stationary) into the future
That a met mast must be at least 100 m tall to be valid
That every reference station reports data in the same units

explanations.a: MCP does not require wind and solar to correlate with each other; it correlates a short record against a long-term reference of the same resource.
explanations.b: Correct — MCP's logic depends on the short-term-to-reference relationship holding into the future, which is exactly what a non-stationary climate (trends, NAO/ENSO phases) undermines.
explanations.c: Mast height is a measurement-setup detail, not the statistical assumption MCP depends on.
explanations.d: Unit consistency is a basic data-handling requirement, not the stationarity assumption at issue.

questions.prompt: Order these phases of the global surface solar radiation record from earliest to most recent.

items.text: Rising industrial aerosol emissions through the mid-20th century
Global dimming: surface solar radiation declining, 1950s-1980s
Clean-air policies reduce aerosol emissions in many regions from the 1980s onward
Global brightening: surface solar radiation recovering, confirmed continuing into the 2000s

questions.explanation: Rising aerosols drove the 1950s-1980s dimming documented by Wild and colleagues (2005); clean-air policy then cut aerosol emissions in many regions from the 1980s, driving the brightening that a 2009 update confirmed continued into the 2000s.

questions.prompt: Match each climate driver to the resource variability it primarily explains.

right.text: Multi-year swings in northern European versus Mediterranean storm-track wind resource
Roughly 2-7 year regional shifts in wind and cloud patterns
Multi-decade projected changes in wind power density under future emissions scenarios

questions.explanation: NAO phase governs multi-year North Atlantic storm-track shifts; ENSO governs a shorter 2-7 year cycle of regional wind/cloud shifts; global climate model ensembles (Karnauskas and colleagues' CMIP5-generation study, followed by newer CMIP6-generation regional studies) project longer-term, multi-decade resource change under emissions scenarios.

lessons.label: Case Studies in Resource Assessment

sections.heading: Wind: Mast Campaign to P90 to Back-Analysis
sections.body: A two-year met mast campaign measures on-site wind speed at hub height. Two years is too short to represent long-term climate on its own, so the record is extended by measure-correlate-predict (MCP) against a nearby long-term reference — an airport station or reanalysis dataset — producing a synthesized long-term on-site record, typically spanning 10-20 years. WAsP or CFD (chosen by how rugged the terrain is) then maps that point measurement across every turbine position, and an uncertainty budget — combining measurement uncertainty, MCP uncertainty, spatial extrapolation, and year-to-year variability — is compressed into a P50 (median expected annual energy) and a P90 (the level exceeded in 90% of years), the conservative figure lenders size project debt against. After 1-2 years of commercial operation, an operational assessment back-analyzes metered production against that pre-construction P50, checking whether the wake, availability, and flow-model assumptions held up.

sections.heading: Solar: Satellite Irradiance and TMY to Yield
sections.body: Few solar sites have a decade of on-site pyranometer data, so developers instead commission a satellite-derived irradiance record — built by applying a per-image cloud-index irradiance retrieval model (the same family as Perez and colleagues' 2002 operational model) to each geostationary satellite image across the historical archive, converting each image's cloud index into a ground-level irradiance value — and validate it against whatever ground measurement exists. That long record is reduced to a Typical Meteorological Year (TMY): not the single sunniest or hottest year, but a synthetic composite built by selecting the most statistically representative month from each calendar month across the full historical record. The TMY drives a PV system simulation (tools like PVsyst) that layers in system-specific losses — soiling, temperature derating, inverter efficiency, module degradation — to produce an annual energy yield with its own P50/P90 spread, the solar counterpart of the wind case's uncertainty budget.

sections.heading: Hybrid and Repowering: Altamont Pass
sections.body: Some of the strongest resource assessments are not new-build projects at all but repowering: replacing an aging fleet with fewer, taller, more efficient turbines at a site whose own decades of production records are a better long-term reference than any nearby weather station. Altamont Pass in California, one of the earliest US wind farms, has seen multiple repowering rounds that each replaced hundreds of vintage 1980s-era turbines (typically well under 100 kW apiece) with a much smaller number of modern multi-megawatt machines, at roughly similar combined nameplate capacity to the fleet they replaced — but producing far more energy because the new turbines are taller (reaching cleaner wind above the rougher surface layer) and dramatically more efficient, while turning far fewer rotors reduces avian mortality risk. Hybrid wind-solar-storage projects get a related advantage: the diurnal and seasonal complementarity between wind and solar output lets a shared grid interconnection carry more usable energy than either resource alone.

lessons.workedExample: A 100 MW wind project runs an 18-month, 80 m met mast campaign measuring a mean 7.4 m/s. MCP against a 20-year airport record lowers the long-term estimate to 7.1 m/s once a brief high-wind bias in the measurement period is corrected. CFD modeling across ridge-top positions flagged for high RIX projects a P50 of 310 GWh/year and, folding in wake, availability, and inter-annual uncertainty, a P90 of 265 GWh/year used to size project debt. Two years after commissioning, metered production averages 296 GWh/year — inside the P50-P90 band but below P50 — and the operational assessment traces most of the shortfall to wake losses under-predicted at three ridge-top turbines, feeding directly back into how the next site's flow model is built.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing a case study is testing whether a student can narrate a project end-to-end rather than list isolated terms. A weak answer says 'we used WAsP' or 'we used a TMY' without connecting the measurement to the statistic to the decision it supported. A strong answer walks the chain: what was measured, how a short record was extended and with what uncertainty, what statistic that uncertainty produced, and what happened once the plant actually operated — because a resource assessment never checked against real production is an unfalsifiable claim. Citing a real precedent like the Altamont Pass repowering shows the student knows these are decisions with track records, not just formulas.

questions.prompt: In wind project financing, what does a P90 annual energy estimate represent?

options.text: The theoretical maximum output the turbines could ever produce
The annual energy production level expected to be exceeded in 90% of years — a conservative figure used to size project debt
The output level exceeded in only 10% of years
The average lifetime output with uncertainty ignored

explanations.a: P90 is a conservative, low-probability-of-exceedance figure, not a theoretical maximum.
explanations.b: Correct — P90 is deliberately conservative: lenders want a figure the project will very likely meet or beat, which is why the lower P90 rather than the median P50 sizes debt.
explanations.c: That description matches a P10 estimate (a high, less-likely-to-be-exceeded figure), the opposite end of the distribution.
explanations.d: P90 exists specifically to represent uncertainty, not to ignore it.

questions.prompt: What is a Typical Meteorological Year (TMY) used in solar yield modeling?

options.text: The single sunniest calendar year on record at the site
A synthetic year built by selecting the most statistically representative month from each calendar month across a long historical record
A randomly chosen real year from the historical dataset
The most recent calendar year of satellite data available

explanations.a: The sunniest year would overstate expected yield; TMY is built to be representative, not extreme.
explanations.b: Correct — TMY splices together the most typical month-by-month conditions from the historical record into one composite representative year for simulation.
explanations.c: TMY is a deliberately constructed composite, not a randomly selected real year.
explanations.d: TMY draws on many years of history, not just the most recent year.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the wind case from met mast installation to post-construction validation.

items.text: Run an on-site met mast measurement campaign
Extend the short record to a long-term estimate via MCP against a reference station
Map the long-term wind climate across turbine positions with WAsP or CFD
Compress the uncertainty budget into a P50/P90 energy estimate
Back-analyze metered production against the P50 after commissioning

questions.explanation: The campaign measures on-site wind first; MCP extends it to a long-term estimate; flow modeling maps that estimate across turbine positions; the uncertainty budget produces P50/P90; and operational back-analysis checks the estimate against reality after the plant runs.

questions.prompt: Match each resource assessment case to what gives it its long-term reference.

right.text: MCP correlation against a nearby long-term weather station or reanalysis
Multi-year satellite-derived irradiance reduced to a TMY
Decades of the site's own historical operational production records

questions.explanation: A new-build wind site leans on MCP against an external reference; a new-build solar site leans on satellite-derived irradiance reduced to a TMY; a repowering project can use its own long operational history, sidestepping much of the uncertainty a first-time site must accept.
